en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Great Chapter of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
1. The Mahākhandhaka: The Discourse on Enlightenment.
Immediately after the recitation of both Pātimokkhas, [the Council was held].
The Great Elders, experts in the Khandhakas, recited them.
Now that the time has come for its commentary, since it is the turn for the exposition,
here follows this commentary on its previously unexplained meanings.
If we were to state again those meanings which have already been explained by whomsoever in the *Padabhājaniya*, when would there ever be an end?
And what is the use of commenting upon those meanings that are already plain and clear?
"However, those points which are not explicitly stated through the underlying intentions, the connections, and the phrasing—
since they cannot be known unless they are explained—
this method of commentary is therefore intended for them alone."
1. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full enlightenment.

Herein, although there is no specific reason for using the locative case—as in expressions such as "at that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, [was staying] in Verañjā"—nevertheless, with respect to the Vinaya, this expression is formulated using the locative case.
"Appropriated" (āropita) should be understood as being stated here by way of the expression "ascended" from the very beginning.
This same method applies to other similar cases that follow this one.
But what is the purpose of stating this? It is to show the origin (nidāna) of the disciplinary acts (vinayakamma), such as the going-forth (pabbajjā), starting from the beginning.
For indeed, it was after attaining full enlightenment and spending seven weeks at the seat of awakening that the Blessed One, in Bārāṇasī,

authorized both the going forth and the higher ordination by saying, "Monks, I authorize the going forth and the higher ordination through these three goings for refuge," as well as the duties toward preceptors and teachers,
and so forth, which were authorized in Rājagaha and other places.

It should be understood that the purpose of this statement is to show, from the very beginning, the origins (*nidāna*) of these disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*)— such as the going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on— by stating: "Having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, having reached such and such places by this sequence, and in such and such matters, these [rules] were laid down."
In this context, "at Uruvelā" means at Mahāvelā; the meaning is "on a great heap of sand. Alternatively, "uru" refers to sand, and "velā" refers to a boundary;
thus the meaning here should be understood as follows: because it was brought [there] due to the transgression of a boundary (velā), it is called Uruvelā.
It is said that in the past, before the Buddhas had arisen, ten thousand sons of noble families went forth into the ascetic life.
While dwelling in that place, they once gathered together and established a formal agreement:

"Physical and verbal actions are indeed evident even to others, but mental action is not evident. Therefore, for whoever conceives a thought of sensual desire, ill will, or cruelty, there is no one else to reproach him; he himself must reproach himself."
"Let him reproach himself by himself, fetch sand in the hollow of his hands, and scatter it in this place;
this shall be his penance. From that time forth, whoever conceived such a thought would scatter sand there with the hollow of his hands.
In this way, a great heap of sand gradually formed there, and then the later generation [took it up].
Having surrounded it, he made it a site for a cetiya. With reference to this, it was said: “At Uruvelā means at Mahāvelā;
the meaning is ‘on a great mound of sand. With reference to that very same thing, it was further said: “Alternatively, *uru* is a term for sand; *velā* means a boundary (*mariyādā*).
Because it was brought [there] due to the transgression of a boundary (*velātikkamana*), it is called *uruvelā*; such is the meaning to be understood here.”
"At the foot of the Bodhi tree": "Bodhi" refers to the knowledge in the four paths.
Because the Blessed One attained that Bodhi there, even the tree received the name "Bodhi tree. "At the foot of the Bodhi tree" means at the base of that Bodhi tree.
"First fully enlightened" means first fully awakened; having become fully awakened, it means at the very beginning of all.
The meaning is as follows: "With one leg crossed" means with a single cross-legged posture that has not been shifted even once, just as it was initially assumed.
"Experiencing the bliss of liberation" means experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Dependent origination" refers to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), for the mode of conditions consists of phenomena that arise together in mutual dependence.
"It causes to arise" (uppādeti) is why it is called "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda). This is the summary here.

However, one who desires a detailed exposition complete in all its aspects should take it from the *Visuddhimagga*. "In direct and reverse order" means both in forward (anuloma) and backward (paṭiloma) sequence.
Therein, the mode of condition beginning with ignorance, stated by way of the formula "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," etc., by itself...

It is called "conformable" (*anuloma*) because it performs the function that ought to be performed. That same [process], when stated in the manner beginning with "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," is called "reverse" (*paṭiloma*) because, by ceasing through non-arising, it does not perform that function; thus, it is so called due to its non-performance of that function.
Alternatively, what was stated according to the former method is conformable to occurrence, while the other is reverse to it.

The meaning here should be understood in this way. However, since [the sequence] has not been stated starting from the beginning up to the end, nor starting from the end back to the beginning, the state of being in direct and reverse order does not apply in any other sense than this.
"He attended to" (manasākāsi) means he brought it to mind (manasi akāsi). In that regard, first, in order to show how he attended to it in direct order:
“It is with ignorance as condition that volitional formations [arise],” and so forth, has been said. In this context, “ignorance-condition” means ignorance which is a condition;
therefore, the meaning in all instances should be understood according to this method: “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be.
This is the summary here. However, one who desires a detailed exposition complete in all its aspects should take it from the *Visuddhimagga*.

In order to show how he attended to [the sequence] in reverse order, it was said: "But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations," and so forth.
Therein, "but from ignorance" (*avijjāya tveva*) means "from ignorance indeed.

"From the remainderless fading away and cessation" (*asesavirāganirodhā*) means from the complete cessation by means of the path, which is characterized as fading away (*virāga*). "Cessation of volitional formations" (*saṅkhāranirodho*) means the cessation through non-arising of volitional formations.

Thus, in order to show that when formations have ceased, consciousness ceases through their cessation; and when consciousness and the other factors cease, name-and-form and the rest likewise cease, it is said:

"With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness," and so forth, concluding with, "In this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this context, the word *kevalassa* (of the entire) means:
"Of the whole" means of that which is either pure or devoid of beings. "Of the mass of suffering" means of the heap of suffering.
"There is cessation" means there is non-arising.
"Having understood this matter" refers to the fact that through ignorance and so forth, there is the origination of the mass of suffering beginning with volitional formations.
And it is said that "cessation occurs by way of the cessation of ignorance, etc.," having understood this matter in all its aspects.

"At that time" means at the time of understanding that meaning. He uttered this *udāna*—this utterance illuminating the power of the knowledge of both the cause and the phenomenon arisen from the cause—when that meaning was understood: "When..."
He uttered this *udāna*—beginning with “When... appear”—which is originated by knowledge associated with joy;
that is to say, he let forth words of gladness. Its meaning is as follows:

“When (*yadā hava*)” means at whatever time or existence (*bhave*). “Appear (*pātubhavanti*)” means they arise. “Dhammas (*dhammā*)” refers to those things that accomplish the penetration of the mode of conditions in their forward order (*anuloma-paccayākāra*).

The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*). Alternatively, "manifesting" means they are revealed; through the power of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they become distinct and evident.

"Dhammas" refers to the dhammas of the Four Noble Truths. "Ardor" (*ātāpa*) is called energy (*vīriya*) in the sense of burning away the defilements (*kilesa*); "ardent" (*ātāpino*) refers to one who possesses the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna*).

"Meditating" (*jhāyanto*) is by way of the characteristic of meditating upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna-lakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of meditating upon the characteristics [of phenomena] (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna-lakkhaṇa*).
And for one who meditates with jhāna. "Of the brahmin" means of one who has banished evil, whose taints are destroyed.
"Then his doubts fade away" means that for him, for whom the Dhamma has thus become manifest, his doubts fade away. "All" refers to those [doubts] such as:
"Who, venerable sir, experiences [this]? 'The question is not appropriate,' the Blessed One said," and likewise, "Which [person], venerable sir..."

“Venerable sir, this is aging-and-death; but for whom is there this aging-and-death?”—to such a question, the Blessed One replied, “That is not a fitting question,” and in this manner, doubt regarding the mode of conditions was stated.
Furthermore, those sixteen doubts that have come down, beginning with “Did I exist in the past?,” which arise because the mode of conditions has not been penetrated—all these vanish.
They pass away and cease. Why? Because he understands that phenomena have a cause;
for he understands, knows, and penetrates this entire mass of suffering, consisting of volitional formations and so forth, as being accompanied by causes such as ignorance.

In the second section: "He uttered this inspired utterance" means that when that meaning had been realized, he uttered this inspired utterance: "But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance..."

The meaning is that he uttered the aforementioned *udāna* as a manifestation of the power of his realization of the destruction of conditions (*paccayakkhaya*), which is designated as *nibbāna* and thus proclaimed as "the cessation of volitional formations" (*saṅkhāranirodha*). Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
because he experienced, knew, and penetrated *nibbāna*, which is the destruction of conditions, therefore, when that brahmin was ardent and meditating, such [realization] occurred for him.
When phenomena become manifest, all those doubts that might have arisen due to his lack of knowledge regarding Nibbāna vanish.

3. Regarding the third occasion—"he uttered this inspired utterance"—this refers to the illumination of the power of that Noble Path by which the meaning of the mass of suffering, consisting of its origin and cessation, was known through its function and its activity as an object.
The meaning is that he uttered an exclamation (*udāna*) of the kind already described. Herein, the summarized meaning is as follows:

"When, indeed, the states (*dhammā*) become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin, then that brahmin stands having shaken off [defilements] by means of those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) that have arisen, or by means of that Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) through which the states of the Four Truths have become manifest."
He stands dispelling, shaking off, and destroying the army of Māra—the army described in the manner beginning with, "Sensual pleasures are your first army.
How so? Like the sun illuminating the sky; just as the risen sun stands illuminating the sky with its own radiance while dispelling the darkness.
Thus that brahmin also, while penetrating the Truths by means of those qualities or that path,
stands shaking off the army of Māra. In this context,
the first udāna is by way of reflecting on the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), and the second is by way of reflecting on Nibbāna.
It should be understood that the third [type of knowledge] arises by way of reviewing the path. However, in the *Udāna* it is said:
"During the first watch of the night, dependent origination in forward order; during the second watch, in reverse order; during the third watch, in both forward and reverse order.
This refers to the attention he produced during the night after the lapse of seven days, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall rise from my seat."

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For at that time, by means of those two preceding udāna-verses which illuminate the power of both the understanding of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) and the attainment of the destruction of conditions (*paccayakkhaya*), the Blessed One brought to mind each single section during the first watch and the middle watch;
however, here on the night of the full moon, he brought them to mind in this manner. Indeed, the Blessed One...
On the night of the full moon of Visākha, during the first watch of the night, he recollected his past lives; during the middle watch, he purified his divine eye;

and during the last watch, by attending to dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, he attained omniscience, thinking, "Now the dawn is about to break. And at the very moment he attained omniscience, the dawn rose.
Then, having spent that day in that very cross-legged posture, at the arrival of the night of the first lunar day (*pāṭipada*),

he attended to his mind in this way throughout the three watches of the night and uttered these inspired utterances (*udāna*). Thus, having attended to his mind on the night of the first lunar day, he spent those seven days—
referred to as "he sat for seven days at the foot of the Bodhi tree in a single cross-legged posture"— right there.
The Discourse on Awakening is finished.
4. The Discourse to the Cowherd.
Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and [departed] from the foot of the Bodhi tree.

Regarding the phrase "he approached the Ajapāla banyan tree," it does not mean that the Blessed One arose from that meditative absorption and immediately thereafter went from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla banyan tree.

Rather, just as when it is said, "having eaten, he lies down," this does not imply that he lay down without first washing his hands, rinsing his mouth, or going near the place where he was to rest; [so too here].
It is said that he "lies down without engaging in any conversation," which means he lies down after eating,

not that he does not lie down at all. Likewise, here too, it is said that "he did not depart immediately after emerging from that concentration," meaning he departed after emerging, not that he did not depart.
This very point is illustrated here.
But what did the Blessed One do immediately after that, without departing? He spent another three weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree itself. Regarding this, the sequential account is as follows:
it is said that once the Blessed One had attained Buddhahood, he remained for seven days in a single cross-legged posture.

As he sat there, the thought occurred to some of the deities: "The Blessed One has not yet emerged from his attainment; could there be other qualities that constitute Buddhahood? Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One emerged from his meditative absorption.
Knowing the doubt of the deities, and for the purpose of dispelling their uncertainty, he rose into the air and displayed the Twin Miracle, thereby [resolving] them.
Having dispelled his doubts, he stood for a short while on the eastern side of the seat, slightly toward the northern direction.

Gazing with unblinking eyes at the seat—the place where he attained the power of the perfections accumulated over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons—and at the Bodhi tree, he spent seven days; that spot is known as the Animisa Cetiya (the Unblinking Shrine).

Thus it was named. Then, walking back and forth on a jeweled walkway that extended eastward and westward between the place where the throne stood and that spot, he spent seven days; that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya (Jeweled Walkway Shrine).
Then, in the western direction, the deities constructed a jeweled house. There, by means of the cross-legged posture...
Having sat down, he spent seven days investigating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and here especially the *Samantapāṭhāna*, which contains infinite methods;
that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya.
Thus, having spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, on the fifth week, from the foot of the Bodhi tree...
He approached the Goatherd’s Banyan tree. It is said that because goatherds would go there and sit in the shade of that banyan tree, it acquired the name “Goatherd’s Banyan.
“Experiencing the bliss of liberation for seven days” means that even there he sat experiencing the bliss of liberation while investigating the Dhamma. To the eastern side of the Bodhi tree...
This was the tree. Now, while the Blessed One was seated there, a certain brahmin went up and asked a question.
Therefore it is said: “Then a certain one,” and so forth. In that context, “of a *huṃhuṅ* disposition”: it is said that he was named Diṭṭhamangalika;
because of his pride and his anger, he used to wander about uttering “*huṃhu*,” and for that reason he is called “of a *huṃhuṅ* disposition.”
It is said. Some also read "one who is prone to hiccoughing.
Having understood this meaning—that is, having understood the ultimate significance of the words spoken by him—he, at that moment, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).
Its meaning is as follows: he who is a brahmin by virtue of having banished evil qualities, and not by virtue of regarding sights as auspicious;

Having been associated with evil qualities such as the utterance of "huṃ-huṃ," yet claiming the status of a Brahmin solely on account of his birth, that Brahmin—because he has cast out evil qualities—is "huṃ-huṃ-less" through the abandonment of the "huṃ-huṃ" sound; because he is free from the taints of passion and the like, he is "taintless";
because his mind is devoted to the practice of meditation, he is "self-restrained"; or because his mind is well-composed through the restraint of virtue.
One who has reached the end (*vedantagū*) because he has gone to the end of the Vedas—meaning the knowledge known as the fourfold path—or because he has reached the end of the Vedas;
one who has lived the holy life (*vusitabrahmacariyo*) because he has fulfilled the holy life of the Path.
He may speak the Brahma-discourse according to the Dhamma, meaning he may speak this discourse, "I am a Brahmin," according to the Dhamma, such that in the entire habitation of the world, nowhere...
"Even regarding a single object, there are no such excesses as the excess of lust, the excess of hatred, the excess of delusion, the excess of conceit, or the excess of views.
The Discourse on the Cowherd is finished.
The Discourse on Mucalinda.
5. "An unseasonable cloud" refers to a cloud that arises when the rainy season has not yet arrived. This one, however, arose in the last month of the hot season.
"A seven-day downpour" means that once it had arisen, there was rain falling continuously for seven days.
"Cold winds and cloudy days" refers to that seven-day downpour accompanied by cold winds mixed with spray, which blew all around.
Because the day had been defiled, it became known as a cold, windy, and cloudy day.
Now, Mucalinda the Nāga King was a powerful Nāga king who had been reborn in a lotus pond near that very Mucalinda tree.
Having encircled [the Buddha] seven times with his coils, he formed a great hood over his head.
Having done so, he remained standing. Within that enclosure, for him, there was a space the size of a storehouse chamber inside the iron palace;
therefore, the Blessed One became as if seated in a gabled hall with the doors and windows closed in a windless place.
"Lest it be cold for the Blessed One," and so forth, is an explanation of the reason for his remaining there in such a manner. For he [thought], "Lest it be cold for the Blessed One..."
"May heat not afflict me; may contact with gadflies and the like not afflict me. Having acted accordingly, he stood there.
In this regard, although there was indeed no heat during that seven-day storm, it would have been appropriate for him to think, "If a cloud were to disperse from time to time, there might be heat;
may even that not afflict me. Thus he thought. "Viddhaṃ" means...
"Ubbiddhaṃ" means it has become distant due to the disappearance of clouds. "Vigatavalāhakaṃ" means free from clouds.
"Devaṃ" means the sky. "Sakavaṇṇaṃ" means one's own form.
"Sukho viveko" means the seclusion of the substrata (upadhi), reckoned as Nibbāna, is blissful. "Tuṭṭhassa" means by means of contentment with the knowledge of the four paths.
"Of one who is content": of one for whom the Dhamma has been heard—that is, for whom the Dhamma has been proclaimed. "Seeing":

seeing that seclusion, or whatever else is to be seen, all of it with the eye of knowledge attained through the power of his own energy. "Non-affliction" (*abyāpajja*) is the state of being unprovoked;
by this, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is shown. "Restraint toward living beings."
And restraint toward beings; the meaning is that the state of non-violence is happiness. By this, the preliminary stage of compassion is shown.

"Happiness is dispassion for the world" indicates that even freedom from passion (*vītarāgatā*) is happiness. "The transcendence of sensual desires"—that which is called "the transcendence of sensual desires" is also happiness, meaning that dispassion is happiness.
By this, the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) is described.
By the phrase "the disciplining of the conceit 'I am'," Arahantship is described; for Arahantship is called the "disciplining through subsiding" of the conceit "I am.
Beyond this there is no happiness whatsoever; therefore he said, "This indeed is the supreme happiness.
The Discourse on the Mucalinda [Tree] is concluded.
The Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree.
6. "At the foot of the Mucalinda tree" means at the foot of the Mucalinda tree situated in the northeastern corner of the Great Bodhi tree.
"To the Rājāyatana tree" means he approached the Rājāyatana tree situated in the southern direction. "And at that time..."—by what [time]?

At that time, it is said that on the very day the Blessed One arose from his seven-day meditative absorption while seated cross-legged at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, at the moment of sunrise, Sakka, the king of the gods, perceiving that "it must be time for the meal," offered him medicinal myrobalan (*osadha-harītaka*).
The Blessed One consumed it; and as soon as he had finished eating, his bodily functions were restored.
Sakka offered water for his face. The Blessed One, having washed his face, sat down at the very foot of that tree.
While the Blessed One was thus seated as the dawn had risen, there were at that time two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, who were brothers.
"Merchants. "From Ukkaḷā" means from the district of Ukkaḷā. They point out that region where the Blessed One dwells.
And in which region does the Blessed One dwell? In the Middle Country. Therefore, the meaning here is that they had set out on the high road to go to the Middle Country.
"Deities who were kinsmen and blood-relations" refers to deities who had previously been their relatives. "He said this."
She, it is said, caused all their carts to stop. Then they offered an oblation to the deities of the road, wondering, "What is this?
At the time of their offering, that deity spoke these words while her body was still visible:
"With *mantha* and honey-cakes... [referring to] unground grain mixed with ground grain, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth.
"Patimānetha" means "attend upon. "Taṃ vo" means that such honoring will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.
"Yaṃ amhākaṃ" means that such receiving [of offerings] would be for our long-term welfare and happiness.
"Bhagavato etadahosi" refers to that which, it is said, was obtained by him during his time of striving: the milk-rice from Sujātā.
As she was still coming to give [the offering], it vanished. Then this thought occurred to him: "I have no bowl;
moreover, previous Tathāgatas do not accept things directly in their hands. In what, then, shall I receive the stirred drink and the honey-cake?
Knowing his reflection, [it was understood that] even before this, the food given by Sujātā had already been consumed by the Blessed One for the purpose of sustaining his vital energy (*ojā*).
He stood there; for all that time, he experienced neither hunger nor thirst nor physical weakness.
But now, because of his desire to accept food, a reflection arose in him according to the method beginning with, "Indeed, Tathāgatas [do not eat in this manner]," and so forth.
Knowing with his own mind that very reflection which had thus arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, [he said], "In the four directions... (catuddisā) means from the four [directions].
"From the quarters. "Bowl made of stone" means a bowl made of green-stone (muggavaṇṇa-sela). It was precisely these that the Blessed One accepted;
it is with reference to these that this was said. However, first the four Great Kings offered bowls made of sapphire (indanīla-maṇi), but the Blessed One did not accept them.
Then all four of them offered these bowls made of green-stone, and the Blessed One—
He took all four bowls for the sake of preserving their faith, not out of great desire.
Having taken them, he resolved that they should become as one bowl; thus, the karmic fruit of the merit of all four became identical.
When they had been resolved into one, the Blessed One accepted the fine, stone-like bowl and the stirred milk-rice.
And the honey-cake. *Paccaggheti* means in that which is of priceless value; the meaning is "separately" or "in that which is of great worth.
Alternatively, *paccaggheti* means in what is fresh or new; the meaning is "at the very moment it was produced. They had two utterances, thus they are called *dvevācikā*.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they attained the status of lay followers (*upāsaka*) by means of two utterances. Those [who have] thus attained the status of lay followers...
Having made their announcement, they said to the Blessed One, “Whom, venerable sir, should we henceforth pay homage to and rise up for?
Then the Blessed One stroked his head; the hair adhered to his hand. He gave it to them, saying, “Keep these.
Having received those relics of the hair, as if sprinkled with the Deathless, they were joyful and elated, and [they paid homage] to the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, they departed.
The Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree is finished.
The Discourse on the Brahmā’s Entreaty.

7. Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and, having completed all those aforementioned tasks, went again from the foot of the Rājāyatana tree to where the Ajapāla banyan tree was.
The reflection arose: as soon as he had sat down there, this [thought] occurred to him, which is the customary practice of all Buddhas.
A reflection arose in his mind. But why does this arise for all Buddhas?
It is because of the reflection upon the greatness, the weightiness, and the profound importance of the Dhamma, and because of the desire to teach it when requested by Brahmā.
For the Buddhas know: "When such a reflection has arisen, Brahmā will come and request the teaching of the Dhamma; thereafter, beings..."
“They will develop reverence for the Dhamma, for the world’s way of life is one that holds the sublime in high esteem. Thus, it is for these two reasons that this thought arises.
In that context, “I have attained” means “this has been attained by me. “Delighting in attachment” refers to beings [delighting] in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
They adhere [to them], therefore they are called "attachments" (*ālaya*). They delight in those attachments, thus they are "delighting in attachments" (*ālayarāma*).

They take pleasure in attachments, thus they are "pleased with attachments" (*ālayarata*). They rejoice greatly in attachments, thus they are "rejoicing in attachments" (*ālayasammudita*). *Yadidaṃ* is a particle.
With reference to its place, it should be understood as "this which," and with reference to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), as "this which."

Regarding the term *idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppāda*: the conditions for these things are "conditions based on this" (*idappaccayā*); the state of being such conditions is "conditionality based on this" (*idappaccayatā*);
and that conditionality is itself dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Thus, it is called "dependent origination as conditionality based on this.
"That would be weariness for me" means that teaching to those who do not understand would be wearisome for me; it would be a vexation for me.
*Attho*: [the meaning]. *Bhagavantam*: [the genitive case] of the Blessed One (*bhagavato*). *Anacchariyā*: not wonderful (*anu-acchariyā*). *Paṭibhaṃsu*:
they became the objects of knowledge known as "inspiration" (*paṭibhāna*); they reached the state of being fit for thorough reflection.
*Haḷaṃ*: here, the syllable *ha* is merely a particle; the meaning is *alaṃ*. *Pakāsituṃ*: to teach. *Alaṃ dāni me*: enough now for me.
"It is said: 'They shall teach this Dhamma attained with difficulty. 'Going against the stream' (*paṭisotagāmi*):
the 'stream' is called Nibbāna; the meaning is 'going toward Nibbāna. 'Stained by lust' (*rāgarattā*): stained by the lust of sensual desire, the lust for existence, and the lust for views.
'They shall not see' (*na dakkhanti*): they shall not perceive. 'Enveloped by a mass of darkness' (*tamokhandhena āvutā*): overwhelmed by the heap of ignorance."
"By way of being free from concern" means by way of a state of lack of exertion; the meaning is:
"by way of not desiring to teach. 8. "In that very world" means in that world indeed.

"He appeared before the Blessed One" means that, having come while taking with him the Great Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems for the purpose of requesting a teaching of the Dhamma, he appeared before the Blessed One.

"Of a nature with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*) means that because there is little dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom (*paññāmaye akkhimhi*), they are of such a character;
thus, they are "of a nature with little dust in their eyes. "They will become knowers of the Dhamma" means they will be those who have penetrated it.
"He appeared" (*pāturahosi*) means he became manifest. "Contemplated by those with stains" means by the six teachers who were stained by the stains of greed and so forth.
It was thought: "Open this"—that is, open this opening. "The door to the Deathless"—the Noble Path, which serves as the door to the Deathless, Nibbāna.

"May they hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One"—may these beings hear the Dhamma of the Four Truths awakened to by the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of the stains of passion and so forth.
"Just as one standing on the summit of a solid rock mountain would see the people all around with his eyes,
so too, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, the Blessed One— the All-Seeing One with the knowledge of omniscience—
having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and made of wisdom, himself free from sorrow, beholds those who have fallen into sorrow."
"Behold and consider the people overcome by birth and old age; arise!
Thus he spoke, requesting the Blessed One to undertake a wandering tour for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Regarding the terms "hero" and so forth:
the Blessed One is a hero because of his possession of vigor. He is one who has won the battle because he has conquered the Māras of the sons of gods, death, defilements, and volitional formations.
He is a caravan leader because of his capacity to lead across the wilderness of birth and so forth.

He is debtless because he is free from the deer-like craving for sensual pleasures. 9. "Entreaty" means a request. "With the Buddha-eye" refers to both the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of others and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies;
for these two types of knowledge are collectively named the "Buddha-eye. "Those with little dust in their eyes" [refers to those who possess] the eye of wisdom.

Those for whom the dust of passion and so forth is slight are "those with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkha*). Those for whom it is great are "those with much dust in their eyes" (*mahārajakkha*).
Those whose faculties, such as faith, are sharp are "those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriya*). Those whose [faculties] are dull are "those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*).
Those whose very modes, such as faith, are beautiful are "those of good disposition" (*svākāra*). Those whose very modes, such as faith, are not beautiful...
These are of two kinds. Those who perceive the reasons already stated can easily be made to understand; they are "easily instructed" (*suviññāpayā*).
Those who view the next world and moral fault as fearsome are "those who see the next world and moral fault with fear. "In a place of blue lotuses" means in a grove of blue lotuses.
The same method applies to the others as well. "Those whose nourishment is submerged within" refers to those which, while actually submerged within the water, [receive their sustenance].
They nourish. "Standing level with the water" means they stand even with the water. "Standing having overflowed the water" means they stand having surpassed the water.
"Open" means uncovered. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path; for it is [the path] to Nibbāna, which is designated as the Deathless.
"Open the door. "Let them all release their faith"—let everyone release their own faith. Regarding the meaning of the latter two lines:
"For I, perceiving this sublime and supreme Dhamma—which is well-mastered and flows smoothly—to be a weariness of body and speech, do not proclaim it among men, that is, among gods and humans."
The Discourse on the Request of Brahmā is finished.
The Discourse to the Group of Five:
10. "Wise" means endowed with wisdom; "skilled" means endowed with proficiency; "intelligent" means...

He was endowed with wisdom pertaining to the present occasion. "One whose nature is free from the dust of passion" means that because his defilements have been suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), he is a being born pure, devoid of impurities. "He will understand" means he will observe and penetrate [the truth].
"Knowledge arose even for the Blessed One" means that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) arose: "On the seventh day from now, having passed away..."
“...reborn in the base of nothingness. “A great loser” (*mahājāniyo*): because he had fallen away from the path and fruit that could have been attained within seven days, he was a great loser;
he was reborn in an inopportune state (*akkhaṇe*). “Died yesterday” (*abhidosakālaṅkato*): he died the day before;
he saw that he too had been reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*). “Of great benefit” (*bahūkārā*): of great assistance.
"Upaṭṭhahimsu padhānapahitattan" means they attended upon him whose being was directed toward striving, by providing water for his mouth and other services.
"Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ" means Upaka saw the Blessed One between Gayā and the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa). "Addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ" means one who has set out upon a long journey.
"Sabbābhibhū" means he stands having overcome all phenomena of the three planes of existence. "Sabbavidū" means [he knows] all phenomena of the four planes of existence.
"I have known, I have understood. "Unstained by all phenomena" means unstained by the defilement of all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
"Having abandoned everything" means established after having relinquished all phenomena of the three planes.

"Liberated through the destruction of craving" means liberated from the object of craving, which is Nibbāna. "Having directly known for myself" refers to all phenomena of the four planes of existence.
"Having known by oneself": whom else could one point to, thinking, "This is my teacher"? "I have no teacher":
regarding the supramundane Dhamma, I have no one who can be called my teacher. "There is no counterpart for me":
there is no person who is my equal. "Become cool": become cool through the extinguishing of the fire of all defilements.
He is "extinguished" (nibbuto) because of the very extinguishing of the defilements (kilesā).

"City of the Kāsīs" refers to the city in the kingdom of Kāsī. "I shall beat the drum of the Deathless" means: "I go thinking, 'I shall strike the drum of the Deathless for the sake of obtaining the Wheel of Dhamma'.

"It is fitting for you, O Conqueror of the Infinite" means it is worthy for you to become a Conqueror of the Infinite. "May it be so, friend" means, "Friend, may it indeed be thus. "Shaking his head" means moving his head.
12. *Saṇṭhapenti*: they made an agreement. *Bāhulliko*: one who practices for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth.

*Padhānavibbhanto*: fallen away from, departed from, and lost to exertion. *Āvatto bāhullāya*: turned back toward abundance, that is, for the sake of having an abundance of robes and other such things.
*Odahatha bhikkhave sotaṃ*: "Listen, monks"—apply your ear; [apply] the faculty of hearing for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
The meaning is: "Make it manifest. "The deathless has been attained" shows that the deathless *nibbāna* has been attained by me.
"By conduct" means by difficult conduct. "By the path" means by the difficult path.
"Do you recognize from me? means do you perceive? The meaning is: "Do you recognize that such a statement was spoken by me?"—that is, this kind of speech was uttered.
The Blessed One was indeed able to convince the group of five monks; he was able to make them know: "I am the Buddha.
(13) "The maker of eyes" is said with reference to the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). From this point on, everything is clear in its literal meaning.

However, regarding the distinctions such as the underlying intention (*adhippāya*), the sequence of connection (*anusandhi*), and the application (*yojana*), one should follow the method explained in the *Papañcasūdani*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.

This should be understood. From this point onward, however, out of consideration for the minds of the general public who fear excessive prolixity, we shall not elaborate on the discourse of the Suttantas, but shall instead explain the discourse of the Vinaya.
"That indeed was the ordination of that venerable one"—on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, together with eighteen koṭis of deities.
For that venerable one who was established together with the fruit of stream-entry, his admission as an *ebhi-bhikkhu* (come, monk) was accomplished by the Blessed One’s words,
"Come, monk. Then, regarding the venerable Vappa and so forth—
at the beginning [of the account]— the Dhamma-eye arose for the Elder Vappa on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipadadivasa*).
It arose on the second day for the Elder Bhaddiya, on the third day for the Elder Mahānāma, and on the fourth day for the Elder Assaji.
Furthermore, in order to purify the defilements that had arisen in these monks regarding their meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), the Blessed One remained within the monastery itself.
Whenever a defilement regarding a meditation subject arose, he would travel through the air and dispel that defilement.
But on the fifth day of the fortnight, having gathered them all together, he instructed them with the *Anattasutta*. Therefore it is said:
“Then the Blessed One [addressed] the group-of-five,” and so forth.
At that time, there were six Arahants in the world; the meaning is that on the fifth day of the fortnight, six men in the world became Arahants.
The Discourse on the Group-of-Five is finished.
The Discourse on the Going-forth 31.
“Successively from of old”: the meaning is, by way of lineage, those that are ancient and more ancient than the ancient. At that time...
"There were sixty-one Arahants in the world" means that including the previous six and these fifty-five, sixty-one men became Arahants within the very same rainy season.
In this regard, the prior spiritual practice (*pubbayoga*) of the young men beginning with Yasa was as follows: it is said that in the past, fifty-five people were companions.
Performing meritorious deeds in groups and tending to the bodies of the destitute, they were wandering about.
One day, seeing a pregnant woman who had passed away, they brought her out to the charnel ground, thinking, "We shall cremate her.
Having left five men at the charnel ground with the instruction, "You cremate her," the rest entered the village. The boy Yasa, having pierced that body—
Having turned [the body] over and burning it, he acquired the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*).
He showed it to the other four people, saying, "Behold, sirs, this impure and repulsive thing! They too acquired the perception of foulness there.
Those five men went to the village and told their remaining companions. But the boy Yasa did not even go home...
Having gone, he told his parents and his wife; they all practiced the meditation on the foul (*asubha*).

This was their prior practice (*pubbayoga*). Therefore, in the case of the Venerable Yasa, the perception of a cemetery arose even toward the members of the theatrical troupe, and through that very excellence of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-sampatti*), the attainment of distinction was produced for them all.

Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: from the time he was staying at Bārāṇasī until the full moon of the latter Kattika month, on one occasion the Blessed One addressed those sixty bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted.
"Divine" means the snares of greed regarding divine objects. "Human" means the snares of greed regarding human objects.
"Let not two go by one way" means do not let two travel together along a single path. "Because of not hearing" means due to the lack of hearing [the Dhamma]. "They fall away" means...
Those who do not attain what has not yet been attained fall away from the attainment of distinction.

33. "End-makers" (antaka) refers to wretched, inferior beings. "Wanderer in the sky" (antalikkhacara) is said with reference to the snare of lust; for he spoke, regarding that [lust] as a "wanderer in the sky. 34.
"From various directions and various countries" means from various directions and from various countries. "I allow you, monks..."
"Now, you yourselves should ordain [them] in those various directions and in those various districts," and so forth—

when one is ordaining a son of good family who desires ordination, one should exclude those persons who were later prohibited by the rules beginning with, "Monks, one afflicted by five diseases should not be ordained," and continuing until,
"one who is blind, mute, or deaf should not be ordained."
A person free from the defects that preclude ordination should be ordained; moreover, he must have been permitted by his mother and father.
We shall explain the characteristics of such permission in this Sutta: "Monks, a son should not be ordained without the permission of his mother and father;
whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing."

Thus, when one is ordaining someone who is free from the defects of renunciation and has been permitted by his parents, if that person’s hair has not yet been cut and there are other monks within the same boundary, he must request the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*) for the purpose of cutting the hair.
Regarding the manner of requesting this, it is said: "I allow you, monks, to seek permission from the Saṅgha for the shaving of the head. Herein—
We shall explain [this]. If there is an opportunity, he should be ordained by himself.
If he is occupied with recitation, interrogation, and so forth, and does not find the opportunity, one young bhikkhu should be told, "Ordain this person.

Even if the young bhikkhu has not been so instructed, it is permissible for him to ordain him with that person as his preceptor. If no young bhikkhu is available, [the procedure continues as follows].
The novice should also be told: "Go, having led him to this broken boundary, having conferred the going-forth upon him, and having clothed him in the saffron robes.
However, the refuges must be given by oneself. In this way, one has indeed gone forth by means of a monk.

For no one other than a monk is permitted to confer the going-forth on a man, and no one other than a nun is permitted to do so for a woman. But a novice or a female novice [may confer it on their respective counterparts].
He may receive the saffron robes by means of an instruction. Having one's hair shaved is well-done whether performed by anyone at all;
however, if he is of suitable appearance, endowed with the necessary causes, well-known, and of noble birth, he should be ordained by himself after having been granted permission [with the words]:
"Take a handful of clay, bathe, moisten your hair, and then come back. And furthermore:
He should not be dismissed. For those who desire to go forth, there is first a strong enthusiasm;
however, later on, upon seeing the saffron robes and the razor for shaving the hair, they become terrified and flee from right there.
Therefore, having led him himself to the bathing place, if he is not too young, he should be told, "Bathe. As for his hair, he himself should take the clay...
They should be washed. However, a young child should be bathed by oneself after descending into the water and rubbing him with cow dung and clay.
Even if he has scabs or pustules, one should rub his hands, feet, and head thoroughly and bathe him without feeling any disgust, just as a mother does not feel disgust for her son.
Why? Because by such service, sons of good family [attain merit].
They possess strong affection for their teachers and preceptors, as well as for the Dispensation; they have intense reverence and are of a nature that does not turn back.
Having dispelled any arisen discontent, they reach the state of an elder (*thera*), being grateful and mindful of what has been done for them.
Thus, at the time of bathing or when shaving the hair and beard, [they say]: "You are renowned and famous; now we..."
He should not be told, "By relying on that, we shall not be troubled by the requisites," nor should any other talk that does not lead to liberation be spoken.
Rather, having said to him, "Friend, examine this thoroughly; establish mindfulness," the meditation subject of the fivefold skin (the *tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*) should be explained.
And while explaining it, one should describe its impurity, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness by way of its color, shape, smell, habitat, and location.
Or, it should be explained by making manifest its state of being soulless and devoid of a living entity.

For if he has previously refined his mental formations and developed his meditation, like an abscess ready to burst awaiting the prick of a thorn, or like a full-blown lotus awaiting the rising of the sun,
then as soon as his attention to the meditation subject is commenced, [the defilements] fall away like Indra’s thunderbolt.
Knowledge proceeds only by grinding away the mountain of defilements on the mountain; one attains Arahantship even on the very edge of a razor.

Indeed, whoever has attained Arahantship on the edge of a razor has all done so after obtaining such a hearing as this, relying on the method given by a good friend and teacher, and not without such reliance.
Therefore, from the very beginning, such a discourse must be delivered to him.

But when the hair has been shorn, having rubbed the head and body with turmeric powder or fragrant powder to remove the scent of a householder, the saffron robes should be accepted—either three times, twice, or once.
Even if the teacher or preceptor puts them on for him himself without giving them into his hands, it is permissible. If...
If he instructs another— whether a young novice, a novice, or a lay follower— saying, "Friend,
take these saffron robes and clothe him with them," or if he instructs that person himself, saying, "Take these and clothe him with them," all of this is permissible.
All of it is considered as having been given by that monk himself.
However, if one wears a lower garment or an upper robe that has not been formally given, it must be removed and given back again.
For a yellow robe is permissible only when given by a monk either with his own hand or by formal authorization;
what has not been given is not permissible, even if it belongs to that same person, let alone if it is held in trust by one's preceptor. This is...

Regarding the phrase, “having first had his hair and beard shaved off, having had him clothed in saffron robes, and having had him arrange his upper robe over one shoulder,” this is the detailed explanation.
“Having had him pay homage at the feet of the monks” means: having had him pay homage at the feet of whichever monks are assembled there.
Then, having had him sit in the *ukkuṭika* (squatting) posture for the purpose of taking the refuges and having him raise his joined palms (*añjali*), he should be told: "Speak thus.

He should be told: "Say what I say. Then the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or the teacher (*ācariya*) should grant him the refuges in the manner beginning with "I go to the Buddha for refuge," following the exact sequence already described.

Not out of order. For if one gives even a single word or a single syllable out of order—whether by giving the refuge to the Buddha three times first and then giving each of the others three times—the refuges have not been granted.
Furthermore, having rejected this ordination through going for refuge, the ordained ordination permitted [by the Blessed One] is for the sake of purity as one.
It is permissible. However, the going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) is permissible only when there is purity on both sides, not when there is purity on only one side.

Therefore, regarding full ordination (upasampadā), if the preceptor performs the formal act (kamma) while avoiding defects in the motion (ñatti-dosa) and defects in the proclamation (kammavācā-dosa), it is well-performed.
But regarding the going forth, these three refuges [must be recited] without the omission of consonants such as the letter *b* or the letter *dh*.
The preceptor and the pupil must both speak without failing in the perfection of the places of articulation and the vocal organs.
If the preceptor is able to speak but the pupil is not, or if the pupil is able to speak but the preceptor is not, or if neither of them is able to speak, it is not permissible.
However, if both are able to speak, it is permissible.

Furthermore, when giving these, they should be given either by making them end in a nasal sound with a single connection, saying: “I go for refuge to the Buddha,” or by making them end in the letter *m* with a pause, saying: “I go for refuge to the Buddha.
In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is said that after announcing one's name: “Venerable sir, I, Buddharakkhita, for as long as life lasts...”
When it is said, “I go for refuge to the Buddha,” that [phrase] is not found even in a single commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), nor is it stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*);
it is merely their own preference, and therefore it should not be accepted. For the refuge of one who does not speak in that manner does not become invalid.
“Monks, I authorize the going forth and the full ordination by means of these three refuges”—thus [he spoke regarding] the Buddha.

The meaning is: "I grant both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) by means of these three goings-for-refuge, spoken thus three times for the sake of purity on both sides, beginning with 'I go for refuge.
In that regard, since full ordination is prohibited later on, it does not take effect now by means of the mere going-for-refuge alone.
However, as for the going-forth, since it is permitted later on— [... —it is therefore valid.
“Monks, by these three goings for refuge, the going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) is authorized. Thus it was indeed permitted;
therefore, even now, that [going forth] succeeds by means of the refuges alone. For at this point, one is established on the ground of a novice.

However, if he is intelligent and of a wise nature, then the training rules (sikkhāpada) should be recited to him right there. How? Just as they were recited by the Blessed One. For this has been said:
“Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and that novices should train in them: abstaining from the destruction of life,
abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from unchaste conduct, abstaining from false speech,

abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, abstaining from eating at improper times, and abstaining from dancing, singing, music, and watching shows...

“Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from intoxicants that cause heedlessness; abstaining from wearing garlands, using perfumes and ointments, and engaging in adornment and beautification; abstaining from high and luxurious beds and seats; and abstaining from accepting gold and silver.
However, in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it says: “Venerable sir, I, named so-and-so, for as long as life lasts, [undertake] the training precept of abstaining from taking life...”
The phrase “I undertake [them]” is mentioned here just as it is in the case of giving refuge;
however, that [specific formula for the training rules] is found neither in the Canon (Pāḷi) nor in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). Therefore, they should be recited exactly according to the Canon.

For going forth is accomplished by the act of taking refuge alone, whereas the training rules are to be known solely for the purpose of fulfilling the training. Consequently, those [rules] are [found] in the Canon.
For one who is unable to learn by means of the traditional method, it is permissible to explain the meaning in whatever language is appropriate. However,
as long as he does not know the training rules (sikkhāpada) that he himself must study, and is not yet skilled in wearing the outer cloak, bowl, and robes, or in standing, sitting, and so forth,
nor in the procedures for drinking, eating, and so on, [he should remain] in the dining hall or the place where the voting tickets are distributed.

Nor should he be sent to another such place; he must be kept close by, cared for like a young child, instructed in all that is proper and improper, and trained in the practical observances of conduct, such as wearing the lower and upper robes.
By him [the teacher] also, [it was said]: "Monks, I allow one who possesses ten qualities..."
Having avoided from afar these ten grounds for expulsion mentioned above— thinking, "I shall cause the novice to be expelled"—
one who fulfills the higher conduct of observance should train thoroughly in the tenfold morality.
The Discussion on Going-forth is finished.
The Second Discourse on Māra. 35.

"Bhikkhus, for me indeed" (*mayhaṃ kho bhikkhave*) means "by me indeed. Alternatively, the meaning is: "by that which is my wise attention (*yoniso manasikāro*), by that cause. Regarding the phrase "non-arising again" (*anuppatti*), one should say "for me" (*mayā*) here by changing the grammatical case.
The Second Discourse on Māra is concluded.
The Discourse on the Bhaddavaggiyas (36).
Regarding the term *Bhaddavaggiya*: it is said that those princes were auspicious (*bhaddaka*) both in appearance and in character, and they moved about in a group (*vaggabandhena*);
therefore, they are called the "Bhaddavaggiyas. In the phrase *tena hi vo*, the word *vo* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).
"The eye of the Dhamma arose" means that for some the path of stream-entry arose, for some the path of once-returning arose, and for some the path of non-returning arose.
For all three of these paths are called "the eye of the Dhamma. It is said that in the past they were the thirty gamblers in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka;
then, having heard the exhortation to Tuṇḍila, they observed the five precepts—this was their prior karma.
The Discourse on the Bhaddavaggiya Group is finished.
The Discourse on the Miracle at Uruvelā.
37. *Pamukha* means a leader; *pāmokkha* means supreme, one of purified wisdom.
38. "Without destroying" means without annihilating. "Fire by fire" means one's own fire [overcomes] the fire of the Nāga.
"I would overcome" means I would surpass it, or I would destroy it. "Malice" refers to anger.
However, an Arahant does not speak while conceiving of himself as "I am an Arahant," thinking, "I am an Arahant."
39. The verses beginning with “Nerañjarāyaṃ bhagavā” were inserted later. 44–9.
*Vissajjeyya* means that one should place it outstretched for the purpose of drying; the sense is that one should set it down after spreading it out.
“Āharahattha” means that he is bent over as if saying, “Venerable sir, bring forth your hand. *Uyyojetvā* means having sent away. *Mandāmukhiyo*... [text fragment]
Fire-vessels are so called. 51.
"For a long time" means from a long period of time onwards.
52. Regarding "mixed with hair" and so forth: hair itself is "hair-mixed. This same method applies everywhere. "A load of khāri" means a burden of one khāri.
The Discourse on the Miracle at Uruvelā is finished.
The Discourse on the Meeting with Bimbisāra.
[At] Laṭṭhivana, that is, the Tāluyyāna park. At the Suppatiṭṭha Shrine, that is, at a certain banyan tree; it is said that this [name] belongs to it.
“Nāmaṃ. Regarding the phrase “with twelve hundred thousand”: here, one *nahuta* is ten thousand. “He addressed them” means he spoke to them for the purpose of cutting through their doubts.

“The advisor to the emaciated ones” (*kisakovadāno*) means that, being himself an advisor and instructor to those ascetics who were called “emaciated” (*kisaka*) due to their bodies having become lean through the practice of asceticism;
or alternatively, being himself an emaciated ascetic (*tāpaso*), he was one who spoke while advising others.
"Anusāsanto" also means "instructing. How was it abandoned? By what cause was it abandoned? This is what is meant:
"Being yourself a teacher who gave counsel to the ascetics dwelling at Uruvelā who tended the sacrificial fires, what did you see that you abandoned [them]?
I ask you this matter: by what cause was your fire-sacrifice abandoned?"
This is the meaning of the second verse: These people praise sensual pleasures such as forms and women, as well as sacrifices (*yañña*).

But I, having understood that all these various types of sensual pleasures—forms and the rest—are a stain upon the aggregates and the bases of existence, and since these sacrifices categorized as *yiṭṭha* and *huta* are themselves called stains, I did not delight in what is sacrificed (*yiṭṭha*) or offered (*huta*); the meaning is that I took no pleasure in either sacrificing or offering.
Regarding the third verse: *atha kocarahi* means *atha kvacarahi*. The remainder is self-evident. Regarding the fourth verse: *padaṃ* refers to the state of Nibbāna.
It is *santaṃ* (peaceful) because its intrinsic nature is peace. It is *anupadhikaṃ* (without acquisitions) due to the absence of the substrata of existence (*upadhi*).

It is *akiñcanaṃ* (possessing nothing) due to the absence of the "clutter" of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. Because it is unattached to the three realms of existence, [it transcends] that which is sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).
They speak of sacrifices; yet even therein, I am unattached to sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*). Because of the absence of birth, aging, and death, I am not subject to change.
It is to be attained only by the path developed by oneself, and is not to be attained by anything else; thus, I am "not led by another" (*anaññaneyya*).
Since I have seen such a state, therefore I did not delight in sacrifice or oblation. What does this show? That which—
“I have not found delight in sacrifices or offerings that accomplish the prosperity of the world of gods and humans;
so what shall I say, ‘My mind here delights in this world of gods and humans’?
Having thus declared his lack of delight in the entire world, the Venerable Uruvelakassapa then said, “I am a disciple.”
Thus he manifested his status as a disciple of the Blessed One, having displayed various miracles in the sky.
"The eye of Dhamma" refers to the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*). 57.
"Aspirations" (*assāsakā*) means hopes; the meaning is "longings. Regarding the phrase "Here I am, venerable sir," although by the very penetration of the path—
The going for refuge is established; therein, however, he has gone by way of definitive arrival. Now, he makes a formal surrender of himself through speech.
Having attained this state of fixed refuge by means of the Path itself, he speaks thus while making it manifest to others through speech and while proceeding with prostrations.
58. *Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo* means having a color equal to that of a piece of refined gold (*siṅgīsuvaṇṇa*). *Dasavāso* means one who has completed his residence in the ten noble dwellings (*ariyavāsa*).
*Dasadhammavidū* means one who knows the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakammapatha*). *Dasabhi cupeto* means endowed with the ten factors of one beyond training (*asekkha*).
*Sabbadhidanto* means tamed in all respects; for indeed, among the Blessed One’s faculties, such as the eye and so forth, there is nothing whatsoever that is untamed.

59. “Having sat down to one side of the Blessed One when he had finished his meal and had removed his hand from the bowl” means that, having observed that the Blessed One had eaten and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, he sat down in a certain place.
“Of those who have need” means of those who have need both of approaching to pay homage to the Buddha and of hearing the Dhamma. “Worthy of approach” means worthy of being approached.
It would be possible. "Not crowded" (*appākiṇṇa*) means not filled with people. "Quiet" (*appasadda*) means quiet in terms of the sound of speech.
"Noiseless" (*appanigghosa*) means noiseless in terms of the clamor of the city. "Free from the wind of people" (*vijanavāta*) means devoid of the bodily wind of people who pass by.

There is also a reading, "free from the talk of people" (*vijanavāda*); the meaning is that it is devoid of internal human chatter. There is also a reading, "free from the movement of people" (*vijanapāta*).
*Pāṭho*; the meaning is "devoid of human traffic. *Manussarāhaseyyakaṃ* means "a place for the secret activities of humans.
*Paṭisallānasāruppaṃ* means "suitable for seclusion," that is, appropriate for solitude.
The Discourse on the Ordination of Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
60. "Sāriputta and Moggallāna" means Sāriputta and Moggallāna. A pact was made between them: "Whoever first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other.

It is said that both of them, who were known by the names Upatissa and Kolita during their time as householders, went to a mountain-top festival accompanied by a retinue of two hundred and fifty young men. There, of those two—
Seeing the great multitude of people, he thought: "Indeed, this vast assembly of beings is mindful of death even before the hundredth year has passed.
Then, as both groups had risen and questioned one another, they shared a single resolve;
with the perception of death firmly established, they deliberated: "Friend, since death is certain, there must be an antidote to it. Come now, let us search for that immortality."

Having gone forth with their retinue in the presence of the wanderer Sañjaya Channa for the sake of seeking the Deathless, they reached the further shore of the range of his knowledge in just a few days;
yet, not seeing the Deathless, they asked, "Teacher, is there perhaps some other essence here?
Having heard him reply, "Friends, there is none; this is all there is," they [realized it was] empty.
"Friends, this is the way out. Now, whoever among us first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other"—thus they made an agreement.
Therefore it was said: "An agreement was made by them," and so forth.
In such expressions as "with a pleasing advance," the instrumental case should be understood as indicating a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). By those seeking [the goal]...
“‘The path pointed out’: this is a statement regarding the reason for following behind. For this is what is meant:
‘What if I were now to follow closely behind this bhikkhu? Why?
Because this act of following closely behind is a path pointed out by those who seek [the goal]; it is a path that is both known and entered upon. This is the meaning.”

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: Nibbāna is that which has been designated merely as "existent" by us seekers in the thought, "If death exists, there must also be the Deathless. He went seeking and searching for it.
"Taking almsfood, he returned" means that having approached a certain base of a wall of the kind described in the Sudinna episode.
[The Elder] sat down. Sāriputta, thinking, "It is not yet the right time to ask the question," stood to one side awaiting the proper moment.

Once the Elder had finished his meal and performed his duties, Sāriputta gave him water from his own water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and having exchanged greetings with the Elder whose hands and feet were washed, he asked the question. Thus it was said:
“Then the wanderer Sāriputta,” and so forth. “I am not able to do that for you” means: I am not able to do those things for you.
And herein, the Elder who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) is certainly not unable to do this much;
rather, thinking, “I shall cause him to develop reverence for the Dhamma,” he spoke thus, having grasped in every way the fact that the domain of the Buddha is beyond his own reach.
"Those phenomena that arise from a cause": the "arising from a cause" refers to the five aggregates; by this, he shows the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). "The Tathāgata has taught their cause":
the "cause" of these is the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*);
he shows that this too was taught by the Tathāgata. "And their cessation": this refers to the cessation of the non-occurrence of both those truths. And...
"The Tathāgata has said" is the meaning. By this, he shows the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).

Although the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is not shown here in its specific form, it is nonetheless shown by way of implication; for when cessation is stated, the path that leads to its attainment is effectively stated as well.
Alternatively, in the phrase "and their cessation," it should be understood as: "both their cessation and the means to that cessation."
"Thus two truths have been shown. Now, in order to establish that very point, he said: "The Great Ascetic speaks thus.

"If this alone is the Dhamma"—that is, even if there is nothing further beyond this, and only this much is to be attained, namely the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*)—nevertheless, "this alone is the Dhamma," is the meaning. "He has reached the state free from sorrow"—that which we were seeking.
"Let us investigate: you have penetrated that state which is free from sorrow; the meaning is that you have attained it.
"Unseen and passed away through many millions of eons"—this means that for us, this state has indeed remained unseen and has passed away through many millions of eons;
thus, by way of the state's being unseen, he demonstrates his own long-standing poverty.
62. "In the profound sphere of knowledge" means in that which is both profound and the object of profound knowledge.
"In the unsurpassed destruction of acquisitions" refers to Nibbāna. "Liberated" means liberated through the liberation that has that as its object.
"He prophesied" means that by saying, "This pair of disciples shall be my foremost auspicious pair," he prophesied regarding the knowledge of the perfection of discipleship.
"That was their full ordination" means that their full ordination was indeed by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*).
Once they were thus ordained, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna established himself in Arahatship within seven days,
and the Elder Sāriputta within half a month.
In the past, it is said, a Buddha named Anomadassī appeared in the world.
A forest-dweller named Sarada, having constructed a pavilion with various flowers in his own hermitage, seated the Blessed One upon a seat of flowers;
he likewise constructed a pavilion for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and prepared seats of flowers, and thus he aspired to the state of being an Aggasāvaka (Chief Disciple). Having made this aspiration—
He sent a message to the merchant named Sirivaḍḍha, saying, "I have aspired to the position of chief disciple; you too, having come, should aspire to a station.
The merchant, having constructed a pavilion of blue lotuses and fed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha there, aspired to the status of the second disciple.
Among them, the ascetic Sarada became the Elder Sāriputta.
"Sirīvaḍḍha and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna"—this was their past karma. Regarding the phrases "because of being childless," etc.:

for those whose sons have gone forth, it is because of their state of being childless; for those whose husbands have gone forth, it is because of their being widowed, that is, the state of being a widow.
By both of these, there is the destruction of the family line. "Sañcayāni" refers to Sañcaya.
*Antevāsikāni*: [The word] *giribbajaṃ* refers to the city of Giribbaja in the kingdom of Magadha.

*Mahāvīrā* means those possessing great heroism (*mahāvīriya*). Regarding *nayamānānaṃ*, it is used among those who are leading. The genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of the locative (*bhumm-attha*), or alternatively, in the sense of the accusative (*upayoga-attha*).
"What envy for those who understand?"—what jealousy can there be for those who understand that they are leading according to the Dhamma?
The Discourse on the Ordination of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is concluded.

The Discourse on the Duties Toward a Preceptor (Upajjhāyavatta-kathā), 64–5. "Without a preceptor" means being deprived of a venerable one who reflects upon what is blameworthy and what is blameless. "Not endowed with proper deportment" means...
"Not perfected in deportment" means they are devoid of conduct befitting a recluse (*śramaṇa*). "Above the food" means on top of the food.
"The bowl for rising" (*uttiṭṭhapatta*) refers to the bowl used for wandering for alms.
For people perceive it as leftover [food] in that [bowl], therefore it is called "the bowl for rising. Alternatively, it is so called because people rise up and offer the bowl; thus it is here.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "I allow you, monks, to take a preceptor (*upajjhāya*)," means "I allow you to accept a preceptor.
"He will establish a mind like that toward a son" means he will establish a mind [toward the preceptor] with the thought, "He is my son," by way of worldly affection.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "Respectful and deferential" refers to both a sense of reverence and a sense of seniority.

"Having attended upon. "Those of similar conduct" means those of a similar livelihood. "Sāhu," "vā," and so forth—these five phrases are synonyms for the acceptance of the status of preceptor (*upajjhāya*).

"He makes known by body" means that when the student has thus said three times, "Venerable sir, be my preceptor," the preceptor, by means of any one of these five phrases beginning with "Sāhu," makes it known by body.
Or, if by means of speech, or by both body and speech, one makes known the taking of a preceptor, saying, "The preceptor has been taken by you," then the preceptor is taken.
For this alone is the "taking of a preceptor" in this context:
namely, the verbal proclamation or the making known of the meaning of any one of these five phrases concerning the preceptor, either by speech or by body.
Some, however, say that this refers to the acceptance [of the request] with the words "Very well. That is not authoritative;
for the preceptor is already accepted by the mere act of giving the request, and acceptance is not a necessary factor here.
It is also permissible for the student to understand: "By this phrase alone, the preceptor has been accepted by me. From this day forward, the Elder is my responsibility."
"I too am a burden to the Elder"—this also ought to be understood.
66. Regarding that which was stated as "one should conduct oneself properly," this is the proper conduct therein:
having risen early and removed one's sandals, if, for the purpose of walking meditation or for the sake of protecting the feet after washing them at the time of dawn...
Or, if sandals have been put on and are still on the feet, they should be removed as soon as one has risen at the proper time.
Regarding the tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*): having brought three types—large, medium, and small—one should give whichever he takes for three days;
from the fourth day onward, the same kind should be given. If, however, no specific rule has been established...
Whether he takes this or that, then whatever kind he receives, that same kind should be given.

Regarding "mouth-water should be given": having brought both cold and warm water, from the fourth day onward, one should give mouth-washing water of the same kind as that which was used for three days. If, however, no specific rule has been made...
He may take either one or the other; however, whatever kind he receives, that same kind must be given back.
If he uses both types, both must be brought back. Having placed water in the place for washing the face, he should sweep starting from the restroom.
When the elder has entered the restroom, the courtyard should be swept; in this way, the courtyard is not left empty. When the elder...
The seat should be prepared while one has not yet stepped out from the restroom.
Having performed the bodily functions and returned, one should perform the duty prescribed for one seated there, beginning with the formula: "If there is rice-gruel," and so forth.
"Uklāpa" means strewn with some refuse; however, if there is no other refuse and there are only drops of water, it may be wiped even with the hand.
"Having made them with a border" means having joined two robes together; those two robes, once joined together, must both be given as *saṅghāṭīs*.
For indeed, every robe is called a "*saṅghāṭī*" because it is stitched together (*saṅghaṭita*); therefore it is said, "the *saṅghāṭīs* must be given.
Regarding the phrase "one should not go too far, nor too near": here, if the preceptor turns back and looks [at the pupil] with one [eye]...
Or, he reaches it with two steps; by this much, it should be understood that he has gone neither too far nor too near.

"The bowl that has been included [in the alms-round] should be received": if, while the preceptor is on his alms-round, the bowl obtained for either rice-gruel or solid food becomes hot or heavy, he should give his own bowl to him and take that bowl.

The meaning is "should be taken. "One should not interrupt the preceptor while he is speaking" means that while he is speaking—whether in a village or elsewhere—one should not initiate another conversation until his speech is finished.
Furthermore, from this point onward, wherever a prohibition is made by means of the negative particle *na*, in all such cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

This must be understood; for this is the nature of the Khandhaka rules. "Speaking near to an offense" means speaking words that are close to an offense by way of such things as minor offenses (*padasodhamma*) or grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla*).
"He should be restrained" means he should be stopped by one who asks, as it were: "Venerable sir, is it permissible to speak such a thing?
Is there no offense? Having resolved, "I shall restrain him," [one says]: "Elder,..."
"You should not say, 'Do not speak thus.
Regarding "having arrived earlier": if the village is nearby, or if there is a sick monk in the monastery, one should arrive earlier than from the village.
If the village is far away and there is no one coming along with the preceptor, [one may arrive later].
Having departed from the village together with him, one should wrap the bowl with the robe and arrive at the midpoint of the road first.
Thus, returning, one should arrive first and perform all the necessary duties, such as preparing the seat.
"Soggy" (*sinna*) means soaked or saturated with sweat. "Having turned up the hem by four finger-breadths" refers to the hem (*kaṇṇa*).
The robe should be folded in this manner, making it exceed [the usual length] by four finger-breadths. For what reason? "Lest there be a break in the middle.
For if it is folded evenly, a break occurs in the middle; thus, being constantly broken there, it becomes weak.
This was said for the purpose of preventing that. Therefore, just as today the break occurs at that very spot, tomorrow...
It does not break; likewise, every day it should be rolled up after being raised four finger-breadths.
"The waist-band should be placed in the fold" means that after rolling up the waist-band and putting it into the fold of the robe, it should be set aside.
"If there is almsfood" refers here to one who has eaten either in the village, within a house, or on the way back.
He arrives, but does not receive alms; thus he has no food. However, for one who has not eaten in the village or who has obtained some alms-food, [the following applies];
therefore it is said, "If there is alms-food," and so forth.
