Even if he has none, if he wishes to eat, water should be given and the alms-food he himself has obtained should also be brought forward. He should be asked about drinking water.
While eating, he should ask for water three times, saying, "Venerable sir, let water be brought.
If there is time, he should eat after his preceptor has finished eating. If the time is drawing near, he should place the water near his preceptor and eat himself.

"Anantarahitāya" means that one should not place the bowl on ground that is not cleared of anything harmful, such as wooden planks, broken pieces of stone, or the like, but rather on ground mixed with dust and gravel.
However, if it is black-soiled earth, or clay bound with lime, or even washed sand, it is permissible to place it on such ground. Washed sand is also suitable for placing it upon.
It is not permitted [to place it] on dust, soil, gravel, and so forth. However, having placed either a leaf or a support there, it should be deposited upon that.

Regarding the phrase "the edge from the far side and the fold from the near side," this is stated for the purpose of inserting one's hand beneath the robe-stand or similar object and then slowly depositing it with the hand facing forward.
Having grasped the edge, [one should place it] with the fold against the robe-stand or similar object.
If one places it on high, the shoulder strikes against the wall; therefore, it should not be done in that way.
"The powder should be moistened" means the bath-powder should be soaked with water and made into a paste.
"It should be placed to one side" means it should be set down in a smoke-free place. "Preparation in the sauna" refers to the providing of charcoal, clay, warm water, and so forth.
"All duties" means all tasks, such as massaging the limbs and so forth, even while in the water.
"He should be asked for drinking water" means that because thirst arises from the heat in the sauna (*jantāghara*), he should therefore be asked.
"If he is able" means if he has the strength; that is, if he is not overcome by any illness—for it is expected that the student (*saddhivihārika*) is not ill.
The entire duty toward the preceptor must be performed even for sixty years; for one who performs it without respect and thereby violates the duty, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, regarding those instances connected with the word "not" (na), there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing for one who performs a prohibited action even when ill.
"Without knocking" means without striking against the ground. "The surface of the door" refers to both the door and...
"And without touching a heap of grain. "A cobweb" refers to any kind of insect nest, spider's web, and so forth.
"First removing from the ceiling" means that starting from the ceiling—that is, beginning with the ceiling—it should be removed.
"The light-fissures and the corners" refers to the parts of the light-fissures and the corners, namely the inner and outer window-frames and shutters.
And the meaning is that the four corners of the bed should be wiped.
"It should be spread out as it was laid out" means it should be spread exactly as it had been laid out previously;
for it is for this very purpose that one should observe how it was laid out, take it away, and set it aside to one side.

The previous procedure has been prescribed. However, if it was previously arranged by someone who did not know [the rule], one should arrange it after leaving a space of two or three finger-breadths all around the wall. For this is the procedure for arranging [the bedding].
If the mattress is too large, it should be cut down, its corners turned back, and tied together before being arranged.
If he does not know how to turn back and tie [the animal] up, it must not be cut.
"The eastern windows should be closed" means the eastern windows should be shut; likewise, the remaining windows should also be closed.
"He should be sent away" means he should be led elsewhere. "He should be made to be sent away" means another bhikkhu should be told: "The Elder..."
"Having taken [him], go elsewhere"—this means he should be separated.
"He should be made to separate" means another person should be told, "Make the elder relinquish his adherence to that view.

"Effort should be made" means that for the purpose of granting the *parivāsa* probation, each respective monk should approach him and make a formal request. If he himself is capable, it should be granted by him alone.
If he is not capable [of doing so], it should be caused to be given by another. "How indeed" (*kinti nu kho*) means "by what means indeed. This method applies everywhere.

"Or he should convert it to a light [penalty]" means that without performing an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), he should perform an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) or an act of demotion (*niyassakamma*).
Therefore, having understood that "the Saṅgha intends to carry out an act of suspension against the preceptor,"...
Having approached each individual bhikkhu, they should request: “Venerable sirs, do not perform a formal act against our preceptor.
If they nevertheless proceed to do so, they should request: “Perform instead a *tajjanīya* (reproval) or a *niyassa* (sending away).
If they still proceed to do so, then the preceptor should request: “Venerable sirs, conduct yourselves properly. Having thus caused him to conduct himself properly—
“Venerable sirs, let the procedure subside,” thus should the monks be requested.
“Turning it over and over again” means having turned it over repeatedly.
“And one must not depart while the drops have not ceased” means that if even a small amount of dye still drips, one must not depart yet.
"Without asking the preceptor, the alms-bowl must not be given to anyone," and so forth—all this was stated with reference to persons who are unsuitable for the preceptor.
"Without asking the preceptor, one must not enter a village": one who wishes to enter for alms or for any other purpose must indeed enter only after having asked permission.
If the preceptor has risen early and [is traveling] far away...
If he wishes to go on almsround, he should say, "Let the young monks enter for alms," and then depart.
If he departs without saying this, it is permissible for him to enter the village after going to his own cell and not seeing the preceptor.
If, while entering the village, he does see him, it is still necessary for him to take leave from the very place where he saw him.
"One should not go to the charnel ground" means one should not go there for the purpose of staying or for the purpose of visiting. "One should not depart for another region":
here, one who wishes to depart must explain the matter and request permission up to three times. If he grants permission, that is well;
if he does not grant permission, then for one living in dependence on him, whether it be recitation, questioning, or the meditation subject—

If it does not succeed—meaning the preceptor is foolish and incompetent, and refuses to let him go merely out of a desire to have him live under his own care—it is permissible to go even when he is thus preventing it.
"One must wait for his recovery from illness" means that one must wait for his recovery from sickness; one should not go anywhere else. If there is another monk who acts as an attendant...
If there is medicine, one should seek it out, place it in his hand, say, "Venerable sir, this person will attend to you," and then depart.
The discussion on the duties toward the preceptor is finished.
Now follows the discussion on the duties toward the co-resident pupil.

67. Regarding the proper conduct toward a pupil by the preceptor: "He should be supported and assisted" means that the preceptor must provide support and assistance to him through recitation and other such means.

In this context, "recitation" (uddesa) refers to the oral transmission of the text. "Interrogation" (paripucchā) refers to the explanation of the meaning of the text. "Exhortation" (ovāda) refers to [the instruction] regarding matters not yet undertaken: "Do this; do not do that."
“Instruction” (*anusāsanī*) refers to when a matter has already arisen. Furthermore, the initial statement regarding a matter—whether it has arisen or not—is “admonition” (*ovāda*);
the repeated statement is “instruction. “If the preceptor has a bowl” means if he has an extra bowl. This same method applies everywhere.
“Requisites” (*parikkhāra*) refers to other requisites of a recluse as well. Here, “exertion” (*ussukka*) means...

The search for means that arises by a righteous method. From here on, beginning with the giving of tooth-sticks and ending with the pouring of water from the rinsing-pitcher, the duty must be performed by the sick student (*saddhivihārika*) alone.
However, the removal of dissatisfaction and so forth must indeed be performed even by one who is not sick. Regarding "while dyeing the robe": "In this way..."
"By one who, having heard the means from the preceptor, becomes impassioned. The remainder should be understood in the manner already stated.
The Discussion on the Duties of a Co-resident is finished.
The Discussion on Improper Conduct, etc.
68. "They do not conduct themselves properly" means they do not fulfill the duties toward a preceptor as they have been prescribed.
"Whoever should not conduct himself properly" means whoever does not fulfill the duties as they have been prescribed; the meaning is that he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"He should be dismissed" means he should be sent away. "There is no excessive affection" means there is no excessive affection based on worldly attachment toward the preceptor.
"It does not exist. "There is no superior development" means there is no superior development of loving-kindness (*mettā*);
the positive side is to be understood by the method of the opposite of what was stated. "Fit to dismiss" means it is appropriate to dismiss.
"If the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) does not dismiss him, he is at fault" means he is blameworthy; he incurs an offense. Therefore, it is not right...

One who is engaged in the duties must indeed be dismissed. Furthermore, as long as the robe-dyeing is not yet completed, if the duties are not performed according to the proper conduct (*sammāvattanā*), there is a loss for the preceptor.
Therefore, for one who fails to perform them—whether their formal dependence (*nissaya*) has been relinquished or not—there is indeed an offense.
For certain individuals, however, there is an offense starting from the giving of the bowl, even while their dependence has not been relinquished.
If the co-residents behave properly but the preceptor does not behave properly, it is an offense for the preceptor.
If the preceptor behaves properly but the co-residents do not behave properly, it is an offense for them.
Even if there are many co-residents, if the preceptor consents to the duty being performed, it is an offense for all of them. If the preceptor says, "My attendant..."
If he says, "There is [time]; you should apply yourselves to your own recitation, reflection, and so forth," there is no offense for the co-residents.

If the preceptor does not know whether [the time] is acceptable or unacceptable, or if he is ignorant, or if there are many co-residents—among them, a bhikkhu endowed with proper conduct [should think], "I shall perform the duty for the preceptor; you..."
“Dwell free from anxiety”— if he thus takes the burden upon himself and dismisses the others, then from the moment he assumes that burden,
there is no offense for them.
The discussion on improper conduct is concluded.
The Story of the Brahmin Rādha (69). Regarding the story of the Brahmin Rādha:

although the Venerable Sāriputta knew that the Blessed One had authorized both the going forth and the full ordination through the threefold taking of refuge at Bārāṇasī, the Blessed One considered that [method] to be too easy.

Having rejected full ordination (*upasampadā*) and having made it a grave matter through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), he wished to grant full ordination [to the brahmin].
Then the Elder, knowing his intention, said: "Venerable sir, how shall I go about ordaining that brahmin and granting him full ordination?
For the assemblies of Buddhas are skilled in discerning intentions, and this Elder was the foremost among the Buddha’s assembly.

Regarding the phrase "by a capable and competent monk" (*byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena*): here, one who is "capable" (*byatta*) is one for whom the Vinaya Piṭaka together with its commentaries has been committed to memory and is active;

in his absence, even one for whom at least this much—the formal proclamation of the motion followed by three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—is well-learned, committed to memory, and active, is also "capable" in this sense. However, one who [suffers] from coughing, consumption, phlegm, and so forth...

Or, due to illness, or because of the impairment of the lips, teeth, tongue, and so forth, or because one has not cultivated proficiency in the scriptures, one is unable to announce the *kammavācā* with complete and rounded words and phrases;
or one omits a phrase or a word, or says otherwise than what should be said—this person is "incapable. One who is the opposite of this [is capable] in this regard.
In this context, "capable" is to be understood [in this sense]. "The Saṅgha should be informed" means the Saṅgha should be made aware.
Thereafter, in order to show what the Saṅgha is to be made aware of, he said, "Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me," and so forth. 71.
"Immediately after being ordained" means having become ordained, immediately thereafter. "He practices improper conduct" means he transgresses the formal rule (paṇṇatti).
He acts [thus]: "May the teacher lift me up, may he pull me out; having raised me from the unwholesome, may he establish me in the wholesome;
or, having raised me from the state of a novice, may he establish me in the state of a bhikkhu. "Out of compassion" means depending on mercy;
the meaning is: "having shown compassion toward me."

73. "It persists" means it proceeds continuously. "The four supports" refers to the four conditions. Because the personal existence (*attabhāva*) proceeds in dependence upon these four conditions, they are called "supports.
The Discourse on the Story of the Brahmin Rādha is concluded.
The Discourse on the Teacher’s Duties.
75. "What kind of monk is this? means: what sort of monk is he?
"To be exhorted and instructed by others" means he is one who must be both exhorted and instructed by others. "Devoted to abundance, namely, to forming a group" means:

because he has this "forming of a group" (*gaṇabandha*) as his abundance, he is called "one devoted to forming a group" (*gaṇabandhika*); that is, abundance. This which is the "forming of a group" is abundance.
“Abundance of names” means that you have fallen into it very quickly for the sake of that [reputation]; this is what is meant.
76. “Incompetent” (*abyattā*) means devoid of the clarity of wisdom (*paññāveyyattiyena*). “One who was formerly a member of another sect” (*aññatitthiyapubbo*) refers to the wanderer Pasūra.
It is said that he, thinking “I shall deceive the Dhamma,” went forth under the Elder Udāyī, and by him...

When being addressed according to the Dhamma, he brought forward a challenge to his opponent’s argument. In the passage beginning, “I allow, monks, a competent monk,” the term “competent” (byatta) possesses the very characteristics already described in the previous commentary on the instructor of nuns.
Furthermore, one who is able to perform services such as nursing for a sick pupil or co-resident is intended here by the term “capable” (paṭibala). And this has also been said:
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may grant full ordination, give formal support, and have a novice attend upon him.
What are the five? He is capable of attending to or having his pupil or co-resident attended to when they are ill;
of calming or having them calmed when they are discontented; of [dealing with] arisen... [disputes].”
“...to dispel remorse regarding the Dhamma, to train them in the Abhidhamma, and to train them in the Abhivinaya.
77. “Regarding those who have gone over to the faction”: this refers to those who have gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas*. “I allow you, monks, a teacher (*ācariya*):
I allow a teacher who instructs in proper conduct and behavior. “A teacher, monks, [should behave] toward his pupil,” and so forth—all of this is as [stated] for the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
This should be understood according to the method stated in the passage beginning with “I am a *saddhivihārika*,” and so forth; for here there is only a difference in terminology.
The discussion on the duties toward the teacher is finished.
Now begins the discussion on dismissal and excusing oneself.
80. Regarding the statement, "The resident pupils do not behave properly toward their teachers," it should be understood here from what was previously stated:
"Due to improper conduct, as long as the duties are not performed—even down to the dyeing of the robes—the preceptor suffers a loss;

therefore, for one who fails to perform them, there is indeed an offense, whether he has been released from formal dependence (*nissaya*) or not. And: "For some, [the offense arises] from the giving of the bowl..."

And although the characteristic [of an offense] has been stated as "an offense occurs only for one who has not released the formal dependence (*nissaya*)," the offense of the dependent pupil (*nissayantevāsika*) should not be understood by that characteristic alone.
For as long as the dependent pupil lives in dependence upon the teacher (*ācariya*), he must perform every duty toward the teacher.
However, this does not apply to those who are pupils in the Dhamma regarding going-forth (*pabbajjā*) or full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Even for those who are independent of formal dependence (*nissaya*), the proper conduct (*vatta*) must be observed from the beginning until the dyeing of the robes;

however, there is no offense for them in giving alms bowls or similar items without having first asked permission. Among these, the student of going-forth (*pabbajjantevāsika*) and the student of full ordination (*upasampadantevāsika*) are the responsibility of the teacher (*ācariya*) for as long as they live.
The student of formal dependence (*nissayantevāsika*) and the student of the Dhamma (*dhammantevāsika*) [are responsible] as long as they remain in his presence.
They remain for just that long. Therefore, the teacher must also behave properly toward them.
For regarding teachers and students, whoever behaves improperly incurs an offense.
The discussion on dismissal and forgiveness is concluded.
83. Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence (*nissayapaṭippassaddhikathā*).
Regarding the cessations of dependence from a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), such as "the preceptor has departed," etc., this is the analysis:
"departed" means he has gone away from that residence, having the desire to dwell apart, and having gone off in some direction. And when he has thus departed...
If there is a provider of formal dependence (nissaya) in the monastery, one should receive dependence from him;
or from one with whom dependence has previously been taken on other occasions, or from one who shares the same communal enjoyment (ekasambhogaparibhoga). There is no exemption for even a single day.
If such a person is not available, and there is another who is modest and amiable, one should receive dependence from that person, provided one recognizes his state of being modest and amiable.
On that very day, one must request formal dependence (*nissaya*). If he grants it, that is well.
But if he asks, "Will your preceptor (*upajjhāya*) arrive soon? and the preceptor has indeed said so, one should say, "Yes, Venerable Sir.
If he says, "In that case, wait for the arrival of the preceptor," that is permissible. However, if by his nature...
If he does not know his good character, one should wait for four or five days to observe whether that bhikkhu is of similar standing,
and then, having requested permission, receive formal dependence (*nissaya*) from him. However,
if there is no giver of dependence in the monastery, and the preceptor says, "I will return in a few days," [one may wait].
Having said, "Do not be distressed," he departed; [the junior monks] receive an exemption from duties until his return.
Even if people there should keep him for five or ten days beyond the fixed period, he must send word to the monastery:
"Let the juniors not be distressed; I shall return on such-and-such a day. In this way also—

An exemption is granted. Now, if on the way back there is an obstruction such as a river in flood or danger from thieves and the like, and the elder waits for the water to recede or searches for companions, and the juniors hear of this situation, an exemption is granted until his return.
However, if he sends word saying, "I shall stay right here," [the exemption does not apply].
There is no exemption. Wherever support (nissaya) can be obtained, one must go there.
However, if [the preceptor] has disrobed, died, or transferred to another faction, there is no exemption even for a single day; wherever support can be obtained, one must go there.
Furthermore, "command" (āṇatti) refers to the dismissal of support (nissayapaṇāmanā). Therefore, [one says]: "I dismiss you..."
Whether by means of this scriptural method— such as saying "Go away," or "Do not come back here," or "Take away your bowl and robes," or "I am not to be attended by you"—
or by a method outside the scripture such as "Do not ask me for permission to enter the village," whoever has been dismissed by the revocation of dependence must ask his preceptor for forgiveness.
If he does not forgive from the very beginning, one should bring him to perform a penance (*daṇḍakamma*) and ask for his forgiveness three times by oneself.
If he still does not forgive, one should take the senior elders (*mahāthera*) of that monastery and ask for his forgiveness.

If he still does not forgive, one should take monks from the neighboring monasteries and ask for his forgiveness. If even this does not suffice, one should go elsewhere and [inform] the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
One should dwell in the presence of those who are like-minded, thinking: "Perhaps they will forgive me once they know that I am dwelling in their presence.
If even then they do not forgive, one should continue to dwell right there.
If it is impossible to dwell there due to factors such as famine, one should return to that same monastery, take formal dependence (*nissaya*) from another, and dwell there.
It is permissible. This is the analysis regarding formal instructions (*āṇattiya*).

Regarding the cessation of dependence (*nissaya*) from a teacher: in the cases where "the teacher has departed" or "the teacher has gone away," some teachers depart after having requested permission, while others depart without having requested permission.
It is the same for the resident pupil (*antevāsika*). In that regard, if the resident pupil...
He asks his teacher, "Venerable sir, I wish to go to such-and-such a place for some business.
When the teacher asks, "When will you return? he replies, "I shall return having risen either in the evening or at night.
The teacher accepts this, saying, "Very well," and at that very moment the formal dependence (nissaya) is suspended.

But if, when he says, "Venerable sir, I wish to go to such-and-such a place," the teacher says, "After you have wandered for alms in such-and-such a village, you will know [the way] later," and he accepts this, saying, "Very well," then if he goes, it is well.
But if he does not go, the formal dependence (nissaya) is not dissolved. Or even if he thinks, "I am going..."
When the teacher says, "Do not go yet; let us deliberate during the night and then we shall know," and having so deliberated he goes, he is one who has gone rightly (*sugata*).

If he does not go, the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not dissolved. However, for one who departs without asking permission from the teacher, the formal dependence is dissolved upon crossing the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*). For one who turns back before reaching the boundary of the precinct, [the dependence remains].
It does not subside. However,
if the teacher informs the pupil, saying, "Friend, I am going to such-and-such a place," and when the pupil asks,
"When?", he replies, "In the evening or during the night," and the pupil accepts, saying, "Very well," [then it subsides].
At that very moment, the formal dependence (nissaya) is dissolved.
However, if the teacher says, "I shall go tomorrow after walking for alms," and the other agrees, saying "Very well," then the dependence is not dissolved for that one day;
on the following day, it becomes dissolved. "In such-and-such a place..."
Having said, "I will know whether I go or do not go after wandering for alms in the village named so-and-so," if he does not go, the formal dependence (nissaya) is not lifted.
Furthermore, even if he says, "I am going," and the pupil says, "Do not go yet;
consult [your teacher] at night and then you shall know," and having consulted, he still does not go, the formal dependence is [not lifted].
It does not cease.
If both the teacher and the pupil go outside the boundary on some business, and if the teacher,
having gone without asking for permission while the thought of traveling has arisen, turns back within the distance of two stone-throws, the dependence [is maintained].
It is not pacified. If he returns after passing two clods' throws, it is pacified.
If the teacher and preceptor reside in another monastery beyond two clods' throws, the formal support (nissaya) is pacified.
When the teacher has departed, died, or joined another faction, it is pacified at that very moment. In the case of an instruction...
Furthermore, even if the teacher, desiring to let go, dismisses the pupil by revoking his formal dependence (*nissaya-panāmana*),
and the pupil remains full of attachment, thinking, "Although my teacher dismisses me, he is nevertheless soft-hearted toward me," the dependence is not dissolved.
Even if the teacher is full of attachment while the pupil is free from attachment, [the teacher thinks], "Now, this..."
If he relinquishes his responsibility, thinking, "I will live depending on him," even so it is not pacified.
However, as long as there is attachment on the part of both, it is certainly not pacified. It is pacified only when both have relinquished their responsibility.
One who has been dismissed must perform penance and ask for forgiveness three times. If he does not forgive, one should proceed according to the method described for a preceptor (upajjhāya).
Regarding the phrase "or has come together with the preceptor (*upajjhāya*)," here "coming together" should be understood by way of seeing or hearing.

For if a resident student (*saddhivihārika*) living under the guidance of a teacher (*ācariya*) sees his preceptor—whether while the preceptor is worshipping at a shrine in the same monastery or walking for alms in the same village—the dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended. [The same applies if] the preceptor sees [the student].
But if the *saddhivihārika* does not see [the offense], it is not pacified.

Or, having seen his preceptor (*upajjhāya*) walking along a path or traveling through the air, because of the distance, he perceives him as "a monk" and does not perceive him as "my preceptor"; thus, it is not pacified.
If he does perceive him, it is pacified. [The preceptor] is staying on the upper floor of the palace, while [the student is] below...
If the co-resident (saddhivihārika), having not seen him at all, drinks the rice-gruel and departs; or, having not seen him sitting in the assembly hall, eats in a secluded spot and departs;

or, having not seen him even though he is sitting in the Dhamma-hall, listens to the Dhamma and departs—the formal dependence (nissaya) is not suspended. In this way, first, the convergence should be understood by way of sight.

Regarding the method of hearing: if, while one's preceptor is preaching the Dhamma or offering an expression of appreciation (anumodanā) in a monastery or within a village, one hears the sound and perceives, "This is my preceptor’s voice," the formal dependence (nissaya) is suspended.
For one who does not perceive it, it is not suspended. This is the detailed analysis in summary.
The Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence is finished.
84. The Discussion on the Five Things to be Ordained.
Now, regarding what was previously stated: "I allow you, monks, a learned and competent monk of ten years' standing..."

In brief, the characteristics of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and the teacher (*ācariya*) have been stated thus: "or one who has more than ten years [of seniority] may grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) or give formal dependence (*nissaya*).
To show this in detail, he said: "Endowed with five factors, O monks... and so forth.
In that context, "with five factors" means with five factors of non-virtue; for he is indeed [unfit] because he is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and the others.
"He is not endowed with the qualities of a limb. "He should not be ordained" means that having acted as an *upajjhāya* (preceptor), he should not ordain [a candidate].
"Support should not be given" means that having acted as an *ācariya* (teacher), support should not be given.

And here, in the three pentads beginning with "not by one who possesses the aggregate of virtue of an Asekkha," "not himself being an Asekkha," and "one who lacks faith," the negation is by way of what is inappropriate.

It is not [improper] by way of the factors of an offense. For if one who is not himself endowed with the aggregates of virtue and so forth of an Asekha, and being unable to encourage others therein, maintains a retinue while being possessed of faults such as lack of faith, his retinue surely declines in virtue and the like;
it does not increase. Therefore, he should not grant full ordination, and so forth.
This was stated by way of what is appropriate, not by way of the factors for an offense.

For the Blessed One did not authorize the status of preceptor or teacher for one who has only destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*). If that alone had been authorized, he would not have said, "If dissatisfaction has arisen in the preceptor," and so forth.
However, because the assembly of one who has destroyed the taints does not decline in virtue and the other qualities, [the Blessed One spoke thus].
Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors may confer full ordination," and so forth.

Regarding the phrases "one who has failed in virtue with respect to higher virtue" (*adhisīle sīlavipanna*) and so on: one who has committed a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa* offense is called "one who has failed in virtue with respect to higher virtue.
One who has committed the other five classes of offenses is called "one who has failed in conduct with respect to higher conduct" (*ajjhācāre ācāravipanna*). Having abandoned right view...
One who possesses an extremist view is said to be "fallen from the view" due to excessive views.

Because he lacks that learning which ought to be possessed by one who leads an assembly, he is "of little learning. Because he does not know what he ought to know—such as the nature of offenses and so forth—he is "of weak wisdom.
In this pentad, the first three terms are used in the sense of being inappropriate.
The latter two have been stated by way of the factors of an offense (*āpatti-aṅga*).
"He does not know the offense" means that when it is said, "I have committed such-and-such," he does not know, "This person has fallen into this particular offense.

"He does not know the rehabilitation" means [he does not know] regarding the offense from which one proceeds either by way of formal rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhāna*) or by way of confession (*desanā*). Thus...

He does not know that this is the emergence from the offense. In this group of five, the first two terms are stated by way of what is improper, while the latter three are by way of the factors of an offense.
"In regard to the training of proper conduct" means he is not capable of training [others] in the duties of the Khandhakas. "In regard to the fundamentals of the holy life" means...
The meaning is that he is not capable of training [others] in the *sekkhapaṇṇatti* (the rules for those in training).

Regarding the *Abhidhamma*, the meaning is that he is not capable of training [others] in the analysis of mind and matter (*nāmarūpapariccheda*). Regarding the *Abhivinaya*, the meaning is that he is not capable of training [others] in the entire *Vinayapiṭaka*.
And in all cases, "not capable of training" means he is unable to instruct. "To separate from the Dhamma" means...
To cause [a monk] to relinquish [an object] by means of a lawful procedure (*dhamma-kāraṇa*). In this group of five, there is an offense in every instance.
In the group of five beginning with "he does not know the offense," there is also an offense in every instance. The same method applies to the group of five ending with "less than ten years.
Thus, the first three groups of five, the three phrases in the fourth, and the two phrases in the fifth—all four groups of five—are stated according to what is improper.
In the fourth pentad there are two items; in the fifth, three; and in the sixth, seventh, and eighth, three pentads each—all four pentads are stated by way of the factors of an offense.
In the bright fortnight (the section on non-offenses), there are eight instances of non-offense.
The discussion of the pentad concerning those to be ordained is concluded.
85. Discussion on the Set of Six Subjects Regarding Ordination (*Upasampādetabbachakkakathā*).

Among the six sets, the phrase "less than ten years" is the specific distinction; that constitutes an offense in every instance. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. In that regard:
"Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have not been properly learned by him in detail."
They are not well-received by way of both the Vibhaṅgas. They are "not well-analyzed" by way of the analysis of the Mātikā.
They are "not well-functioning" by way of being mastered through recitation. They are "not well-determined" by way of the Suttas and the Anubyañjana;
that is, they are not properly determined according to both the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga.
The Discussion on the Sixfold Set of Those to Be Ordained is finished.

86. The Discussion on the Case of One Formerly a Member of Another Sect. Regarding the case of one formerly belonging to another sect: as for this Pasūra, because he had gone over to another sect, he was not [ordinable].

He should be ordained. However, in order to show what must be done for anyone else who comes here who has not previously gone forth, the Buddha said, "But whoever, monks, that other person... and so forth.
In that context, "four months' probation should be given to him" refers to what is called *titthiyaparivāsa*; it is also termed *appaṭicchannaparivāsa*. This, however—
It should be given only to a naked wanderer, an Ājīvika, or a naked ascetic (acelaka).
Even if such a person arrives wearing a cloth, a woolen blanket, or any other sectarian emblem (titthiyaddhaja), probation (parivāsa) must not be granted to him.
Furthermore, it should certainly not be given to others, such as those who are "ash-smeared" ascetics (tāpasa-paṇḍaraṅga) and the like.
First, by the words "hair and beard," etc., he shows his initial going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera).

However, when those who are ordaining him are seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, the elder bhikkhus should not be addressed with such words as, "You ordain him," "You be the teacher (ācariya)," or "You be the preceptor (upajjhāya).
For if they were so addressed, should they—acting in the capacity of his teacher and preceptor—[fail to do so]...
Feeling disgusted, they do not accept him; then, thinking, "These people do not have faith in me," he might depart in anger.
Therefore, having led him aside, his teachers and preceptors must be sought out.
(87) In this way, monks, one who was formerly a member of another sect becomes successful; in this way, he is unsuccessful. This is his [distinction].
The summary (mātikā) is for the purpose of showing the duties of one who has completed his probationary period. And how, monks, etc., is the analysis (vibhaṅga) of that very same [summary].
Therein, "he enters the village too early" means he enters the village for alms at the very time when the monks' duty of performing the formalities is taking place.
"He returns too late in the day" means he engages in domestic conversation with women, men, boys, girls, and so forth, within the houses.
While [the monks] are eating right there, or while they are putting away their bowls and robes, or while they are engaged in recitation or questioning, or while they are in seclusion, he arrives;
he performs neither the duty toward his preceptor nor the duty toward his teacher, but instead enters his dwelling place and sleeps.
In this way too, monks, one who was formerly a member of another sect...
“He is one who does not win over” means that even by acting in this way, he is neither a fulfiller nor a completer of the probationary observance (*parivāsa-vatta*).

Regarding the phrases “frequenting prostitutes,” and so forth: “prostitutes” (*vesī*) refers to women who live by their beauty and are easily approached for sexual favors through the giving of material goods, trifles, and the like.
“Widows” (*vidhavā*) refers to women whose husbands are deceased or absent; they [may associate] with anyone whatsoever.
They seek friendship. "Maidens of mature age" refers to girls who have reached puberty or have passed beyond it;
they wander about with the intention of sexual union and seek friendship with anyone at all.

"Eunuchs" refers to those of the neuter sex whose defilements are excessive and whose feverish agitation is unappeased; overcome by the force of that agitation, they [seek friendship] with anyone at all.
They long for friendship. "Bhikkhunīs" refers to women who have gone forth together with one;
with them, intimacy arises quickly, and from that, virtue is broken.

In that regard, having become a *kulūpaka* (one who frequents families) among the families of prostitutes, or by making excuses such as wandering for alms-food and so forth, [one acts] out of affection and familiarity born therefrom.
If, out of a desire for frequent sight and conversation, he approaches them with his heart [set on them], he is called "one who frequents prostitutes" (*vesiyāgocara*);
before long, he becomes subject to the report: "He has gone with such-and-such a prostitute. This same principle applies in all cases.
However, if prostitutes and others provide *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals) and so forth, he may go together with the bhikkhus.
It is permissible for her to come having eaten together with them or having taken [food] from them.
It is permissible for nuns who are ill to go together with monks who are going to exhort them, teach the Dhamma, or provide instruction, questioning, and so forth.
However, one who comes in such a manner but then goes out of a desire for friendship and intimacy is not one who succeeds.

"High and low duties" refers to major and minor tasks. Among these, those duties that must be performed by a complete Saṅgha after striking the gong and assembling—such as the restoration of a cetiya or a great palace—are called "high.
Those included in the Khandhaka, such as the washing and dyeing of robes, as well as the practical observances (*ābhisamācārika*) such as the conduct regarding the fire-hall, are [the minor ones].
"Avacāni" means "to speak. In that context, "he is not skillful" means he is not clever or well-trained in those tasks.

"He is not untiring" means he is not endowed with initiative and energy; having heard, "There is work for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," he performs his meal duties early in the morning, enters his inner chamber, sleeps as much as he likes, and only leaves in the evening. "Tatrupāyāya" means...

Regarding those tasks, he was not endowed with the wisdom that arises at that very moment—namely, the investigative wisdom (*vīmaṃsā*) which serves as the means for those actions—to discern: "This should be done in this way; this should not be done in that way.
He was not capable of acting or arranging it, meaning he was not able to do it even with his own hands. [He said: "Take them, venerable sir!"
"Take it up, young man! Take it up, novice!
If you will not do it, or we will not do it, who indeed will do this now?"—having thus generated such enthusiasm, he is unable to arrange it or to have it done by one another.
When the monks say, "We shall perform the formal act," he makes some pretext of illness; [this refers to] the monks' formal act.
He wanders about merely in their vicinity when they are practicing; he shows only his head; such a person is also one who fails to win over others.
"He does not have intense desire" means he does not have powerful desire. "In the recitation" refers to the mastery of the textual tradition (*pāḷi*).

"In questioning" refers to hearing the meaning. "In higher virtue" refers to the *pātimokkha* morality. "In higher mind" refers to the cultivation of mundane concentration (*samādhi*). "In higher wisdom" refers to...
"Through the cultivation of the supramundane path.
"Has transferred" means he has come here. "Of that teacher" means of the owner of that religious system (*titthāyatana*).
"By his view" means by the tenet belonging to him. Now, since that very tenet belongs to that founder of the school (*titthakara*), [it is said:]...
It is both approved and liked, and grasped with a firm insistence as "this alone is the truth";
therefore, it is said that one takes up its approval, its liking, and its adoption. Hence it is stated: "by his approval, by his liking, by his adoption.
Regarding the phrase "when dispraise is being spoken": when censure is being uttered. "Dissatisfied" means one whose intention is not fulfilled; not...

"With uplifted mind": *udagga* means with body and mind raised up. "This, monks, is the 'Saṅghātanika' [discontent] regarding that which is not to be approved by one who was formerly a follower of another sect"—this, monks, refers to the displeasure (*anattamanatta*) that produces bodily and verbal manifestations when the dispraise of that teacher and his doctrine is being spoken, thinking, "Why are these people censuring others?", as well as [the displeasure toward] the Buddha and the rest.
The state of being pleased when dispraise is being spoken, the state of being pleased when praise is being spoken of that very teacher and that very doctrine,

and the state of being displeased when the praise of the Buddha and others is being uttered— this is the characteristic mark of one who was formerly a member of another sect regarding what is not to be propitiated;
it is the mark for one who is non-propitiatory, who has undergone the probationary period, and who has not fulfilled the formal act.

This means it is said: "This is the characteristic; this is the fixed measure. Thus, "O monks, one who has previously belonged to another sect and has come here, if he does not satisfy [the requirements], should not be ordained"—meaning that if he possesses even one of these factors, he should not be ordained.
On the bright side (the positive case), everything should be understood by reversing what was stated.
"Thus, monks, one is a seeker of favor": thus, by not entering the village too early, by not returning from it too late,
by not frequenting the quarters of prostitutes and the like, by being skillful in the affairs of one's fellow practitioners, by having intense zeal for the recitation of the scriptures and so forth,

by being pleased when the disparagement of other sectarians is spoken, by being displeased when the disparagement of the Buddha and the others is spoken, and [by being pleased] when the disparagement of other sectarians...
If he is one who has come from another sect and is able to fulfill these eight sectarian observances— namely, dissatisfaction when the praises of the Buddha and so forth are being spoken,
and satisfaction when the praises of the Buddha and so forth are being spoken— he is to be granted full ordination as a monk who has pleased and satisfied [the Saṅgha].
However, if he breaks even a single observance within the ordination hall itself, he must again undergo the four-month probationary period.

Just as probationary training rules and formal permission for training are granted again to a trainee (sikkhamānā) whose training has been broken, so too there is nothing further to be given to this person.
For his probation is indeed the very same probation previously granted;
therefore, he must again undergo probation for four months. If, while undergoing probation, he [attains] the eight attainments...

[Such a person] brings [the offense] to birth; what is called a mundane dhamma has the nature of provocation and should not be conferred upon. Only one who has fulfilled the four-month probationary practice may be conferred.

However, if while undergoing probation he comprehends the four great elements, delimits derived matter, defines name-and-form, and, having applied the three characteristics, initiates insight, [he is fit for ordination].
A worldly person (lokiya-dhamma) is one whose nature is subject to agitation; he must not be ordained.
However, if he has developed insight and attains the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), his duties are indeed fulfilled.
Since all views have been eradicated and the dart of doubt has been pulled out, he may be ordained on that very day, even if he is currently wearing the sectarian marks of a heretic (titthiya-liṅga).
He is a stream-enterer; there is no requirement for a probationary period (*parivāsa*). On that very day, he should be granted the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
"A robe should be sought based on the preceptor" means that making the preceptor the authority, one must seek a robe for him.
The same applies to the alms-bowl. Therefore, if the preceptor has a bowl and robe, [one should say]: "For this..."

He should be told, "Give [it]. If there is none, and others wish to give, they too must give it to the preceptor himself, saying, "Having made this for you, please give it to him. Why? Because those of other sects are contrary;
having said, "The bowl and robes were given to me by the Saṅgha; why am I dependent on you?", they would not provide instruction or admonition.
But because his livelihood depends upon the preceptor, he will follow his word;
therefore it is said, "He should seek robes with the preceptor as the basis. For the purpose of shaving the hair: this discussion on shaving will come later.
"Fire-worshippers" means those who attend to the sacrificial fire. "Matted-hair ascetics" means forest-dwelling recluses. "These, monks, are proponents of action" means these [hold that] action...
They do not reject them; they hold the view that "there is karma, there is the ripening of karma.
For all Buddhas, while fulfilling the perfection of renunciation, fulfilled it precisely by going forth into homelessness; I too have fulfilled it in the same way.
Going forth in their teaching is not contrary [to the Dhamma]; therefore, they should be ordained, but they do not require a period of probation.
"It should be given. "Monks, I give this special privilege to my kinsmen;
I grant them this distinct, specific favor. Why did he say this? Because even though they had gone forth in other sectarian orders, they were not seekers of disrepute for the Teaching;
rather, they spoke in praise, saying, "This is the Teaching of our most excellent kinsman. It was for this reason that he said so.
The Discourse on the Previous Life as a Follower of Another Sect is finished.
The Discourse on the Five Diseases: 88.
"In the Magadhas there are five diseases that are prevalent"—this refers to both humans and non-humans in the country named Magadha.
Five diseases have become prevalent, increased, and reached a state of severity. The account of Jīvaka Komārabhacca will appear in the Cīvarakkhandhaka.

"Monks, one who is afflicted by five types of ailments should not be ordained. This means that one who is afflicted and overcome by those five ailments, such as leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) and so forth, when they have become prevalent, should not be ordained.

In this context, "leprosy" (*kuṭṭha*) refers to whether it be red leprosy or black leprosy; it is stated that whatever variety there may be, such as *kiṭibha*, *daddu*, or *kacchu*, all are indeed leprosy.
If even a patch the size of a fingernail is situated on a part of the body intended for growth, he should not be ordained.
However, if [the disease] is covered by the lower garment (*nivāsana*) or the upper robe (*pārupana*) in a place normally concealed, and is the size of a fingernail—

If it is situated on the non-growing side [of the nail], it is permissible. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that if it is situated on the face, the back of the hand, or the back of the foot—even if it is smaller than the surface of the nail—even though it is on the non-growing side, it is certainly not permissible.

When one who has been treated medically is to be ordained, he should be ordained only when his natural appearance has returned. Even one whose body is covered with powder resembling the back of a monitor lizard [is not to be ordained].
It is not permissible to grant him the going-forth.
Regarding "a boil": whether it be a carbuncle or any other kind of boil, even if it is only the size of a jujube fruit, if it is on the side of increasing, he must not be granted the going-forth.
However, if it is in a concealed place, the size of a jujube fruit, and on the side of not increasing...
It is permissible [to ordain] one who is stationary [in growth]. However, it is not permissible even for one who remains on the side of not growing in uncovered areas such as the face and so forth.
Even when one intends to ordain after having them treated medically, they must be ordained only after the body has been made smooth-skinned.
Those called "woolly goiters" (uṇṇigaṇḍā) hang here and there like cow-horns or fingers; these too are simply goiters.
If these [boils] are present, it is not permissible to grant the going-forth. There are what are called milk-boils in childhood and hard boils in youth;
they disappear in old age and do not count as swellings (*gaṇḍa*); if these are present, it is permissible to grant the going-forth.
However, other hard boils on the body are called *aparā-padumakaṇṇikā*, and others are like mustard seeds.
Even those [eruptions] as small as mustard seeds that spread over the entire body are all of the leprous type (*kuṭṭha-jātika*). When these are present, one should not be ordained.
As for *kilāsa* (leucoderma): it is a non-ulcerating, non-exuding leprosy, white in color like the petals of a lotus or a water lily, by which the body becomes spotted like that of cattle;
regarding this *kilāsa*, the determination should be understood in the same manner as stated for the previous case.

"Sosātika" refers to one suffering from consumption (*sosabyādhi*); if such a person exists, he should not be ordained. "Apamāra" refers to either a bile-induced delirium (*pittummāra*) or a spirit-induced delirium (*yakkhummāra*);

in that case, if he is seized by a non-human being (*amanussa*) with whom he has a prior enmity, he becomes difficult to cure. Furthermore, even if there is only a slight delirium, he should not be ordained.
The Discussion on the Five Grounds of Non-Obstruction is finished.
The Discussion on the Ground of the King’s Servant (90).
Regarding the ground of the king’s servant: “Clear away the borderlands” means to expand the borderlands; having driven out the bandits...
The meaning is: having settled the village that had been abandoned due to fear of thieves, and having provided protection, you should cause agricultural work and other such tasks to proceed.
However, because the king was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), he did not command, "Kill the thieves! Strike them! [When asked], "Venerable Sir, should the preceptor's head be cut off?
and so forth, [the Buddha replied]: "In the religious life, the preceptor is the most excellent; after him, the teacher; after him..."
Thinking, "It is a group," they said, "This has come down in common parlance regarding the adjudication of debts. "Monks, one who is a royal servant (*rājabhaṭa*) is not to be ordained.

Herein, whether he be a minister, a high official, a servant, or one who has attained some rank or not—whosoever is supported by the king through food and wages, all such are reckoned as a "royal servant."
He should not be ordained. However, it is permissible to ordain his sons, grandsons, or brothers who do not receive food or wages from the king.

But as for one who returns to the king alone whatever fixed income or monthly or annual allowance he has received from the king, or who causes his son or brother to take over that position and then says to the king, "I no longer..."
If one asks for leave, saying, “I am the king’s servant,” or if the work for which wages were received has been completed,
or if one has been permitted by the king, saying, “Let him go forth,” it is permissible to ordain such a person as well.
The discussion on the case of the king’s servant is finished.
91. Discussion on the Cases of Thieves:

Regarding the phrase "having seen [them] among the cases of thieves"—those who have previously seen him during his time as a householder, or those who hear from others that "this is he," become terrified upon seeing him...
[and so forth] ...even closing their doors. However, those who do not know him...
He receives almsfood in their houses. "Not so, monks," said the Blessed One, the Master of Dhamma himself;
therefore, in order to prevent such an occurrence in the future, he spoke thus while laying down a training rule for the monks.
In this context, one who "wanders about like one who has hoisted a banner" is called a *dhajabandho*. This means that he is as well-known in the world as Mūladeva and others. Therefore, whoever...

If someone wanders about committing village raids, highway robberies, or acts such as housebreaking in a city, and it is known that "such-and-such a person is doing this and that," he should not be ordained.
However, if a prince commits village raids and the like out of a desire for kingship, he may be ordained; for kings are pleased when he has gone forth.

But if they are not satisfied, he should not be ordained. If a thief who was previously well-known among the public later abandons his thievery and undertakes the five precepts and so forth, and people know him as such, he may be ordained.

However, those thieves such as those who steal mangoes and jackfruits, or those who break into houses by tunneling walls, who commit theft while remaining hidden even afterwards—[he should not be ordained].
Even those for whom it is not known who did what by name may be ordained. 92.
"Having broken the prison" means having broken the bonds of fetters and so forth. Regarding the term *abhayūvarā*: here, those who cease (*uparamanti*) because of fear are *bhayūvarā*;
however, these [monks] are called *abhayūvarā* because they have obtained freedom from fear. Furthermore, in this context, the letter *pa* has been changed to *va*.
It should be understood that "katā" means this. "Monks, one who has broken out of prison (kārabhedaka) should not be ordained"—here, "kāra" refers to a prison.

In this context, however, it may be a bond with fetters, or a bond with chains, or a bond with ropes, or confinement to a village, or confinement to a town, or confinement to a city, or guarding of men, or confinement to a district, or confinement to an island.
Or, whoever, having broken, cut, released, or opened any one of these bonds—
whether people see him or do not see him— and flees, he is reckoned as a "breaker of the prison. Therefore,
such a thief who has broken the prison and gone to another island must not be ordained, even if he has reached another land.
However, one who is not a thief, but was merely bound by royal officials and others for performing manual labor with the thought,
"He will do it for us without complaining," may be ordained even if he has escaped after breaking his confinement. On the other hand, one who has been imprisoned for failing to pay taxes on villages,
market towns, ports, and so forth, and who returns after having escaped, must not be ordained.
If someone who has earned wealth through farming and other such means is imprisoned by another on the grounds of slander,
claiming, "He obtained this treasure," it is not permissible to ordain him right there;
however, if he has escaped and gone elsewhere, it is permissible to ordain him at that new location.
93. "Monks, regarding the term 'one who is marked' (*likhitaka*): here, a 'marked one' does not refer merely to one for whom it is decreed, 'Wherever he is seen, there he shall be slain.
Rather, it refers to anyone who, having committed theft or some other grave offense against the king, has fled;
and the king, on a leaf or in a book, has written: 'The person named so-and-so, wherever he is found, shall be seized and executed.'"

Or if one causes it to be written: "His hands and feet are to be cut off," or "He is to be made to pay such-and-such a fine," this is called a "written offender" (*likhitaka*); he is not to be ordained.

94. Regarding the phrase "one who has undergone punishment for having been whipped": herein, one who is beaten for failing to perform verbal orders, errands, and the like, is not one who has undergone punishment for having committed an offense.

But if someone, having taken or eaten something from Keṇiya or otherwise, being unable to give it back, is beaten with whips while saying, "Let this itself be your punishment," he is one who has undergone the penalty of being whipped.
Whether he has been beaten with whips or with any other instrument such as a half-stick, he must not be ordained as long as the wound is still moist. Regarding the wound:
However, having made them normal, he should be ordained.
But if he has been freed after being struck by the knees, by the temples, or by coconut stones and the like, and lumps are visible on his body, he should not be ordained.
Only when the lumps have subsided and he has been made healthy should he be ordained.

95. Regarding the phrase "one struck with a mark and for whom the penal rite has been performed": here, the state of having had the penal rite performed should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

However, if a mark has been struck upon his forehead or his thighs and other such parts with heated iron, he must not be ordained as long as he remains a free man (*bhujissa*) and the wound is still moist.
Even if his wounds have healed and the skin has grown back level, [he is still not to be ordained].

The characteristic mark is not discernible; if the upper robe is made over the three circles of cloth and it is in a concealed place, it is permissible to grant him the going-forth, but if it is in an unconcealed place, it is not permissible.
The Discussion on the Robe of a Thief is finished.
The Discourse on the Matter of the Debtor (Iṇāyikavatthu).

96. “Monks, ‘one who is a debtor’—in this context, a debtor is one whose father or grandfather took a loan, or who himself has taken a loan, or for whom something was taken by his parents after being promised.”
He who owes that debt to others is called a debtor (*iṇāyika*). However, one whom other relatives have seized and taken something from is not a debtor;
for they have no authority to seize him, therefore it is permissible to ordain him, whereas the other is not.
But if his kinsmen and blood relations say, "We will pay [the debt], ordain him," then he is [effectively] free of debt.
They provide the means, or someone else, seeing his excellence of conduct, says, "Ordain him; I will pay the debt," and it is permissible to ordain him.

If those [three] are absent, the bhikkhu should inform such a supporter as well, saying, "This being has a cause for not being ordained due to the obstacle of debt. If he acts accordingly, [he may be ordained].
He should be ordained. Even if he has his own allowable goods, he may be ordained with the thought, "I shall give this [to him].

However, if neither relatives and so forth take responsibility for him, nor does he have his own wealth, it is not permissible to ordain him with the thought, "Having ordained him, I will support him by wandering for alms and then release him.
If one ordains him in such a case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even one who has run away may be brought back and...
It must be paid. If he does not pay it, the entire debt becomes his personal liability. There is no offense for one who ordains someone without knowing [of the debt].
However, if he sees [the debtor], he should bring him back and show him to the creditors. For one who does not see him, there is no liability.
If the debtor goes to another country and, even when questioned, says, "I owe nothing to anyone," [then there is no offense].
A man goes forth into homelessness; meanwhile, his creditor, searching for him, arrives at that place. Seeing him, the youth flees.
The creditor approaches the elder and says, "Venerable sir, by whom was this man ordained?
He has fled after taking such-and-such an amount of my wealth. The elder should say, "Lay follower, he told me, 'I am free from debt.'"
“Having gone forth, what shall I do now? Look at my mere bowl and robes”—this is the proper course in that case. However, there is no liability for the debt if he has fled.
But if, having seen him in the presence of the elder, he says, “This man is my debtor,” he should be told, “You yourself must deal with your own debtor.
Even in this case, there is no liability. If, moreover, he says, “This man has now gone forth...”
If he says, "Where will he go?", the Elder should be told, "You yourself must know. In this way, even if he flees, there is no offense.
However, if the Elder says, "Where indeed will he go now? Let him stay right here," and he nevertheless flees, there is an offense.
If he is a person endowed with the causal factors and perfect in his duties, the Elder [should consider]: "One such as this..."
"this should be said. If the creditor releases [the debt] saying "Very well," this is good.
But if he says, "Give me half and half," it must be given. At another time, if he becomes very helpful, then even when told, "Give it all," it must indeed be given.
But if he is skilled in recitation, interrogation, and so forth, and is of great assistance—
"Even for monks, having sought [alms] according to the rule of alms-round, a debt must indeed be repaid.
The Discussion on the Matter of Debtors is finished.
The Discussion on the Matter of Slaves.
97. "Monks, regarding the term 'slave,' there are four kinds of slaves: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, one brought by force, and one who has entered into slavery of his own accord.
Therein, 'one born in the house' means a slave by birth, the son of a female slave of the household.
'One bought with wealth' means that, having given wealth to his parents or to his master, [he enters] the state of servitude."

One who has been sold after being pledged—these two also should not be ordained. When ordaining them, one should ordain them by making them undergo the proper conduct (cāritta) in various places as if they were slaves.
One brought from another kingdom as a "prisoner" refers to those who have been plundered from a foreign country or enticed away from a foreign kingdom, yet are free men.
They bring [slaves] from abroad; or, when some person within the kingdom has committed an offense, the king commands, "Plunder that village," and then they bring even human beings from there.
In that state, all the men are slaves and the women are slave-girls.
Such a slave brought as a convict (karamarānīta), whether living in the presence of those by whom he was brought or bound in prison, is guarded by men.
Or he should not be ordained. However, if he has fled and gone elsewhere, he may be ordained at that place where he has gone.
Or, if his release from bondage has been effected—either by a king who, being pleased, says, "Release those brought as captives," or by some other common means—he should certainly be ordained.
One who has entered into servitude of his own accord is one who, for the sake of livelihood or for the sake of protection, has himself said, "I am your slave."
He has entered into a state of servitude. Like those who tend the elephants, horses, cattle, buffalo, and goats for kings, such a slave should not be ordained.
The sons of the king’s concubines (*vaṇṇadāsī*) are similar to the sons of ministers; they too should not be ordained.
However, it is permissible to ordain the sons of independent women (*bhujissitthiyo*) who, though unrestrained, associate with the king’s concubines. If [the father] himself...

If they enter the formal agreement (*paṇṇa*), it is not permitted. Even slaves belonging to groups such as those of hired laborers (*bhaṭiputtaka*) must not be ordained if they have not been given away by their masters.
In monasteries, there are those known as "monastery-attendants" (*ārāmika*) or "slaves" who have been granted by kings; it is also not permitted to ordain them.

However, it is permitted to ordain them after first making them free men (*bhujissa*). In the *Mahāpaccarī*, regarding those born inside [the monastery] or those purchased with money, having brought them to the Saṅgha of monks...
It is said: "If they give [the land] saying, 'We give it to the monastery attendant,' they are just like those who have poured sour gruel over one's head;

it is permissible to ordain them. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is said: "If they give it using the formal expression 'We give it to the monastery attendant,' regardless of the specific terminology used, he must not be ordained.
[This refers to those who think: "We shall live depending on the Saṅgha," being people of poor means.

If there are authorized attendants (*kappiyakāraka*) in the monastery, it is permissible to give the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) even to these [slaves]. It is not permissible to give the going-forth to one whose parents are slaves, or to one whose mother is a slave while the father is not a slave.
However, it is permissible to give the going-forth to one whose mother is not a slave but whose father is a slave.
Or, if a monk’s relatives or supporters give a slave [to him], saying, "Give this person the going-forth," [it is permissible].
"He will perform service for you. Or, even if he has his own slave, he should be ordained only after he has been made free.
If the owners give the slave [saying], "Ordain this one; if he finds it agreeable, he shall no longer be a slave;
but if he should disrobe, he will remain our slave," this is called "temporary" (tāvakālika), and it is not permitted to ordain such a person—thus it is stated in the Kurundi.
It has been stated: one who is a slave without an owner—even he must be made free before being ordained.
If, after having ordained or given full admission to someone, one later discovers that he is a slave, it is permissible to make him free.
To illustrate this point, they cite this story: it is said that a certain family slave was [in love] with a certain man...
Having fled from Anurādhapura and living in Rohaṇa, she gave birth to a son. After he had gone forth and received full ordination, he became modest and scrupulous.
Then one day he asked his mother: "Lay sister, do you have no brother or sister?
I do not see any relative of yours. "Dear son, I was a family slave in Anurādhapura."

“Having fled with your parents, I am living here. The virtuous bhikkhu, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon thinking, “My going-forth was indeed impure,” asked his mother for the name and clan of that family.
Having arrived at Anurādhapura, he stood at the door of that family’s house. Even when told, “Pass on, venerable sir,” he did not pass through; they came toward him...
"What is it, venerable sir? they asked. "Is there a female slave of yours named so-and-so who has run away?
"There is, venerable sir. "I am her son; if you grant me permission, may I receive the going-forth. You are my masters.
They, being delighted and joyful, said, "Venerable sir, your going-forth is pure," and having made him a free man, [they established him] in the Mahāvihāra.
They had him dwell there, tending to his needs with the four requisites. While residing in dependence upon that family, the Elder attained arahantship.
Thus ends the Story of the Servant.
Now begins the Story of the Blacksmith’s Anvil and Other Matters.
"Kammārabhaṇḍu" refers to the son of a goldsmith, a shaven-headed man who was a weigher; "Pañcasikha" means a young boy—this is what is meant.
"For the purpose of shaving, having informed the Saṅgha" means: "I authorize [you] to ask for permission from the Saṅgha for the sake of shaving.
Herein, this is the procedure for asking permission: having assembled the monks within the boundary (sīmā),...
Having led the one seeking ordination there, one should say three times, twice, or once: "Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for the shaving of this boy.
And in this context, one may say either, "I request the shaving of this boy," or "I request the making of him a recluse," or "I request his ordination."
It is indeed permissible to say, "This person wishes to become a recluse," or "This person wishes to go forth.
If it is a common area where ten, twenty, or thirty bhikkhus reside, and their boundaries are known,
one should go to the place where they are standing or sitting and request permission in the same manner as described before.

Even if one sends young bhikkhus or novices instead of someone seeking ordination, it is permissible to have them request permission in such a manner as: "Venerable sirs, there is one seeking ordination; we ask for his shaving.
If some bhikkhus have entered a dwelling or a grove and are sleeping or engaged in the duties of a recluse...
Or they perform [the act], and even while seeking those who have not yet asked for permission, they perceive that "all have been asked by us," thinking that ordination (*pabbajjā*) is a light matter;
therefore, the one ordained is indeed well-ordained, and there is no offense for the one who ordains.
However, if it is a great monastery inhabited by many thousands of monks, it may be difficult even to assemble all the monks.

Furthermore, it is not necessary to request permission in the proper sequence; rather, one may be ordained while standing within a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), or after traveling to a river, the ocean, or similar locations.

However, for one who has a new shorn head, one who has gone forth from another sect (*vibbhantaka*), one belonging to such groups as the Nigaṇṭhas, or one whose hair is two finger-breadths long or less than two finger-breadths long, there is no requirement for shaving the hair;
therefore, one may perform the *bhaṇḍukamma* (shaving) even without requesting permission.

It is appropriate to ordain such a person. However, one whose hair exceeds two finger-breadths—even if they wear it in a single tuft—must first request permission for the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*) before being ordained.
The story of Upāli is exactly as described in the method set forth in the Mahāvibhaṅga. 100.
"By the plague of snake-venom" means by the pestilence of death (*māri-byādhi*); for wherever that disease arises, that family [of humans and quadrupeds]...
Everything is lost for one who escapes by breaking through a wall or the roof, or who has gone beyond the village boundary;
such a person is released. Likewise, in this case, father and son were both released. Therefore it is said: “The father and son are the exceptions.

As for the “crow-scaring man”: one who, sitting with a clod of earth held in his left hand, is able to scare away crows as they arrive and eat the food placed before him—he is called a crow-scaring man, and it is permissible to ordain him.
102. "Ittarā" means short; the meaning is that the stay will be for only a few days.
103. "Ogaṇena" means with a diminished group; the meaning is with a small number of monks in the Saṅgha. Regarding "abyattena yāvajīvaṃ":
here, if he does not find an elder teacher, [he may remain] even if he has been sixty or seventy years since his full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Or let it be so; even from one who is younger but competent, having sat down in the kneeling posture (ukkuṭika) and extended the hands in reverential salutation (añjali), one should receive dependence (nissaya) by saying three times:
"Friend, be my teacher; depending upon the Venerable One, I shall live.
Even when asking for permission to enter a village, one must likewise sit down in the kneeling posture and extend the hands in reverential salutation.
"Teacher, I ask permission to enter the village," he should say. This same method applies to all requests for permission.
Regarding the groups of five and six here, whatever is required for one who is independent of formal support (nissaya) has been stated in the commentary on the "Exhorter of Bhikkhunīs.
It should be understood that if such a person is absent, one is "of little learning," and if present, one is "of great learning. The rest is according to the method already explained.
The Discourse on the Blacksmith’s Tools, Clothing, and So Forth is concluded.
The Discourse on the Story of Rāhula, 105:
“He set out on a wandering tour toward Kapilavatthu”—herein is this sequential account. King Suddhodana the Great...

It is said that from the day of the Bodhisatta’s Great Renunciation, he lived with his ear attentively tuned to hear news of the progress [of the Bodhisatta], thinking, "My son has gone forth because he will become a Buddha; has the Buddha now been born?
Hearing of the Blessed One’s practice of striving, his attainment of enlightenment, and his turning of the Wheel of Dhamma and so forth, he thought, "Now indeed it seems my..."
Having heard that his son was living in dependence on Rājagaha, he commanded a minister: "Dear one, I am old and advanced in years;
it would be well if you were to let me see my son while I am still alive. Having assented with "Very well," the minister went to Rājagaha accompanied by a thousand men.
He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down. Then the Blessed One preached a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
Having gained confidence, he requested both the going-forth and full ordination. Then the Blessed One ordained him with the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) ordination;
having attained arahantship along with his retinue, he dwelt right there, experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
By that same means, the king dispatched eight other messengers, and all of them, together with their retinues, did likewise.
Having attained *arahantship*, they remained right there. No one reported even a mere rumor to the king as to why they were not coming.
Then the king, desiring to send the minister named Kāḷudāyin—who was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta—together with the Bodhisatta, [sent for him].
He requested [permission] in the same manner as before, and he said, "If I am permitted to go forth, I shall show him to you.
The king sent him with the instruction, "Even after going forth, you must show my son to me.
He too, having gone accompanied by a thousand men, attained Arahantship together with his retinue. One day, when all the crops had ripened and the laborers were left idle, [he...]

When the people of the countryside were in full bloom with land and water flowers, and a path fit for travel had been prepared, he paid homage to the Blessed One and praised the journey with about sixty verses. The Blessed One asked, "What is this?
[He replied,] "Venerable Sir, your father, the Great King Suddhodana, is advanced in years; show your son to me while he is still alive."
“He has sent me, saying: ‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would show favor to his kinsmen; it is time to set out on the journey. In that case, announce to the Saṅgha:
‘The bhikkhus will fulfill the duties of those traveling. “Very well, venerable sir,” the Elder replied, and he did so.
The Blessed One [set out] with ten thousand noble sons dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha, and [those] dwelling in Kapilavatthu...
“Let us go,” he said; and surrounded by all twenty thousand of those whose taints were destroyed, he departed from Rājagaha.
Thinking, “I shall reach Kapilavatthu, which is sixty yojanas from Rājagaha, traveling one yojana each day in two months,” he set out on a journey without haste.
Therefore it is said: “He set out on a journey toward Kapilavatthu.”
When the Blessed One had thus departed, the Elder Udāyī began from the day of his departure to perform the meal service in the house of King Suddhodana.

After the king had served the Elder, he rubbed the bowl with scented powder, filled it with the finest food, and placing it in the Elder’s hands, said, "Give this to the Blessed One. The Elder did exactly so.
He did so. Thus the Blessed One consumed his alms-food along the road belonging specifically to the king.
At the conclusion of each day’s meal, the Elder also informed the king: "Today the Blessed One has come this far.

And through discourse connected with the qualities of the Buddha, he inspired faith in the Blessed One among the Sakyans. For that very reason, the Blessed One declared of him: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost..."
He placed him in the foremost position among his disciples, the monks who inspire confidence in families, saying:
"That is to say, Kāḷudāyī. And when the Sākiyas arrived, thinking, "We shall see our most excellent kinsman," they gathered together;
and while searching for a suitable dwelling place for the Blessed One, they perceived that the Nigrodha Sakka’s park was delightful.
There, having performed all the rites of reception, they went out to meet him with perfumes, flowers,
and other offerings in their hands; first, they sent forth young city boys and girls adorned with every ornament,
and immediately after them, the princes and princesses went in person with perfumes, flowers, powders, and so forth.
Honoring the Blessed One, they took him and went to the Nigrodha Monastery.
There, the Blessed One sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted.

The Sakyans, being of proud nature and stiff with pride, thought, "Prince Siddhattha is younger than we, our junior, our nephew, our son, and our grandson," and so they [treated him] as one very young.
The princes said, “You should pay homage; we shall sit behind you.
While they were sitting thus, the Blessed One, observing their inclination, thought, “My kinsmen do not pay me homage; come now, I shall have them pay homage.
