He then entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for supernormal power, and emerging from it, by means of his psychic power—
Having ascended into the sky, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, he performed a miracle at the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree similar to the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
Seeing that marvel, the king said: "Blessed One, on your auspicious day, when you were led before the brahmin to pay him homage, your feet turned around and were placed upon the brahmin’s head."
Having seen you even then, I paid homage; this was my first act of homage.

On the auspicious day of the sowing of seed, seeing that while you were reclining on a glorious couch in the shade of a rose-apple tree, the shadow of the tree did not shift from you, I bowed at your feet;
this was my second act of homage. Now, having seen this miracle never before witnessed, I bow at your feet once again.
“This is my third salutation,” he said.
When the Blessed One had been saluted by the Great King Suddhodana, there was not even a single Śākyan who remained standing without having saluted him; indeed, they all saluted him.
Thus, having caused his kinsmen to salute him, the Blessed One descended from the sky and sat upon the seat prepared for him.
While the Blessed One was seated, the assembly of kinsmen reached its peak; they all gathered together with one-pointed attention.
Then a great cloud rained down a shower of lotuses, and the copper-colored water flowed away below with a roar.
Not even a single drop fell upon anyone’s body; seeing this, everyone was struck with wonder and amazement. The Blessed One—
“It is not only now that the rain falls like a shower of lotuses when I am gathered with my kinsmen; it also fell so in the past.
On this occasion, he related the Vessantara Jātaka. Having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, they all rose, paid homage, circumambulated him, and departed.
Not even a single king or royal minister said, “Please accept our alms tomorrow.”
There was no one who, having spoken thus, departed.
On the second day, the Blessed One entered Kapilavatthu for alms accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus;
yet no one came out to meet him, nor invited him, nor took his bowl. Standing at the city gate, the Blessed One directed his attention inward.
“How indeed did the Buddhas of the past wander for alms in their native cities?
Did they go to the houses of wealthy people out of order, or did they practice systematic alms-round? Then, seeing that not even a single Buddha had gone out of order, [he thought]:
“I too must now uphold this lineage and this tradition; and in the future, may it be so for me.”
“May my disciples also, training in accordance with me, fulfill the practice of wandering for alms.
Thus he went for alms from house to house in regular succession, starting from the house situated at the corner.

Hearing the news, “It is said that the noble Prince Siddhattha is wandering for alms,” the great multitude became intent on seeing him, opening the lion-windows in their palaces of four stories and more. Rāhula’s mother also—

The queen thought, "It is said that my noble son, having previously wandered through this very city with great royal splendor in golden palanquins and the like, now shaves his hair and beard, wears saffron robes, and wanders for alms with an alms-bowl in hand; does he shine or not?
Opening the lion-window, she gazed out at the Blessed One, who was radiant with various colors— ... [the rest of the sentence would follow here] ... [of light].

Having seen him illuminating the city streets with the radiance of his body and shining with the glory of a Buddha, [the man] praised him from the crown of his head down to the soles of his feet with eight verses known as the *Narasīhagāthā*. Then, going into the presence of the king, he announced to the king:
"Your son is walking for alms. The king, his heart moved with emotion, [tore] his upper garment with his hand...
Composing himself, he hurried out in great haste, went with speed, stood before the Blessed One, and said:
"Venerable sir, why do you put us to shame? For what purpose do you wander for alms?
Did you think that food could not be obtained for so many bhikkhus? "Great King, this is our traditional custom."
"Venerable sir, is it not true that our lineage is called the Kṣatriya Mahāsammata lineage, and in that lineage there has never been even a single kṣatriya who went about for alms?
"Great king, this is indeed your lineage; however, ours is the lineage of the Buddhas.
And all the Buddhas were alms-seekers. Standing in the middle of the street, he said:
“Arise! Do not be negligent! Practice the Dhamma that is well-conducted.
One who lives by the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.
He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, the king realized the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
“One should practice the Dhamma well-conducted, and not practice what is ill-conducted;
one who lives by the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.
Having heard this verse, he was established in the fruit of a once-returner; having heard the Dhammapāla Jātaka, he was established in the fruit of a non-returner.
He attained [the state of a noble one] while lying upon his glorious couch beneath a white parasol at the time of death.
For the king, there was no need for the practice of striving through dwelling in the forest.
Having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he took the Blessed One’s bowl and [invited] the Blessed One together with his assembly.
Having ascended the great palace, he served him with excellent hard and soft foods.
At the conclusion of the meal, the entire harem came and paid homage to the Blessed One, with the exception of Rāhula’s mother.
Although she was told by her attendants, "Go and pay homage to the noble son," she replied, "If I possess any virtue, the noble son will [come to me] of his own accord."
Having said, "He will come; when he has arrived, we shall pay him homage," she did not go.
Then the Blessed One, having had the king take his bowl, went with his two chief disciples to the princess's bedchamber.
Saying, "The princess may pay homage as she pleases; she is not to be spoken to," he sat down on the prepared seat. She came quickly and [touched] his ankles.
Taking her by the back of the feet and repeatedly turning her head toward him, he paid homage according to his desire.
The king spoke of the princess’s perfection of qualities, such as her affection and great respect for the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “It is not surprising, Great King, that the princess, being protected by you now that her wisdom is fully matured, has protected herself.”
"Previously, while wandering at the foot of a mountain without protection, we protected ourselves while our knowledge was yet unripe," he said, and related the *Candakinnarījātaka*.

On that very day, for Prince Nanda, there were five great auspicious ceremonies: the ceremony of shaving the hair, the investiture with the royal fillet, the domestic blessing, the marriage blessing, and the umbrella-blessing. The Blessed One had Nanda take his bowl and [performed] the blessing.
Having spoken thus, he rose from his seat and departed. Seeing the prince departing, Janapadakalyāṇī said, “Noble son, please return quickly,” and she craned her neck to look after him.
He too, unable to say to the Blessed One, “Please take your bowl,” went straight back to the monastery. Even though he was unwilling, the Blessed One—
He ordained him. Thus, having arrived at Kapilavatthu, the Blessed One ordained Nanda on the second day.
On the seventh day, Rāhula’s mother, having adorned the boy, sent him into the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
"Look, dear, at this ascetic surrounded by twenty thousand monks—golden-hued, with the appearance of a Brahmā. This...
“Father, he had great treasures; since his departure we have seen none of them.
Go and ask for that inheritance. Father, I am a prince who will raise the royal parasol and become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin);
I have need of wealth, so give me wealth, for a son is indeed the master of what belongs to his father. Thus spoke Prince Rāhula.
Having approached the Blessed One and regained his paternal affection, he stood with a joyful heart, saying, "How pleasant is your shade, O ascetic!
and spoke much else that was appropriate to himself. After the Blessed One had finished his meal and performed the expression of thanks, he rose from his seat and departed.
The youth also said, "O ascetic, give me my inheritance; give me my inheritance."
“Give me my inheritance, ascetic! he pursued the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: “Wandering by stages on his journey, [he arrived] at Kapilavatthu... ‘Give me my inheritance, ascetic!
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta. Thus the Blessed One did not cause the prince to turn back.
Even his retinue was unable to turn him back as he was departing with the Blessed One. Then, having gone to the monastery, [he thought]:
"Whatever wealth this man desires from his father’s estate is subject to the cycle of existence and brings suffering;
well then, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth obtained at the seat of enlightenment, and make him the heir to the supramundane inheritance."
He addressed the Venerable Sāriputta. Having addressed him, he said: “In that case, Sāriputta, you must give the novice Rāhula the going-forth.
Since this youth asks for his inheritance, the meaning is: “Therefore, give him the going-forth so that he may obtain the supramundane inheritance.
Now, as for that going-forth and full ordination which was authorized by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī through the threefold taking of refuge—

Therefore, because full ordination (*upasampadā*) was prohibited and established as a weighty matter before being permitted by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), whereas going forth (*pabbajjā*) was neither prohibited nor subsequently permitted, a doubt will arise among future monks:
"This so-called going forth was formerly similar to full ordination; what then of it now?"
"Is it to be performed by means of the formal ritual (kammavācā) alone, just like full ordination (upasampadā),

or rather by means of the three goings for refuge? Having understood this matter, and desiring to further authorize the novice’s going-forth (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) by means of the three goings for refuge, the Dhammasenāpati,
perceiving the Blessed One’s intention and wishing to have the Blessed One authorize the going-forth once more, said:
“How, venerable sir, shall I cause Prince Rāhula to go forth?
Then the Venerable Sāriputta caused Prince Rāhula to go forth.
Elder Mahāmoggallāna shaved the youth’s hair, gave him the saffron robes, and administered the Three Refuges. Elder Mahākassapa was the preceptor who gave him instruction.

Since both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) are rooted in the preceptor (upajjhāya), and the preceptor alone—not the teacher (ācariya)—is the authority therein, it was therefore said: "Then the Venerable Sāriputta gave the going-forth to Prince Rāhula.
Having heard thus that "the prince has gone forth," King Suddhodana, with a heart moved by the spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that arose, then [acted].

Everything should be stated. In that regard, since it is inappropriate for one who has gone forth and lives by the practice of gleaning to say "I ask for a boon" when told "Ask," and because such a thing is not the custom of the Buddhas, it was said:
"The Tathāgatas, Gotama, have transcended boons. And as for what is allowable and blameless for you, venerable sir... [and] for yourselves...
The meaning is: "It is permissible to give it, it is blameless, and because of my receiving it, I shall not be censured by the wise;
therefore, I ask for it. Likewise, regarding Nanda and Rāhula as "excessive":

just as the fortune-tellers prophesied that the Bodhisatta would become a wheel-turning monarch on his auspicious day, so too did they prophesy for both Nanda and Rāhula that they would become wheel-turning monarchs.
Then the King, filled with the desire to see his son’s glory as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), experienced great frustration regarding the Blessed One’s renunciation.
Thereupon, he generated the hope, "I shall see Nanda’s glory as a wheel-turning monarch," but the Blessed One ordained him as well.
Thus, enduring that suffering as well, [he thought], "Now I shall see Rāhula’s glory as a wheel-turning monarch..."
He generated the aspiration, "I shall go forth," and the Blessed One ordained him as well. Consequently, because he thought, "Now even my family lineage is cut off;
from where shall the glory of a wheel-turning monarch come? an even greater suffering arose within him. Therefore it was said:
"In the same way, [it was] excessive in Nanda and Rāhula. It should be understood that after this, the King attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
“Excellent, venerable sir, noble one!”—why did he say this? It is said that he thought:

“If even I, who am devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha, am unable to endure the suffering of separation from my own beloved sons when they are being ordained, how will other people endure it when their sons and grandsons are ordained?”
"Therefore, let such suffering not befall others as well," he said.

The Blessed One, thinking, "The king speaks of the cause for deliverance within the Teaching," delivered a discourse on the Dhamma and established a precept, saying: "Monks, a son must not be ordained without the permission of his mother and father."
In this context, "by mother and father" is said with reference to one's progenitor and parent. If there are two, both must be asked for permission.
If the father is dead or the mother is dead, whoever is living must be asked. Those who have gone forth (monastics) must also certainly be asked.
When asking, one should either go oneself and ask, or send another, or send that very person [with the message]: "Go to the mother and father..."
"Having asked for permission, come. If he says, "I have been permitted," he should be ordained by one who has faith.
If the father himself has gone forth and wishes to ordain his son, he should ordain him only after asking the mother's permission.
Or if the mother wishes to ordain her daughter, she should ordain her only after asking the father's permission. If the father has fled, being indifferent toward his wife and children...
If the mother gives her son to the bhikkhus, saying, "Ordain him," and when asked, "Where is his father?
she replies, "He has run away to play with toy carts," it is permissible to ordain him.
If the mother has run away with some man, but the father gives him [to the monks], saying, "Ordain him," the same principle applies here as well. If the father is absent, the mother...
If one says, "Ordain your son," and when asked, "Where is his father?", he replies, "What business is it of yours?
I shall know," it is permissible to ordain him; so it is stated in the Kurundi.
If both parents are deceased and the boy has been raised in the presence of his maternal aunt or others, when he is being ordained, his relatives...
They either engage in quarrels or speak with disparagement; therefore, for the sake of ending disputes, one must seek permission before granting the going-forth.
However, there is no offense for one who grants the going-forth without seeking permission.
Those who take [a child] at a young age and raise him are called "parents," and the same principle applies to them as well. A son lives by depending on himself, whereas parents do not. Even if...
If he is a king, he must be ordained only after having been formally asked for permission.

If, after being ordained with the parents' consent, he disrobes—even if he disrobes after having been ordained a hundred times—he must be ordained again and again, each time after asking for permission whenever he returns.
If they say: "This man has returned home after disrobing; he does not [belong to us]..."
"Having gone forth, he does not fulfill your duties; there is no need to consult him regarding this matter—whenever anyone arrives, you should ordain them.
When he has been thus relinquished, it is permissible to ordain [another] even without consulting him again.
Also, if at the very time of childhood [he was given with the words], "This one is given to you; whenever you wish, then ordain him," thus...
If he has been given [in charge], he too must be ordained again each time he arrives without having asked for permission.

However, one who, while still a child, was granted permission by saying, "Venerable sir, please ordain him," but later, when he has reached adulthood, is not granted permission, should not be ordained without asking for permission. One person, having quarreled with his parents, comes saying, "Ordain me!"
When told, “Go after taking leave,” he replied: “I will not go.

If you do not ordain me, I shall either burn down the monastery, or strike you with a weapon, or cause harm to your relatives and supporters by cutting down the grove and so forth, or I shall die by throwing myself from a tree, or enter among thieves, or go to another country.”
If he says this, it is appropriate to ordain him for the sake of protecting his very life.

However, if his parents come and say, "Why have you ordained our son?", one should explain the matter to them and say, "We ordained him for the sake of protecting him; look after him as your son. [He thinks: "I shall jump from a tree."
However, once he has climbed up, it is indeed permissible to ordain him even if he lets go of his hands and feet.
Even if a single person goes to a foreign land and requests ordination, if he went after having asked for permission, he should be ordained.
If not, a young bhikkhu should be sent to have permission requested, and then he should be ordained; if the distance is too great, he may be ordained and then [sent] together with the bhikkhus.
It is proper to send someone and show [them] [the way]. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*:
"If it is far away and the path is a great wilderness, it is proper to grant the going-forth [with the thought], 'We shall go and take leave [of them].
But if the parents have many children and say, "Venerable sir, among these children, you may let whichever one you wish go forth," then [regarding] the children...

Having investigated, whoever he desires may be ordained. Even if permission has been granted by an entire family or village, saying, "Venerable sir, you may ordain whomever you wish from this family or village," whoever he desires may be ordained.
Or, "to whatever extent he is able" means to whatever extent he is capable.
The Story of Rāhula’s Case is finished.
The Story of the Cases Concerning Formal Punishment for Violating the Training Rules: 106.
Among the ten training rules, the transgression of the first five constitutes a case of forfeiture; the transgression of the latter five constitutes a case of formal punishment.
107. *Appatissa* means they do not establish the monks in the position of seniority or the position of authority.

*Asabhāgavuttika* means they do not share a common livelihood; the meaning is that they lead dissimilar lives. *Alābhāya parisakkati* means he exerts himself so that they do not obtain gains. *Anatthāya* means for their misfortune.
*Avāsāya* means [he acts] so that [they think], "How can we [remain] in this residence?"...
"He exerts himself so that they shall not dwell [there]. "He reviles and scolds" means he both reviles and threatens by showing them fear.
"He causes division" means he causes division by instigating slander. "To create an obstruction" means to make a prohibition, saying, "Do not enter here.
"Wherever he dwells or wherever he retreats" means wherever he dwells or enters.
Or; by both [terms], one's own cell and the lodging obtained through the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) are meant.
"They create an obstruction to food that enters the mouth" means they prevent it by saying, "Do not eat today! Do not consume!
Regarding the statement, "Monks, an obstruction should not be made to food that enters the mouth," [it refers to] "Do not eat! Do not consume! here.
Even for one who says, "I will stop providing food," or who puts away his bowl and robes inside [the monastery], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all such actions.
However, it is permissible to administer a disciplinary measure to an ill-behaved and difficult-to-correct novice, and then, having shown him the rice-gruel, the meal, or the bowl and robes, to say:
"When such-and-such a disciplinary measure has been imposed, you shall receive this. Thus [it was said] by the Blessed One.
For indeed, the *daṇḍakamma* (penance) itself was stated to be a form of restraint (*āvaraṇa*).

However, the Theras who compiled the Dhamma stated that it may also involve making [the offender] fetch water, wood, sand, and so forth, in accordance with the nature of the offense; therefore, that too should be performed.

And this should be done out of compassion, thinking, "He will desist, he will refrain," and not out of an evil disposition such as, "He will perish" or "He will disrobe," and so forth. This is the *daṇḍakamma*.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to have [the person] lie down on hot stones, to have stones, bricks, or the like placed upon their head, or to have them immersed in water.
The discussion on the basis for disciplinary action according to the training rules is concluded.
108. The Discussion on the Matter of Not Informing the Preceptor, etc.: “Monks, one should not act without informing the preceptor.
In this regard, if it has been said three times, “This is the offense of your novice; inflict a disciplinary act upon him,” and yet the preceptor does not inflict the disciplinary act—

It is appropriate for him to do it himself. Even if the preceptor says at the very outset, "When there are faults in my novices, you must carry out the disciplinary action," it is still appropriate for him to do so.
And just as it is with novices, it is also appropriate for him to carry out disciplinary action against those who live with him (saddhivihārikas) and those who are his pupils (antevāsikas).
“*Apalāḷenti* (they entice)” means they win over others for the sake of receiving service for themselves, saying, “We will give you a bowl; we will give you a robe.

“Monks, one must not entice the assembly of another” means that here, whether they be novices or fully ordained, it is not permitted to break apart and take for oneself the assembly belonging to another—even if it is the assembly of a monk who is immoral.
However, it is permissible to point out the danger: "By you, who have come to bathe, acting like one smeared with excrement, you have acted by living in dependence upon one who is immoral.
If he, having understood this himself, requests the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) or formal dependence (nissaya), it is permissible to grant it.
Regarding the rule "I allow you, monks, to expel a novice endowed with ten factors," the commentary on the Kaṇṭaka training rule [provides the details].
Among the three methods of expulsion mentioned, it is the expulsion by means of the removal of the emblem (liṅganāsanā) that is intended here.
Therefore, whoever commits even a single deed such as the taking of life must be expelled by the removal of the emblem.
Furthermore, while monks incur various offenses for acts such as the taking of life, this is not the case for novices. For a novice, even after killing a small insect or an ant, or even a fish-egg...
Having broken it, it reaches the very state of being destroyed; at that very moment, his taking of the refuges, his choosing of a preceptor, and his taking possession of a dwelling cease;
he no longer receives a share from the Saṅgha, and only the mere outward sign remains.
If he is one whose faults are manifold and does not abide in future restraint, he should be expelled. But if—
If, having suddenly become disenchanted [with the life of a monk], he thinks, "I have done wrong," and desires to stand once again in restraint, there is no requirement for the removal of his marks.

The refuges must be given to him while he remains exactly as he was dressed and robed; an upajjhāya must be appointed, but the training rules (sikkhāpada) are accomplished by the going for refuge alone.
For the going for refuge of novices is equivalent to the formal act of ordination (upasampadā-kamma-vācā) for monks.
Therefore, just like the fourfold purification precept (*catupārisuddhisīla*) of the bhikkhus, these ten precepts are indeed already undertaken by this [act].
Nevertheless, they should be given again for the purpose of strengthening them and for the purpose of establishing oneself in future restraint.

If one has taken the refuges again during the earlier period (*purimikā*), one will receive the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) during the later period (*pacchimikā*). If [one takes them] during the later period...
Once they have been accepted, the Saṅgha should grant the gain after obtaining formal permission.
Regarding the taking of what is not given: even by the mere act of taking a blade of grass; regarding unchastity: by committing an offense in any of the three ways;
regarding false speech: even by speaking a lie with the intention of joking—one becomes a non-monk (assamaṇa) and must be expelled.

He commits an offense. Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, however, for a bhikkhu who drinks an intoxicant starting from the seed even without knowing it is such, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
A novice (sāmaṇera) who drinks while knowing it commits a breach of virtue (sīlabheda), but not if he does so without knowing.

As for his other five training rules (sikkhāpada), if these are broken, he should not be expelled; rather, a disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma) should be performed. But regarding the training rule [on intoxicants], again...

It is permissible whether [the substance] has been given or not given. However, it must be administered by means of a formal act of punishment (daṇḍakamma) for the purpose of establishing restraint in the future.
This is the distinction: for novices, the drinking of intoxicants is a matter of defeat (pārājika) involving a conscious intention.

Furthermore, regarding the speaking of dispraise, there is the case of the Buddha—by way of contradicting such statements as "The Arhat is the Perfectly Enlightened One"—or regarding the Dhamma, by way of contradicting such statements as "Well-expounded."
Whether by disparaging the Dhamma through its opposites, or by disparaging the Saṅgha through the opposites of "one who has practiced well" and so forth,
one who speaks ill of or reviles the Triple Gem must be restrained by his teachers,

preceptors, and others after they have shown him the danger in speaking such disparagement, saying, "Do not speak thus. If, even when told up to three times, he does not desist, [he commits an offense].
"In order to remove the thorn [of the wrong view], he should be expelled"—this is stated in the *Kurundi*. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
"If, when being addressed in this way, he relinquishes that adherence, he should be made to perform penance and be made to confess his transgression.

If he does not relinquish it, but remains having taken up and maintained it just as before, he should be expelled by means of the removal of the [monastic] marks (*liṅga-nāsanā*). This refers to that.
This is appropriate; for it is precisely this [form of] expulsion that is intended here.

The same method applies even in the case of one with wrong view. Indeed, if one who holds either the eternalist or annihilationist view, when being exhorted by teachers and others, relinquishes [the view], then after having imposed a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*), he should be made to confess his transgression. If, however, he does not relinquish it...

"He should be expelled. Herein, although a violator of a bhikkhunī is certainly included by the term "one who does not live the holy life" (*abrahmacārī*), it is permissible to grant the refuges and confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon one who does not live the holy life provided he desires to abide in restraint for the future.
However, even one who violates a bhikkhunī and desires to abide in restraint for the future does not receive even the going forth (*pabbajjā*), let alone full ordination; such is the meaning.
It should be understood that the phrase "one who violates a bhikkhunī" was stated as a separate tenth factor in order to demonstrate this.
The discussion on the matter of not asking for permission regarding the granting of protection is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the matter of the paṇḍaka.
109. "Dahare dahare" means "the young ones, the very young. "Moḷigalle" means those with stout bodies. "Hatthibhaṇḍe assabhaṇḍe" means elephant-keepers and horse-keepers.
"Paṇḍako bhikkhave" (O monks, the paṇḍaka): here there are five types of paṇḍakas—the *āsittapaṇḍaka*, the *usūyapaṇḍaka*, the *opakkamikapaṇḍaka*, the *pakkhapaṇḍaka*, and the *napuṃsakapaṇḍaka*.
Among these, [the one] who, having taken another's *aṅgajāta* (genital organ) into his mouth...
One whose fever is pacified by being sprinkled with impurity is a *āsittapaṇḍaka*.
One whose fever is pacified when envy arises upon seeing others’ transgressions is an *usūyapaṇḍaka*.

One from whom the seeds have been removed by means of an external application is an *opakkamikapaṇḍaka*. Furthermore, some [become so] during the dark fortnight through the power of the ripening of unwholesome karma.
One who is a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) is one whose feverish passion subsides during the bright fortnight; this is a *pakkhapaṇḍaka*.
However, one who is born as a non-male from the very moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is a *napuṃsakapaṇḍaka*.

Among these, ordination is not prohibited for the *āsittapaṇḍaka* and the *usūyapaṇḍaka*, but it is prohibited for the other three. Even among those, [ordination is prohibited] for the *pakkhapaṇḍaka*.
It is stated in the Kurundi that ordination is prohibited for one who is a paṇḍaka (a eunuch) during the very same period in which he is such.
And with reference to one whose ordination is thus prohibited, this was said: "One who has not been fully ordained should not be ordained;
one who has been fully ordained should be expelled. He too must be expelled by the mere removal of his gender-mark. From here on, [the term] "should be expelled" [is used].
The same method applies to those [other cases] that have been mentioned as well.
The Discussion on the Case of Paṇḍava is finished.
The Discussion on the Case of One Who Lives in Communion by Theft.
110. "A son of an ancient noble family" (*purāṇakulaputto*) means a son of a family that has gradually reached a state of decay.

One whose maternal and paternal lineages (*kolañño*) have become exhausted, ruined, and dead is called "one of exhausted lineage. "Not attained" (*anadhigataṃ*) means not reached. "To cause to increase" (*phātiṃkātuṃ*) means to expand. "Come now" (*iṅgha*) is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.

"Being urged" (*anuyuñjiyamāno*) refers to [the process] of being led to one side and [instructed] regarding the ritual procedures for shaving the hair and beard, receiving the saffron robes, going for refuge, taking a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), and the duties of dependence (*nissaya-dhamma*).
"Being questioned, he related this matter": he explained this very fact of his own going forth from the beginning.
"A thief-living monk, O monks"—here there are three kinds of thief-living monks: one who steals the outward sign, one who steals the communion, and one who steals both.
Among these, he who, having gone forth himself and entered a monastery, does not count the years of his monkhood [is a thief-living monk].
One who does not accept a salutation according to seniority, does not decline a seat, and does not appear at the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies—
this person is called a "liṅgatthenaka" (one who has stolen the outward signs) because he has merely misappropriated the mere appearance [of a monk].
Furthermore, one who, though having been ordained as a novice by monks, goes abroad and says, "I am ten years or twenty years [ordained]," [is also such a person].
Or, having spoken falsely thus, if he counts his years as a bhikkhu, accepts veneration according to seniority,
refuses a seat, or appears [together] at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other ceremonies— this is called a "thief of co-residence" because he has stolen even the mere fact of co-residence.
For in this context, every variety of action, such as counting one's years as a bhikkhu, should be understood as "co-residence."
The same principle applies even to one who, having renounced the training (*sikkhā*), acts with the thought, "No one knows me. However,
he who has himself gone forth, goes to a monastery, counts his years as a monk (*bhikkhu-vassa*), accepts veneration according to seniority, declines seats [for others],
and is seen participating in the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other ceremonies— he [is considered a monk] by virtue of both his outward marks (*liṅga*) and...
Because of his deceptive nature regarding living together, he is called a "deceiver in both ways. This threefold deceiver in communal living—if unordained, must not be ordained;
if already ordained, must be expelled; and even if he requests the going-forth again, he must not be admitted to the going-forth.
Furthermore, for the sake of avoiding confusion, this supplementary matter should be understood here:
“Whether due to fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies,
or for the sake of obtaining robes, whoever here assumes the outward mark—
if he does not consent to co-residence as long as his mind remains pure;”
"He is not yet called one who lives in communion by theft.
Herein is the detailed method: Suppose here a certain man is angry with someone;
thinking, "In this way my safety will be secured," he takes the [monastic] emblem himself and flees. Seeing him, they report it to the king. The king says, "If he has gone forth..."

Thinking, "I cannot do anything about that," he subdues his anger; such a person, realizing "the danger from the king has subsided," should be ordained even if he returns having taken up the marks of a householder without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, if one has developed a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "I have obtained my life by relying on the Dispensation; come now, let me go forth," then by that very [realization]—
If one comes in the guise of a wanderer and does not consent to the duties of a guest, yet— whether questioned by the monks or not— discloses his true identity as it is and requests ordination,
he should be ordained after that disguise has been removed. However, if he consents to the duties,
points out the dwelling place of those who have gone forth, and follows all the procedures previously described, such as the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth, [he is to be ordained].
This person should not be ordained.
However, in this case, there is someone who, being unable to survive during a famine, takes up the robes of his own accord and eats the alms-food provided for all religious sects;
yet, when the famine has passed, he returns having taken up the layman’s dress without ever having entered into the midst of the Saṅgha.
Everything is exactly as before.
Another person desires to cross a great wilderness, and the caravan leader is traveling while taking along renunciants.
Thinking, "The caravan leader will take me along in this way," he himself takes on the outward signs and [joins] the caravan leader.

Having crossed the wilderness together and reached a place of safety, he did not descend into the midst of the Saṅgha but returned having taken on the marks of a layperson; all of this is exactly as before.
Another, being unable to live when a danger of disease arose, took the marks himself and [partook of] the alms-foods of all the various sectarians.
While he was eating, the danger of illness subsided; yet, without having returned to the midst of the Saṅgha, he came back having assumed the marks of a householder—all of this is exactly as before.
Another man had an enemy who was angry with him and was wandering about seeking to kill him; [the former thought], "In this way, my safety will be secured."

Taking the very robes himself, he fled. The enemy, searching for him and hearing that he had fled after going forth, thought, "If he has gone forth, it will not be possible to do anything to him," and thus he let go of his anger toward him.
Thinking, "The danger from my enemy has been stilled," he returned without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having taken up the garb of a householder.
Everything is exactly as before.
Another [monk], having gone to his family’s home, renounced the training and became a householder, thinking: "These robes will be ruined here;
even if I were to take these and go to the monastery, they would seize me on the way, saying, 'He is a thief. What if I..."
Thinking, "I shall go having made [myself] fit for the body," he puts on his lower robe and wraps himself in his upper robe to go to the monastery.
Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and young monks come forward and perform their duties of service.
He does not accept this; he reveals himself as he truly is. If the monks say, "Now..."
Thinking, "We shall release him," they desire to ordain him by force; having removed the saffron robes, he must be ordained again.

However, if—thinking, "These [monks] do not know my state of having returned to the lower life"—he acknowledges that very status as a monk and undertakes the entire procedure previously described, such as the calculation of the years of seniority and so forth, he is not to be ordained.
Another great novice, having gone to his family home and left the order, became oppressed by the burden of performing manual labor.

Thinking, "Now I shall become a recluse once more; moreover, even the Elder does not know that I have left the order," he took that same bowl and robe and returned to the monastery, yet he did not inform the monks of this matter or of his status as a novice.
If he admits [his status], he is indeed a thief-living-in-congregation (theyyasaṃvāsaka) and does not receive the going-forth.

Even if, at the very time of receiving the signs [of ordination], he thinks, "I will not tell anyone," yet having gone to the monastery, he confesses it, by that very act of taking [the signs] he is a thief-living-in-congregation.
Or even if the thought arises in him, "I will declare it at the time of taking [the signs]," and having gone to the monastery, [he asks], "Where..."
When addressed with the words, "Friend, you have gone [to the forest]," if he deceives them by saying, "They do not know me now," and does not disclose it, or if he thinks,
"I will not disclose it," and thereby abandons his responsibility, he too is one living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). However,
if at the time of being apprehended the thought "I will disclose it" has arisen in him, and he discloses it even after going to the monastery, he may receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) once again.
Another case is that of a young novice, or one who is grown but incompetent;
having left the monastic life in the same manner as before, he does not wish to perform household tasks such as tending calves.

His relatives, having clothed him in those very same saffron robes and placed an alms-bowl or a vessel in his hand, send him out from the house, saying, "Go, remain a recluse. He [goes] to the monastery...

He goes away; neither do the monks know, "This person, having disrobed, has now re-ordained of his own accord," nor does he himself know, "One who ordains in such a manner is called a thief-living (theyyasaṃvāsaka).

If they confer full ordination upon him when he has reached the full age, he is well-ordained. However, if [the offense occurs] while he is still in the period before full ordination, during the determination of the Vinaya...
If he hears it while it is being recited, saying, “One who goes forth in this manner is called a ‘thief-living’ (theyyasaṃvāsaka),” he must declare to the monks,
“I have done this,” and thus he receives the going-forth again. If, thinking, “Now no one knows me,” he does not report it,
he becomes a thief-liver at the mere moment of abandoning his responsibility.

A bhikkhu who, having renounced the training but not discarded the outward signs, performs an act of immorality— whether he does so or not— and then again undertakes the entire procedure previously described,
such as the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth, is one who dwells in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). One who,

without having renounced the training and while remaining in the outward signs, engages in sexual intercourse [and then undertakes] the procedure such as the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth...
One who commits [an offense] does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft); he merely receives the status of one who has gone forth (*pabbajjāmatta*).
However, in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that such a person is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*; that should not be accepted.
A certain bhikkhu, while still desirous of wearing the saffron robe, put on white clothes, engaged in sexual intercourse, and then again [put on] the saffron robes.
If, having dressed himself, he undertakes the entire procedure— including the counting of the years of seniority and so forth— he is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who dwells in communion by theft),
but merely receives the status of one who has gone forth. However, if he sets aside the saffron robes, puts on white clothes, engages in sexual intercourse,
and then again puts on the saffron robes and undertakes the entire procedure including the counting of the years of seniority and so forth, he is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.

A novice (sāmaṇera), while remaining within his own status, does not become a "one who dwells in communion by theft" even if he commits an act such as sexual intercourse that renders him non-monastic.

Even if, while still having an aspiration for the saffron robes, he removes them, engages in sexual intercourse, and then puts on the saffron robes again, he is not a "one who dwells in communion by theft.
However, if he has laid down the burden of the saffron robes and is either naked or...
If one who was previously dressed in white becomes a non-recluse by engaging in sexual intercourse and so forth,
yet puts on the saffron robe, he is a "one living in communion by theft. Even if, desiring the state of a householder,

he wears the saffron robe by folding it as a loincloth or in some other manner like the dress of a layman for the purpose of testing whether "does this mark of a householder suit me or not," [he is still a thief-communing].

He protects [the robe] for the time being. But having accepted it with the thought, “It looks beautiful,” if he subsequently consents to the mark [of the robe], he becomes one who dwells in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).
The same principle applies to testing or accepting [the robe] after putting on a white lower garment.
However, if he tests it or accepts it after putting a white lower garment over the saffron-colored robe already worn, [he does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*].
She indeed guards [the robe]. The same principle applies to a bhikkhunī as well. For even she, if desiring the state of a householder, might put on the yellow robe of a householder's dwelling;
if it is for the purpose of testing whether "does this mark of a householder suit me or not," she still guards [the robe] for the time being.
But if she accepts it, thinking "it suits me," she does not guard it. This also applies to the testing and acceptance [of the robe] after having put on white [clothing].
The same principle applies here. However, if one who is already wearing a saffron robe puts on a white cloth over it and then either investigates or accepts alms, he still protects himself.

If someone who has gone forth late in life—disregarding his seniority and not even staying by the edge of the bowl—comes up from one side and, when a morsel of food is lifted with a ladle into large bowls and such, holds out his bowl and takes the piece of meat like a hawk seizing its prey, [he does not protect himself].
One who is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion through theft) does not become so by counting and taking [the seniority] as a novice (*sāmaṇera*).

However, one who counts and takes [the seniority] as a monk (*bhikkhu*) becomes a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*. One who, while still a novice, counts and takes fraudulent years according to the sequence of novices does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*. A monk who counts and takes fraudulent years according to the sequence of monks is to be dealt with according to the value of the stolen property.
The Discussion on the Matter of the *Theyyasaṃvāsaka* is finished.

The Discussion on One Who Has Gone Over to Other Sects (*Titthiyapakkantaka-kathā*). Regarding the phrase "one who has gone over to other sects, monks": here, one who has gone over to, or entered among, the *titthiyas* (heretics) is called a "one who has gone over to other sects.
Not only should such a person not be ordained (*upasampadā*), but he should also not be given the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). In this regard, the following is the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*).

If a fully ordained monk, thinking, "I shall become a member of another sect," goes to their dwelling while still wearing his own monastic robes, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every step he takes.
As soon as he has taken on their distinctive mark, he becomes one who has gone over to another sect.
Even if he himself, thinking, "I shall become a member of another sect," puts on grass garments and the like, he likewise becomes one who has gone over to another sect.

But if one who is naked, while bathing, looks at himself and thinks, "My state as an Ājīvaka is becoming," and goes to the Ājīvaka monastery naked without taking up the saffron robes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every step taken.
However, if a sense of shame and moral dread (hirottappa) arises within him along the way, he is released from those offenses after confessing them. For them...
Even if he goes to their residence and is exhorted by them, or if he himself thinks, "The going-forth for these people is too painful," and turns back,
he is still released from the offense. However, if— after being asked, "What is so superior about your going-forth?"— he is told, "It is the plucking out of hair and beard,
etc.," and he then causes even a single hair to be plucked, or undertakes such practices as the *ukkuṭika* posture or exertion, or [accepts] peacock feathers and so forth...
or puts them on, adopts their outward signs, or—thinking "this renunciation is the best"—takes up that state as being supreme, he is not released;
he becomes one who has gone over to the faction of the sectarians (*titthiya-pakkantaka*).

However, if he puts on grass-cloths and so forth, or binds his hair into a matted lock (*jaṭā*), or carries a carrying-pole (*khārikāja*) for the purpose of testing whether "does this renunciation of the sectarians suit me, or does it not suit me?", [he is not yet a *titthiya-pakkantaka*].

Or, as long as one does not accept [the new status], one's original conviction (*laddhi*) protects one; but at the very moment of acceptance, one becomes a defector to a non-Buddhist sect (*titthiyapakkantaka*).

However, one whose robes have been stolen, while wearing garments of kusa grass and so forth, or one who adopts the insignia of a non-Buddhist sect out of fear of kings and the like, does not become a defector to a non-Buddhist sect because of the absence of that conviction.
And this one called "one who has gone over to another sect" (titthiyapakkantaka) is described by one who is already ordained as a bhikkhu;

therefore, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that even if a novice (sāmaṇera) goes to the sphere of another sect while still wearing his own [monastic] marks, he may again receive both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā).
However, the former "one living in communion by theft" (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is described by one who is not yet ordained; therefore, one who is ordained [but acts as such] is a counterfeit rain-cloud.

Even one who counts [the years] is not a non-monk. Even one who, while still aspiring to the outward signs, commits a *pārājika* offense and counts his monastic years and so forth, is not a "one living in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).
Thus ends the discussion on those who have gone over to the faction of other sects.
The Discourse on the Matter of Animals (Tiracchānagatavatthukathā) 111. Regarding the phrase "he is terrified by the nāga-birth":

although during his lifetime he enjoys a mastery and prosperity equal to that of the gods as a result of wholesome kamma-vipāka, nevertheless, for one who has received rebirth-linking through unwholesome kamma-vipāka, there is [fear] regarding sexual intercourse with those of his own kind.
And when he has cast off sleep and set out, his nāga-body appears—wandering in the water and feeding on frogs;
therefore, he is distressed by that nāga-birth. *Harāyati* means he feels shame. *Jigucchati* means he feels disgust for his own physical form.
*Tassa bhikkhuno nikkhante* means when that bhikkhu has departed. Alternatively, *tassa bhikkhuno*.

The meaning is "departing. "He fell asleep with his guard down" means that while he had not yet departed, he did not relinquish his mindfulness due to the fear of a sudden outcry, but merely slept through the influence of monkey-drowsiness;
once he had departed, however, having relinquished his mindfulness, he fell into a deep sleep with his guard down and free from apprehension.
"He let out a cry" means that, out of fear, he abandoned the perception of him as a recluse and made a hideous, loud noise.

“*Tumhe khottha*”: this means “you indeed are”; it is stated thus by eliding the vowel *a*. “You indeed are [those] incapable” (*nāgā*) because you lack the capacity for the jhānas, insight, the path, and the fruit;
thus, in this Dhamma and Discipline, you are of a nature that does not grow, you do not become of a nature that grows—this is the summarized meaning here.
“Of her own kind” (*sajātiyā*) means of a female nāga herself. But when [she is] of another kind, such as a human woman and so forth—

When it consumes [its food], it is like a young god (*devaputta*). And here, in the context of the course of existence (*pavatti*), it is said that "there are two conditions" by way of showing the frequent manifestation of its natural state.
However, for a nāga, the manifestation of its natural state occurs at five times:

at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), at the time of shedding its skin, at the time of mating with its own kind, at the time of emerging from a relaxed sleep, and at the time of death (*cuti*).

"An animal, monks"—in this context, whether it be a nāga, or any other such being like a supaṇṇa or a māṇavaka, including even Sakka, the king of the gods—anyone belonging to the class of non-human beings (amanussa) should be understood as an "animal" in this sense.
Such a person may neither be ordained nor given the full admission; even if already fully admitted, he must be expelled.
The Discussion on the Case of Animals is finished.
112. Regarding the Discussion on the Cases of Matricides and Others:
"They would cause her to go forth" means they would cause her to leave, to depart, or to be led away.
"Should do"—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "a matricide, O monks":

here, one who has intentionally deprived of life his own biological mother, who was a human female, while he himself is also of human birth, is a matricide by virtue of that immediate (*ānantariya*) act of matricide;
for such a person, both going forth and full ordination are prohibited. However, as for one by whom [a woman] who was a human female...
If a mother who gives suck, one who nourishes, a foster-mother, a great-mother, a junior-mother, or even a biological mother—
who is not a human female— is killed, his going forth is not forbidden, nor does it constitute an immediate offense (*ānantarika*). Likewise,
if one kills a human female mother while being a non-human animal oneself, he also does not commit an immediate offense, because of his being an animal.
Going forth is prohibited. The rest is self-evident. The same principle applies to a patricide as well.

For even if he is the son of a courtesan and does not know, "This is my father," if he kills the one by whose procreation he was born, he is reckoned as a patricide and incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
114. Even the "murderer of an Arahant" (arahantaghātaka) should be understood by way of a human Arahant alone.

For if one intentionally deprives of life—even if only a child or a girl—anyone belonging to the human race who has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava), even if they have not gone forth, one becomes a murderer of an Arahant, incurs an immediate retribution (ānantariya), and his going-forth is forbidden. However, as for a non-human Arahant...
Having killed a human being or any other noble person (ariyapuggala), one does not incur an immediate retribution (ānantariya) offense;

his going forth (pabbajjā) is not forbidden, yet the kamma is powerful. Even a beast having killed a human or an arahant does not incur an immediate retribution offense, yet the kamma is grave—this is the distinction here.
"They are led away for execution" means for the purpose of killing.
*Onīyanti* means they are being led away, that is, they are being led away to be executed.
As for what is stated in the Pāḷi, “*sacā ca mayaṃ*,” its meaning is simply “*sace mayaṃ*” (if we). For while one should say “*sace*,” the particle *sacā ca* is used here.
Alternatively, the reading is simply *sace ca*. In that context, *sace* is a particle used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*), and *ca* is used merely as a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*).
“*Sacajja mayan*”—this is also a reading. Its meaning is: “If today we [should do so]. 115.
Regarding the phrase “a violator of a bhikkhunī, O bhikkhus”: here, one who violates a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhunī by means of any of the three paths is called a “violator of a bhikkhunī.
For such a person, both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full admission (*upasampadā*) are forbidden. However, as for one who...
If one causes the destruction of virtue through physical contact, his going forth and full ordination are not barred.
Even one who defiles a woman against her will by force, making her wear white garments, is indeed a "defiler of a nun" (*bhikkhunī-dūsaka*).
However, one who defiles a woman against her will by force while she is wearing white garments is not a "defiler of a nun. Why is that?
Because she becomes a non-nun (abhikkhunī) at the very moment the state of being a householder is accepted.
However, one who later defiles her after she has once fallen from virtue, or who misconducts himself with a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), does not become a defiler of a nun;
he may even receive both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā).

Regarding the phrase "one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, O monks": here, one like Devadatta, who—having rendered the Teaching contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya—splits the Saṅgha by means of any one of the four formal acts (kamma), is called a "schismatic.
For such a person, both the going-forth and the full ordination are prohibited.

Regarding the phrase "one who causes the appearance of blood, monks": here too, whoever—like Devadatta—with a wicked mind and a murderous intent causes even as much blood as could be drunk by a tiny fly to appear on the living body of a Tathāgata, such a person is called a "causer of the appearance of blood.
For him, both going forth and full ordination are forbidden. However, for one who [causes blood to flow] for the purpose of curing a disease...
Just as Jīvaka, having cut open [the body] with a knife, removes putrid flesh and blood and restores it to health,
so too one generates much merit.
The discussion on the cases of matricides and others is concluded.
The Discussion on the Matter of the Hermaphrodite (Ubhatobyañjanaka-vatthu-kathā) 116. "Bhikkhus, one who is a hermaphrodite" (*ubhatobyañjanaka*):

because he possesses both sexual characteristics (*byañjana*)—namely, the karma that produces the female characteristic and the karma that produces the male characteristic—he is called a hermaphrodite. "He acts" means [he acts] toward women by means of the male characteristic.
He commits an act of sexual misconduct. "Causes to be done" means that, having incited another, he causes it to be done upon his own female organ;
this is of two kinds: one who possesses both female and male characteristics (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*), and one who possesses both male and female characteristics (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*).
Among these, for the one possessing both female and male characteristics, the female organ is manifest, while the male organ is concealed.
For a hermaphrodite male (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*), the male characteristic is manifest and the female characteristic is concealed.
For a hermaphrodite female (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) who assumes the state of a male among women, the female characteristic is concealed and the male characteristic becomes manifest.
For a hermaphrodite male who approaches the state of a woman among men, the male characteristic... [is concealed].
The female characteristic is concealed, while the male characteristic is manifest. A hermaphrodite female (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive;
however, a hermaphrodite male (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka) does not conceive himself but causes another to conceive—this is the distinction between them.
But in the *Kurundi* it is said: "If, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the male organ..."
"The female characteristic arises in the course of existence; if the female characteristic [arose] at rebirth-linking, then the male characteristic would arise in the course of existence.
The detailed sequence of analysis regarding this should be understood from the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
However, for this two-fold type of hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), there is neither going-forth (*pabbajjā*) nor full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This much should be understood here.
The discussion on the basis of one who possesses both sets of characteristics is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the basis of one who has no preceptor, and so forth.
117. Now at that time: at the time when the training rule had not yet been laid down by the Blessed One.
"Without a preceptor" means having not taken a preceptor, being entirely devoid of a preceptor.
Those who have been ordained in this manner receive neither spiritual nor material support; they simply decline.

They do not increase. "Monks, one who has no preceptor" means that one should not be ordained without having been made to take a preceptor—that is, one should not be ordained as one who lacks a preceptor.
"Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). From the time this training rule was established, there is an offense for one who ordains in this manner;
however, the formal act (*kamma*) itself is not invalidated. Some say it is invalidated.
That [ordination] is not to be accepted. This same method applies to the cases beginning with "by a Saṅgha" and "by an Upajjhāya," ending with "one who is both-sexed.
The discussion on the subject of those without an Upajjhāya and so forth is concluded. Now follows the discussion on the subject of those who have not fallen into an offense and so forth.
118. "They wander for alms with their hands" means they wander for the sake of whatever alms can be obtained in their hands.
"Just like the sectarians" means just like the sectarians known as Ājīvakas; for they eat only alms-food placed in their hands after it has been mixed with soups and condiments.
"There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that the offense belongs to the one who confers full ordination in this manner; [the formal] act—
However, it does not become an offense. The same principle applies to the grounds such as "without a robe" (acīvaraka) and so forth.
"Borrowed" (yācitaka) means taken after requesting, saying, "Please give this until we perform the full ordination (upasampadā)";
the meaning is "temporary. For one who confers full ordination using such a bowl, robe, or both bowl and robe, there is indeed an offense.
However, the kamma does not fail; therefore, one should be ordained only when possessing a full set of bowl and robes.

If he has none, and his preceptor and teacher wish to give them, or if other monks give after having relinquished their own belongings without attachment, then a bowl and robes sufficient for formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) should be given. But as for one seeking admission who is like a withered leaf—

It is permissible to grant the going-forth even with a bowl and robe that have been borrowed; it is also permissible to grant the going-forth after taking [the requisites] on trust in a place where they are common property.

However, if someone has arrived having taken an unbaked bowl and cloths intended for robes, one should provide him with unclaimed almsfood while he resides in the monastery until the bowl is baked and the robes are finished.
It is permissible; it is permissible to eat from a shallow dish; it is permissible to give a portion of food equal to the novice’s share before the meal.

However, the drawing of lots for lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*), as well as tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*), designated meals (*uddesabhatta*), invitations (*nimantana*), and so forth, are not permissible.
After the meal, it is also permissible to give a medicinal portion consisting of oil, honey, molasses, and so on, equal to the novice’s share. If he is ill...

It exists; it is permissible to provide medicine for him, and all duties of attendance are to be performed just as they are for a novice (sāmaṇera). The discussion on the case of those who have not received the full ordination, etc., is concluded.
Now follows the discussion on the case of those with severed hands, etc.

119. Regarding the cases of those whose hands have been cut off, and so forth: "One whose hand has been cut off" refers to one for whom one or both hands have been severed at any location whatsoever—whether on the palm, at the wrist, or at the forearm.
"One whose foot has been cut off" refers to one for whom one or both feet have been severed at any location whatsoever—whether at the toes, at the ankles, or in the shank.
"Hand-and-foot-cut" refers to one whose two, three, or all four hands and feet have been cut off in the manner already described.
"Ear-cut" refers to one whose one or two ears have been cut off either at the base of the ear or the earlobe.
However, in the case of one whose ears are pierced and [the piercings] are cut, it is possible...
Regarding "one whose ear is sewn together": having sewn the ear together, he should be ordained.
Regarding "one whose nose is severed": this refers to one whose nose has been cut off anywhere—whether at the base, at the tip, or in a single fold.
However, if his nose can be rejoined, he should be ordained after it has been made functional. One whose both ear and nose are severed should be understood according to both criteria.
"One whose fingers have been cut off" refers to one for whom one or more fingers have been severed without leaving even a trace of the nail visible.
However, it is permissible to grant the going forth to one for whom even a mere thread of nail remains visible.
"One whose thumbs have been cut off" refers to one for whom one or more thumbs have been severed from among the four [thumbs], in the same manner as described for the fingers.
They exist. "With tendons severed" means one whose large sinews called *kaṇḍara* have been cut either in front or behind;
because even one of them has been severed, he walks on his toes or he walks on his heels, or he is unable to plant his foot firmly.
One who has hands like a cobra’s hood, whose fingers are joined together like the wings of a bat— if one desires to ordain such a person,
one should have the spaces between the fingers slit open, remove all the skin from between them,
and make it functional before ordaining him. Likewise, if one has six fingers, one who desires to ordain him should have the extra finger cut off, make it functional, and then ordain him.
"Khujja" refers to one whose body is hunched due to a protrusion from the chest, the back, or the side.
However, it is permissible to ordain anyone whose various limbs and members are only slightly crooked. For only the Great Man possesses a perfectly erect body like Brahmā;
there is no other being who can truly be called "not hunched."
"Vāmana" means one who is stunted in the shanks, or stunted at the waist, or stunted in both.
For one stunted in the shanks, the lower body from the waist downwards is short, while the upper body is well-proportioned.
For one stunted at the waist, the upper body from the waist upwards is short, while the lower body is well-proportioned. For one stunted in both, both bodies are short—those for whom...
Because of its density, the physical form (*attabhāva*) is like a large pot with a narrow opening, resembling a hollowed-out tree trunk;

it is not permitted to ordain anyone who possesses even one of these three types. "One with a goitre" (*galagaṇḍī*) refers to one who has a swelling on the neck like a *kumbhaṇḍa* fruit. This is merely an illustration; [it applies] to anyone in whom—
However, if there is a boil in any part [of the body], he should not be admitted into the Order.
The detailed explanation regarding this is to be understood in the same manner as stated in the passage: "Monks, one afflicted by five kinds of diseases should not be admitted into the Order.

As for what should be said concerning those who have been branded, those who have been struck with a stick, and those who have been tattooed, that has already been stated in the passages beginning with: "Monks, one who has been branded... and so forth.
"Sīpadī" refers to one with club-footed legs. One whose foot is thick, covered in warts, and rough should not be ordained.

However, if it has not yet become so rough, it is possible—by applying a poultice, immersing it in a water-pool, and filling it with water and sand—to make the veins visible and the shank appear like an oil-tube.
It can be made to wither in this way; therefore, it is appropriate to ordain such a person after having rendered his foot thus.
If, however, it grows back again, even one who confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) must do so only after having treated it in that same manner.

One who has a foul disease (*pāparogī*)—that is, one who is constantly afflicted by any disease among those such as hemorrhoids, fistula, bile-disorders, phlegm-disorders, coughs, or consumption, and whose disease is incurable, loathsome, and unpleasant—this person should not be ordained.
"One who defiles the assembly" (*parisadūsaka*) is one who defiles the assembly because of his own deformity. He is either too tall, reaching the height of others' heads or navels;
or too short, like a figure consisting of both types of dwarfs; or too dark, like a charred stump in a burnt field;
or too fair, with the color of polished copper after being rubbed with curd, buttermilk, and so forth; or too thin, with little flesh and blood, a body composed only of bones, veins, and skin.
Or one who is excessively fat, or has heavy flesh; or one with a large belly like a great elemental being;
or one with an excessively large head, as if standing with a basket placed upon his head; or one with an excessively small head, endowed with a head so tiny it is disproportionate to the body;
or one with a peaked head, endowed with a head resembling a cluster of palm fruits; or one with a crest-like head.
Or one with a head that is gradually tapered from top to bottom; or one with a tubular head like the joint of a large bamboo;
or one with a cleft head or a flattened head, with the head tilted toward any one of its four sides;
or one with a scarred head, a putrid head, or hair like a cluster of buds, as if on a field eaten by insects.
He is endowed with hair that has grown here and there like blades of grass; or he has a hairless head, or thick and stiff hair, or hair like the fibers of a palm tree;
or his head is white with natural graying, or his hair is naturally tawny, or he is endowed with hair as if it were aflame;
or he has a "swirl-headed" appearance, with hair standing upright like the whorls on the bodies of cattle.
He is endowed with hair-whorls; or his facial hair, together with the hair of his head, forms a single continuous mass, as if his forehead were covered by a net;
or he has joined eyebrows, or hairless eyebrows, or monkey-like eyebrows; or his eyes are too large, or his eyes are too small.
Or one with eyes like those of a rhinoceros hide, resembling wounds inflicted by a bamboo thorn;
or "uneven-eyed," endowed with one large eye and one small eye;
or "uneven-eyebrowed," endowed with eyes and eyebrows that are unevenly positioned, such as one being high and the other low; or "squinting" (kekara), having deep-set eyes.
Or one whose eye-pupils appear like reflections of stars in a deep well;
or one with protruding eyes whose pupils are bulging out like those of a crab; or one with "elephant-ears," endowed with large flaps of skin on the ears;
or one with "mouse-ears" or "bat-ears," endowed with small flaps of skin on the ears.
Or one whose ears are merely perforated, meaning that for him there is only the ear-hole itself without ear-rings;
or one with unperforated ears, such as a Yavana by birth, who does not corrupt the assembly; for that is his very nature.
Or one suffering from ear-fistula, possessed of an ear that is constantly putrid; or one with "goiter-ears," possessed of an ear from which pus is always trickling.
Or one with ears like a goad-point, or endowed with ears resembling the tip of a cow’s fodder-stalk;
or one with excessively tawny eyes—though it is permissible to ordain those with honey-tawny eyes;
or one with eyes free of film, or with eyes that water with tears, or with blossoming eyes, or with eyes afflicted by inflammation.
One with a nose that is too large, or one with a nose that is too small, or one with a flat nose, or one with a crooked nose that does not stand straight but is bent to one side,
or one with a long nose, or one endowed with a nose from which mucus constantly drips, such that it could be licked by a tongue as well-formed as a parrot's beak.

Or one with a "large mouth," whose mouth-sign alone is large like that of a grasshopper or a frog, while the actual mouth is like a gourd and extremely small; or one with a split mouth, or a crooked mouth;
or one with large lips, possessing lips resembling the rim of a mortar; or one with thin lips, [or] with teeth like the skin of a drum, unable to close them together.
He is endowed with lips that are either large on the lower lip and thin on the upper lip, or thin on the lower lip and large on the upper lip;
or his lips are severed, or his mouth is like that of a wild beast, or his mouth is distorted, or his snout is constricted;
or he is endowed with lips that are dark outside and excessively red inside; or his mouth has a foul-smelling, corpse-like odor.
One who has "large teeth" is endowed with teeth resembling those of a boar; or one who has "asura-teeth," meaning teeth that protrude either from below or above;
however, it is permissible to ordain one whose protruding teeth can be covered by the lips and are visible only while speaking, not when not speaking.
One who has "rotten teeth" or "missing teeth"—that is, one for whom there is a gap between the teeth—[is likewise ineligible].
He has teeth as fine as those of a kalandakan bird; he is fit for ordination.
Or he has a large jaw, or is endowed with a jaw like that of an ox; or he has a long jaw, or a flat jaw, or is endowed with an extremely short jaw as if it were sunken inside;
or he has a broken jaw, or a crooked jaw, or is without mustache and fangs.
Or one with a face like a bhikkhunī’s; or one with a long neck; or one endowed with a neck like that of a crane; or one with a short neck, as if the neck were drawn inward;
or one with a split neck; or one with drooping shoulder-tops; or one without a hand; or one with only one hand;
or one with excessively short hands; or one with excessively long hands; or one with a split chest; or one with a split back.

"Having itchy limbs," "having scabby limbs," "having eruptive skin conditions," or "having 'lizard-skin' limbs"—that is, one from whose limbs the scales fall off like those of a lizard—all this is stated in detail with reference to various types of disfigurement.
However, the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) here should be understood according to the same method explained in the passage: "Monks, [one should not give] for five kinds of diseases."
One who has a humpbacked back or a large hump, with the flesh of the hump rising high like the peak of a hearth;

or one with large thighs, or a wind-swollen body, or large knees, or knobby-kneed, or long shanks, or shanks like staffs, or one who is deformed, or one with a cleft leg, or one with protruding calves—this [latter type] is of two kinds: those with calves that hang down low or those with calves that rise high.

Or he is endowed with large calves; or he has large shanks, or thick calves, or large feet, or large heels, or a foot with a prominent instep, or shanks that rise from the middle of the foot, or crooked feet—this is of two kinds:
either the feet turn inward or outward, or the toes are knotted like the bulbs of ginger.
One who possesses [such defects], or one with blind nails, or one with black-colored, putrid nails—every such person is a defiler of the assembly.
One who is a defiler of the assembly in this manner should not be ordained.
"Blind" means either naturally blind from birth or having impaired vision due to cataracts and the like; that is, one who is sightless in both eyes or in one eye.

If he does not see, he should not be ordained. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, one with a single eye is called "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*), while one blind in both eyes is included under the category of "blind" (*andha*).
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, one born blind is called "blind. Therefore, both [definitions] are appropriate as alternative explanations.
"Lame" (*kuṇī*) means one who is lame in the hand, lame in the foot, or lame in the finger; for whomsoever there is some such defect among these, such as the hands and so forth...

One who appears crooked is called *kuṇī*. A "lame one" (*khañja*) is one whose knee-joints are bent, or whose shins are broken; or one who is lame because the feet are contracted at the middle, like a cripple (*kuṇḍapādaka*);
or one who is lame because the feet are contracted at the tips while walking on the back part of the feet;
or one who is lame because they walk only on the tips of the feet; or one who is lame because they walk on their heels.
Whether he is lame from the outside edge of the foot while walking, or lame from the inside edge of the foot while walking,
or lame with the entire back of the foot due to a fracture above the ankles—
all such persons are indeed lame, and they must not be ordained.
"Pakkhahata" means one for whom one hand, or one foot, or even half the body does not function comfortably.
"Chinniriyāpatha" refers to one who is a cripple (pīṭhasappi). "Jarādubbalā" means one who is weak due to old age and is unable even to perform tasks such as dyeing his own robes.
However, one who is elderly yet strong and capable of looking after himself—
He should be ordained. "Blind" refers to one who is blind from birth. "Dumb" refers to one whose vocal articulation does not function;

even if it does function, if he is unable to recite the formula for going for refuge in its entirety, such a person—even if he is merely mute—is not permitted to be ordained. However, one who is able to recite at least the complete formula for going for refuge may be ordained.
"Deaf" refers to one who does not hear at all in any way whatsoever. However, it is permissible to ordain one who hears loud sounds.

Those such as the blind and the mute are mentioned by virtue of having both defects. For those whose admission into the order (pabbajjā) is prohibited, their full ordination (upasampadā) is likewise prohibited.
But if the Saṅgha should nevertheless confer full ordination upon them, [the same applies to] all those with severed hands and so forth.
They are fully ordained; however, the community of makers (the *kāraka-saṅgha*) as well as the preceptor and the teacher are not released from the offense. And he will say:
"Monks, there is a person who has not reached restoration (*osāraṇa*); if the Saṅgha restores him, one is well-restored and another is poorly restored.
The meaning of this will be clarified at the very place where it occurs.
The Discussion on the Cases of Those with Severed Hands, etc., is finished.
120. Regarding the Discussion on the Cases of Dependence on Shameless Persons:
"Living in dependence upon shameless persons" is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative; that is, living in dependence upon individuals who are shameless.

The meaning is as follows: "As long as I know the commonality with the monks" means that one should know the commonality—that is, the sense of shame—of the monk who provides dependence (nissaya) with other monks.

Therefore, when one has gone to a new place and is told, "Come, monk, take dependence," one should wait four or five days to examine whether the provider of dependence possesses a sense of shame before accepting the dependence.
If, having heard from the bhikkhus that "the elder is modest," one wishes to receive dependence on the very day of arrival, it is permissible for the elder to say, "Wait for now;
you will know when you have lived here," and after observing his conduct for a few days, grant dependence.
However, one who goes to a place for receiving dependence as usual must receive it on that very day; even for a single day...

There is no exemption. If there is no opportunity for the teacher during the first watch of the night, and he lies down thinking, "I will receive it at dawn," and does not even notice that the sun has risen, there is no offense.

However, if he lies down without forming the intention, "I will receive it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when the sun rises. Having gone to a place never visited before, two or three...
One who wishes to depart after having stayed for several days may stay without formal dependence (*anissita*).

However, one who intends to stay for seven days and forms an attachment [to the place] must take formal dependence (*nissaya*).
