If the elder asks, "What need is there for formal dependence for one staying for seven days?", from that point on he receives the same privileges as one who has been granted leave.
The Discussion on the Basis for Reliance on the Shameless is finished.
121. The Discussion on the Bases for Reliance such as for Travelers, etc.
*“Nissayakaraṇīyo”* means reliance that is to be performed; it is a reliance that must be performed by me. The meaning is: “it is to be taken up.”
"By one not obtaining dependence" means that when there is no one to grant dependence among those traveling together on the road, one is said to "not obtain dependence.
One who does not obtain it thus must travel for many days without being dependent.
If he enters any monastery where he has previously lived after having taken dependence, even by staying there for a single night—
One must receive formal dependence (*nissaya*). If one stays for a few days while resting along the way or while seeking a caravan, there is no offense.

However, during the rainy season, one must reside in a fixed location and receive formal dependence. But for one traveling by boat, there is no offense if, even when the rains arrive, one does not obtain formal dependence.

"By one being asked": that sick person, being asked [to leave], should dwell without being dependent [on others]. If, even when told "Please ask me," the sick person does not ask out of pride, one should go.
"It is comfortable": it is comfortable by way of attaining serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Indeed, neither stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), nor once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), nor non-returners (*anāgāmī*), nor arahants obtain this exemption; nor do those whose concentration or insight has reached firmness.

Or [if he is] one who has attained [insight], there is no question at all regarding an ordinary worldling (*bālaputhujjana*) who has abandoned his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). However, one for whom serenity (*samatha*) or insight (*vipassanā*) is still tender receives this exemption;

it is for such a person alone that the inclusion in the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇa-saṅgaha*) is permitted. Therefore, even when the teacher has gone after being invited by this person, [the thought arises]: "When a suitable..."
If one forms the intention, "The provider of dependence will come; I shall dwell under his dependence," it is permissible to live without dependence until the full moon of Āsāḷhī.
However, if the teacher does not arrive during the month of Āsāḷhī, one must go to a place where dependence can be obtained.
122. “One may announce even by clan”: the meaning is that I authorize one to announce after having stated the clan thus, “He is desirous of full ordination under Mahākassapa.

123. “Two [may be ordained] by a single announcement”: this refers to two being announced together; that is, while one teacher announces the *kammavācā* for one person and another for the other, I authorize the conferring of full ordination by two teachers simultaneously through a single announcement.
Two or three persons may be made the object of a single announcement, provided they have a single preceptor (*upajjhāya*), according to the same procedure as before.
I authorize the performance of the proclamation (*anussāvana*) by one person; and the meaning is that I authorize this act of proclaiming by means of a single preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
Therefore, two or three [novices] may be proclaimed by a single teacher (*ācariya*).
Or, by two or three teachers, each separately for one [novice], two or three *kammavācā* formulas should be performed simultaneously in this manner. If...

However, if they have different teachers and different preceptors—such as when the Elder Tissa makes the Elder Sumana’s pupil announce [the full ordination], and the Elder Sumana makes the Elder Tissa’s pupil announce it, and they each serve as the one who completes the quorum for the other—it is permissible.
But if they have different preceptors and only one teacher, it is not allowed; for it is said: “But certainly not with different preceptors.”
Because it has been rejected, it is not permissible; for this very reason, this rejection was made.
The discussion on the grounds for dependence, such as those for one going on a journey, is concluded. Now follows the discussion on the procedure for full ordination (*upasampadā*).
126. "First, one should have [the candidate] take a preceptor (upajjhāya)": here, one who contemplates (upanijjhāyati) what is faulty and what is not faulty is an *upajjhā*;
that is the *upajjhā*. Having had him say, "Venerable sir, please be my preceptor," he should be made to take one.
"Becoming bloated" means their limbs become swollen. "Whatever has been born" means whatever has been born, produced, or exists within your body—that.
"When asked in the midst of the Saṅgha, one who is present should say 'I am,' and so forth. "Ullumpatu maṃ" means "may he lift me up.
The discussion on the procedure for full ordination (*upasampadā*) is concluded.
Now follows the discussion on the four supports (*nissaya*), etc.
128. "Tāvadeva" means immediately upon full ordination. "The shadow must be measured" means the shadow must be measured as being one person’s height, two persons’ heights, and so forth.
"The measure of the season must be announced" means the measure of the season must be announced as "the rainy season," "the winter," or "the summer.
And here, the season itself is the measure of the season. If the rainy season and so forth are incomplete, [it should be stated] by how much...
Having observed which days of the month the season for a particular person is incomplete, that portion of the day should be pointed out.
Alternatively, the measure of the season should be pointed out in this way: "This is the season, and it is either complete or incomplete.
The portion of the day should be pointed out as "forenoon" or "afternoon. This is called *saṅgītī*.
Having combined all of this together, when asked, "What do you receive? What is your shadow? What is the measure of the season?
What portion of the day is it?", you should explain it thus: "I receive such-and-such—either the rainy season, or the winter, or the summer;
this is my shadow; this is the measure of the season; this is the portion of the day. Thus should it be declared.
129. *Ōhāya* means having abandoned. *Dutiyam dātun ti*: I allow [the preceptor] to give a companion to one who is going from the ordination hall to the courtyard;
the meaning is that he should explain the four things not to be done (*akaraṇīyāni*).
*Paṇḍupalāso* is a leaf that has turned yellow. *Bandhanā pavutto* means fallen from its stalk. *Abhabbo haritatthāyā ti*: incapable of becoming green again.
One is incapable of becoming green (harita). "Large stones" (puthusila) means great rocks. 130.

When unity (sāmaggi) cannot be obtained, there is no offense in sharing communal life or living together, as long as unity is not obtained for the purpose of performing a formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) against him;
during that time, one may share communal life with him and perform acts such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies.
"And there is no offense in co-residing. The remainder is self-evident, as it is easy to understand according to what has been stated throughout the Mahāvibhaṅga.
The discussion on the four requisites, etc., is concluded.
From the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the meaning of the Great Khandhaka, adorned with one hundred and seventy-two topics,
is finished. The commentary on the Great Khandhaka is finished.
2. The Uposatha Khandhaka: Discussion on the Permission for Assembling, etc. 132. In the Uposatha Khandhaka—regarding the term *aññatitthiyā* (those of other sects):
here, *tittha* refers to a tenet (*laddhi*); those who have a different tenet [are called *aññatitthiyā*].
"Another sect" (*aññatittha*); those who have another sect are "adherents of other sects" (*aññatitthiyā*); this means they hold views other than this [Buddhist] one.
"They speak of the Dhamma" means they discourse upon what is to be done and what is not to be done according to their own system.
"They receive" means those people receive [offerings]. "Mute pigs" refers to pigs with stout bodies.
135. Regarding the phrase "either has not committed [an offense] or, having committed one, has emerged from it":
here the meaning should be understood as follows—that offense which a bhikkhu has either not committed, or which he has committed and then emerged from—that is called a "non-existent" offense.
As for the question "What happens in the case of intentional lying?": what happens to this intentional lying that is said to belong to him, in terms of an offense; which [offense] is it?
The meaning is that "there is an offense. "There is a *dukkaṭa*" means there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);

and this is not by way of the characteristic of false speech, but rather it should be understood as an offense originating from non-action through the door of speech, by virtue of the Blessed One’s own word. For he will say:
"Not conversing with anyone among men..."
"Even if others should speak harsh words to us,
one might incur verbal misconduct but not bodily misconduct;
this question was pondered by those skilled in wholesome states."
"Obstructive" means that which creates an obstacle. "For what purpose is there comfort? means for what aim is there comfort? "For the attainment of the first jhāna":
for the sake of attaining the first jhāna, there is comfort and ease for that bhikkhu.
This same method applies everywhere. Thus the Blessed One presented the first recitation of the Pātimokkha both by way of summary and by way of detailed exposition.
136. *Devasikaṃ* means day by day. Regarding the phrase "on the fourteenth or the fifteenth":
for one particular season, it occurs twice—on the fourteenth of both the third and the seventh fortnights—and for the remaining seasons, six times on the fifteenth.
This is first one interpretation. However, this is stated according to the natural course of conduct (*pakaticāritta*): "once every fortnight, on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth."
Furthermore, from the statement “or,” it should be understood that when such conditions exist, it is permissible to recite on whichever fourteenth or fifteenth day [of the half-month] is appropriate;
for while the resident monks have the fourteenth as their date, the incoming monks have the fifteenth.
This is also to be understood from the statement: “If the residents are more numerous, the incoming monks must follow the residents.”
The Discourse on the Recognition of the Boundary (Sīmānujānanakathā) 138.
First, regarding the proclamation of the boundary markers: the holder of the Vinaya must ask, "What is the marker in the eastern direction?
[If the reply is] "A mountain, venerable sir," then the holder of the Vinaya must say, "This mountain is the marker. Thus...

The sign (nimitta) should be defined. However, it is not permissible to define it by saying: "We are making this mountain the sign," "we will make it," "the sign has been made," "let it be the sign," "it is," or "it will be. The same method applies to rocks and so forth.
[Likewise for] the intermediate eastern direction, the southern direction, the intermediate southern direction, and the western direction.
"In the western intermediate direction, in the northern direction, and in the northern intermediate direction, what is the sign? 'Water, Bhante. [The teacher says:
'Without standing here, saying "This water is the sign," again, in the eastern direction, what is the sign?
'A mountain, Bhante. 'This mountain is the sign. Thus, having first designated the sign that was pointed out, it should be established."
In this way, one sign is joined with another sign. Having thus proclaimed the signs, the boundary (sīmā) must then be formally established by means of the *kammavācā* recited immediately thereafter.
At the conclusion of the *kammavācā*, the boundary lies within the signs, while the signs themselves are outside the boundary.
In that regard, once the signs have been proclaimed, they remain proclaimed for good, even if they were proclaimed only once; so it is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.

However, it is stated that the boundary circle must be defined by describing the landmark three times. As for the description—“Venerable sir, there is a mountain... [etc. ...there is water”—it is perfectly permissible for either one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or one who is not fully ordained to state it. Now, the following analysis regarding the mountain landmarks and so forth should be understood: a mountain is of three kinds—a mountain of pure soil, [The text continues: a mountain of rock, and a mountain of both soil and rock. Among these, a mountain of pure soil is one consisting solely of earth, such as the Vulture Peak (*Gijjhakūṭa*). A mountain of rock is one consisting solely of stone, such as Mount Vebhāra. A mountain of both soil and rock is one where both earth and stone are present, such as Mount Isigili. Regarding these, when defining the boundary, one should describe the mountain itself as the landmark, saying: “Venerable sirs, this mountain is the landmark; this mountain is the boundary. Or else, one may describe a specific part of the mountain as the landmark, saying: “Venerable sirs, this peak is the landmark; this slope is the landmark; this cave is the landmark; this rock is the landmark; this tree is the landmark; this stream is the landmark; this pond is the landmark; this well is the landmark; this tank is the landmark. In this way, the mountain should be described as the landmark. Furthermore, even if the mountain is not visible, it is still permissible to describe it as the landmark, provided that it was previously seen and remembered. If the mountain is not visible and has not been previously seen or remembered, then it is not permissible to describe it as the landmark. This same principle applies to the other landmarks, such as the rock. However, in the case of a river, one should describe it as the landmark only if its flow is constant; if it is intermittent, it is not permissible. In the case of a tree, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a single tree; if it is a grove, it is not permissible. In the case of a pond, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a natural pond; if it is an artificial one, it is not permissible. In the case of a well, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a natural well; if it is an artificial one, it is not permissible. In the case of a tank, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a natural tank; if it is an artificial one, it is not permissible. In the case of a house, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent structure; if it is temporary, it is not permissible. In the case of a heap of grain, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a large heap; if it is a small heap, it is not permissible. In the case of a charnel ground, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent site; if it is a temporary one, it is not permissible. In the case of a road, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a major highway; if it is a minor path, it is not permissible. In the case of a field, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a large field; if it is a small plot, it is not permissible. In the case of a threshing floor, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent structure; if it is temporary, it is not permissible. In the case of a village, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a large village; if it is a small hamlet, it is not permissible. In the case of a city, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a large city; if it is a small town, it is not permissible. In the case of a monastery, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent establishment; if it is temporary, it is not permissible. In the case of a forest, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a vast expanse; if it is a small grove, it is not permissible. In the case of a thicket, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a dense growth; if it is sparse, it is not permissible. In the case of a mountain pass, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a prominent feature; if it is insignificant, it is not permissible. In the case of a boundary post, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a fixed marker; if it is movable, it is not permissible. In the case of a cairn, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent pile of stones; if it is a temporary heap, it is not permissible. In the case of a fire, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent hearth; if it is a temporary flame, it is not permissible. In the case of a cloud, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent formation; if it is a passing cloud, it is not permissible. In the case of a star, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a fixed star; if it is a moving planet, it is not permissible. In the case of the sun, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is the rising or setting sun; if it is the midday sun, it is not permissible. In the case of the moon, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is the full or new moon; if it is the crescent moon, it is not permissible. In the case of a deity, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent shrine; if it is a temporary image, it is not permissible. In the case of a relic, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent deposit; if it is a temporary offering, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a permanent impression; if it is a temporary mark, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in mud, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is indistinct, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in sand, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is blurred, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in dust, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is faint, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in snow, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is melted, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in ash, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is scattered, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in charcoal, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is extinguished, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in salt, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is dissolved, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint in water, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is submerged, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a wall, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is blurred, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a floor, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is worn away, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a roof, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is obscured by rain, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a door, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is worn smooth, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a threshold, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is blurred, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a step, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is worn down, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a stairway, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is faded, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a bridge, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is broken, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a causeway, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is eroded, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a ford, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is submerged, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a bank, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a clear impression; if it is washed away, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a cliff, one should describe it as the landmark only if it is a distinct impression; if it is crumbled, it is not permissible. In the case of a footprint on a slope, one should describe it as the landmark only if
There are three kinds: a mountain of pure rock, and one that is a mixture of both. All three of these are permissible. However, a heap of sand is not permissible.

Furthermore, even the other [types] are not permissible if they are smaller than the size of an elephant. But from the size of an elephant upwards, even up to the size of Mount Sineru, they are permissible.
If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three in the three [directions], or if there are four or three [mountains], [it is permissible].
It is proper to appoint [the boundary] by means of mountain signs alone; however, it is not proper to appoint it by means of two signs or even one.
This same principle applies to the subsequent signs, such as rock signs and so forth. Therefore, when making a mountain sign, one must ask:
"Is it connected [to another] or not connected? If it is connected, it should not be made; for that [connected area] belongs to the four...
Or even when praising [the monastery] in the eight directions, it is only a single sign that has been praised; therefore,
having praised that mountain which stands surrounding the monastery in the shape of a wheel from one direction,
and having excluded it from the other directions, other signs should be praised within.
If they wish to include a third part or half of a mountain within the boundary, they should not designate the entire mountain;
rather, they should designate a specific landmark—such as a tree, an anthill, or the like—growing on that very mountain, located beyond the portion of the area they wish to include within.
If they wish to include the entire mountain, measuring one or two *yojanas*, within [the boundary]...
When they wish to do so, the signs on the ground beyond the mountain—such as trees, anthills, and so forth—should be pointed out.
Regarding a stone sign—even an iron ball is counted as a stone; therefore, any kind of stone is suitable.
However, in terms of size, one the size of an elephant is considered a "mountain," and thus it is not suitable. [A stone] the size of a large bull or a large buffalo...
However, it is permissible. At its minimum limit, the size of thirty-two *pala* lumps of sugar is permitted;

anything smaller than that, whether as small as a brick or even larger, is not permitted. A heap of stones that has not yet been shaped into a formal object is not permitted, much less a heap of dust or sand.
Likewise, a flat stone like a threshing-floor or a stone protruding from the ground like a stump is not permitted.
If it exists, that too is permissible provided it is of a measurable size. Even a back-rock (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*), though very large, is still reckoned as a rock;
therefore, if they wish to demarcate a single part of a large back-rock within the boundary, they should not demarcate that [part], but rather another rock should be demarcated upon it.
If they build a monastery around the back-rock, then by the middle of the monastery...
Or, if a back-slab passes through [the ground] after piercing it, such a back-slab is not permissible.

For if they were to mark that [slab], the monastery would be situated above the boundary marker; and since the boundary marker itself is outside the boundary, the monastery would also come to be outside the boundary.
A back-slab standing so as to encircle the monastery must be marked at one place and not marked elsewhere.
Regarding "a forest" (*vananimitta*): a forest of grass or a forest of trees such as *taca*, *sāra*, *tāla*, or coconut palms is not permitted.
However, a forest of trees with pithy wood, such as *sāka* or *sāla*, or trees containing pithy wood, is permitted;
provided that, at the very least, there are four or five trees, for less than that it is not permitted, but even up to a hundred leagues it is permitted. If...
However, if they are constructing a monastery in the middle of a forest, the forest itself should not be designated.
Even if they wish to designate a portion within the boundary (sīmā), they should designate the trees, rocks, and so forth therein, without designating the forest.
Having surrounded the monastery, the forest standing there should be designated in one place and not designated elsewhere.
Regarding the sign of a tree: a tree with only bark and sapwood, such as the *tāla* or coconut, is not permitted;
however, one that has inner heartwood while still alive is permitted, even if it is only eight finger-breadths in height or the size of a needle’s shaft in girth.
Anything smaller than that is not permitted, but even a well-established *nigrodha* tree twelve leagues in height is permitted. As for seeds in bamboo, reeds, bowls, and so forth—
Even if it has been planted and grown until it has reached its full size, it is not permissible [to consecrate it].

However, having removed it from there and replanted it in the ground at that very moment, having constructed a fence and poured water upon it, it is permissible to consecrate it. The emergence of new roots and branches is not a valid reason [for it to be considered established].
This, however, applies when it has been planted after cutting the trunk. And by the one who consecrates it, saying "tree,"...

It is permissible to say, “The *sāka* tree is also a *sāla* tree. However, it is not permissible to designate [a boundary] at one place and then designate it again elsewhere as a single continuous unit, such as a well-established banyan tree.
Regarding landmarks for the path—forests, fields, rivers, ponds, roads, and so forth are not permitted; rather, either a footpath or a cart-track [is allowed].
Or it is permissible for one who, having become disillusioned, travels two or three *gāmantara*s (distances between villages).
However, if a footpath descends from a cart-track and then re-enters that very same cart-track, or if there are footpaths and cart-tracks that are not accessible [to both], those are not permissible.
Only those footpaths and cart-tracks that are being used by both foot-travelers and carts are permissible. If there are two paths...

Having gone out, they later become one again like the yoke of a cart; whether at the place where they were split in two or at the place where they are joined, having once designated it, it should not be designated again, for this constitutes a single continuous boundary-mark (*ekābaddhanimitta*).
If four roads leading to the four directions encircle the monastery, having designated one in the middle—
It is not permissible to mark out the further side; for this constitutes a single continuous sign.
However, it is permissible to mark out the path that has been traversed after passing through a corner. But the path traversed by passing through the middle of a monastery must not be marked out;
if it were marked out, the monastery would be situated above the sign. If the sign is the track of the final wheel of a cart on a road...
If they mark the boundary on a road outside the monastery grounds, the road itself is outside the boundary;

the rest belongs to the interior of the boundary. When designating a road, it is permissible to designate it by any one of the ten names: "road" (maggo), "path" (pantho), "way" (patho), or "track" (pajjo). Having surrounded the monastery with a ditch in the shape of a moat...
Once a path has been designated in one place, it is not permissible to designate it elsewhere.
Regarding the ant-hill sign: as for the lower limit, even an ant-hill eight finger-breadths high, the size of a cow’s horn, that was formed on that very day is permissible;
anything smaller than that is not permissible, while anything larger—even one resembling the Himalaya mountains—is permissible. [Regarding] the monastery...
However, if [the boundary] stands as a single continuous enclosure, it is not permitted to recite the kamma at one place and then recite it elsewhere.

Regarding the river-marker: this refers to a river where, during the time of righteous kings, when the rain falls without exceeding the limits—either every half-month, every ten days, or every five days—and the flow is cut off as soon as the clouds have vanished. This is...
It does not count as a river. However, that stream which, even during such a period of good rainfall, does not have its flow interrupted for four months of the rainy season,
and which wets the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) of a nun who has covered her three circles and is crossing anywhere across it—
that counts as a river and serves as a boundary marker for those establishing a formal boundary (*sīmā*).
For a bhikkhunī, this same river applies even when crossing to the other side, when performing sangha formal acts such as the Uposatha, or when demarcating the boundary on the far side of the river.

However, if a river flows so as to encircle a monastery—either in the shape of a cart-track or a moat—it is not permissible to designate it in one place and then designate it again elsewhere. [This applies] to the four directions of the monastery.
The same method applies even when four rivers have flowed away from one another after being separated. However, it is permissible to designate all four as unmixed rivers.

If, like someone building a fence, they obstruct the river's current by planting stakes at the base of trees and binding them with creepers, straw, and so forth, such that the water is dammed up and the obstruction remains in place, it is permissible to establish the sign (*nimitta*).
However, just as water does not flow when a dam has been built, it is not permissible to establish the boundary mark (*nimitta*) for a river that is not flowing.
It is permissible to establish the river-mark at the place where it flows and the water-mark (*udakanimitta*) at the place where it does not flow.
But if, due to drought or during the summer heat, it does not flow because it is devoid of water, that is permissible. [This applies] from a great river...
They drain out the water from the reservoir; it becomes like a small stream and flows constantly, providing for three crops.

Although it flows thus, it is not permissible to establish a boundary marker. However, that which, though originally issuing from a great river at its source, later breaks through the riverbank by the same path it emerged and flows on its own—flowing further ahead, crowded with crocodiles and other such creatures—is [also considered a natural stream].
If there is a river that must be crossed by boat and so forth, it is permissible to make a mark for that purpose.
Regarding water-marks: it is not permissible to establish a water-mark by filling a place devoid of water with water using a boat, a bucket, or similar vessels;

it must be water already existing on the ground. Furthermore, this refers to water that does not flow away, such as that found in pits, lotus ponds, tanks, natural lakes, salt mines, the ocean, and so forth.
However, water that is stagnant—or water in flowing rivers, streams, canals, and the like—is not permissible.
In the *Andhaka-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Water that must be drawn up from deep pits and such should not be made the basis for the sign (*nimitta*).
This is poorly said and is merely one's own personal opinion. As for stagnant water, even if it is only enough to fill a pigsty, it is [permissible] for village children...
Even in the case of a pleasure pond, if at that very moment a pit is dug in the ground and filled with water brought in by jars,
it is permissible provided the water remains until the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā), whether it be little or much. However, in that place,
for the purpose of establishing a perception of the sign (nimitta-saññā), there should be a heap of stones, sand, soil, and so forth, or a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar.
It may be made; it is permissible for a monk both to make it himself and to have it made. However, it is not permissible within the boundary for the distribution of gains (*lābhasīmā*).
But the boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*) does not cause oppression to anyone; it merely effects the disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*) of the monks.
Therefore, it is permissible here.
It is indeed permissible to establish a boundary using these eight types of landmarks, whether they are unmixed or mutually mixed.
When established in this manner, that boundary is considered unbound if it is defined by only one or two landmarks;
however, starting from three, it is considered bound even by a hundred of the aforementioned types of landmarks. It may be triangular in shape, like a crossroads.
It may be square with four sides, or it may have the shape of a crossroads, a half-moon, a *mudiṅga* drum, or other such forms;

with more than those [sides], it may be of various shapes. Those desiring to bind it [the boundary] should ask the monks in the neighboring monasteries about the delimitation of the boundary for each respective monastery:

for monasteries where a boundary has already been bound, they should ask about the interval between boundaries (*sīmantarika*), and for monasteries where no boundary has been bound, they should ask about the precinct (*upacāra*) of the boundary.

Excepting the monks who travel from region to region during times when there is no movement of people, if they wish to establish a boundary within a single village district, they should send word to the monks in those monasteries where a boundary has already been established, saying: "We shall establish a boundary today;
you must not go outside the limits of your own boundaries. To the monks in those monasteries where no boundary has been established...
They should be assembled together, and the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it must be brought forward.
If they wish to include other village districts as well, the monks who reside in those villages must also come;
for those who do not come, their consent must be brought forward—thus said the Elder Mahāsumma. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma [said]: "As for what are called 'separate village districts'..."
"Individual boundaries (*pāṭekkā sīmā*) are like separate territories; consent (*chandā*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*) do not come from them.
However, monks who have gone within the boundary markers must return," he said, and then spoke again:

"At the time of delimiting a common-assembly boundary (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*), both coming and not coming are permissible. But at the time of delimiting a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), [monks] who have gone within the boundary markers..."
"Those who have not come must come; for those who do not come, their consent (chanda) must be brought.

When the monks have thus assembled and the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, [the boundary] should be established outside the monastery for the purpose of quickly bringing visiting monks within hand's reach at various paths, river crossings, village gates, and so forth, and for the purpose of establishing the outer boundary (bahisīmā).
Excluding the monastery attendants and the novice monks, having given the signal by means of a drum or a conch shell,

the boundary should be bound with the formal proclamation beginning with "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs," as stated immediately after the description of the marks. At the very conclusion of the formal proclamation,
the boundary is established by excluding the marks from the outside and taking as its limit the water below that supports the earth.

Now, when those who are establishing this common boundary (samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā), they should first establish a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) for the sake of facilitating the formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the rites of going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā). Those establishing it, however, must understand the proper procedure (vatta).
For if they were to establish it in a monastery built after all sites—such as the Bodhi tree shrine, the dining hall, and so forth—have already been established, [it would be improper].
They should not be tied in the middle of the monastery or in a place where many people gather, but should be tied in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery.

When tying them in a monastery that has not yet been built, those who do so should first observe the locations for all sites, such as the Bodhi tree and the shrine, and then tie them in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery, ensuring it is a place that will remain secluded once the sites are established. At the very least, they should be [placed]...
If he takes twenty-one monks, it is permissible; less than that is not permissible, but even if he takes more than a thousand monks, it is permissible.
Those who are binding it must place boundary-marking stones around the precinct of the boundary-marked area (*sīmāmāḷaka*).

One should not bind a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) by standing within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), nor a partial boundary by standing within a great boundary; [this applies] only within a partial boundary.

However, a *khaṇḍasīmā* (small boundary) should be established by standing within it, and a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) by standing within the *mahāsīmā* itself. The procedure for establishing it is as follows:
having designated the boundary marks all around, saying, "This rock is a boundary mark," the boundary should be formally authorized by means of the *kammavācā*.
Then, for the purpose of strengthening that very boundary, the *avippavāsa-kammavācā* (the formal act regarding non-separation) [should be performed].
It must be done in this way; for if they have come thinking, "We shall abolish the boundary," they will not be able to abolish it [if it has not been properly established].
After the boundary has been formally established, stones should be placed outside the boundary. A space of one *ratana* at the western limit of the boundary is permissible;
a space of one span (*vidatthi*) is also permissible according to the *Kurundi*; a space of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) is also permissible according to the *Mahāpaccarī*.
It has been said. However, if the monastery is large, two, three, or even more than that *khaṇḍasīmā*s (fragmentary boundaries) should be established.

Having thus designated the *khaṇḍasīmā*, at the time of the formal authorization for the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary), they should exit from the *khaṇḍasīmā* and, standing within the *mahāsīmā*, walk around it on all sides while designating the boundary-stone markers (*sīmantarika-pāsāṇa*). Then, the remaining boundary markers...

Having recited the boundary markers while not departing from hand’s reach, and having formally designated the common-residence boundary (*samānasamvāsaka-sīmā*) by means of the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*), one should also perform the ritual proclamation for non-separation (*avippavāsa-kammavācā*) in order to strengthen that [boundary].
For in this way, those who have come with the intention, “We shall abolish the boundary,” will not be able to abolish it.
However, if, after reciting the boundary markers of a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), [one proceeds] from there to the intermediate boundary (*sīmantarikā*)—
Having designated the markers for the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), they designate the markers for the [other] boundaries;

thus, having designated the markers in these three places, it is permissible to bind first that boundary which they desire. Even so, according to the method already stated, it should be bound starting from the fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
However, once the boundaries have been bound in this manner, those standing within the fragmentary boundary...
Monks who are performing an act within the great boundary do not invalidate it; nor do those standing within the great boundary invalidate an act being performed within a broken boundary.
However, those standing in the intermediate space (sīmantarikā) invalidate the acts of both.
But those standing in the village precinct invalidate an act being performed by monks standing within the village precinct, for the intermediate space belongs to the village precinct.
Furthermore, this so-called *sīmā* is not bound only on the surface of the earth;
rather, it is indeed bound even on the back of a rock, in a hut, in a cave, in a palace, or on the summit of a mountain.
In that regard, when binding it on the back of a rock, one should not establish a boundary-mark (*nimitta*) by carving a line on the rock surface or by digging a mortar-hole.
It should be done as follows: having placed stones at the boundary marks, the marks should be designated.
At the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), the boundary descends, making the water that supports the earth its limit.
Since the boundary-mark stones do not remain in their original positions, therefore either a line should be raised all around, or stones should be driven into the four corners.

Having said, "This is the boundary delimitation," the letters should be cut out. Some envious people, thinking, "We shall burn down the boundary," set fire to it; however, only the stones burn, not the boundary.
Even when building a house with a hut, one should not omit the wall, [ensuring] that the space for twenty-one bhikkhus is within.
Having made stone markers and established them, the boundary should be formally designated; the boundary exists only within the walls.
If there is no space for twenty-one monks within the walls, it should be designated after placing markers on the stones at the entrance.
If even this is not sufficient, it should be designated after placing markers even at the place where the drainage water falls outside.
When it has been thus agreed upon, however, the entire hut or house becomes established within the boundary.

Even in the case of a cave with four walls, those performing the demarcation should not mark the plastered walls, but rather the stones themselves. If there is no space inside, the markers should be placed at the entrance.
If that is not possible, they may even be placed outside at the spot where water drips down.
Having placed boundary stones and designated the markers, the boundary should be formally established. In this way, the boundary exists both inside and outside the cave.
On an upper story of a palace as well, the boundary should be established by placing boundary stones inside without designating the walls.

If that is not possible, it should be established by placing boundary stones even at the front entrance. When established in this manner, it belongs only to the upper story of the palace, not to the area below.

It does not descend. However, if in the case of many pillars, a wall on the lower floor of a palace built upon beams stands so that it is within the limits of the signs, being erected and fixed as one continuous unit with the beam-pillars, then even below, it descends.
But if a boundary is tied to the upper floor of a palace with a single pillar, [and] at the top of the pillar, among twenty-one...

If there is space for the monks, it descends below. If they bind the boundary by placing stones on the eaves and other projections that extend out from the walls of the palace, the palace wall is within the boundary.

However, whether it descends or does not descend below that [wall] should be understood according to the method already stated. Even when the lower part of the palace is being measured, the wall and the wooden pillars are not [included].
It should be marked. However, it is permissible to mark [the boundary] on stone pillars fixed to the wall.
When thus marked, the boundary lies strictly within the boundary pillars of the lower story of the palace.
But if the wall of the lower story is connected with the upper floor, it extends upward into the upper story as well. If, outside the palace, at the place where water falls...
They establish the boundary markers, and the entire palace comes to lie within the boundary.
On the mountain summit there is a level area sufficient for twenty-one bhikkhus; there they bind the boundary as if on a flat rock.
The boundary extends down to the lower mountain by that same demarcation. It also extends to the Tālamūlaka mountain.

A boundary fixed above descends below. However, in the case of one shaped like a canopy (*vitāna*), where there is space for twenty-one monks above but none below, the boundary fixed above does not descend below.
Likewise, whether it be shaped like a drum (*mudiṅga*) or shaped like a small drum (*paṇava*), if the measurement of the boundary exists either below or in the middle—
There is none; the boundary fixed above it does not descend below at all.

However, for one whose two peaks stand close together and the space above even one of them is insufficient for the measure of the boundary, the boundary should be formally established above after the space between the peaks has been built up, filled in, or made into a single connected whole.
There is a mountain resembling the hood of a cobra; because it exists above the area of the boundary, they establish the boundary [around it].
If there is a hollow space beneath it, the boundary does not descend into it. However, if in its center there is a porous rock the size of the boundary, it does descend.
And that rock remains strictly within the boundary. Furthermore, even if below it there is a cave...
The wall stands touching the very tip [of the roof]; it descends, and there is only the boundary both below and above.
However, if there is a cave inside from the far side of the upper boundary’s limit, the boundary does not descend outside.
Or again, if there is a cave outside from the near side of the upper boundary’s limit, the boundary does not enter inside. Or again...
Above the boundary, the demarcation is small; below, the cave is large and stands beyond the limit of the boundary.

In this case, the boundary exists only above and does not descend below. However, if the cave is small—measuring no more than the very last extent of the boundary—and the boundary above is large, standing so as to encompass it, then the boundary descends. But if the cave is too small...
It does not reach the full measure of the boundary; the boundary remains only above and does not extend downward.

If even half of it breaks off and falls away, then even if it reaches the measure of the boundary, that which has fallen outside is not part of the boundary. However, if that which has not fallen does reach the measure of the boundary, it certainly remains the boundary.
A boundary that has a low base becomes high once it is filled up; it remains the boundary itself.
If one builds a house within the boundary, it belongs to those who stand within the boundary. If one digs a lotus pond within the boundary, it remains the boundary itself.

When a flood overflows the circle of the boundary and flows away, it is permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) after erecting a watchtower (*aṭṭa*) within the precinct of the boundary. Below the boundary...

There may be a river; if a bhikkhu possessing supernormal power sits there, and if the river flowed there first and the boundary was subsequently bound, it does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*).
However, if the boundary was bound first and the river flowed there afterwards, it invalidates the formal act.
But if he stands on the surface of the earth below, he certainly invalidates it.
At the boundary-mark there is a banyan tree; its branches or the shoots emerging from them reach down to touch the ground within the great boundary, or trees growing there and so forth touch it.
Having cleared the area of the great boundary, the formal act (kamma) should be performed;
or else those branches and shoots should be cut off and placed outside. If a monk climbs onto branches and such that do not touch [the ground], [he is not considered to have entered].

It must be brought within arm’s reach. Thus, if a branch or a sprout of a *jāta*-tree grows within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), it must be established within the boundary enclosure (*sīmāmāḷaka*) in the manner already described;
or, having cleared the boundary in the manner already described, the formal act (*kamma*) may be performed;
or those branches and sprouts must be cut off and placed outside.

If, while the work at the boundary enclosure (*sīmāmāḷaka*) is being performed, any monk enters within the boundary enclosure and sits on a branch suspended in the air, or his feet touch the ground, or his lower garment (*nivāsana*) or upper robe (*pārupana*) touches the ground, it is not permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
However, it is permissible to perform it after having him lift his feet and his lower and upper robes. And this—
The characteristic should be understood according to the previous method. However, this is the distinction:
there, it is not permitted to do so after having caused [the object] to be lifted up; it must be brought within arm’s reach.

If a mountain rises up from within the boundary, the monk standing there must be brought within arm’s reach. Even if one has entered inside the mountain by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), the same rule applies. While being bound...

For in this way, a boundary does not enter a place that lacks a fixed measure. Whatever has arisen within a formally established boundary (baddhasīmā), wherever it may be, if it is connected as one, it is reckoned simply as being within the boundary.
140. Regarding the phrase "not exceeding three yojanas": here, "three yojanas" is its maximum measure; thus, it is "that which has three yojanas as its maximum. That...

The maximum [extent] is three *yojanas*. However, when appointing [the boundary], one should stand in the center and appoint it in such a way that there is one and a half *yojanas* in each of the four directions.
But if, standing in the center, they were to make it three *yojanas* from each direction, it would become six *yojanas*, which is not permitted.
When appointing a square or a triangle, [one must ensure] from the corner...

A corner is three *yojanas*; it should be authorized in this way. For if, by any boundary whatsoever, it exceeds even a hair’s breadth beyond three *yojanas*, one incurs an offense and the boundary becomes a non-boundary.

Regarding "the river-crossing" (*nadīpāra*): here, that which carries across is a "crossing" (*pāra*). What does it carry across? The river. The crossing of a river is a "river-crossing" (*nadīpāra*); that [is what is meant].
"To the further shore of the river"; the meaning is "overflowing the river.
And here, the definition of a river is exactly as stated in the section on river-boundaries.

"Where there is a permanent boat" means where, at the fords located at the boundary-marking places of the river, there is a boat that is constantly used for crossing, which—at the very least—can carry three people along with a steersman.

It carries people across. However, if that boat has been taken upstream or downstream for some business with the intention of returning again, or if it has been seized by thieves, it is certainly recoverable;

but that which has been carried to the middle of the river by the wind or by waves because its moorings were severed is certainly not to be recovered, and it remains merely a drifting boat. Even when the water has receded and it has been hauled onto dry land...
Even if it is filled with lime-paste and the like and set up, it is indeed a permanent boat (*dhuvanāvā*).
If it is broken or its planks are disassembled, it is not permissible. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said:

"Even if they bring a temporary boat, place it at the site where the boundary is to be bound, and then mark the signs, it is still considered a permanent boat. Regarding this, the Elder Mahāsiva said: "The sign..."
Or it goes by way of the boundary or by way of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), not by boat. Since a permanent boat was permitted by the Blessed One, therefore only a fixed boat is allowable.
"Or a permanent bridge" means where there is a bridge made of a collection of trees, or one bound with planks, or a footpath-bridge for elephants and the like.

There must be a great bridge fit for people to cross; or, at the very least, even a footpath-bridge made by cutting down a tree at that very moment counts as a permanent bridge if it is fit for people to walk upon.
However, if one cannot cross it even by holding onto creepers, rattan, or similar materials tied above, it is not permissible.

"To designate such a river-bank boundary" means: I authorize the designation of such a river-bank boundary where there exists, precisely at the landing place facing [the monastery], either a permanent boat or a permanent bridge; this is the meaning.
If neither a permanent boat nor a permanent bridge exists at the landing place facing [the monastery], having ascended slightly further upstream...
Or, having descended below, it exists; in this way as well, it is permissible. However, the Elder Karavīkatissa said, "It is permissible even within the space of a *gāvuta*.

Furthermore, by one who is demarcating this river-bank boundary, standing on one bank and having designated a landmark on the upper stream bank, he should then surround himself starting from there, and whatever extent of boundary he desires—of that...
At the lower end, having marked a sign on the riverbank, one should mark a sign on the opposite bank directly facing it.
From there, according to whatever extent of boundary one desires,
one should mark signs along the riverbank as far as the upper end, directly facing the first sign that was marked, and then return.

It should be joined with the first-mentioned boundary marker. Then, having brought all the monks standing within the boundary markers into hand’s reach, the boundary should be authorized by means of the formal act (*kammavācā*). Those standing in the river, even if they have not yet arrived, do not invalidate the act.
At the conclusion of the authorization, excluding the river itself, [the area] on both the opposite bank and this side of the boundary markers [is defined].
And it becomes a single boundary. However, a river does not fall under the category of a "bound boundary" (*baddhasīmā*); rather, it is simply a river boundary (*nadisīmā*) in its own right.

If there is an island within the river, and one wishes to include it within the boundary, then—just as in the previous method—one should mark the boundary signs on the bank where one is standing oneself, and also mark a boundary sign on both the near shore and the far shore of the island. Then...
Having designated the sign on the opposite bank of the river at the spot directly facing the original sign,
one should then designate signs starting from there in the same manner as before, all the way upstream until reaching the sign first designated at the mouth of the stream.
Then, having designated the signs at both the far and near ends of the island, and having returned [to the start], one should [proceed] with the first designated sign.

It should be joined together. Then, having brought both banks, the island, and all the monks within arm’s reach, the boundary (sīmā) should be formally established by means of the ritual proclamation (kammavācā).
Those standing in the river who do not come [to join] do not invalidate the act.
At the conclusion of the formal authorization, with the exception of the river itself, the two banks and the island constitute a single boundary; however, the river remains simply the river-boundary.
If, however, the island is larger than the boundary of the monastery— either extending above or below it—
then one should mark a sign directly facing the sign that marks the monastery boundary on the near edge of the island; starting from there, while encircling the peak of the island,
one should again mark a sign on the far edge directly opposite the sign on the near edge.
Thereafter, in the same manner as before, having first identified the landmark on the opposite bank facing him,
and having designated the landmarks of the opposite bank as well as the landmarks for the near and far edges of the island,
a connection must be made with the previously designated landmark. Having thus designated it, the boundary is established as a mountain range.
If, however, the island extends further both above and below the boundary of the monastery grounds,
the delimitation of the signs must be performed by encircling both peaks of the island with signs, using the same method as before.
Having thus designated it, the boundary established is in the shape of a drum (mudiṅga).

If an island is within the boundary limits of the monastery and is small, the boundary markers must be designated on that island according to the very first method. Having thus designated them, the formally established boundary takes the shape of a drum.
The discussion on the authorization of boundaries is concluded.
Now follows the discussion on the Uposatha hall and so forth.

141. *Anupariveṇiyaṃ* means in each respective cell within a great monastery that shares a single boundary. *Asaṅketena* means without having made a prior agreement. *Ekaṃ samūhanitvā* means having abolished it by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*). 142. *Yato pātimokkhaṃ suṇātīti*:
because one hears the Pātimokkha while sitting within arm’s reach of the monks, wherever that may be;
the meaning is, "From whom has his Uposatha been performed? This is stated by way of the actual matter (*vatthu*), [referring to] being within arm’s reach.
However, even if one is seated and does not hear it, the Uposatha is indeed performed. Regarding the "proclamation of signs":

it is permissible to designate any sign whatsoever—whether small or large, such as stones, bricks, pieces of wood, staves, and so forth—as a marker for the Uposatha leader, having established a clear recognition of it anywhere, whether in the open air or within a hall and the like. Alternatively, [one may do so by means of a boundary flag].
"The signs should be proclaimed" means that they should be proclaimed—whether they possess signs or are signless—for the purpose of knowing the boundaries.
Regarding the phrase "those bhikkhus should assemble first," if the Elder does not arrive first, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the phrase "the Uposatha should be performed by all having assembled together," if...
If there is an ancient dwelling in the middle of the monastery that is capable of providing a place for the monks to sit,
the Uposatha should be performed after assembling there. If the ancient dwelling is both dilapidated and cramped,
and another dwelling established later is not cramped, the Uposatha should be performed there.

Or, regarding the phrase "wherever an elder monk dwells": here too, if the elder’s dwelling is sufficient for everyone and is comfortable, the Uposatha should be performed there. But if that dwelling is in a border region or on uneven ground, the elder should be told:
"Venerable sir, your dwelling is in an uncomfortable location; it is not possible for everyone [to stay] here."
“There is space; there is space in such-and-such a residence, so it is proper to go there.
If the Elder does not come, one should bring his consent and purity, and the Uposatha should be performed by all in a comfortable place that can accommodate everyone.
This concludes the discussion on the authorization of the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).
143. Regarding "Andhakavinda": three *gāvutas* from Rājagaha is the place named Andhakavinda;
the Elder dwelt there, and from there he was coming to Rājagaha for the Uposatha.

Indeed, all eighteen great monasteries surrounding Rājagaha constitute a single boundary (*ekasīmā*), a boundary established by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta); therefore, [the Elder joined] the Saṅgha at Veḷuvana.
The meaning is: "He came for the purpose of giving alms in a group. "Crossing the river" means crossing over the river named Sippi.

"He was carried away by the current" means he had almost reached the state of being swept away. It is said that the river, having descended from Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa), flows with a violent current;
there, the Elder, not paying attention to the water coming with such force, [was carried away].
It was soaked, yet not actually ruined; his robes became wet, having been struck by the water.

144. From the moment this formal act (*kammavācā*)—“This boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a non-separation from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts”—arises, the previous formal acts of the bhikkhus are no longer valid.
For this [robe] alone is indeed permanent. However, for bhikkhunīs, this one is not permitted; only the former is permitted. Why?

Because the bhikkhunī-saṅgha dwells within the village. If it were otherwise, she would not receive the privilege of the three robes through this formal act (kammavācā), yet there is such a privilege for her;
therefore, only the former is permitted. For the bhikkhunī-saṅgha...
Two boundaries may be established. Therein, it is permissible to establish a boundary for the bhikkhunīs even by encompassing the boundary of the bhikkhus;
the same principle applies to the boundary of the bhikkhus within the boundary of the bhikkhunīs.

For they do not serve as the quorum-filling members for each other’s formal acts (*kamma*), nor do they constitute a quorum for the formal act itself. And in this regard, [the same applies to] villages and cities as well.
The inclusion [of these] should be understood as being like that of a village.

"Village precinct" (*gāmūpacāra*) refers to the enclosure of an enclosed village, or the area where an enclosure would stand for an unenclosed one. A monk who has resolved upon his three robes (*adhiṭṭhitatecīvarika*) does not receive the privilege [of being outside the boundary] with respect to those two.
Thus, the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) for monks consists of both the village and the village precinct.
It does not extend [beyond]; it extends only as far as the boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*).

And here, the boundary of common affiliation proceeds according to its own inherent nature. However, the boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) proceeds exactly where the boundary of common affiliation is;
for there is no separate designation of signs for it. In that regard, if at the time of the formal authorization (*sammuti*) for non-separation, a village...
There is [an area], which she does not cover. However, if a village is settled later within a boundary that has already been authorized, that too comes to be counted as part of the boundary.
And just as with what is settled later, so also an area that has expanded after being first settled comes to be counted as part of the boundary.
Even if houses have already been built at the time of the authorization of the boundary, [they do not invalidate it].
There is the attachment [of the thought], "I shall enter," yet people have not entered;

or perhaps they have abandoned the ancient village or their own homes and gone elsewhere, so that this is indeed a non-village (*agāma*), and the boundary (*sīmā*) covers it. However, if there is even a single family that has entered or returned, it is indeed a village, and the boundary does not cover it.
And furthermore, monks, in this matter of abolishing the non-separation from the three robes, the monk who is abolishing it must know the proper procedure (*vatta*). Herein, this is the procedure:
standing within a minor boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*) must not be abolished;
likewise, standing within the non-separation boundary, the minor boundary must not be abolished. However, by one standing within a minor boundary, only the minor boundary [is to be abolished].
It must be abolished; likewise, while standing within one boundary, the other must be abolished. They abolish a boundary for two reasons:

either because it was originally small and they wish to make it large again for the sake of expanding the residence, or because it was originally large and they wish to make it small again for the sake of giving space for other monasteries.
In that regard, if both the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*)...

Those who know [the boundary] will be able both to abolish and to establish it. Furthermore, those who know the *khaṇḍasīma* (broken boundary) but do not know the *avippavāsa* (non-separation) will also be able both to abolish and to establish it.

Those who do not know the *khaṇḍasīma* but do know the *avippavāsa*, standing in places free from apprehension such as the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*), the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa*), or the Uposatha hall (*uposathāgāra*), might perhaps...
They will be able to abolish it, but they will certainly not be able to bind it.
If they were to bind it, they would create a division of the boundary and turn a monastery (*vihāra*) into a non-monastery; therefore, it must not be abolished.

However, those who do not know both [the rules] will be unable to abolish it nor to bind it by that very fact. For this so-called "boundary" (*sīmā*) is established by means of a formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*).
Or, it becomes non-boundary either through the disappearance of the Teaching, or because it is not possible for those who do not know the boundary to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*);

therefore, it need not be dismantled. However, having thoroughly understood [the situation], it should indeed be dismantled and re-established. This concludes the discussion on village boundaries and so forth.

147. Having thus demonstrated both the state of common residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and the state of a single *uposatha* by means of a delimited boundary (*baddhasīmā*), he now speaks the passage beginning with “Monks, when a boundary has not been authorized and not established,” in order to demonstrate that same state even in places where no boundary has been delimited.
In this context, “not established” (*aṭṭhapitā*) means not demarcated (*aparicchinnā*). Furthermore, by the mention of a “village” (*gāma*) here, a “city” (*nagara*) is also included. Therein...
Whatever area of that village the lords receive as tax—whether that area be small or large—it is reckoned simply as the village boundary.
This same principle applies to the boundaries of cities and market towns (*nigama*).

Furthermore, even if the king, having demarcated a certain portion within the field of a single village, gives it to someone [else] saying, "Let this be a separate village," [that portion is still included].

That too is indeed the boundary of a separate village. Therefore, both that [boundary] and the other—namely, the natural boundaries of villages, towns, and market towns—are exactly like established boundaries;
however, they do not receive the exemption from being separated from the three robes.
Having thus shown the delimitation of the boundary for those living within a village, he now shows the delimitation of the boundary for forest-dwellers:
He said, “And if it is in a non-village,” and so forth. Therein, “and if it is in a non-village” means in a wilderness region not delimited by the boundaries of a village, market town, or city.
Alternatively, “and if it is in a non-village” means that a bhikkhu dwells in a forest resembling a thicket of reeds; then, the area extending seven *abbhantara*s (approx.

280 meters) all around his standing place constitutes the boundary for common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*). This boundary also serves as a protection against the offense of being separated from one’s three robes.
He obtains it. Therein, one *abbhantara* measures twenty-eight cubits (*hattha*).
For one standing in the middle, there are seven *abbhantaras* on each side, making fourteen in total by way of depth.
If two Saṅghas perform separate legal acts (*vinayakamma*), another *abbhantara* between the two sets of seven *abbhantaras* is for the purpose of the boundary (*upacāra*).

It should be set aside. The remaining discussion regarding the seven inner boundaries should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Udositasi-kkhāpada* in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.
"All rivers, monks, are without boundaries"—whatever river possesses the characteristics of a river, having designated its landmarks, [one should say]: "This..."
Even if one says, "I shall establish a boundary," it remains a non-boundary;
however, by its very nature, it resembles a bound boundary, and it is permissible to perform all *saṅghakamma* (formal acts of the Saṅgha) therein.

The same principle applies to oceans and natural lakes (*jātassara*). Here, a "natural lake" refers to a pool that has not been dug by anyone, but is formed naturally and remains filled with water flowing in from all directions.

Having thus rejected the notion that rivers, oceans, and natural lakes possess fixed boundaries, he spoke the passage beginning with “In a river, monks,” etc., to further demonstrate the absence of fixed boundaries therein. In this context,
“the range of a splash of water all around for a man of medium height” refers to that area delimited by the splash of water from a man of medium height on all sides.
But how should the water be thrown? Just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so should one take water or sand in the hand and throw it with all the strength of a man of medium build.
Wherever that thrown water or sand falls, this constitutes one "throw of water" (*udakukkhepa*). Within its range, up to the distance of a handspan (*hatthapāsa*), [one may dig].
Having left [the assembly], he stands and causes a disturbance in the formal act (*kamma*). As long as the assembly increases, so too does the boundary (*sīmā*) increase.
The measure is simply the distance of a water-splash from the edge of the assembly. This same principle applies to natural lakes and the ocean as well.
And here, if a river is not very long, the Saṅgha may [perform the act] everywhere from its source up to its mouth.
He sits down; there is no act of establishing a boundary by throwing water, for the entire river belongs to these very monks.

As for what was stated by the Elder Mahāsumma—that "even in the case of a river flowing for a *yojana*, it is permissible to perform the ritual after leaving half a *yojana* above and below"—that was refuted by the Elder Mahāpaduma himself.

For the Blessed One stated this as the measure of a river: "Wherever a bhikkhunī crosses while covering the three circles [of her body], if her inner robe becomes wet, it is a river. This does not refer to a *yojana* or half a *yojana*.
Therefore, regarding a river that possesses the characteristics previously mentioned according to this sutta, one may perform a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) starting from its source.

"It is permissible. However, if many monks perform the ritual separately here, they must all establish another boundary for the throwing of water between their own and others' boundaries for the purpose of marking the limit (sīmāntara).
More than that is indeed permissible; however, it is stated that less than that is not permissible. The same principle applies to natural lakes and oceans as well.

However, when those who have gone to a river thinking, "We shall perform the ritual there," find that the river is full and level with its banks, they should perform the ritual within the river itself even while wearing their bathing robes (*udakasāṭikā*).
If they are unable to do so, it may be performed even while standing in a boat.
But it is not permitted to perform it in a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary (*sīmā*) extends only as far as the splash of water; therefore—
A boat passes through [the boundary] very quickly. This being the case, there would be a motion (*ñatti*) for one boundary and a proclamation (*anusāvanā*) for another;
therefore, having moored the boat with a rudder, or having it weighed down with stones, or having it tied to a tree growing within the river, the formal act (*kamma*) should be performed.
It is permissible for those standing on a raft tied within the river or on a tree growing within the river to perform it.

If, however, the branch of a tree or a shoot emerging from it is established on the outer bank of a river, or within the boundary of a monastery (*vihāra-sīmā*), or within the boundary of a village (*gāma-sīmā*),
the formal act (*kamma*) must be performed after either clearing the boundary or cutting off the branch.
Or, in the case of a tree grown on the outer bank of a river, one may tie a boat to its branch or shoot that has entered into the inner part of the river.
It is not permissible to perform [the formal act]. Those performing it must either clear the boundary or destroy its status by cutting it so that it stands outside.
However, in the case of a boat moored at a riverbank after a stake has been driven into the ground, it is likewise not permissible.
If they build a bridge over a river, whether the bridge or the bridge-piers are entirely within the river, for those standing upon the bridge—

It is permissible to perform the ritual action. However, if the bridge or the bridge-piers are established on the outer bank, it is not permissible to perform the ritual action; the boundary must be cleared away before it is done.
If the bridge-piers are on the inner side, while the bridge itself stands in the air above both banks, it is permissible. If there is a rock or an island within the river, as much of that area as...
During the four months of the rainy season at the time of the natural rains as previously described, the water covers [the area] and it is reckoned simply as a river.
However, in the case of excessive rain, the place covered by a flood must not be accepted;
for that is reckoned only as a village boundary.
When they are removing the source from the river, they create a dam in the river;
if the water flows over it or through it, it is permissible to perform the work everywhere the water flows.
But if the flow is cut off by the dam or by the construction of a weir, and the water does not flow, then at the place where it does not flow—
It is not permissible to perform construction work. It is also not permissible to build a dam.
However, if a site for a dam is completely submerged by water—just like the previously mentioned rocky island site—it is permissible there;
for that place is then merely counted as a river. They destroy the river and construct a reservoir, and having built an embankment below, the water...
If it comes and remains filling the pond, it is not permitted to perform work there.
It is permitted starting from the place where water, having overflowed the river from below after being discarded at the upper point of flow, begins to flow down.
Even in a dry river during the winter or summer when the rain has ceased, it is permitted. However, it is not permitted for a channel dug out from the river.

If, after some time, it breaks apart and becomes a river, it is permissible. If a certain river, after some time, rises up and flows so as to overflow the boundaries of a village or town, it remains a river and it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
However, if it overflows the boundary of a monastery (*vihāra*), it is reckoned simply as the monastery’s boundary.
Even in the ocean, those performing the work must not do so in a place where the rising tide or natural waves come with force and inundate it.
However, that area where the natural waves, having inundated it, settle down is called the "inner sea" starting from the water's edge; those standing there may perform the work.
If the force of the waves is oppressive, one should perform the act while standing on a boat or a platform.

The detailed analysis regarding these should be understood according to the method already stated for rivers. In the case of the ocean, there is a "back-rock" (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*); sometimes the waves come and wash over it, and sometimes they do not.
It is not permissible to perform the act there, for that place is considered merely as the village boundary (*gāmasīma*).
However, if it is submerged by its natural water even when waves have arrived or not yet arrived, it is permissible.
Or if there is an island or a mountain, if it is distant and not on a path accessible to fishermen, it is reckoned as a forest boundary (*arañña-sīmā*).
But within the limit of their access, it is reckoned as a village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*). Regarding the village boundary therein:

It is not permissible to perform formal acts (kamma) after having filled [the area]. If the ocean stands having overflowed the boundary of a village or the boundary of a town, it remains simply the ocean;
it is permissible to perform formal acts there. However, if it overflows the monastery boundary (vihārasīma), it is reckoned simply as the monastery boundary.

Even for those performing work at a natural pond (*jātassara*), if during the rainy season—of the kind previously described—the rain has just ceased and there is no water available for drinking or for washing one’s hands and feet, and it dries up, this is not a natural pond;
it merely counts as village-field land, and work should not be performed there. However, where water remains standing during the rainy season of the aforementioned type, [it is a natural pond].
This is the Jātassara lake. In whatever area of it the water remains during the four months of the rains, it is permissible to perform work there.
If the water is deep, one may build a platform (aṭṭaka) and perform work even while standing upon it;
this applies even to a platform built on a tree growing within the Jātassara. However, regarding the Piṭṭhipāsāṇa and Dīpaka rocks here in the river—

The analysis is exactly as stated [above]. However, if a pond that is capable of holding water during the time of the uniform rains dries up during a period of drought, or in the summer or winter seasons, and becomes devoid of water, it is permissible to perform a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) there.
As for what is stated in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*: "When every pond is dried up and without water, it belongs exclusively to the village precinct."

That [area] should not be included. However, if they dig a pit or a lotus pond and so forth here for the sake of water, that place becomes an "unborn lake" (*ajātassara*) and is reckoned as part of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
