The same principle applies even when a hedge of *lābu*, *tipusa*, and so forth is planted.
But if, after filling it, they turn it into dry land, or if they build an embankment on one side, then the entire area— [is reckoned as part of the village boundary.]
They construct that great pond, and even though it is entirely a natural lake (*ajātassara*), it is reckoned as a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
A salt-water pool is likewise reckoned as a natural lake. It is permissible to perform work on the site of the water during the four months of the rainy season.
148. "They join one boundary to another" means they join their own boundary to a boundary already established by others.
For if, to the east of an ancient monastery, there are two trees— an *amba* tree and a *jambu* tree—
whose branches are intertwined with one another, and if among them the *jambu* is on the western side of the *amba*,
and the monastery boundary has been established by including the *jambu* within it and excluding the *amba*, then later, to the east of that monastery...
When they establish a monastery in a certain direction and bind a boundary, they do so by including that mango tree within it and excluding the rose-apple tree;
thus the boundary becomes intermingled with another boundary. This is what the group of six (Chabbaggiyas) did, which is why it is said:
"they cause one boundary to intermingle with another. "They cause one boundary to overlap another" means they cause their own boundary to overlap a boundary bound by others.
They bind their own boundary, making either the entire area already bound by others, or a portion of it, the interior.

Regarding the phrase "having set aside the interval between boundaries, they should establish the boundary": here, if the boundary of the monastery established earlier has not yet been formally approved (*sammata*), the precinct of that boundary must be set aside. If it has been approved, [the precinct] from its western limit...
A space the size of a hand should be left between the boundaries. In the *Kurundi*, it is stated that even a span’s width is permissible;
in the *Mahāpaccarī*, even a space of four finger-breadths is said to be suitable. Furthermore, even a single tree can serve as the marker for two boundaries;
however, as it grows, it causes a confusion of boundaries, and therefore one should not do this.
149. Discussion on the Breaking of the Uposatha, etc.
Regarding the terms "fourteenth-day" and "fifteenth-day": here, for the preliminary duties of the fourteenth-day [Uposatha], one should say, "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha.
In the cases such as "a faction by means of what is not Dhamma," if there are four monks living in a single monastery, [one should take] the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*) of one...
If, having brought [the consent] of three, they perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, or if, while three are present,
they bring the consent and *pārisuddhi* of one and two recite the *Pātimokkha*, it is an illegal and incomplete Uposatha act. However,
if all four have assembled and perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, or if three or two recite the *Pātimokkha*, [it is valid].

By illegality, it is called "unanimous. If, among four persons, they recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the purity of one person, or if, among three persons, they perform the Uposatha of purity after bringing the purity of one person, it is called "legally incomplete.
However, if four persons living together all assemble...
They recite the *pātimokkha*; they perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* in three ways; they perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* by mutual declaration to one another;
this is called a legal and harmonious assembly.
This is the Discourse on the Reciter of the *Pātimokkha*.
150. Having recited the introduction, the remainder should be announced by means of the hearing: "Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me...
[as before] ...for when it has been disclosed, there is ease for him. Having recited this introduction—"Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited;
therefore I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask... [as before] ...thus do I understand this"—[the rest follows].
"Furthermore, the four *pārājika* rules have been heard by the Venerable Ones... [as before] ...they should train without disputing.
In this manner, the remainder should be announced by means of what has been heard (*suta*). By this same method, the remaining four recitations of the *Pātimokkha* are also to be understood.
Regarding "danger from savages," this refers to the danger of wild men in the forest. Regarding "obstacles such as kings," if among the monks there is the thought, "We shall perform the Uposatha..."
When they are seated, the king arrives—this is an obstacle caused by the king. Robbers arrive—this is an obstacle caused by robbers.
A forest fire approaches, or a fire breaks out in the dwelling—this is an obstacle caused by fire. A cloud arises, or a flood comes—this is an obstacle caused by water.
Many people arrive—this is an obstacle caused by people. [A] monk...
A *yakkha* seizes him; this is an obstacle caused by non-human beings (*amanussa*). Fierce wild animals such as tigers and the like approach;
this is an obstacle caused by beasts of prey (*vāḷa*). Snakes and the like bite the bhikkhu; this is an obstacle caused by reptiles (*sarīsapa*).
The bhikkhu becomes ill, or passes away, or his enemies seize him, desiring to kill him; this is an obstacle to life (*jīvita*). People [seize] one...
Or many monks may seize them, desiring to cause them to fall away from the holy life; this is an obstacle to the holy life.
In the event of such obstacles, the Pātimokkha should be recited in brief, or the first section should be recited, or two, three, or four sections at the beginning.
And herein, among the second and subsequent sections, if an obstacle arises before a section has been completed, [the recitation should be concluded].
He too should be informed by the son himself.
"Without being requested" means not being commanded or not being asked. And here, the request belongs either to the Dhamma-requester authorized by the Saṅgha or to the Elder of the Saṅgha;
in the absence of that Dhamma-requester, it is done after having consulted the Elder of the Saṅgha.
If requested by him, he may speak. Even by the senior of the Sangha, if there are many preachers of the Dhamma in the monastery, they should be addressed in turn:
"You, preach the Dhamma; speak on the Dhamma; give the gift of the Dhamma.
When thus addressed, the Dhamma should be spoken according to all three methods. However, when told, "Recite [the Pāṭimokkha]," one must recite it alone.
When told, "Speak," he speaks; when told, "Recite the *sara-bhañña*," he recites the *sara-bhañña*.
Furthermore, even a senior monk of the Sangha, if seated on a higher seat, is not permitted to request [recitation].
If both the preceptor and the resident pupil are present, and the preceptor, seated on a high seat, says to him, "Recite," [then he may do so]. Regarding the private recitation (*sajjhāya*):
Having made a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*), one should recite. However, if there are junior monks present, one should say, "I am reciting.
If the senior monk of the Saṅgha in that monastery causes only his own dependents to recite and does not request others who are skilled at recitation, he should be addressed by others:
"Venerable sir, please have such-and-such a person recite. If he says, "Have them recite," [then it is permissible].
If he remains silent, it is permissible to ask him to speak. However, if he objects, one should not ask him to speak.
If the Dhamma discourse has already begun with the senior monks of the Saṅgha before he arrived, there is no need for the formal act of asking permission once he has arrived.
But when he begins to speak after the discourse has concluded, he may speak either after asking permission or without having asked permission. While he is speaking...
The same rule applies when he returns.
Even during informal conversation, the senior monk of the Saṅgha is the master;
therefore, he himself should speak, or he should tell another monk, "Speak," but not while seated on a higher seat. As for laypeople, however—
It is appropriate to say, “Speak. When people ask a bhikkhu whom they know [to answer], he should ask the Elder; having asked the Elder, he may then speak.

If the Sangha Elder, when asked, “Venerable sir, these people are asking questions,” either says, “Speak,” or remains silent, it is appropriate to speak. This also applies during the giving of thanks (*anumodanā*) and so forth while inside a house.
The same principle applies here. If the senior monk of the Saṅgha gives permission, saying, "You may speak even without asking me," it is considered permissible;
it is allowed to speak in all such cases.
Even when one is engaged in recitation, the senior monk must still be asked for permission. If another [monk] is reciting after having asked permission from one [senior], [the first]...
When he returns, there is no further need for formal permission.

If he returns while [the other] has set it aside thinking, "I will rest," then even one who is beginning again must ask for permission. The same rule applies even when one has begun reciting while the Sangha-thera has not yet arrived.
Once one Sangha-thera has given leave, saying, "Recite as you please without asking me," [then permission is no longer required].
It is permissible to recite [the texts] at one's own convenience. However, when another person has arrived, one must first ask their permission before reciting.
151. "Or one may authorize oneself": this means that one may authorize oneself. But the one who asks should look at the assembly; if there is no danger to oneself, the Vinaya may be asked about. 153.
"Even when the opportunity has been granted, one should weigh the individual" means: "Is there a danger for me from this, or is there not? Thus [one should consider].
"Having investigated. "First ours" means first for us. "Right away" means even earlier.

"Having weighed the person, I authorize you to grant leave" means that having investigated thus—"Does he speak of an offense that is actually real, or one that is not?"—I authorize you to grant leave. This is the meaning.

The Discussion on the Protesting of an Unlawful Act (Adhammakamma-paṭikkosanādikathā) 154. An unlawful act (adhammakamma) is exactly as described by the method already stated. "To protest" means to prevent it.
"To make one's view known" means to declare one's own view in the presence of another, saying, "This is an unlawful act; it is not acceptable to me. "By four or five," and so forth.
This was said for the sake of their safety. "They do not recite intentionally" means they recite slowly and deliberately with the thought, "We shall speak in such a way that they do not hear.
155. "Dependent on the elders" (*therādhika*) means dependent upon the elders; the meaning is that it must be subject to the elders. It is also called "the domain of the elders" (*therādheyya*).
As for the recitation, therefore, it should either be recited by the Elder himself or another person should be requested to do so;
and the procedure for making such a request is exactly as described in the section on requesting [the recitation of] the Dhamma. Regarding the phrases "he does not know the Uposatha," and so forth:

he does not know the Uposatha, which is twofold according to the distinction between the fourteenth and the fifteenth [lunar days], and ninefold according to the distinction between the Saṅgha-Uposatha and others; nor does he know the fourfold Uposatha ritual.
He does not know; he does not know the two-fold Pātimokkha; he does not know the nine-fold recitation of the Pātimokkha.

Regarding the phrase "whatever monk there is who is experienced and competent," although the Pātimokkha is permitted even for a young monk who is experienced, nevertheless, this is the intended meaning here:
if the Elder knows five, four, or three [sections]...
The recitation of the Pātimokkha does not come [to them]; however, two [sections] are unbroken, well-defined, and mastered by word of mouth, so that the Pātimokkha depends entirely on the Elder.
But if one cannot even make this much clear, it depends on a learned monk.

"Nearby residences" means a residence in the vicinity. "Together with" means for the purpose of arriving on that very day. "He should instruct a new monk": here, one who is capable of learning should be instructed, not a fool.
156. Discussion on the Permission to Receive the Counting of the Fortnight, etc.:
Regarding the phrase *katimī bhante*, here *katimī* means "the completion of how many? *Kālavato* means "at the very time"; the sense is "even earlier. 158.
Regarding the phrase *yaṃ kālaṃ sarati*: here, even in the evening, it is permissible to announce, "Today is the Uposatha; please attend."
159. Regarding the phrase "the senior bhikkhu should direct a junior bhikkhu":

here too, one who is performing some task, or one who is always alone, or one who carries out heavy burdens, or one who is a reciter of the *sutta* or a preacher of the Dhamma, and so forth—none of these should be directed for the purpose of sweeping the Uposatha hall.
However, the remaining ones may be directed in turn. If he has been directed...
One does not even obtain a broom for the duration of one's stay; one must sweep after having had a twig-bundle made allowable (*kappiya*).
For one who cannot even obtain that, it becomes allowable once it has been obtained. 160.
Regarding the instruction to prepare seats as well, he should be instructed in the same manner already described. And by the one so instructed, if in the Uposatha hall...
If there are no seats, one may bring them from the communal dwelling (saṅghikāvāsa), arrange them, and then take them back again.

In the absence of seats, it is permissible to arrange even straw mats or wooden planks; if even these are lacking, one should arrange branches of trees after having had them made allowable (kappiya) by a kappiyakāraka.
For one who cannot find a kappiyakāraka, that which has been made allowable by another is deemed allowable.
161. Regarding the preparation of a lamp, he should be instructed in the same manner as previously described.

And while instructing him, he should say: "In such-and-such a place there is oil, or a wick, or a bowl; take that and prepare it. If the oil and other materials are not present, they must be sought out;
for one who has sought them but cannot find them, it becomes permissible once they are obtained. Furthermore, a fire should also be kindled in a pan.
The Discourse on the Foundation of Gathering and So Forth (Disaṃgamikādivatthukathā) 163.
“He should be gathered”: he should be gathered with endearing words such as, “It is good, venerable sir, that you have come; here alms-food is easy to obtain, there is curry and condiments;
dwell here without weariness. By means of performing this repeatedly, [he is gathered].
He is to be assisted. He is to be won over by making him give the reply, "Yes, I will stay. Alternatively, he is both to be supported and assisted with the four requisites.
He is to be won over with affectionate words; the meaning is that he is to be addressed in a manner pleasing to the ear.
He is to be served with powdered incense and so forth. Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*): if the entire Saṅgha...
If he does not do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for all. In this case, neither the elders nor the juniors are exempt; he must be attended upon by everyone in turn.

For one who fails to attend upon him during his own turn, there is an offense. Furthermore, he must not accept from the great elders such things as the sweeping of their courtyards or the offering of tooth-sticks.
Even so, the great elders must come to attend upon him every morning and evening. By him, however—
Knowing of their arrival, one should go first to attend upon the great elders (*mahāthera*).
If he has fellow monks who serve as his attendants, he should say: "I have attendants; you may remain free from anxiety.
Even if he has no fellow companions, there might nevertheless be one or two in that very monastery who are perfected in their duties.
They say, “We shall do what must be done for the elder; let the rest dwell in comfort,” and there is no offense for any of them.
That residence must be gone to; it must be gone to every half-month for the purpose of performing the Uposatha.
However, that should be during the dry season (utuvasse); but to show what must be done during the rainy season (vassāne), he said, “Fools and the incompetent dwell for the rains,” and so forth.
In this regard, "Monks, those monks should not spend the rains retreat in that residence" means that one should not enter the rains retreat without a reciter of the Pātimokkha for the earlier period.

If he departs, disrobes, or dies after those who have entered the rains retreat, it is permissible to stay for the later period provided another person is available; if no one else is available, one must go elsewhere.

For those who do not go [to the residence], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, if one departs during the later period, or renounces the training, or passes away, one must have resided for two months.
The Discussion on the Bestowal of Purification.
164. "Communicates by body" means that one communicates—that is, makes known—the giving of purity by means of any limb or member of the body;
however, if one is able to utter speech, one communicates by speech; if one is able to do both, one communicates by both body and speech.
"The Saṅgha should go there and perform the Uposatha" means that if there are many such persons who are ill, the Saṅgha [should go].
Standing in sequence, everyone must be within arm’s reach. If they are far apart and the Saṅgha is not complete, the Uposatha should not be performed on that day;
indeed, the Uposatha must never be performed by an incomplete Saṅgha.
"He departs from right there" means he goes somewhere else without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha. "The novice declares himself [to be one]" means...
"He declares, 'I am a novice,' or he reports his actual status as a novice, or he subsequently remains on the level of a novice"—this is the meaning.
This same method applies in all cases. "He departs when the Saṅgha has assembled" means:
[he departs] when those who have gathered for the purpose of the Uposatha have reached the very minimum limit.
He departs after reaching arm’s reach of four monks. This same method applies everywhere.

And here, even if many [monks] bring their purity, it is as if it has been brought by one. However, if he sees another monk on the way and gives his own purity as well as the purity of those from whom he received it, then [the purity belongs] to him alone.
The *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) comes [to be formally presented]; however, the other, known as the "cat's chain" *pārisuddhi*, does not come.

Regarding the phrase "he does not announce while asleep": having arrived, he sleeps; he does not announce, saying, "Purity has been given by so-and-so. Regarding the phrase "there is no offense for the one who brings the *pārisuddhi*":
here, if he intentionally fails to announce it, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing); nevertheless, the *pārisuddhi* has indeed been brought.
It occurs. However, because it was neither intentional nor reported, there is no offense; and the Uposatha has indeed been performed by both.
165. Regarding the giving of consent (*chandadāna*), the analysis is exactly the same as that stated for the giving of purity (*pārisuddhi*). By one who gives purity...
Regarding the phrase "to give consent as well": here, if one gives only the purification (*pārisuddhi*) and not the consent (*chanda*), the Uposatha is performed;

however, whatever formal act (*kamma*) the Saṅgha performs is considered unperformed. If one gives only the consent and not the purification, both the Uposatha and the formal act of the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha are indeed performed; yet for the giver of consent, the Uposatha...
It is considered unperformed. Even if some bhikkhu comes after having resolved upon the Uposatha within a river or a boundary, he is not permitted to remain thinking, "I have performed the Uposatha";
rather, either concord (*sāmaggī*) or consent (*chanda*) must be given. 167. "He remembers the Uposatha, yet he does not remember":

at one time he remembers, and at another time he does not remember. "There is one who does not remember at all": for one who never remembers at all, there is no requirement to grant formal authorization (*sammuti*). Even if he does not come, he does not invalidate the legal act (*kamma*).
168. Regarding the discussion on the *saṅghuposatha* and so forth:

"Having swept that place" means having swept that area; here the direct case (*paccatta*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayoga*). "Drinking water, water for washing," and so forth, have meanings already explained.
Why, then, was this stated? It is for the purpose of showing the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) and other requirements for the *uposatha*.
Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.”
Thus, these four are called the "preliminary duties. "The declaration of consent,
the purity of the assembly, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation—
these are said to be the preliminary tasks for the Uposatha."
Thus, these five things which are to be done after the preliminary duties have been performed are called "the preliminary tasks" (*pubbakicca*).
[As it is said: "The Uposatha, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act, and there being no common offenses..."
"And there are no persons to be avoided therein;
thus it is called 'the right time' (pattakalla).
Thus, these four are declared to be "the right time."
"Together with them" means that having performed these preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) and so forth together with those who have arrived, the Uposatha should be observed.
Regarding the phrase "Today is my Uposatha," if it is the fifteenth day, it is permissible to resolve: "Today is my fifteenth-day Uposatha.
The same method applies even when it is the fourteenth day.
169. Discussion on the Procedure for the Expiation of Offenses:

It should be understood that the Blessed One’s injunction, “The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense,” was established by the very statement beginning with “For whomsoever there may be an offense,” as well as by the establishment of the giving of purity and the establishment of the purity-Uposatha.
“Such-and-such an offense”: having taken the name of one among the offenses such as a thullaccaya, it should be stated thus: “the thullaccaya offense,” “the pācittiya offense. “I confess that”:
even if this is said as “I confess that in your presence, I confess that in your presence,” it is well-said. “Do you see it? and this means: “Friend, do you see that offense?”
“Do you see that offense, venerable sir?”—this is how it should be said. As for “Yes, I see it,” this is well-said even when expressed as “Yes, venerable sir, I see it;

yes, friend, I see it. Regarding “You should exercise restraint in the future,” if the person is senior, one should say, “You should exercise restraint in the future. When this has been said, [the reply] “Very well...”
"I shall restrain myself well"—this indeed is what must be said.
Regarding the phrase "when he is free from doubt," the Andhaka-ṭīkā states that if he is not free from doubt, it is permissible to confess after first specifying the object (*vatthu*).
Herein, this is the method of confession: if the sun is obscured by clouds...
If one eats while doubting, "Is it now the right time?", that bhikkhu should confess the matter thus: "Venerable sir, I ate while doubting.
If it was the right time, I have committed several *dukkaṭa* offenses; if it was not the right time, I have committed several *pācittiya* offenses.
Having thus declared the basis of the offense, he should say: "Venerable sir, regarding those several *dukkaṭa* offenses in this matter..."
"Whatever offenses, whether *pācittiya* or others, I have committed, I confess them before you. This same method applies to all offenses.

Regarding the phrase "not a common offense" (*na sabhāgā āpatti*): here, when two people commit an offense through a common basis, such as eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*), such a similarity of basis is called "common" (*sabhāgā*). [This refers to] on account of eating at an improper time.
However, it is permissible to confess an offense committed due to eating what is not left over (anatiritta) in the presence of one who has also committed that same offense.
Furthermore, even this [offense] which shares the same basis (vatthusabhāga), once confessed, is indeed well-confessed.

On the other hand, both the confessor—who acts as the cause for the confession—and the recipient—who acts as the cause for the acceptance—fall into a *dukkaṭa* offense; since that [offense] pertains to different bases, it is therefore permissible to confess it to one another.
Regarding the statement, "A neighboring monk should be addressed thus," it is said here that only one who is similar (sabhāga) should be spoken to.
For if one speaks to someone who is dissimilar (visabhāga), quarrels, disputes, schisms in the Saṅgha, and so forth may arise;

therefore, without speaking to him, the Uposatha should be performed after making the mental resolve: "Having emerged from this [confession], I shall make amends. This is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.
172. Discussion on the Fifteen Cases of No Offense (*Anāpatti-paṇṇarasaka*):
Regarding "they did not know"—this means they did not know whether [the monks] had entered the boundary or were entering it.
Furthermore, regarding "other resident monks are coming"—this refers to those who have come from either a village or a forest due to some business.
Having gone, they return to the place where those [other monks] are sitting. "A faction [perceiving itself as] united" means that because they have entered the boundary, they are a faction;
yet because they do not know the fact of having entered the boundary, they perceive themselves as being united. 173. Regarding the fifteen cases of perceiving a faction as a non-faction:
"They know" means that standing on a mountain or on dry land, they see those who have entered or are entering the boundary. The fifteen cases of doubt are likewise straightforward.

175. Regarding the section on those overcome by remorse (*kukkuccapakata-pannarasaka*): just as one who is overwhelmed by desire is called "overcome by desire" (*icchāpakata*), so too, even though they have previously made a resolution, at the moment of performing the act they are to be understood as "overcome by remorse," being overwhelmed by the remorse known as the perception of what is unallowable (*akappiya*) regarding what is unallowable.
176. In the section on the fifteen cases where schism is the primary concern—due to the strength of unwholesome states—a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is stated.

177. In the section on the formula for resident monks regarding visiting monks—just as in the previous formula for resident monks regarding resident monks, it says: "They do not know... [and so forth].

Then it was said, “There are other residents,” and so forth; in this same manner, everything should be understood according to the sequence beginning with, “They do not know that there are other visitors.

In the *peyyāla* (formulaic repetition) concerning the visitor and the resident, just as it appeared in the previous *peyyāla* as “the resident monks assemble,” so too should it be brought in as “the visiting monks assemble. In the *peyyāla* concerning the visitor and the visitor:
However, it should be applied in both cases by way of those who have arrived as guests.
Regarding the statement, "For the resident monks it is the fourteenth day; for the guest monks it is the fifteenth":
here, it should be understood that those for whom it is the fifteenth have either come from another kingdom or have observed the previous Uposatha on the fourteenth day. For the resident monks...
“Should follow along” means that when the resident monks are performing the preliminary duties, thinking, “Today is the Uposatha day of the fourteenth,” one should follow along and not object.
“Should not be given unwillingly” means it should not be given against one’s will.
This concludes the discussion on the observation of gender and other characteristics.
179. "The mode of the residents" means the manner of the residents. This method applies everywhere.

"Mode" (*ākāra*) refers to that by which their perfection or non-perfection in observance of duties is grasped as a form of conduct. "Sign" (*liṅga*) means that which makes them known when they are hidden here and there;
the meaning is that it causes them to be recognized even when they are not visible. "Characteristic mark" (*nimitta*) means that by seeing which one knows, "They exist."
They are known. "Enumeration" (uddesa) means that by which they are designated as being of such a kind of requisite; the meaning is that they receive a specific designation.
All of this is a synonym for well-arranged beds, chairs, and so forth, as well as for words and sounds, and it should be applied accordingly.
This same method applies to the forms of guests and so on. In that context, "unknown" (aññāta) means belonging to others.

“Pouring out the water from washing the feet” (*pādānaṃ dhota-udakanissekaṃ*) means the pouring out of the water after the feet have been washed. One should understand the singular number used for the plural.
Alternatively, the reading is “*pādānaṃ dhota-udaka-nissekaṃ*”; the meaning is the pouring out of the water used for washing the feet.

180. Regarding the cases concerning those of a different communion (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*) and so forth—“the view that they are of the same communion” (*samānasaṃvāsaka-diṭṭhiṃ*) means the view that “these [monks] are of the same communion.”
"They do not ask" means they do not ask about their tenets; without even asking, they perform the Uposatha together after having performed the duties and counter-duties.
"They do not overcome" means they are unable to crush or subdue the state of being of different affiliation;
the meaning is that they do not cause them to relinquish that view.
181. Discussion on the Section Concerning Whither One Should and Should Not Go.

"From a residence where there are monks": from whichever residence there are monks who perform the Uposatha, if one is unable to return to that very same residence on that day, one must not depart from that residence without having performed the Uposatha. "Except with the Saṅgha."

"Without a sufficient number of monks from the Saṅgha" means without those required for a formal act of the community. "Except in the case of an obstacle" means except for the ten kinds of obstacles mentioned previously.
However, at the very least, it is permissible to go with oneself as the fourth person, provided there is an obstacle.
"A non-residence" refers to any place whatsoever, such as a construction site or a workshop. And just as one should not go to a residence or similar places, so too—
If they perform the Uposatha in the monastery, one should not go even to the river or to the boundary for the purpose of determining the Uposatha.
However, if there is a certain monk there, it is permissible to go into his presence.

It is also permissible to go from a residence where the Uposatha has been neglected; having gone thus, one is also permitted to determine [the boundary]. On the Uposatha day, even by a forest-dwelling monk...
Having wandered for alms in the village, one should return to one’s own monastery. If one enters another monastery, one must return only after performing the Uposatha there;
it is not permitted to do otherwise.
(182) "If one should know: 'I am able to go this very day,' that is, if one should know: 'I am able to go there this very day';"
A residence of such a kind may be visited. For by performing the Uposatha there together with the monks, this person will not have created an obstacle to the Uposatha.
The Discussion on Pointing Out Persons Who Should Be Avoided.

183. Regarding the phrases "in the assembly where a bhikkhunī is seated," and so forth, the measure [of distance] is simply the reaching of hands or feet. "Except when the assembly has not yet risen":
for this so-called giving of a deferred purification is not permitted from the moment the assembly has risen;
however, it is permitted while the assembly has not yet risen. Therefore he said: "except when the assembly has not yet risen."
Its characteristic is to be understood from the commentary on the giving of consent (*chandadāna*) for one who has been suspended (*parivāsika*) in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.
"On another Uposatha day" means on any day other than these two Uposatha days, namely the fourteenth and the fifteenth.
"Except for the reconciliation of the Saṅgha" refers to when the reconciliation of the Saṅgha is performed after it has been split, as was the case with the monks of Kosambī.
Having set aside such a formal concord of the Saṅgha, it should then be performed by saying: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
today is the Uposatha day for concord. However, those who have set aside the Uposatha over some trivial matter and subsequently become reconciled must perform the Uposatha itself.
The commentary on the Uposatha Khandhaka is finished.
3. The Khandhaka on Entering the Rains Retreat:
The Discussion on the Permission to Enter the Rains Retreat.
184. In the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*: "Not laid down" (*apaññatta*) means not permitted or not established.
"Those monks here" (*te idha bhikkhū*): the word "here" (*idha*) is merely a particle. "Bringing about destruction" (*saṅghātaṃ āpādentā*) means bringing about ruin.

"They will dwell together" (*saṅkasāyissantīti*) means they will dwell in a fixed residence with little concern for other activities. "Birds" (*sakuntakā*) means birds. "To enter the rains-residence during the rainy season" (*vassāne vassaṃ upagantuṃ*).

The meaning is that during the three months named the rains (vassa), one must enter the rains retreat (vassa). "How many, indeed, are the entries into the rains? means how many are the acts of entering the rains.
Regarding the phrase "on the following day having arrived" (*aparajjugatāya*): here, it is "one for whom the following day has arrived," thus *aparajjugatā*;
[the locative case] *tassā aparajjugatāya* means "when the following day has passed," that is, on the next day. In the second method as well, [it refers to] when the month has passed.
"Assā" means having reached a month; "tassā māsagatāya" means of that which has reached a month; the meaning is: when a month has elapsed and is complete.

Therefore, on the first day (pāṭipada) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī, or on the very first day following the next full moon after the Āsāḷhī full moon, one should attend to the monastery, provide drinking water and water for washing, and perform all the respectful duties such as the worship of the cetiya.
Having finished [the repairs], one should enter the rains residence by uttering the words once or two or three times: "I enter the rains residence for this three-month period in this monastery.
One must enter the rains residence after having uttered the words.
185–6. Discussion on the Prohibition Against Wandering During the Rains Retreat, etc.
"Whoever should set out": here, the offense should be understood as occurring either by departing without looking back or by causing the dawn to rise elsewhere.
"Whoever should overstep": here, the offenses should be understood according to the number of monasteries. If...
If he enters the vicinity of a hundred monasteries on that day and passes beyond them, there are a hundred offenses.
But if, having passed beyond the vicinity of one monastery, he turns back without entering the vicinity of another monastery, there is only one offense.
If, due to some obstacle, he does not enter the earlier *pavāraṇā*, he should enter the later one.
"Desiring to postpone the rains" means desiring to postpone the first month called "Vassa";
the meaning is that, instead of making it the month of Sāvaṇa, one wishes to make it the month of Āsāḷhī again. "In the coming month, in the dark fortnight" means in the coming month.
Regarding the statement, "I allow you, monks, to follow the kings," there is no disadvantage whatsoever for the monks in postponing the rains.
It is permitted to follow [the instruction] "there is none"; therefore, one should also follow in other lawful (dhammika) matters.
However, in regard to what is not lawful (adhammika), one should not follow anyone at all.
The Discussion on the Permission for a Seven-Day Task.

187–8. Regarding "on account of business to be done within seven days" (*sattāhakaraṇīya*): "to go on account of business to be done within seven days" means that whatever must be performed within the interval of seven days is "business to be done within seven days";
the meaning is that I authorize one to go by means of that business to be done, which serves as the cause for going.
Regarding "when sent": the meaning is that I authorize one to go only when sent by these seven types of persons, beginning with the monk (*bhikkhu*).
"A seven-day stay must be made" means that one must return within seven days; the meaning is that the eighth dawn must not be spent right there.
"For the sake of the community of bhikkhunīs" means that from this point forward, these three—namely, the latrine, the bathhouse, and the bathhouse hall—are excluded.
189. *Udositādi* and so forth are already explained in the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning *udosita* and the rest. *Rasavatī* is called a meal-house.
*Vāreyya* is already explained in the training rule concerning acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*). "Before this discourse (*suttanta*) falls into ruin" means:
as long as this discourse does not fall into ruin, as long as this discourse does not perish. Or else, there is some other duty or obligation for it.
By this [formula], whatever duty is so designated is included. And in all cases, one should go when sent with this very appropriate formula:
“I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the bhikkhus,” or with a synonym for these.
The sequence of the elided portions (peyyāla), however, should be understood as follows: “By a lay follower...”
Monasteries and other dwellings have been constructed intended for the Saṅgha; or intended for many bhikkhus, one bhikkhu, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, many bhikkhunīs, one bhikkhunī,
many sikkhamānās, one sikkhamānā, many sāmaṇeras, one sāmaṇera, or many sāmaṇerīs.
It is said: "A dwelling was being built for one's own sake with reference to a single novice nun. In the same way, all should be stated [for the other cases]:

"with reference to a female lay follower (upāsikā), a monk (bhikkhu), a nun (bhikkhunī), a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), or a female novice (sāmaṇerī) with reference to the Saṅgha.
When these seven kinds of business have been sent forth, one must go.
193. The Discussion on Granting Permission Even When Sent by Five [Persons]:
Regarding the phrase "for the seven-day business of five," this refers to fellow practitioners such as monks and others, thinking:
"I shall seek out, inquire after, or attend to a meal for the sick, a meal for those nursing the sick, or medicine."
By such reasons as these, which have been shown in detail by others, one should go even when not invited, let alone when invited.
A bhikkhu is ill; dissatisfaction has arisen; remorse has arisen; a wrong view has arisen;
he has committed a grave offense and is subject to probation; he is subject to being sent back to the beginning.

One should go into the presence of a monk for ten reasons: [if he is] deserving of the *mānatta* penance, deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the Saṅgha wishes to perform a formal act (*kamma*), or a formal act has already been performed by the Saṅgha.

One should go into the presence of a nun for nine reasons; one should go into the presence of a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) for six—namely, the first four, plus [the cases where] her training has lapsed.

"He is, he desires to receive full ordination. For a male novice (sāmaṇera), there are six [cases]: by means of the first four, and "he desires to ask about the rains-residence" and "he desires to receive full ordination.
For a female novice (sāmaṇerī), excluding the case of full ordination, there are five, including "he desires to give the training rules (sikkhāpada).
Beyond this, the same method applies even to the point where parents have given their permission. In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*...

However, as for what was said—that "it is permissible to go even when uninvited by those who attend upon one's parents, whether they be relatives or strangers"—this was stated neither in the Commentary nor in the Canon; therefore, it should not be accepted.
This concludes the discussion on permission being required.
199. *Bhikkhugatika* means a person living together with monks in a single monastery. *Undriyati* means it falls apart.
*Bhaṇḍaṃ chedāpitaṃ* means the materials and components of the goods have been caused to be cut. *Āvahāpeyyuṃ* means they would cause to be brought.
*Dajjāhaṃ* means "I would give. *Saṅghakaraṇīyena*: herein, whatever [is required] for the affairs of the Saṅgha in the Uposatha hall or other dwellings—
Or it may be done for shrines, parasols, railings, and so forth; even a private dwelling for a monk is entirely a matter for the Saṅgha.
Therefore, one must go to procure the materials and requisites for its completion, or to cause food, wages, and other such things to be given to carpenters and others.
Now, here is the decision regarding the determination of the night’s limits outside of the formal text (pāḷimuttaka): it is not permissible to go to hear the Dhamma if one has not been invited.

However, if at a large residence a prior agreement has already been made—“One should assemble on such-and-such a day”—then one is indeed considered as having been invited, and it is permissible to go. [Also permissible] is to go thinking, “I will wash my robes.”
It is not permissible to go. However, if the teacher or preceptor sends one, it is permissible.
If the monastery is not too far away, it is permissible provided that one is unable to reach it and return on the same day after going there.
It is also not permissible to go for the sake of recitation, questioning, and so forth. But one may go with the thought, "I will see my teacher. If, however—
If the teacher says, "Do not go today," it is permissible. One does not obtain permission to go to see a family of supporters or a family of relatives.
This concludes the discussion on the non-offense regarding obstacles and the cutting short of the rains residence.
201. Regarding such instructions as "one should go toward the village," if the village is not far away, one should wander for alms there and then return to the monastery itself to stay.
If it is far away, one should wait until dawn occurs every seven days.
If that is not possible, one should stay right there in a suitable place. If people provide regular offerings such as *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals) and so forth...
The monks should say, “We did not reside in that monastery. However, when it is said, “We do not give [the food] to the monastery or the palace;
we give it to you. Eat wherever you are staying,” then they may eat as they please, for that [food] accrues to them alone. Or, [if told], “Eat after having it brought to your place of residence.”
But when it has been said, one should take [the robe] after leading [the monks] to where they reside and having them reach the end of the rainy-season residence (*vassa*).
If they give the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) at the time of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), it should be accepted provided they have caused the dawn to rise within the seven-day period.
However, those whose *vassa* was interrupted should say, "We did not reside there; our *vassa* was interrupted. If...
If they say, “Let those to whom our lodgings were assigned take them,” it should be accepted.

However, as for any goods such as robes or other articles subject to distribution that were brought here from the monastery with the thought, “May they not be lost,” one should go back to that very place, inform [the residents], and divide them there.
One should tell the stewards, “Give four requisites to the venerable ones from this.”
The same principle applies even to property arising from that source, such as land, buildings, and so forth, when they have been given.

For regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha that is subject to distribution—whether it be inside the monastery or outside the boundary—it is not permissible to divide it after merely consulting those who are outside the boundary.
However, even if it is situated in both places, it is certainly permissible to divide it after consulting those who are inside the boundary.
202. Discussion on the Absence of Offense Regarding the Schism of the Saṅgha and the Interruption of the Rains Retreat:
Regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha is split," there is no need to go once the Saṅgha has actually been split;
however, with reference to one who suspects, "it will be split," it is said, "it is split. The Saṅgha was split by several bhikkhunīs.
In this context, it should not be understood that "the Saṅgha is split by bhikkhunīs. For it has been said:

"Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not split the Saṅgha. However, this was said with reference to a case where, relying on these [bhikkhunīs] and making them a supporting force, there might be the apprehension that "the bhikkhus would split the Saṅgha."
203. The Discussion on Entering the Rains Retreat at Vaja and Other Places.
*Vaja* is the dwelling place of cowherds. Regarding the phrase "to where there is *vaja*," there is no offense for one who has gone with a caravan to a place where the rains retreat is interrupted.
*Upakaṭṭhāya* means when it is near [the time]. Regarding the phrase "to enter the rains retreat in a caravan," here, on the day of entering the rains retreat, by him—
The monk should say to the lay followers, “It is permissible to obtain a hut.
If they give one after it has been built, he should enter it and say three times, “I enter the rains residence here.

If they do not give one, he should take up residence beneath a cart standing in the vicinity of a hall. If even that is not obtained, he should establish his dwelling [elsewhere]. However, in the case of a caravan...
It is not permissible to enter the rains residence [at that time]. "Attachment" (*ālaya*) means the mere arising of the thought, "I shall dwell here for the rains.
If the day of the *pavāraṇā* ceremony falls while the caravan is still on its journey, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* right there.

However, if the caravan passes beyond the place where the monk intended to stay even though it was within the rainy season period, he should stay at the intended place and [perform the *pavāraṇā* there].

In that case, one should perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) together with the monks. Furthermore, if the caravan stays within the boundary itself or disperses at a certain village along the way, one must stay in that very village together with the monks and perform the invitation ceremony;
it is not permitted to proceed further without having performed the invitation ceremony.
Even one who has entered the rainy season residence on a boat must enter it in a hut. If he cannot find one after searching, he may establish a temporary dwelling (*ālaya*).
If during the three months the boat remains at sea, the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) must be performed right there.
If the boat reaches shore and he wishes to go further, it is not permitted to go; [he must remain] only in the village reached by the boat.
Having stayed [there], one should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with the bhikkhus.

Even if the boat goes elsewhere along the riverbank, and the bhikkhu wishes to stay first at a village he has reached, let the boat go; the bhikkhu, having stayed right there, should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with the bhikkhus.
Thus, when there is a threat from weapons or armies, in these three cases there is no offense for interrupting the rains retreat, and one is permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
However, in the preceding cases— beginning with "they are harassed by wild beasts" and ending with "there is a schism in the Saṅgha"—
there is simply no offense, yet one is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
204. “Monks, regarding ‘in a tree-hollow’: here, it is not permitted [to stay] in a mere empty tree-hollow.
However, it is permitted to approach after having constructed a small hut with a thatched roof inside a large tree-hollow and provided it with an entrance door.
It is likewise permitted to construct a small hut with a thatched roof on top of a tree stump after cutting down the tree.”
Regarding "on a tree branch": here too, it is not permitted on a mere clean branch.
However, having built a platform on a large branch and constructed a small hut there with a thatched roof, one may approach it. Regarding "one who has no lodging":
this refers to one who does not possess a lodging covered by any of the five types of roofing materials and provided with fitted doors and fastenings.
"One must not approach it. Monks, 'in a charnel-house'—a charnel-house means a hut consisting of various types such as those with iron spikes or beds;
it is not permitted to approach one there. However, it is permitted to build another hut on the cemetery grounds and approach that.
'Monks, under a canopy'—here too, having set up a canopy upon four pillars and made a screen, [one may enter] the door..."
Having joined it, it is permissible to approach; this is what is called a "parasol-hut" (*chattakuṭikā*). Regarding the term "cauldron" (*cāṭī*):
here too, having constructed a hut in the manner described for the parasol using a large potsherd, it is permissible to approach.
[End of] the discussion on unrighteous agreements and so forth.

205. Regarding the phrase "such an agreement": the meaning here is that whatever other such unrighteous agreement (*adhammikā katikā*) there may be, it must not be made. Its characteristics are stated in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*. 207–8.
Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for making a promise: here, the offense does not arise only from promising, "Stay here for these three months for the rains retreat";
it also arises from [promising], "Accept alms-food for these three months; both of us..."
In cases such as, “We shall spend the rains retreat here; we will assign [the duties] together,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each respective promise.

This applies when one was initially pure in mind but later deceives; however, if one was already impure in mind at the time of the promise, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the promise and an offense of wrong-doing for the deception—thus, the offense of wrong-doing is joined with the offense of expiation.

Thus, regarding the phrase "on that very day it is not to be done," and so forth: if one departs without having entered the rains residence, or if having entered it one spends seven days outside, and neither the earlier period (*purimikā*) nor the later period (*pacchimikā*) is recognized, there is an offense for the formal declaration (*paṭissava*).
However, for one who has entered the rains residence and departs on that very day for a seven-day business without waiting for dawn, even if he returns within those seven days, [there is no offense].
There is no offense; how much less so for one who stays for two or three days and returns within seven days?

Regarding the phrase "having stayed for two or three days," here too, the breaking of the rains residence (*vassaccheda*) should be understood to occur only when one has passed beyond the precincts without any further expectation [of staying]. If there is the thought, "I will stay here," it constitutes a break;
however, if there is no such intention, the rains residence is not entered. The lodging that was taken is well-taken, and the rains residence is considered broken.
If he does not exist [in that place], he is indeed permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Regarding the phrase "seven days before the *pavāraṇā*," it is permissible to go from the ninth day onwards; whether he returns or not, there is no offense. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka* is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Invitation (Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka). Discussion on Living Uncomfortably. 209.
In the Chapter on the Invitation: regarding the phrase "we shall neither speak to nor converse with [them]," here "speaking" (ālāpa) refers to the first word.
"Conversation" refers to their final words. "By leaping hand-to-hand" means by raising the hands. "Living like cattle" means living as cattle do.
For even cattle do not inform one another of the pleasure or pain that has arisen within themselves, nor do they exchange greetings;
these [monks] acted in the same way, and therefore their way of life is called "living like cattle."

It is said. This same method applies everywhere. "Monks, the practice of silence is not an undertaking of the sectarians" means that one should not undertake a vow such as "I shall not speak for these three months," for this is an illegal agreement (*adhamma-katikā*).
"Mutual compliance" (*aññamaññānulomatā*) is the state of being compliant with one another in speech. For when someone says, "Let the venerable ones speak to me," it is possible [to respond].

One may say something, but not anything else. "The state of emerging from offenses" (*āpattivuṭṭhānatā*) means the state of emerging from offenses while making the discipline (*vinaya*) one's primary concern.
For when one says, "May the venerable ones speak to me," it is said that such a person will emerge from offenses and will dwell having placed the discipline before them.
210. “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the Pavāraṇā. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā.
This is the motion known as the “all-inclusive. When this has been stated, it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā by means of three statements, two statements, or one statement;

however, performing it with the same number of statements [as the motion] is not permissible. But when it is said, “One should perform the Pavāraṇā by means of three statements,” then it must be performed by means of three statements only.

It is permissible; anything else is not permissible. When it is said, “One should invite with two utterances,” both two-utterance and three-utterance invitations are permissible, while one-utterance and simultaneous-year invitations are not permissible.

However, when it is said, “One should invite with one utterance,” one-utterance, two-utterance, and three-utterance invitations are permissible, but only the simultaneous-year invitation is not permissible. Regarding “simultaneous-year”:
When this has been said, everything is permissible.

211. "They remain" means they stay seated and do not rise. "In the meantime" (*tadantara*) means within that interval; the meaning is "for that length of time. This concludes the discussion on the breaking of the *pavāraṇā*.

212. Regarding the phrases "on the fourteenth" and "on the fifteenth": on the fourteenth day, the preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*) should be performed thus: "Today is the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) on the fourteenth"; on the fifteenth day, it should be: "Today is the invitation ceremony on the fifteenth.

Among the formal acts of invitation (*pavāraṇakamma*), if five monks are residing in a single monastery, they may perform the invitation by bringing the invitation of one monk and then performing it after four have established the motion of the group (*gaṇañatti*). If four or three are residing [there], [they may do so] by bringing the invitation of one [monk].

If, having brought [the monks], three or two perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) after proposing a motion for a group (*gaṇa*), all this is an invitation procedure that is illegal and a factional assembly (*adhammena vagga*).
But if all five persons together assemble and perform the invitation after proposing a motion for a group;
or if four, three, or two dwelling together assemble and perform the invitation after proposing a motion for the Saṅgha—all this is...
An *adhamma* (unlawful) *pavāraṇā* procedure that is not in concord:
if five persons perform the *pavāraṇā* by bringing the *pavāraṇā* of one person and establishing a motion (*saṅghañatti*) for the four;
or if four or three persons perform the *pavāraṇā* by bringing the *pavāraṇā* of one person and establishing a group-motion (*gaṇañatti*) for the three or two.
All this is a *pavāraṇā* procedure that is discordant because it is contrary to the Dhamma.
However, if all five persons assemble together and perform the *pavāraṇā* by establishing a motion of the Saṅgha;
or if four or three assemble together and perform the *pavāraṇā* by establishing a motion of a group (*gaṇa*); or if two [perform it] with one another—

They perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*); one staying alone performs the formal determination of the invitation (*adhiṭṭhāna-pavāraṇā*). All this is called a legal act of invitation performed by a complete assembly (*dhammena samaggaṃ pavāraṇakammaṃ*).
This is the discourse on the authorization for granting the invitation.
213. "The invitation has been given": regarding this, when the invitation has been thus given, the one who conveys the invitation should approach the Saṅgha and invite them in this way:
"Venerable sirs, the monk [Name] invites the Saṅgha with regard to what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Saṅgha, out of compassion, speak to him if they see [any fault]."
"He will make amends. For a second time... [and] for a third time, venerable sirs, the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ... "He will make amends. But if he is senior, one should say, "Venerable sir, the venerable Tissa";
for in this way, he has invited on his behalf.

Regarding the phrase "one giving the *pavāraṇā* may also give consent (*chanda*)," the manner of giving consent here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Uposatha-kkhandhaka*.
And here too, the giving of consent is for the sake of the remaining formal acts.

Therefore, if one giving the *pavāraṇā* gives consent, then once the *pavāraṇā* has been brought forward in the manner already described, both that monk and the Saṅgha have indeed performed the *pavāraṇā*.

Then, if he gives only the invitation (pavāraṇā) and not the consent (chanda), once his invitation has been announced and the Saṅgha has performed the invitation ceremony, the invitation of all is well-performed; however, any other formal act (kamma) is invalidated.
If he gives only the consent and not the invitation, neither the Saṅgha’s invitation nor the remaining formal acts are invalidated; nevertheless, by that monk—

The invitation has not yet been performed. However, on the day of the invitation (pavāraṇā), even one who has arrived after having resolved upon the invitation outside the boundary (sīma) must give their consent (chanda);
by this means, the Sangha’s formal act of invitation is not invalidated.

218. Regarding the phrase "Today is my invitation": if it is the fourteenth day, one should resolve thus, "Today is my invitation, the fourteenth"; if it is the fifteenth day, one should resolve thus, "Today is my invitation, the fifteenth."
219. "Then there is the offense for not performing the *pavāraṇā*," and so forth, is exactly as stated in the previous method.
222. Regarding the discussion on the fifteen cases of non-offense (*anāpatti*) and so forth:

"One should perform the *pavāraṇā* again" means that after again performing the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*) and putting forward a formal motion (*ñatti*), one should perform the *pavāraṇā* starting from the senior monk of the Saṅgha. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the Uposatha Khandhaka.

228. Regarding the rule that "the incoming monks (āgantuka) must follow the established residents (āvāsika)": "Today is the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) on the fourteenth day"—this very preliminary duty (pubbakicca) must be performed.

This same method applies to the case of the fifteenth-day ceremony as well. Regarding the instruction that "the residents must go outside the boundary (nissīma) to perform the invitation ceremony," at the conclusion of this [text], there is this decision not found in the canonical word (pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya):
if five monks have entered the rains-residence during the earlier period, [and so forth].

There are also five [cases] for the later group: having set aside the motion (*ñatti*) by those of the earlier group, when they have performed the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), the purity-observance (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) should be performed by those of the later group in their presence; two motions should not be set aside at a single observance site (*uposathagga*).
Even if there are four, three, two, or only one who has arrived during the later period, the same rule applies. Now, if there are four [monks] during the earlier period...
The same method applies if there are four, three, two, or even one [monk] who has entered for the later invitation (*pacchimikā*).
Furthermore, if there are three for the earlier invitation (*purimikā*) and three or two for the later invitation, the same method applies. This is the characteristic here:

if those who have entered for the later invitation are fewer than or equal in number to those who entered for the earlier invitation, and they complete the quorum for a communal invitation (*saṅghapavāraṇā*), then a motion (*ñatti*) should be established by way of that communal invitation.
If, however, there are three in the earlier invitation and one in the later invitation, then together with him there are four;

it is not permissible for them to perform the *pavāraṇā* after setting aside a motion (*ñatti*) for a *saṅgha* of four. But by means of a motion for a group (*gaṇa*), he becomes the one who completes the number;
therefore, having set aside a motion according to the group, they should perform the *pavāraṇā* with the former ones, while the other [monk] does so in their presence.
The Uposatha of purity should be performed. If there is one [monk] during both the first and the second rains-residence periods, or two in each, this same procedure applies.
If there is one monk during the first period and also one during the second period, one should invite [the other] in the presence of the other, and one should perform the Uposatha of purity.
However, if those who entered the first rains-residence [period] [meet with] those who entered the second rains-residence [period]...
If there are more [monks] by even one, then after first reciting the Pātimokkha, they should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony in the presence of those who are fewer.
However, at the Kattika Cātumāsinī Pavāraṇā, if [the monks] have first performed the Mahāpavāraṇā upon entering the rains retreat...
If those who have entered the rains residence later are more numerous or equal in number, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) should be performed after setting aside the formal motion (*ñatti*).
Once they have invited, the others should subsequently perform the Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*).

Now, if at the Great Invitation (*mahā-pavāraṇā*) there are many monks who have invited, while those who have entered the rains residence later are fewer or even only one, then when the Pātimokkha has been recited—
Afterwards, he should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony in their presence.

233. "Monks, one should not perform the *pavāraṇā* when there is no *pavāraṇā*, except for the sake of the harmony of the Saṅgha"—here, "harmony" should be understood as being similar to the harmony [restored] at Kosambī.
If it is said, "Today is the *pavāraṇā*; [let us achieve] harmony," then this preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*) must be performed. As for those...
However, if they become reconciled after setting aside the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for some minor reason, they must perform the invitation ceremony at that very time.

And those performing the invitation ceremony for the sake of concord (*sāmaggī-pavāraṇā*) must do so between the first invitation ceremony and the full moon of the Kattika four-month festival, starting from the first day of the waxing moon;
it is not permitted to do so either before or after that period.
234. Discussion on the Invitation Ceremony with Two Utterances, etc.:
Regarding the phrase "to invite with two utterances," when laying down the motion (*ñatti*), one should say: "If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha invite with two utterances.
For the single-utterance ceremony, one should say: "Let [the Saṅgha] invite with one utterance. This also applies to those of the same seniority (*samānavassika*).

“One should perform the *pavāraṇā* with those of the same year of seniority (*samānavassika*)”—this is what should be said; and here, even many who have the same year of seniority are permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* together.
Regarding the discussion on the suspension of the *pavāraṇā*:
"When it has been spoken, uttered, but not yet concluded"—here, there are two kinds: that which includes all [monks] and that which pertains to an individual.
The suspension of the *pavāraṇā*. In that regard, from the point where the presiding official says, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me...
[etc. ...let the Saṅgha perform the *pavāraṇā* by means of three utterances," up until the letter *r*, the *pavāraṇā* is spoken and uttered but remains incomplete.
If, in the interval between these points, he suspends it even for a single word, the *pavāraṇā* is suspended. However, when the syllable *yya* is reached, it is completed.

Because it exists [as a formal act], therefore, even if one were to set it aside from that point onward, what was set aside remains as if not set aside. However, in the case of setting aside for an individual—saying:
"Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha... up to... For the third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen...
up to... seeing it, may you speak to me"—from the beginning until this very last syllable *ṭi*, it is spoken and uttered but remains incomplete.
The invitation (pavāraṇā) is suspended; even by one who stops at a single word within this interval, the invitation is suspended.
However, when it is said, "I shall do so," it is completed. Therefore, when the word "I shall do so" has been reached, although [the procedure] was suspended, it is as if it were not suspended.
This same method applies to the two-word, one-word, and same-year invitations as well. For in these cases too, the field for suspension extends only up to the end of the syllable *ti*.
237. *Anuyuñjiyamāno*: being questioned according to the method stated later, namely, "In what did you place him?
*Omadditvā*: having spoken these words, "Enough, monk, do not quarrel," and so forth; for here, "pressing" (*omaddanā*) is intended as the pressing of words.
*Anuddhaṃsitaṃ paṭijānāti*: he confesses, "I have been falsely accused (*anuddhaṃsito*) by him with a groundless offense involving defeat (*pārājika*)."
Thus he confesses. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means: for an offense of Saṅghādisesa, there is a Pācittiya; for others, a Dukkaṭa.
"Having destroyed" means having destroyed by means of the destruction of the characteristic marks.

Regarding the statement, "She has atoned for this in accordance with the Dhamma," one should say only this much and then invite [the Sangha to admonish her]; however, one must not specify, "It was such-and-such an offense," for that is the opening to quarrel.
239. Discussion on the Establishment of the Matter, etc.:

Regarding the statement "this matter is evident, but not the person," it is said that thieves, having taken fish from a lotus pond in a forest monastery, cooked them, ate them, and departed. Seeing that misfortune, [the monk] [saw] something in the monastery...
Having seen the disfigurement caused by Dhutta and observing that "this must have been done by a bhikkhu," he spoke thus.
"The Saṅgha should perform the Pavāraṇā after setting aside the case" means: "When we know who that person is, then we will charge him;
for now, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā. [If one says: "Tell him right now. If...
The meaning is: "If you suspect any person on account of this matter, point him out right now.
If he points him out, one should investigate that person and then perform the *pavāraṇā*. If he does not point him out, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* thinking, "We shall investigate and find out.
Regarding the phrase "this person is known, but not the matter": here, a certain monk [decorates] a *cetiya* with garlands, perfumes, and ointments...
Or he honored [the Buddha], or he drank *ariṭṭha* liquor; consequently, his body had a corresponding odor.
Referring to that odor, and intending to explain the basis for saying, "This bhikkhu has such a bodily odor," he spoke thus.
"The Saṅgha should perform the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) setting aside this individual" means: let the Saṅgha perform the invitation ceremony having set aside this person. "Tell him right now."
Regarding the person whom you have designated, speak of that person’s fault right now.

If he says, "This is indeed his fault," then after having cleared that person [of the charge], the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) should be performed. But if he says, "I do not know," then the invitation should be performed with the thought, "We shall find out after investigating."

"The object and the person are both evident" means that, according to the previous method, having seen the place where the thieves had caught fish, cooked them, and eaten them, as well as the place where they had bathed with perfumes and other scents, he thought, "This is the work of a renunciant," and spoke thus.
"Tell me about him right now" means: tell me about that person who is suspected on account of this very incident right now.
But having seen both of these, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* only after making a formal determination from the very moment they were seen.
"It is fit to speak" means it is fit for censure; the meaning is that it is permissible to censure. Why?

Because [the matter] was not determined prior to the *pavāraṇā*, and because it was censured after being seen subsequently. "The offense of *pācittiya* for reopening [a settled matter]" refers to both of these cases prior to the *pavāraṇā*.
Since the monks perform the invitation ceremony only after having seen [the fault] and having judged it, therefore there is an offense for one who reopens that matter.
Regarding the discussion on the basis for being a quarrelsome person (bhaṇḍanakāraka):
"Two or three Uposatha days should be made on the fourteenth"—here, the fourth and fifth [days] are two, but as for the third...
"By nature, it is indeed the fourteenth. Therefore, either two or three *cātuddasika* (fourteenth-day) observances should be performed—either the third and fourth, or the third, fourth, and fifth.
If they hear [the proclamation] when the fourth has been performed, a fifth *cātuddasika* must be performed;
in this way, there are two *cātuddasika* observances. Those who act in this manner [ensure that] for those who cause strife, [the observance falls on] the thirteenth or the fourteenth.

Or these [monks] will perform the Pavāraṇā on the fifteenth day. And while they are performing it, having placed the novices outside the boundary and hearing that "they are coming," they should assemble very quickly and perform the Pavāraṇā.
To show this matter, it was said: "If those, monks... pe... let them act thus."
“Unprepared” means lacking preparation for the purpose of knowing the arrival; the meaning is that they have not made arrangements beforehand.
“Having caused them to become confused” means having created delusion by such means as saying, “You are tired, rest for a moment,” and so forth.
“If they do not obtain [permission]” means if they are not permitted to go outside the boundary; this refers to those who are quarrelsome.

They are constantly followed by novices and junior bhikkhus. Regarding the statement "we shall perform the invitation ceremony when the moon is full," they have put forward a formal motion (ñatti) with this intention;

however, on that full-moon day of the month of Kattika (Āgama-juṇha), which is the fourth month of the rainy season (Komudi Cātumāsini), the invitation must be performed even against one's will—it must certainly be performed—for it is not permitted to postpone the invitation beyond that time.
“Monks, when those monks are performing the *pavāraṇā*, that is, when the *pavāraṇā* is being performed at the end of the four months.
Regarding the discussion on the inclusion of the *pavāraṇā*:
‘A certain state of well-being’ means either nascent serenity (*samatha*) or nascent insight (*vipassanā*). ‘We shall become excluded’ means...”
"Unable to accomplish the practice of meditation due to having no fixed place for staying by night or day, we shall become outsiders.
By this, he rejects the granting of consent (*chandadāna*).

For at the time of reconciling a split Saṅgha through the settlement by "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*), and in this inclusion of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*), [consent is not required].
In these three instances, it is not permissible to grant the formal consent (*chanda*).

This "invitation-inclusion" (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*) should not be granted to those who have abandoned their meditation subjects, nor to those who possess well-established serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and the like.

However, it must indeed be granted even for the sake of a single individual—whether they be all those who have attained nascent serenity and insight, or half of them, or even just one person. Once it has been granted...
In the summary of the *pavāraṇā*, there is an exemption during the rainy season; incoming monks are not permitted to take their lodgings.

Furthermore, those who have completed the rains retreat should not be considered as having broken the retreat; however, it is said that after performing the *pavāraṇā*, they are permitted to set out on a journey even in the interim.
It is for the purpose of showing this that the Buddha said, "If, monks, by them... and so forth. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Pavāraṇā-khandhaka is finished.
5. The Leather Khandhaka:
The Discourse on the Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa.
242. In the Chapter on Leather (Cammakkhandhaka): "Possessing sovereignty and lordship" means endowed with both the state of being a lord (*issara*) and the state of being a ruler (*adhipati*).
"Kingship" (*rajja*) refers either to the status of a king or to the duties to be performed by a king. Regarding the phrase "Soṇa Koḷivisa":

here, *Soṇa* is his personal name, while *Koḷivisa* is his clan name (*gotta*). "Hair on the soles of the feet" refers to fine hairs, the color of collyrium, growing upon the reddened soles of the feet.

The hairs grew back with their natural luster restored. It is said that formerly, when he was the leader of eighty thousand men, he built a leaf-hut for a Paccekabuddha at his dwelling place together with them;
he then took his own beautiful woolen rug and placed it as a foot-wiping mat in the spot where the Paccekabuddha’s feet would tread.
For three months, however, they all attended upon the Paccekabuddha. This was the prior connection (pubbayoga) of him and those eighty thousand village headmen.
"Eighty thousand village headmen" means eighty thousand sons of good family living in those villages.
"On some business" means as if on some business; for he had no business whatsoever other than that of his [the Paccekabuddha].
Regarding "for the sake of seeing": it is said that the king, while convening those eighty thousand sons of good family, convened them thinking, "In this way, Soṇa will come without being suspected.
Regarding "benefits pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika-attha*):

it refers to benefits for the welfare of this world according to such methods as, "Agriculture, trade, and so forth should be carried out righteously; mother and father should be supported righteously," and so on.
"Having instructed. "He is our Blessed One" means: "He, the Blessed One, will instruct us regarding our welfare in the future life.
"I inform the Blessed One" means: I make it known to the Blessed One. "Having submerged at the landing-stone" means: having submerged at the half-moon-shaped stone at the bottom of the stairs.
"Venerable sir, when the Blessed One deems it the right time for them" means: for those [monks].
The Blessed One knows the time for performing what is beneficial. "In the shadow of the monastery" means in the shade at the edge of the monastery.
"They attend to it" means they direct their minds toward it again and again by way of serene confidence. "To a still greater degree" means:
show it yet more distinguishedly; this is the sense. "It disappears" means it becomes invisible.
The Story of Soṇa’s Going-forth. 243.
“Smeared with blood” means covered with blood. “A place for slaughtering cows” means a place where cows are killed; such a place is the meaning.
“Skilled” means skilled in playing the lute (*vīṇā*). “In the strings and tones of the lute” means in the strings of the lute.

*Sarā*: "Accāyata" means excessively extended, being harshly tightened. "Saravatī" means endowed with resonance (*sarasampannā*). "Kammaññā" means capable of work (*kammakkhamā*). "Atisithilā" means loosely tied, being slackly bound.
"Same guṇe paṭiṭṭhitā" means having established [the string] on an even pitch, it is tied when placed upon the middle tone.
"Vīriyasamataṃ adhiṭṭhahā" means resolve upon the balance associated with energy; [resolve] energy by means of serenity (*samatha*).
The meaning is "you should apply. And he penetrates the evenness of the faculties (*indriyasamata*), that is, the state of balance among the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*).

Therein, by joining faith with wisdom and wisdom with faith, energy with concentration and concentration with energy, he penetrates the evenness of the faculties. And therein, "grasp the sign" means in that...

When serenity (samatha) is present, grasp and produce that sign by which [the fruit] should arise—just as the reflection of a face appears in a mirror—namely, the sign of serenity, the sign of insight (vipassanā), the sign of the path (magga), and the sign of the fruit (phala); this is the meaning. 244.
“I would declare another” means I would make known: “I am an Arahant. “Six grounds” means six reasons. One who is intent...
