"Having penetrated and made manifest" means he stands having realized it directly. "Devoted to renunciation," and so forth—all this is stated with reference to Arahantship.
For Arahantship is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from all defilements; it is "seclusion" (*paviveka*) because it is secluded from those very same defilements;

it is "non-affliction" (*abyāpajja*) because of the absence of affliction; and it is the "destruction of clinging" (*upādānakkhaya*) because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging, and at the end of the destruction of craving (*taṇhā*).
Because it has arisen, it is called the "destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaya*); because of the absence of delusion, it is called "non-delusion" (*asammoha*).
"Merely faith" (*saddhāmattaka*) means merely faith that is devoid of penetration, unmixed with the wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*).
"Accumulation" (*paṭicaya*) refers to growth through repeated performance. "From being free from lust" (*vītarāgattā*) [refers] to lust by means of the penetration of the Path.
Because he is free from [defilements], he has penetrated and stands firm in Arahantship, which is termed "renunciation" (nekkhamma).
The meaning is that he dwells precisely by means of the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti), and his mind is inclined toward that alone. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"Gain, honor, and renown" (lābhasakkārasiloka) refers to the acquisition of the four requisites, the state of those very things being well-prepared, and the speaking of praise regarding them.
"Nikāmayamāno" means desiring, longing for. "Pavivekādhimutto" means one who is intent upon seclusion;
such is the meaning when he thus declares his attainment of Arahatship.
"Sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ" refers to the mere grasping of what has been taken up after clinging to rules and observances. "Sārato paccāgacchanto" means considering it to be the essence.
"Knowing by way of its essence. "Devoted to non-affliction" means he declares non-affliction, which is Arhatship; this is the meaning.
In this same manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
"Powerful" means strong. "They do not overwhelm his mind": having seized the mind of this one whose taints are destroyed...
They are unable to remain stable. "Unmixed" (*amissīkata*) means made unmixed. The defilements mix the mind with its object;
because of their absence, it is "unmixed. "Stable" (*ṭhita*) means firmly established. "Attained to imperturbability" (*āneñjappatta*) means attained to immovability.
"And he contemplates its passing away" means he perceives both the arising and the passing away of that mind.
"Of one intent upon renunciation" means of one who stands having penetrated to arahantship. By the remaining phrases as well, only arahantship is spoken of.
"Of the destruction of clinging": the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. "And of non-delusion of the mind": of one intent upon the non-delusion of the consciousness.
"Having seen the arising of the sense-bases": having seen both the arising and the passing away of the sense-bases.

“Rightly the mind is liberated”: by this means—through this practice of insight (vipassanā) as the correct cause and method—the mind is liberated by way of the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti);

it is resolved upon Nibbāna as its object. “Of one with a peaceful mind” means of one whose mind is extinguished (nibbuta). “Such a one” (tādi): he is “such” because of his immovability through attraction or repulsion toward the desirable and the undesirable; [the text refers to] that such one.
245. Discussion on the Prohibition of Double-layered Sandals, etc.
"Explaining something else" means explaining [the attainment of] Arahatship. "And the meaning has been stated" means that the meaning by which one is known as an "Arahant" (worthy) has been stated.
However, the specific meaning of the sutta must be understood from the commentary on the sutta itself. And "the self is not introduced."
"I am an Arahant"—thus the self is not presented here by way of its literal expression (*byañjana*).
However, "some foolish men" refers to other empty persons who, as if laughing, explain what is non-existent as existent merely through words.
"Single-palāsa" means having a single layer. "A load of eighty carts": here, two cart-loads constitute one [unit].
It should be understood as "vāho. Regarding the phrase "an army of seven elephant-units" (*sattahatthikanīka*): here, six female elephants and one male elephant constitute one unit (*anīka*).
Seven such units are called an "army of seven elephant-units. "Twofold" means having two layers; "threefold" means having three layers.
"Multi-layered sandals" (*gaṇaṅguṇūpāhana*) refers to those starting from four layers upwards.
246. Discussion on the Refutation of "All Blue," etc. "All blue" means everything is blue.
This same method applies to "all yellow," and so forth. In this context, "blue" has the color of flax flowers;
"yellow" has the color of *kaṇikāra* flowers; "red" has the color of *jayasumana* flowers; and "mañjiṭṭhika" (madder-red) has the color of madder.

Likewise, it may be black, the color of a stone from Addariṭṭha, dyed with a great dye the color of the back of a centipede, or dyed with *mahānāma* [lac] such that its color is mottled and resembles the color of a withered leaf.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated that it may be "the color of a lotus flower.
Having obtained any of these, it is permissible to wear the dye after wiping it with a cloth and breaking up the color. It is indeed permissible even if the color is broken up by only a small amount.
“Nīlakabaddhikā” means those that are blue only on the upper part. This same method applies everywhere.
These too should be worn after distinguishing them by color. “Khallakabaddhā” refers to those made by binding a leather strap to the sole for the purpose of covering the heel.
“Puṭabaddhā” refers to Yavana sandals, which cover the entire foot up to the ankles. “Pāliguṇṭhimā” means having wrapped around...
It is made [so as to cover] only the upper part of the foot, not the calf. A "cotton-filled" one is made by stuffing it with cotton wool.

A "partridge-feathered" one is variegatedly bound in the shape of a partridge feather. A "ram-horn-topped" one is made by attaching projections shaped like ram's horns at the position of the ear-flaps.
The same method applies to those with goat-horn tops and so forth. There is also the "scorpion-ribbed" one.
These are made by joining pieces of wood shaped like scorpions and their stingers right there.
"Sewn with peacock feathers" means they are sewn with peacock feathers resembling thread onto either the leather or the wooden parts. "Variegated" means diverse;
having obtained any of these, if it is possible to use them after removing the buckles and so forth, they should be used. Among those—
However, for one who uses it while being mindful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Lined with lion-skin" means that on the borders of the robe, the lion-skin is joined as if it were a fringe. "Lined with lynx-skin" means lined with the skin of a bird-lynx.
In these cases as well, whatever [skin] is obtained, that skin must be removed before the robe is worn.
247. *Omukkaṃ* means having been put on and then removed. *Navā* means unused. 248.
Regarding the phrase *abhijīvanikassa*:
it refers to the cause of that craft by which they live, by which they make their livelihood. The Discourse on the Prohibition of Sandals within the Monastery.

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "In this matter, O bhikkhus" (*idha kho taṃ bhikkhave*): here, *taṃ* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*); the meaning is, "In this matter, O bhikkhus, you should shine.
"Yaṃ tumhe" means "you who. Alternatively, it is said "yadi tumhe" (if you). For this particle has the sense of the word "yadi" (if).

In the passage beginning with "among teachers" (*ācariyesu*), there are: the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*), and the teacher of recitation (*uddesācariya*).
These four are also merely teachers (*ācariya*) here. For one who has been ordained for six years, [the preceptor] is merely a teacher.

This is because, when he was four years ordained, he lived in dependence on him; likewise, for one with one year of seniority, [the preceptor] is seven years senior; for one with two years, eight years; for one with three years, nine years;
and for one with four years, ten years. These too are merely teachers. [The relationship] of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is that of a visible companion.
Furthermore, those who are fellow monks, or whoever else is senior by ten years, all such are called "mere preceptors" (*upajjhāyamatta*).
When these many monks are walking about barefoot, there is an offense for one who walks about wearing sandals. 249.
"A foot-thorn affliction" means that flesh resembling a wooden stake has protruded from the foot.
251. *Tiṇapādukā* means sandals made from any kind of grass. *Hintālapādukā* means sandals made from *khajjūrī* leaves;
even those made from *hintāla* leaves are not permitted. *Kamalapādukā* refers to a certain grass called *kamala*; sandals made from that are so named; some also call them *usīrapādukā*.
*Kambalapādukā* means sandals made from wool. *Asaṅkamanīyā* means [sandals] that should not be stepped upon.
Firmly established on the ground, immovable, and unshakable.

(252) "Touching the private parts" means they touch the private parts with the private parts themselves. "Drowning after having plunged" means they seize [the victim] firmly within the water and kill them.
This concludes the discussion on the prohibition against vehicles and so forth.
253. "Drawn by women" means drawn by cows. "With a man [as driver]" means with a male charioteer. "Drawn by men" means drawn by oxen.
"With a woman [as driver]" means with a female charioteer. "At the Gaṅgā festival" means at the festival of the Gaṅgā-Mahā.
Regarding "a handcart drawn by men": here, whether it is drawn by men with a female charioteer or with a male charioteer, both are permissible.
As for the hand-mill, whether women or men turn it, it is indeed permissible.
"By the jolting of a vehicle" means that when one mounts a vehicle, the entire body shakes; on account of that [shaking]. A *sivika* is a palanquin carried on seats.
A *pāṭaṅki* is a cloth litter suspended from bamboo poles.
254. Regarding the phrase "high and large beds and seats": here, a "high bed" (*uccāsayana*) is a couch that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.

A "large bed" (*mahāsayana*) is one with an improper covering. Among items such as chairs (*āsandī*), a "chair" refers to a seat that exceeds the prescribed dimensions. A "couch" (*pallaṅka*) is one made by attaching animal figures to its legs.
A "woolen rug" (*gonaka*) is a large woolen carpet with long hair; it is said that its hairs are more than four finger-breadths in length.
*Cittaka* is a woolen coverlet variegated with woven patterns. *Paṭika* is a white woolen coverlet.
*Paṭalika* is a thick, flowered woolen coverlet of red color, which is also called an *āmalakapaṭṭa*. *Tūlaka* is simply a natural cotton-down mattress.
*Vikatika* is a woolen coverlet variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth. *Uddalomi* is one on which the wool has been shorn from one side.
A woolen rug (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*); there is also a reading, "with hair upwards" (*uddhalomī*). "With hair on one side" (*ekantalomī*) refers to a woolen rug with the hair standing up on both sides.
A "cotton-padded coverlet" (*kaṭṭissa*) is a cotton-padded coverlet sewn with jewels.
"Silk" (*koseyya*) is a silk-thread coverlet sewn with jewels; however, plain silk is permitted.
*Kuttaka* refers to a woolen rug suitable for dancing, upon which sixteen dancing girls stand to perform.
*Hatthatthara* and *assatthara* are simply rugs used for covering the backs of elephants and horses respectively; the same principle applies to *rathatthara*.
*Ajinappaveṇī* is a mat made by sewing together deerskins to the size of a bed. *Kadalīmigapavarapaccattharaṇa* is... [the excellent spread made from the skin of the kadalī-deer].
There is such a thing as the skin of a kadali deer; a choice covering made from that means an excellent covering.
It is said that they make it by spreading the kadali deer skin over a white cloth and sewing it together.
"With an upper canopy" (sauttaracchada) means together with an upper covering; the meaning is together with a red canopy fastened above.
Even a canopy is not permitted if there is an improper covering beneath it; however, it is permitted if there is none.
"Red pillows on both sides" refers to a head-pillow and a foot-pillow; such a bed with red pillows on both sides is not allowable.
But if there is only one pillow that is red on both sides, or has the color of a lotus, or is variegated, [it is permitted].
Or, if it is of a suitable size, it is permissible. However, a large cushion (mahāupadhāna) is prohibited.
255. Regarding the discussion on the prohibition of all skins:
"A young panther" means a cub of a panther. "Are woven" means they are bound by wrapping them around wall-frames and the like.

256. *Abhinisīditun* means to sit down leaning against [something]; the meaning is to sit having made it a support. Regarding the phrase "by a sick monk wearing sandals": here, one who is called "sick" is one who is unable to enter a village without sandals.
257. *Kurara-ghare*: in a city of that name; by this, his alms-village is stated.
*Papatake pabbate*: on a mountain named Papataka; by this, his place of residence is stated. *Soṇo*: that is his name. *Koṭi-agghanakaṃ*: worth ten million.
However, because he wears an earring, he is called "Kuṭikaṇṇa," which means "Point-eared.
"Pāsādika" means producing confidence. "Pasādanīya" is a synonym for that same meaning.
"Uttamadamathasamatha" refers to the highest self-control and tranquility, as well as wisdom, concentration, bodily tranquility, and mental tranquility.
The meaning is as follows: "Tamed" (*danta*) means tamed because all crookedness and agitation have been cut off; the meaning is that his defilements are exhausted.
"Guarded" (*gutta*) means guarded by the protection of restraint. "With peaceful faculties" (*santindriya*) means with restrained faculties. "Without blemish" (*nāga*) means free from fault (*āgu*).
"After the passing of three years" means after the lapse of three years from the day of my going forth.
"I received the full ordination" means: "I obtained the upasampadā. "With black soil on top" (kaṇhuttarā) means having black clay on the upper surface;
the meaning is that it was built up with black clay on top. "Damaged by cow-hoof marks" (gokaṇṭakahatā) means damaged by the cow-hoof marks arising from ground trodden by the hooves of cattle.
It is said that they [the shoes] were single-soled leather sandals intended to protect against those cow-hoof marks.
They cannot [bear it]; thus they become rough. *Eragū*, *moragū*, *majjārū*, and *jantū*—these are four kinds of grass.
With these, they make straw mats (*kaṭasāraka*) and floor-mats (*taṭṭikā*). Here, *eragū* refers to *eraka* grass; that is coarse.
*Moragū* grass has copper-colored tips, is soft, and pleasant to the touch; a mat made from it, as soon as one rises after lying down upon it—
Furthermore, having become bloated, it remains so. They even make garments from the marrow and flesh. The person's complexion becomes like that of a jewel.
"He prepared a seat" means he prepared either a mattress or a straw mat;
and having prepared it, he informed Soṇa: "Friend, the Teacher wishes to dwell in the same dwelling as you, right in the Fragrant Chamber."
"The lodgings have been prepared. 258.
"This indeed is the time for him" means this would be the proper occasion. "He will show it" means he will point it out.
"'Say this and that' means: 'Now is the time for what my preceptor has made known to me; come now, I shall announce it.'"
"This is the teaching"—this is the intended meaning here.
259. "With the holder of the Vinaya as the fifth" means with the teacher of the proclamation as the fifth. Regarding the rule:
"I allow you, monks, in all border regions, sandals with double soles," here it is said that, excluding human skin, sandals may be made from any kind of leather whatsoever.
It is permissible. The same rule applies to shoe-cases, knife-sheaths, and key-cases. Regarding "skins as coverings":
here, it is permissible to spread out any kind of sheepskin or goat skin and lie down or sit upon them.
As for deer skins, these are: the enī-deer, the vāta-deer, the pasada-deer, the kuraṅga-deer, the migamātuka, and the rohita-deer.
Only the hides of these [animals] are permitted. However, for others— namely,
the monkey, the black lion, the sarabha, the kadali-deer,
and whatever other wild beasts there may be— their hide is not permitted.

In this context, "wild beasts" (*vāḷamiga*) refers to lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas. However, it should be understood that not only these, but all others—down to cows, buffaloes, hares, and cats—who are not included among those whose hides are permitted, are to be regarded as wild beasts for the purposes of this rule.
For the hides of all these are not permitted; thus, they do not yet come within the scope of the calculation [of allowable items].

"As long as it has not come into one's hand" means: as long as it has not been brought and given, or as long as it has not been announced by sending word that "Venerable Sir, a robe has arisen for you," it does not enter into the count.
If it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), it is permissible; the meaning is that once it has been determined, it does not enter into the count.
But when it has been brought and given, or when one has heard that it has arisen, from that point on—
Starting from that point, he receives the exemption for ten days only.
The commentary on the Cammakkhandhaka is finished.
6. The Bhesajjakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Medicines).
260. Discussion on the Five Medicines, etc.
In the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*: “By an autumnal affliction” means by a bile-affliction that arises during the autumn season;
for at that time they are drenched by rainwater, trampled by mud, and from time to time exposed to harsh sunlight.
Because it is hot, their bile becomes localized within the hollow of the stomach. "It would serve the purpose of food" means it would accomplish the function of food. 261.

"They do not clear [the stomach]" means they do not digest, nor are they able to alleviate a wind-disease (*vātaroga*). "Glossy" means smooth. "By one who covers the meal" means by one for whom the meal has no appetite. 262.
In the cases of *acchavasa* and so forth, the determination should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the *Nissaggiya* rules. At the proper time...
Regarding "received" and so forth: the meaning is that after having been received before midday has passed, it is cooked and strained.
"To use by means of oil for consumption" means to use it as oil for consumption permitted during the seven-day period.
263. The determination concerning medicinal roots and so forth has already been stated in the *Khuddakavaṇṇanā*. Therefore, whatever [is mentioned] here...

We shall describe that very same thing which was not mentioned previously. *Vacatta* means white *vacā*. *Nisada* and *nisadapota* refer to the grinding stone and the grinding stone’s young (or powder).
*Phaggu* is a species of creeper. *Nattamāla* is the *karañja* tree. *Hiṅgu*, *hiṅgujatu*, and *hiṅgusipāṭikā* are all varieties of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
*Takataka*, *pattitaka*, and *takapaṇṇi* are varieties of lac (*lākha*).
"Sāmudda" (sea salt) remains like sand on the seashore. "Kāḷaloṇa" (black salt) is natural salt.
"Sindhava" (rock salt) is white-colored and arises from a mountain. "Ubbhida" (soil salt) arises as a sprout from the earth.
"Bila" (cave salt) is cooked together with various ingredients; it is red in color.
264–6. “The body is foul-smelling”: for some, such as horse-riders, the odor of the body is [unpleasant];
for them too, either *sirīsa*, *kosumbha*, and other powders, or perfumed powders (*gandhacuṇṇa*), are all permissible. “Chagaṇa” means cow dung. “Boiled dye” refers to a decoction of dye.
It is also permissible to bathe by pounding ordinary powder, moistening it with water, and using it; this too is included within the category of “boiled dye.”

"He ate raw flesh and drank raw blood" does not mean that the bhikkhu ate or drank; rather, a non-human being (amanussa), having eaten and drunk, departed. Therefore it is said: "That affliction caused by the non-human being subsided for him.
"Ointment" (añjana) is a term inclusive of all types. "Black ointment" (kāḷañjana) is one species of ointment. "Juice-ointment" (rasañjana) is made from various ingredients.
"River-ointment" (sotañjana) is ointment produced in river currents and the like. "Geruka" refers to golden geruka.
"Kapalla" refers to a vessel taken from the rim of a lamp. "With grinding substances for collyrium" means with things to be ground together with the collyrium;
for indeed, there is nothing that is not permitted as a grinding substance for collyrium. "Sandalwood" refers to any kind, such as red sandalwood and so forth.
"Tagara" and the others are well known, but other things such as blue lotuses (*nīluppalādi*) are also certainly permissible.
"Made of bone" means made of all other bones except human bone. "Made of ivory" means made of all types of ivory, such as elephant tusks and so forth.
There is nothing unallowable even among those made of horn; those made of reed and so forth are exclusively allowable.
"A substitute for a tally-stick" means that I authorize either a hollow tube or a bag for that place where one inserts a tally-stick. "Shoulder-strap."
A shoulder-sling for a small ointment-box. A twin nostril-pipe (*natthukaraṇī*) means a single nozzle made from two tubes with equal openings.

267. “I allow you, monks, the preparation of oil (*telapāka*): whatever medicinal substances are added, all of it is indeed permitted. “With too much marrow added” means with excessively added marrow;

the meaning is that they were prepared by putting in a large amount of marrow. “Joint-wind” (*aṅgavāta*) refers to wind in the hands and feet. “Decoction of various ingredients” (*sambhāraseda*) refers to a decoction made from various kinds of leafy herbs. “Great decoction” (*mahāsedo*).

The meaning is: "I allow [you] to sweat the body by filling a pit the size of a man with glowing embers, covering it with dust, sand, and so forth, spreading various wind-dispelling leaves upon it, and then lying down there on a limb smeared with oil, turning over and over.
*Bhaṅgodaka* means water heated with the crushed fragments of various leaves.
Water: having repeatedly sprinkled [the area] with those leaves and water, it should be fomented. "A water-tub" means:
I allow the performance of fomentation by entering there after filling a trough or a wooden tub in a water-tub with hot water—this is the meaning.
"There is wind in the joints" means: wind pierces each joint. "To discharge blood" means: [to draw] blood with a lancet.

To cleanse. "To prepare a foot-wash" means to prepare a foot-wash by adding various medicinal substances such as coconut and so forth, whereby split feet are restored to their natural state; the meaning is to boil a medicine suitable for the feet.
"Need for sesame paste" means need for ground sesame seeds. "A bolus" means a lump of sesamum paste applied to the opening of a wound.
"To insert. "With a wall of mustard seeds" means with a paste of mustard seeds. "Swelling flesh" means excess flesh that protrudes like a bolt.
"To cut with salt-grit" means to cut with a razor. "A wick" refers to a cloth used for soaking oil.
"Every treatment for a wound" means whatever is called a treatment for a wound; the meaning is that I authorize all of it.
268. "Having taken it oneself" means that this is not only for one bitten by a snake;
when there is any other poisonous bite, one may take and consume it oneself. However, in other circumstances, it is permissible only if it has been formally received (*paṭiggahita*).
Regarding the rule "once prepared, it need not be received again": if it has already reached the ground, it must be received; but if it has not yet reached it, it is permissible to take it.

269. *Gharadinnakābādho* is a disease arising from a potion used for subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*). *Sītāloḷi*: the meaning is that I allow [the use of] clay clinging to the plowshare of one who is plowing, having mixed it with water and given it to drink.
*Duṭṭhagahaṇiko*: one whose digestion is impaired; the meaning is that excrement is expelled with difficulty. *Āmisakhāra*:
alkaline water that has dripped from the ashes after burning dry rice. *Muttaharītaka*: [a preparation] saturated with cow’s urine.
Harītaka is the yellow myrobalan fruit. "With a body full of humors" means with a body in which the dosas (humors) have increased. "Clear rice-gruel water" refers to the scum of rice-water.

"Unfermented bean-soup" is a drink made from boiled mung beans that is not greasy. "Fermented and putrid" refers to that same soup when it has been washed and is greasy. "With a meat broth" means with a sauce made of meat. This concludes the discussion on the permission for sugar and other such substances.
272. “Monks, if even cooked mung beans grow,” means that even if cooked mung beans do grow, they may be consumed as one pleases; for because they have been cooked, they are indeed allowable.
274. “Grown within” means grown in an unallowable hut. “Cooked by oneself”:
herein, it is not permitted for a monk to cook any kind of foodstuff himself. Even if he [has] hot gruel, or *sulasī* leaves, or *siṅgivera*...
If they add salt, it is not permissible to stir it even then; however, it is permissible to stir it thinking, "I shall cool the gruel.
Even if one receives rice with no grains left (uttaṇḍula-bhatta), it is not permissible to cover it. But if people give it after having already covered it, it is permissible;
or it is permissible to cover it so that "the rice does not go cold. However, in the case of milk, buttermilk, and so forth—
It is permissible to place fire on [food] that has already been cooked once, because cooking it again is permitted.
"They eat even lumps of charcoal" means that *biḷā* (mungoose), mice, monitor lizards, and *maṅgusa* (lizard) eat them. "Tame animals" refers to scavengers (*vighāsāda*). 276.
"Brought out from there" means brought out from the place where those who have been invited are eating.
278. "Grown in the forest" (*vanaṭṭha*) means grown both in the woods and in a lotus thicket. "Seedless" (*abīja*) refers to a young fruit whose seed does not produce a sprout.
"From which the seed has been extracted" (*nibbaṭṭabīja*) refers to things such as mangoes and jackfruits that are to be consumed after the seed has been removed and set aside.
279. "A wound difficult to heal" (*duropayo vaṇo*) means it heals with difficulty; the meaning is that it becomes natural [to heal] only with great hardship. "Difficult to maintain" (*dupparihāraṃ*).
"Surgery" means that one should perform surgery with difficulty in a cramped place. "Surgical treatment or vaginal treatment" refers to cutting,
tearing, piercing, or scraping within a delimited area by means of any kind of instrument— whether a knife, a needle, a thorn,
a lancet, a stone splinter, or a fingernail.

It must not be done; for all of this is merely surgical treatment (*satthakamma*). Furthermore, one must not perform a vaginal compression (*vatthipīḷana*) using any skin or cloth; for all of this is merely vaginal treatment (*vatthikamma*).
And here, the phrase "two finger-breadths around the narrow passage" is stated specifically with reference to surgical treatment; however, vaginal treatment applies to the narrow passage itself.
This is prohibited. However, in that case, it is permissible to take up caustic alkali and bind it with any kind of string.
If it is cut by that [string], it is considered well-cut. Even in the case of the disease of testicular enlargement (*aṇḍavuḍḍhi*), surgical treatment is not permitted;

therefore, one must not perform the act of cutting open the testicle, extracting the seeds, and thinking, "I shall cure the illness. Regarding the heating with fire and the application of medicinal ointments:

However, there is no prohibition [regarding the following]. A medicinal applicator smeared with medicine, or a bamboo tube, is permitted for use in the anus—by means of which they perform the act of cleansing or introduce oil. 280.
"Meat that has come into being" refers to the meat of one who is dead. "A day of sacrifice" means that on that day, nothing at all may be obtained by anyone.
To deprive of life. *Potthanika* is said to be a meat-cutting knife.
*Kimpimāya* means "what indeed with this? *Na bhagavā ussahati* means "the Blessed One is not able. *Yatra hi nāma* means "since indeed. *Paṭivekkhi* means he investigated;
it is equivalent to saying he questioned. *Appaṭivekkhitvā* means without having investigated, i.e., without having questioned. However, if [he says], "It is the flesh of such-and-such..."
If one knows [the nature of the meat], there is no need to ask; however, one who does not know must eat only after having asked.
281. Regarding the discourse on the prohibition of elephant meat and so forth:
"Dog meat"—in this context, those known as *araññakokā* are like dogs; their meat is permitted.
However, the meat of one produced from the union of a village female dog with a male jackal, or a male jackal with a village female dog, is not permitted;
for such an animal partakes of both [species]. "Snake-meat" refers to the meat of any footless creature of the long-bodied class, which is not permitted.
Lion-meat and the like are already well known.
And herein, human flesh is forbidden because it is of the same species; the flesh of elephants and horses because they are royal mounts;
the flesh of dogs and snakes because they are repulsive; and the flesh of lions and the other four [beasts] for the sake of one’s own safety.
The flesh, bones, blood, skin, and hair of these ten—human and the rest—are all not permitted; nothing whatsoever [from them is allowed].
Whether one knows it or not, there is indeed an offense for one who eats. When one becomes aware of it, it must then be confessed.

For one who takes [the food] thinking, "I will eat after asking permission," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the moment of receiving; for one who takes it thinking, "I will eat after asking permission," there is no offense.
However, there is an offense only for one who eats knowing that it was prepared specifically for them; one who becomes aware of it afterwards is not to be charged with an offense.
The Story of the Gruel and Honey-Ball, etc., 282.
"Alone" means being single; the sense is that there is no second for him.

"Having had plenty of gruel and honey-balls prepared"—it is said that he had them prepared by spending a hundred thousand [pieces of money]. At the conclusion of the verses of thanksgiving, "for those who aspire..."

The phrase "icchatan" (of one who desires) is connected with "alameva dātun" (it is indeed enough to give). However, if there is a reading "patthayatā icchatā" (by one who aspires, by one who desires), that alone should be accepted. 283.
"Bhojayāguṃ" refers to that which generates an invitation. "Yadaggena" means starting from which point. "Saggā te āraddhā" means the heavens have been commenced for you.
The meaning is that merit producing rebirth in heaven has been accumulated. "He should be dealt with according to the rule" means he should be dealt with for eating in succession;
for the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) occurs through the offering of food (*bhojjayāgu*).
284. "I do not know you, Kaccāna," [he said]. It is said that when there was sugar remaining, deities added subtle nourishment (*sukhumoja*) to it.
It does not apply to others; therefore, he spoke thus. "Sugar for one who is ill" means that I authorize sugar after the meal for one who is afflicted by such an illness.
The Discourse on the Site of Pāṭaligāma.
285. "Laid out entirely" means in such a way that it is completely covered.
286. "Sunidha and Vassakāra" refers to Sunidha and Vassakāra, two brahmins who were high ministers and chief counselors to the King of Magadha.
"For the sake of warding off the Vajjis" means for the purpose of cutting off the sources of revenue for the Vajji royal clans. "Sites" means...

"House-sites. It is said that those deities, having become intent upon the bodies of the geomancers (*vatthuvijjāpāṭhakā*), thus incline their minds so that they might construct dwellings. Why? The meaning is: "They will show us honor appropriate to ourselves.
"By the Thirty-three" means: it is said in the world that, including Sakka the king of the gods and Vissakamma, [there are] the Thirty-three.
The title "Paṇḍita" (the Wise One) has arisen; for that very reason he says, "by the Tāvatiṃsa [gods]," meaning they construct it as if consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
"As far as the noble domain" means as much as there is a place of resort for noble persons.
"As far as the marketplace" means as much as there is a place for buying and selling where merchants have their goods brought together in heaps.
There is a name [for it]. "This shall be the chief city" means that among those market-towns of the noble ones (ariya), this will be the foremost city.
"Puṭabhedana" means a place for breaking open packages; what is meant is a place for unloading. In the phrase "or from fire," etc., the word "or" has the sense of a conjunction.
For there, from one part [of the danger] it is from fire, from another from water, and from another from within.
There will be an obstacle due to mutual dissension. A *uḷumpa* is made by driving in stakes for the purpose of crossing to the other shore.
A *kulla* is made by binding together reeds and the like.
An *aṇṇava* refers to a body of water at least one *yojana* in depth and breadth.
This is a synonym. Here, "rivers" (sara) are intended. This is what is meant:
those who cross the deep and wide lake of craving do so by making a bridge, which is the Noble Path, and having abandoned the quagmires, they do not touch even the low-lying places filled with water.
But this person, though desiring to cross even this small amount of water, [uses] a raft...
The attendants cling [to the raft], but the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha—those wise ones—know how to cross over even without a raft.
287. *Ananubodha* means by way of not awakening. *Sandhāvita* means having run on from one existence to another existence.
*Saṃsarita* means having wandered on by way of going again and again. *Mamañceva tumhākañca* means "by me and by you."
Alternatively, "sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ" means that the running and wandering—both mine and yours—has occurred;

this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Saṃsitaṃ" means "wandered. "Bhavanetti samūhatā" means that the craving-rope, which is the cause for going from one existence to another—that is, the running through existences—has been thoroughly struck down, severed, and rendered non-functional.
289. "Blue" (nīla) is a term that encompasses everything. "Of blue color," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of showing its specific divisions.
In this context, their natural color is not blue; rather, this is said by way of the variety of blue ointments. "He turned back" (paṭivaṭṭesi) means he warded off.

"You should give with its provisions" (sāhāraṃ dajjeyyātha) means you should give it together with the surrounding territory. "They snapped their fingers" (aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ) means they snapped their fingers.
They moved [the assembly]. "Ambakāya" means "to the woman. "Oloketha" means "look. "Apaloketha" means "look again and again.
"Upasaṃharatha" means "bring near. The meaning is: "By means of your own minds, bring this Licchavi assembly to the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods; look upon it as equal to the Tāvatiṃsa realm."
The Story of Sīhasenāpati, etc. (290).
“Explaining the Dhamma and its conformity” means they speak of a reason that accords with the reason stated by the Blessed One.
“A reasoned discussion in accordance with the Dhamma” means that, being supported by a reason through what has been stated by others, your argument is subject to censure by the wise.
"Does not even some slight reason come forward?"—this is what is meant: "Is there not, even by every possible means, a ground for censuring your doctrine?
"Not wishing to misrepresent" means not wishing to declare [faults] after having overcome [the opponent]. "Having investigated thoroughly" (anuviccakāraṃ) means:
"Act in a way that must be done after having understood, reflected upon, and weighed [the matter]. This is what is said.
“Of well-known people” means those who are famous in the world. “It is good” means it is beautiful.
“They should carry a banner” means they should wander about the city raising a banner and proclaiming [the news]. Why? Thinking, “In this way our greatness will be established.
“Like a well” means standing like a prepared water-pool. “Family” means a household. “Should be given.”
“Maññeyyāsī” means: “Do not interrupt the gift of these [people]; for what has been obtained must indeed be given. Thus he instructs.
“Okāro” means a state of deficiency or inferiority. “Sāmukkaṃsikā” means taken up by oneself alone;
the meaning is that it is not shared with others. “Uddissa kataṃ” means made specifically for [someone].
294. *Paṭiccasakamma* means "done in dependence upon oneself. Alternatively, *paṭiccasakamma* is a designation for "causal action" (*nimittakamma*);
because that causal action exists therein, it is called *maṃsapaticcasakamma*.
For whoever consumes such meat is also a co-heir to that action, just like the killer.
The intention is that even for him, there is the act of taking life. "They will perish" means they perish;

those who slander do not perish, in the sense that they do not reach the end of their slander. The discussion on the triple purity has been stated in the commentary on the Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada. This is the discussion on the authorization of the *kappiya-bhūmi* (the area where things may be made allowable).
295. "Surrounded by wagons" (sakaṭaparivaṭṭa) means they remain having formed a perimeter as if with wagons. "Bordering" (paccantima) is merely a way of speaking;

however, because it is stated that "the Saṅgha may desire [this]," even a primary monastery (dhuravihāra) may be authorized. This is permissible not only by means of a formal act (kammavācā), but also by a simple announcement (apalokana).
"The sound of crows' cawing" refers to those who have entered here and there for the purpose of eating food.
The sound of the crows gathered there was like the cawing of those that have descended.
Yasoja was the foremost among the five hundred who went forth at the conclusion of the *Kapila Sutta*.
Regarding the terms beginning with "ussāvanantikā," first, the *ussāvanantikā* should be performed as follows: [the procedure] for one who is upon the pillars or at the base of a wall...
Or, when a monastery is being built by digging [into the ground], the stones used as foundations for the pillars beneath it remain part of the earth itself.

However, when many people are surrounding the first pillar or the first base of the wall, lifting it up while shouting the words, "We are building a *kappiya-kuṭī*! We are building a *kappiya-kuṭī*!"—then [the stone becomes a formal object].
When establishing [a structure], one should establish it either by touching it or by lifting it oneself, placing it upon a pillar or at the base of a wall.
However, in the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī* commentaries, it is stated that after saying "the kitchen (kappiyakuṭi), the kitchen," it should be established.
In the *Andhaka-ṭṭhakathā*, it says, "I resolve this as the Saṅgha’s kitchen. Yet, even without saying that, [it is still valid].
There is no fault in stating it according to the method explained in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, the common characteristic here is that the fixing of the pillar and the conclusion of the speech must occur simultaneously.

For if the pillar is fixed while the speech is not yet finished, or if the speech is finished while the pillar is not yet fixed, the *kappiyakuṭi* (permissible hut) is not properly made. Therefore, in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
It is said: “It should be spoken of after being surrounded by many; for in this case, the completion of the speech of even a single person and the fixing of the pillar will necessarily coincide.
However, in the case of huts made of bricks, stone, clay, or wattle, they may build them either with or without a foundation below.

From the moment they wish to erect a wall, they should first take a brick, a stone, or a lump of clay and construct a *kappiyakuṭi* (a hut for allowable goods) according to the method already described. For bricks and the like are not permitted beneath the first bricks and so forth of a wall;
however, pillars do rise above [the ground], and therefore they are permitted.
In the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "When constructing with pillars, four pillars should be established at the four corners;

on the brick wall, two or three bricks should be established at each of the four corners. However, there is no fault even if it is not done in that way, for what is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is indeed the authoritative standard.
There are two kinds of "cow-path" (gonisādikā): the cow-path of the monastery (*ārāmagonisādikā*) and the cow-path of the dwelling (*vihāragonisādikā*).
Among these, where neither the monastery nor the lodgings are enclosed, this is called the "cow-path of the monastery.
Where all or some of the lodgings are enclosed, but the monastery is unenclosed, this is the "cow-path of the dwelling."
Thus, in both cases, the fact that the monastery is unenclosed is the sole criterion.
However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*, *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, *Aṭṭhakathā-paccarī*, and other texts that even if a monastery is half-enclosed or mostly enclosed, it is indeed called "enclosed.
In such a case, it is permissible to obtain a kitchen-shed (*kappiyakuṭi*).
“Householder” (*gahapati*) refers to those who, having built a dwelling, say, “We give this as a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a lawful hut); please make use of it.
This is what is called a “householder. It is likewise permissible when they say, “We give [this] to build a *kappiya-kuṭi*.
However, in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Except for a monk, from the hands of all other fellow practitioners of the Dharma and of gods and humans...”
It is said: "Receiving, storing, and what has been kept overnight—these are permissible for a monk if they belong to those [laypeople].
Therefore, their houses or a suitable hut (kappiyakuṭi) given by them are called 'the householder's'. Furthermore, it is said:
"Excluding the monastery of the Saṅgha of monks, [the dwellings] of the nuns' quarters, of the monastery attendants, or of the heretics..."
"If it is said that 'the celestial palace of the devas, or of the nāgas, or even of Brahmā, becomes a kappiya-kuṭi,' that is well said;

for indeed, only what belongs to the Saṅgha—or a house belonging to individual monks—is not a gahapatikuṭikā. What is called 'formal authorization' (sammutikā) is that which is made by proclaiming the formal act (kammavācā)."
Whatever food has been stored within these four types of allowable enclosures (kappiyabhūmi) does not count as "stored indoors" (antovuttha).
Indeed, it was for the purpose of releasing the restrictions regarding storage indoors and cooking indoors for both monks and nuns that the allowable huts (kappiyakuṭi) were authorized.
However, whatever belongs to the Saṅgha that has been stored in an unallowable place (akappiyabhūmi), such as a house large enough for two people to lie down together—
If something belonging to an individual monk or nun has been set aside for even a single night, it is called "stored overnight";

anything cooked therein is termed "cooked overnight," and this is not permitted. However, items intended for use within seven days (*sattāhakālika*) and those for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*) are allowable.
Regarding this, the following is the detailed analysis: a novice brings food such as rice to a monk at the *kappiyakuṭi* (the kitchen).
If one sets it aside and then cooks and gives it on the following day, it is not considered "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*).
In that regard, if one puts anything—such as ghee or other items—into what has been placed in an improper shed (*akappiyakuṭi*) and then gives it, it is called "oral storage" (*mukhasannidhi*).
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* it is stated: "It is stored overnight. In this case, the only difference is merely in the terminology. [If] a monk [places it] in an improper shed...

If one cooks clarified butter that has been set aside and leaf-vegetables intended for life-long use together and consumes them, it is permissible for seven days as long as they are not mixed with non-medicinal food (*nirāmisa*).
If, however, one consumes them after mixing them with non-medicinal food, they are considered both "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*) and "self-cooked" (*sāmaṃpāka*).
By this same principle, all types of admixture (*saṃsagga*) are to be understood.
When, however, do these *kappiyakuṭis* (permissible sheds) lose their structural basis? First, regarding those established by formal proclamation (*ussāvanantikā*):

if it was constructed by driving [posts] into the ground above the pillars or at the base of the walls, it loses its structural basis once all the pillars and the bases of the walls have been removed.
But if they move the pillars or the bases of the walls, whichever one remains...
It remains established in each respective place; even when all other parts have been turned over, it does not abandon its original basis.

However, a structure built with bricks and so forth—starting from the brick, stone, or lump of clay placed on top for the sake of a wall—loses its basis once it has perished. But as for those bricks and so forth by which it was supported, even if they are removed...
When other [buildings] have been established there, it remains with its original site intact.
In the case of a *gonisādikā* (a small hut), once an enclosure such as a wall has been constructed, its original site is abandoned.

In that case, it is necessary to obtain a separate *kappiyakuṭi* (a storehouse for allowable goods) within that same monastery. However, if the walls and so forth are broken here and there again, then from those points...
The cows enter [the enclosure], and it becomes a *kappiyakuṭi* (a place for lawful food) once again.

However, the other two [types of enclosures] become abandoned in their structural basis when the entire roof has perished, with the exception of the mere rafters. If there is even a single eave-support or circular ridge-pole above the rafters, it remains protected.
But where none of these four types of *kappiyabhūmi* exist, what should be done? [One should rely on] one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Having given it away and made it his own property, it may be used. Here is the story regarding this:
It is said that the Elder Karavikatissa, a preeminent master of the Vinaya, went into the presence of the Elder Mahāsīva.
Seeing a jar of ghee by the light of a lamp, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is this? The elder replied, "Friend, a jar of ghee was brought from the village for the day of coarse food."
“I shall eat with ghee,” he said. Then the Elder Tissa replied, “It is not permitted, Venerable Sir.
On the following day, the Elder had it placed at the head of the hall. When the Elder Tissa returned one day, he saw it and asked the same question;
[the other] replied, “Venerable Sir, it is not permitted to place it in a spot sufficient for two people to lie down together. On the next day, the Elder...
Having had it carried outside, he had it set down; thieves stole it. On another day, when the Elder Tissa arrived, he said to him:
"Friend, that jar which you told me was not permissible has been carried outside and stolen by thieves.
Then the Elder Tissa said to him: "Was it not, venerable sir, to be given to one who is not fully ordained? To one who is not fully ordained..."
"For it is indeed permissible to use [these things] after having given them away and made them his own.

296–9. The *Meṇḍaka* story is self-evident. Furthermore, regarding the statement "I allow you, monks, the five milk-products (*gorasa*)," the meaning is that I also allow these five milk-products to be used separately as individual items of consumption. "One should seek provisions for the journey" means...
In this regard, if some give having understood for themselves, that is good;
if they do not give, it should be sought from a place where one’s relatives have invited [one] or by means of the practice of wandering for alms.

If one does not obtain it in that way, it may be taken even after requesting it from a place where those who are not relatives have invited [one]. On a journey that can be completed in a single day, one should seek only enough for a single meal.
Over a long journey, one should seek out as much [provisions] as it takes to cross the wilderness.
300. The Story of the Foul-Tufted Keniya:
"Having had them carried by carrying-poles" means a thousand jars of well-prepared jujube juice, using five hundred carrying-poles.
Having had [them] recite [the verses], and having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, he said:

"It was well, monks, that you did not raise the claim that 'the disciples of the ascetic Gotama do not drink water because they are addicted to many requisites,' and that you showed respect for me and caused respect for me to arise in you; it is for this reason that I [say] to you..."
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma in the manner beginning with “You are well-pleased,” he said: “I allow you, monks, eight kinds of drinks,” and so forth.
In that context, *ambapāna* (mango drink) is a drink made from mangoes, whether raw or ripe.
Regarding that, one making it from raw fruit should break open young mangoes, place them in water, cook them by the heat of the sun, strain them, and [use those] received on that very day.
It should be prepared by mixing honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth. What is thus prepared is permissible only before the meal.
However, having received what was prepared by those not fully ordained, if it is accepted before the meal, it is allowable even for consumption with solid food;
after the meal, it remains allowable for consumption without solid food until the rising of the dawn. This same method applies to all drinks.
Among these, *jambupāna* is a drink made from jambu fruits. *Cocapāna* is a drink made from the seeds of plantain fruits.
*Mocapāna* is a drink made from plantain fruits that are seedless. *Madhukapāna* is a drink made from the natural juice of *madhuka* flowers;
that is permissible when mixed with water, but it is not permissible if it is pure. *Muddikapāna*...
*Ambapāna*: juice made by crushing grapes in water, like the drink made from mangoes. *Sālūkapāna*:
juice made by crushing the roots (*sālūka*) of red lotuses, blue lotuses, and so forth. *Phārusakapāna*: juice made from *phārusaka* fruits, like the drink made from mangoes.
These eight drinks are permitted whether they are cold or heated by the sun; they are not permitted if heated by fire. *Dhaññaphalarasa*: the juice of grain and fruit.

The juice of the fruit of the seven grains. "Juice of *ḍāka*" means the juice of ripe *ḍāka* (potherbs). For the juices of vegetables that may be consumed at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), only the juice before the meal is permissible.
For those [vegetables] that may be kept for life (*yāvajīvika*), once they have been accepted and cooked together with ghee and so forth that may be stored, they are permissible for seven days.
However, if one cooks them with plain water, they are permissible even for the duration of one's life. [This applies to] milk and so forth as well.
However, it is not permissible to cook it together [with other food]. Even that which has been cooked by others is considered merely a vegetable juice (*ḍākarasa*).

In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated: "Even for those things that may be consumed at any time (*yāvakālika*), if they have been crushed with cold water, it is permissible whether they are prepared as a juice or roasted by the sun.
Regarding the phrase "except for the juice of *madhuka* flowers," here the juice of *madhuka* flowers may be either fire-cooked or sun-roasted.
Or, it is not permitted after the meal. Even before the meal, any liquid that people take and use to make intoxicants is not permitted from the very beginning.

However, as for *madhuka* flowers—whether fresh, dried, or roasted, or the molasses made from them—from the point at which they no longer produce intoxicants, all of that is permitted before the meal.
Ucchu-rasa (sugarcane juice) is permissible after the meal when it is unrefined. Thus, by permitting these drinks, these four flavors are also permitted.
In such passages as "Sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their chief," it is said that the fire-oblation is the best; the fire-oblation is the "mouth" [the foremost].
The Discourse on the Story of Roja Malla and Others.
301–2. The story of Roja is easy to understand. In this context, "they made a compact" means they made an agreement.

"This is indeed noble for you" means this is indeed excellent for you. "I have not come here, venerable Ānanda, because I am busy" shows that he did not come because he was occupied with great reverence and faith toward the Buddha and others.
"And all kinds of potherbs" refers to any kind of potherb, whether cooked with ghee and other ingredients or uncooked.
“Parched grain” (*piṭṭhakhādanīya*) means food made from flour. It is said that Roja had both of these prepared by paying a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
“Gentle” (*mañjukā*) means sweet-spoken. “Eloquent” (*paṭibhāneyyakā*) means endowed with ready wit in their own craft. “Skillful” (*dakkhā*)...
"Skilled" means diligent. "Of pure craft" means of faultless craft. "With a nāḷi measure and a sifter":
a *āvāpaka* (sifter) is that into which they pour or deposit whatever they have obtained; this is what is meant.
And as for the rule, "Monks, one who was previously a barber must not take up a barber's kit," it is not merely forbidden to carry it after having taken it up.
It is permissible to have one’s hair cut by someone else’s property. However, if one has it cut for a wage, it is not permissible.
It is also permissible for one who has never had his hair cut before to maintain it himself; likewise, it is permissible to have one’s hair cut using either that person’s hair or another’s.

304. “Having given a share” means having given a tenth part. This, it is said, was the ancient custom in Jambudīpa; therefore, having divided [the crop] into ten portions, one portion must be given to the owners of the land.
The Discourse on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesakathā) 305.
"Monks, that which has been declared by me, 'This is not allowable,'—the Blessed One spoke these four great authorities for the sake of monks grasping the method.
Therein, the Elder Theras who compiled the Dhamma, having taken up the Sutta and scrutinized it, [said]: this...
They saw this. With the exception of the juice of grain and fruit, the juices of the seven types of grain are prohibited because they are not permitted after the meal.

The palmyra, coconut, plantain, breadfruit, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, *pussaphala*, *tipusaphala*, and *eḷāluka*—these nine great fruits and all other non-grain vegetables—belong to the category of grain (*dhaññagatika*). Although these are not specifically prohibited, [they are treated as such].
Now, it conforms to what is allowable; therefore, it is not permissible after the meal. Eight drinks have been authorized.
The remaining small-fruit drinks—such as those made from vetta, tintiṇika, mātuluṅga, kapittha, kosamba, karamanda, and so forth—fall under the same category as the eight drinks.
Although they have not been specifically authorized, they nevertheless conform to what is allowable; therefore, they are permissible. With the exception of...

For there is no other fruit-drink that is not permissible which possesses the flavor of grain-fruit in accordance with the rule; indeed, all such drinks are only for the duration of a watch (yāmakālika), as stated in the *Kurundi*.
Six types of robes were authorized by the Blessed One. By the Elders of the Council (*Dhammasaṅgāhakathera*), six others were authorized as suitable for them:
*dukūla*, *pattuṇṇa*, *cīnapaṭṭa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, *iddhimayika*, and *devadattiya*.
In this context, "cotton" (*pattuṇṇa*) refers to cloth produced by insects in the Pattuṇṇa country.
Two types of cloth are mentioned by their very names. These three are suitable for silk; *dukūla* is suitable for hemp, while the other two are suitable for cotton, or for all [three materials].
Having rejected eleven types of bowls, the Blessed One permitted two: the iron bowl and the clay bowl.
Furthermore, an iron bowl, a clay bowl, and a copper-iron bowl are the corresponding types for those [three]. The Blessed One permitted three kinds of water-pots (*tumba*):
an iron pot, a wooden pot, and a fruit-pot. A water-flask (*kuṇḍikā*), a golden vessel, and a water-pot are the corresponding types for those.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: "Water-strainers and water-scoops are the corresponding types for these."
It has been stated. Two types of waistbands were permitted: the *paṭṭikā* and the *sūkaranta*; waistbands made of cloth strips or rope are their appropriate counterparts.
Three types of umbrellas were permitted: the white umbrella, the palm-leaf umbrella, and the leaf umbrella;
the single-leaf umbrella is the appropriate counterpart to those very ones. Following this method, the *pāḷi*...
Without relying solely on the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), other points that are consistent with what is allowable and what is not allowable should also be understood.
The statement, "What is received on that very day is allowable at the proper time," and so forth, was said with reference to [drinks] whose flavors have been mixed together.
For if the drink has been received together with the entire coconut fruit, without even removing the husk, [it is not allowable].
Having removed the coconut shell, it is permissible even at an improper time.
When they give cold milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top, having removed the ghee that is not mixed with the rice, it is allowable to consume it for seven days.
The same principle applies to solidified honey, molasses, and so forth. [Likewise,] alms-food adorned with cardamom, nutmeg, and other such items...
Those teeth, having been extracted and washed, may be used for as long as one lives.

The same principle applies to ginger and other such things that were given after being added to gruel, or to lac and madhuka and other such things that were given after being added to oils and the like.
Thus, whatever remains unadulterated in its flavor, even if it was received as a single mixed item, it becomes pure in the same way [as if it had been received separately].
It is permissible to wash or chop it and consume each [ingredient] according to its respective time-period.
However, if it has become mixed in flavor—that is, if they have been blended together—it is not permissible.

For when things of different time-periods are mixed in flavor with one another, those of the "yāmakālika" (night-time) period and so forth cause even the three [other types], including the "yāvakālika" (immediate-time), to assume their own nature; likewise, the "yāmakālika" causes even the two [others] to do so.
Things such as those kept for seven days bring their own specific nature [to what they are mixed with];
even that which is kept for seven days, when mixed together with that which is kept for life, brings only its own specific nature [to the latter].

Therefore, if one has received it on that same day, then a lifetime-allowance (yāvajīvika) received on that same day, or one received earlier, is permissible for seven days; if received two days prior, for six days; if received three days prior, for five days.
It should be understood that what has been received for five days... [and so on] ...up to seven days is allowable on that very day.
For this very reason, it was not said, "Monks, by means of a seven-day medicine, life-long medicine may be received on that same day," but rather, "What is received is allowable for seven days.

Furthermore, regarding the passing of the time, the watch of the night, and the seven days, [the distinctions are made] by way of the training rules concerning eating at the wrong time, storing food, and medicines.

The offenses are to be understood [as follows]. Furthermore, among these four types of "time-limited" (kālaka) substances, only the two—namely, that which is for as long as life lasts (yāvakālika) and that which is for a watch of the night (yāmakālika)—are subject to both "storing within the monastery" (antovutthaka) and "making a hoard" (sannidhikāraka).

However, that which is for seven days (sattāhakālika) and that which is for as long as life lasts may be placed even in an improper storehouse (akappiyakuṭi), and they do not produce the state of being a hoard. The remainder is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is finished.
7. The Chapter on the Kathina:
The Discourse on the Permission for the Kathina.
306. In the Kathina-kkhandhaka—“The Pāveyyakas” means those who dwell in the kingdom of Pāvā. Pāvā is the name of a kingdom located in the western part of Kosala;
it means “those dwelling there. This is a designation for the Bhaddavaggiya Theras, who were paternal cousins of the King of Kosala.
Among them, the eldest was a non-returner (anāgāmī), and the youngest...
There is not even one stream-enterer, nor an arahant, nor an ordinary person (puthujjana).

They are "forest-dwellers" (*āraññika*) by virtue of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), not merely by the fact of living in the forest. The same principle applies to their being alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*) and so forth.
This was stated with reference to their heads. However, these thirteen ascetic practices are undertaken and then maintained. In the phrase "by the gathering of water," it is by water...
"Bound together, joined, and mingled" means they have become one in water, both on dry land and in the depths.
"In a muddy quagmire" means that wherever one steps, a muddy quagmire rises up and strikes as far as the buttocks;
such is the meaning of "in a quagmire. "Filled with water" means full of water. It is said that their robes were thick.
The water that falls upon them does not flow away; because of its density, it remains as if bound in a sack. Therefore it is said: "with robes filled with rain.
There is also a reading: "with robes filled with floods" (*oghapuṇṇehi*).
Regarding the phrase "we spent the rains without quarreling," here, due to the lack of comfort in the lodgings at the place where newcomers arrived, [the Blessed One]...

Because of their lack of gain from seeing [the Buddha] and because of their dissatisfaction, those bhikkhus did not dwell in comfort; therefore, they did not say, "We have spent the rainy season in comfort without dispute.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma—the discourse on the *Anamatagga* (Without-End)—the Blessed One spoke to those bhikkhus.
At the conclusion of that discourse, they all attained Arahantship right where they were sitting.
They departed by leaping into the air; it is with reference to this that it is said: "Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One thought:
"If the Kathina ceremony had been established, these monks would not have come so exhausted, traveling in only their inner and outer robes while setting aside one robe;
moreover, this Kathina ceremony has been authorized by all the Buddhas."
Having reflected and desiring to authorize the spreading of the *kaṭhina*, he addressed the monks; and having addressed them, he said, “I authorize you, monks,” and so forth.
In this context, *atthatakathinānaṃ* is merely a particle (*voti nipātamattaṃ*), and it is a variant form (*vokāro*); its meaning is “of those for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread. For it is thus:
When there is another [person], it is appropriate [to say], "That shall be for them. Alternatively, *vo* is simply a genitive particle.
In the phrase "that shall be for them" (*so nesam*), the meaning is: "That robe-offering shall be for those whose *kathina* has been spread.
In that context, "going without having asked permission" means that as long as the *kathina* has not been removed, it is permissible to go about without having asked permission.

The meaning is that there will be no offense by means of the training rule on conduct (*cāritta-sikkhāpada*). "Wandering without having formally undertaken [the robes]" means wandering without having formally accepted the three robes;
the meaning is that being separated from one's robe will be permissible. "Eating in a group" means that eating in a group will also be permissible.
"Robes as much as required" means as much robe-cloth as is needed, even if it has not been determined (*anadhiṭṭhita*) or assigned for distribution (*avikappita*).
The meaning is "it shall be appropriate. And as for "whatever robe-offering arises there":

whether it be a robe for the deceased within that boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread, or what is given specifically for the Saṅgha, or what is brought by means of a contribution intended for the Saṅgha—in whatever manner a robe belonging to the Saṅgha arises there, the meaning is that it shall belong to them.
And furthermore, monks, regarding the instruction "the kaṭhina should be spread in this manner," who receives the spreading of the kaṭhina and who does not?
First, by way of number, at the minimum five persons receive it; above that, even a hundred thousand may do so, but below five, they do not.
By way of having completed the rains residence, those who have entered the rains residence during the first period and [participated in] the first invitation ceremony...

Those who have been invited receive [the benefit]; however, those whose rains-residence is cut short, or those who have entered for the later rains-residence, do not receive it, nor do those who have completed their rains-residence in another monastery—thus it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

But for those who have entered for the earlier rains-residence, all become "fillers of the quorum," yet they do not receive the special privilege (*ānisansa*); that privilege belongs only to the others. If, during the earlier rains-residence...
If four, three, two, or even one [monk] has arrived, the *kaṭhina* should be spread by making the others fulfill the quorum.

Now, if four monks have arrived and one novice (*sāmaṇera*) who is of full age (*paripuṇṇavassa*) receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) during the later period, he both fulfills the quorum and receives the benefit. [Likewise if there are] three monks and two novices, or two monks...
The same principle applies here as well: [the case of] three novices, one bhikkhu, and four novices.

If those who have arrived during the first period are not skilled in the spreading of the *kaṭhina*, then elders who are reciters of the *Khandhaka* and are skilled in the spreading should be sought out and brought there.
Having announced the formal act (*kammavācā*), having had the *kaṭhina* spread, and having partaken of the gift, they will depart.
The benefit, however, belongs only to the others.
By whom may the *kaṭhina* be given? It is permissible for it to be given by anyone—whether a deva or a human—or by any one of the five who share the same Dhamma.
There is a duty for the giver of the *kaṭhina*; if he asks because he does not know it, [it should be explained].
—“Venerable sir, how should the kaṭhina be given? To him it should be explained thus:
“It is permissible to give, at the time of sunrise, a cloth sufficient for any one of the three robes, saying, ‘We give this as a kaṭhina-cīvara.
For the purpose of preparing it, there should be this many needles, this much thread, and this much dye; [this is] the preparation.”
"It is proper to give rice gruel and food for this many monks.
Furthermore, the one who spreads the *kaṭhina* cloth must know the proper conduct when spreading the *kaṭhina* that has been acquired in accordance with the Dhamma and justice.
For it is not permissible to use a robe that is stained with grain-dust, even if it was brought from a weaver's house; nor is a soiled robe permissible.

It is not permissible; therefore, having obtained a cloth for the Kathina ceremony, one should wash it thoroughly, prepare the needle and other requisites for sewing, and together with many bhikkhus, sew it on that very day.

Once the needlework is finished, it should be dyed, the *kappa-bindu* mark applied, and the Kathina spread. If another cloth for the Kathina is brought while that one has not yet been spread, [the same procedure must be followed].
He also gives many other items that constitute grounds for the benefits of the kaṭhina; the kaṭhina should be spread using the property of whoever gives the great benefit.
As for the other person, he should be exhorted and persuaded in whatever way necessary.
But by whom should the kaṭhina be spread? By him to whom the Saṅgha gives the kaṭhina robe-cloth. However, by the Saṅgha...
To whom should it be given? To one whose robes are worn out. If many have worn-out robes, it should be given to the senior.
Even among the seniors, it should be given to one who has a large following and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day.
If the senior is unable and a junior is able, it should be given to him. Furthermore, by the Saṅgha, [it should be given] to the Great Elder...
It is appropriate to make a collection; therefore, one should say, "Venerable sir, you take [the robe]; we shall make it and give it to you.
Among the three robes, that which is worn out should be given for its replacement. For a robe that is normally double-layered (*dupaṭṭa*), only a double-layered one should be given.
Even if his single-layered robe (*ekapaṭṭa*) is thick and his Kathina-cloth is thin, [a double-layered one] should be given for the sake of propriety.

Only enough for two layers (*dupaṭṭa*) should be given; even if one says, "I will wear a single-layered robe if I do not receive [enough]," it is permissible to give two layers. However, it should not be given to one who is of a greedy disposition.
Furthermore, that person should not accept it with the thought, "Having spread out the *kaṭhina*, I will later sew it and make two robes. But as for the one to whom it is given...
In order to show the procedure by which it should be given, the text begins with, "And thus, monks,
the kaṭhina should be spread," and first states the formal act of giving (*dāna-kammavācā*) beginning with, "Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. Now,
when the kaṭhina has been given in this manner, if that kaṭhina-cloth is already prepared for use, then this...
This is wholesome. If the preliminary work has not been completed, it is not permissible for even a single person to say, "I am an elder" or "I am one of great learning," and thus fail to do it;
rather, everyone must assemble and complete the washing, sewing, and dyeing.
For this is called the Kathina-duty, praised by the Buddha. In the past, even the Blessed One Padumuttara [praised] the Kathina-duty...
He performed it. It is said that his chief disciple, the Elder Sujāta by name, took up the *kaṭhina*;
the Teacher, sitting together with six million eight hundred thousand monks, performed it.
Once the *kaṭhina* ceremony was completed, the monk who had spread the *kaṭhina*, having taken up the *kaṭhina* robe, [said]: "If, with the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), the *kaṭhina*..."
When one wishes to spread the *kaṭhina*, the old outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) must be relinquished and the new outer robe formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*).
One must utter the words: "By means of this outer robe, I spread the *kaṭhina*. The *kaṭhina* is to be spread according to the procedure stated in the *Parivāra* beginning with these words.
Having spread it, that monk who has spread the *kaṭhina* [should address] the Saṅgha...
Having approached, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, he should speak thus:
‘Venerable sirs, the kaṭhina has been spread for the Saṅgha; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma; please express your appreciation.
Those monks who are expressing appreciation, having arranged their upper robes over one shoulder and extended their hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus: ‘It has been spread...’
"Friends, the kaṭhina belongs to the Saṅgha; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma; let us express our appreciation.
By means of this very procedure stated in the Parivāra, one should have the appreciation expressed, and the others should express their appreciation.
In this way, the kaṭhina is considered spread for all. For it is said in the Parivāra: "The kaṭhina is considered spread for two types of persons..."
“...and for the one who spreads [the robe] and the one who gives thanks. Furthermore, it is said: “The Saṅgha does not spread the *kaṭhina*;
a group (*gaṇa*) does not spread the *kaṭhina*; an individual (*puggala*) spreads the *kaṭhina*.
Through the Saṅgha’s giving of thanks, through the group’s giving of thanks, and through the individual’s spreading, the *kaṭhina* becomes spread for the Saṅgha; it becomes spread for the group.”
"The kaṭhina has been spread; the kaṭhina has been spread for an individual.

Now, when the kaṭhina has been spread in this manner, if the donors give the benefits brought along with the kaṭhina-cloth, saying, "We give them only to the one who accepted our kaṭhina," the Saṅgha of monks has no claim to them. Then, without even investigating—

Having given [the robes], they depart; the Saṅgha is the master. Therefore, if the remaining robes of one who has performed the *kathina* ceremony are also worn out, the Saṅgha, having obtained permission, should give cloth for their sake as well.

However, only a single formal act (*kammavācā*) is required. For the remaining benefits of the *kathina*, [one may provide] strong cloth by means of the *vassāvāsika-ṭhitikā* (the practice of providing robes for the rainy season).
They should be distributed; in the absence of a fixed order of precedence, they should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior monk. Valuable goods (garubhaṇḍa) must not be divided.
However, if there are many monasteries within a single boundary (ekasīmā), all the monks should be assembled and the kaṭhina cloth should be spread out in one place;
it is not permissible to spread it out separately in each location.
308. Now, in order to show in detail the procedure for how the kaṭhina is properly spread and how it is not properly spread, [the Buddha] said:
"And thus, monks, the kaṭhina is properly spread, and thus it is not properly spread.

Having stated this, he first demonstrated the twenty-four characteristics of what is not properly spread—beginning with "not by mere scratching," and so forth—which consist of both things that should not be done and those pertaining to the great grounds.
He demonstrated [the first] mode. Thereafter, demonstrating the characteristic of being spread, he demonstrated seventeen modes beginning with "spread with new cloth.
For in the *Parivāra* as well, this very definition is stated: "In twenty-four modes the kaṭhina is not spread; in seventeen modes the kaṭhina is spread."
In this context, "by the mere act of scratching" means by the mere taking of measurements in terms of length and breadth.
For one who takes measurements scratches with their fingernails or the like, showing the boundaries for the purpose of identifying each respective part, or rubs it on the forehead and so forth;
therefore, that taking of measurements is called "the mere act of scratching. "By the mere act of washing" means...
“By the mere washing of the cloth for the kaṭhina”: by the mere washing of the robe-cloth intended for the kaṭhina ceremony. “By the mere sorting of the robe-cloth”:
by the mere sorting [of the threads] with the thought, “Let it be fivefold, or sevenfold, or ninefold, or elevenfold.

“By the mere cutting”: by the mere cutting of the cloth as it has been sorted. “By the mere sewing”: by the mere application of the waste-thread (the binding thread). “By the mere making of the border-strips”: by the mere making of the *ovaṭṭika* (border-strips).
"By merely sewing it long according to the pattern of a false thread"; "by merely making a seam" means by merely binding the corners with cloth;
"by merely making it firm" means by merely sewing two pieces of cloth together after joining them as one.
Alternatively, it means by merely sewing a stiffened cloth (kaṭhina-sāṭaka) after having fixed the first piece of cloth and made that inner layer its lining.
This is the meaning. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: “By the gift of a dwelling for a regular robe. In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated:
“By merely attaching a lining (*kucchicimilika*) so that a regular robe bound with a border (*pattabaddha*) may be made double-layered (*dupaṭṭa*).

“By the mere act of making a wind-layer (*anuvātakaraṇa*)” means by the mere application of a wind-layer to the back. “By the mere act of making a fringe (*paribhaṇḍakaraṇa*)” means by the mere application of a wind-layer to the front.
"By the mere act of adding a border" means by the mere application of a border to a newly acquired robe.
Or, having taken a border from a *kaṭhina* robe, it means by the mere application of a border to another robe that is not a *kaṭhina* robe.
"By the mere act of softening the wool" means by applying once even a tooth-colored dye or a pale-leaf-colored dye to the cloth during the process of dyeing.
Or: if it is suitable even once or twice during the night, it is permissible.
"By making a sign" means by making a sign such as, "I shall spread the kaṭhina with this cloth. For only this much is stated in the Parivāra;
however, in the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathās), it says: "This robe is beautiful; it is possible to spread the kaṭhina with this."
"Having performed such a preparatory act (nimittakamma), [the robe] is obtained," it is said. "By means of indirect speech (parikathā)" means:
by what has been produced through indirect speech such as, "It is proper to give a kathina; one who gives a kathina generates much merit. Regarding the kathina: it must be of the highest quality;
it is not even proper to request it from one's own mother; it must be exactly like something fallen from the sky.
