"It is allowable" means: "by what is done for a short time" (*kukkukata*) refers to that which is temporary. Regarding "by what is stored" (*sannidhikata*): here, "storing" (*sannidhi*) is twofold—storing by making (*karaṇa-sannidhi*) and storing by accumulation (*nicaya-sannidhi*).
Among these, "storing by making" is the act of setting something aside without having made it on that very day.
For example, if the Sangha receives cloth for the Kathina ceremony today and gives it away on the following day, this is "storing by accumulation."

"By means of what is to be forfeited" (nissaggiyena) means by means of that which is to be forfeited at dawn. It is also stated in the *Parivāra*: "What is called 'to be forfeited' is when dawn breaks while [the robe] is being made.

"By means of what is not formally accepted" (akappakatenā) means by means of that which has not received even a drop of formal acceptance (*kappa*). Regarding the phrase "except for the outer cloak" (*aññatra saṅghāṭiyā*) and so forth:

setting aside the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*), upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), it refers to whether another item, such as a bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*), has been spread out or not.

"It is allowable" means: except for one made of five or more than five [patches], it is permissible only if it has been made by cutting it into five or more pieces and displaying large and small circular patches (*maṇḍala*). For in this way it becomes "patched with circles" (*samaṇḍalika*);
apart from that, it is not permissible if it is uncut or consists of only two, three, or four pieces. Except for... [the rest of the sentence continues].
"Spreading for an individual" means that once the spreading has been performed for an individual, it does not become spread by any other spreading for the Saṅgha or a group.
"He gives thanks while standing outside the boundary" means he gives thanks while standing outside the *upacāra-sīmā* (the precinct boundary).
"With new [cloth]" means with that which has not yet been used. "With what is like new" means with that which resembles new cloth, having been worn only once or twice.

Or with one that has been washed. "With a rag (*pilotikā*)" means with a cloth from a shop. "With a refuse-rag (*paṃsukūla*)" means with a refuse-rag obtained from the twenty-three [specified] places.

It is also stated in the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī* commentaries that it refers to a robe made from rags obtained by a refuse-rag monk (*paṃsukūlika*) after wandering for alms for such rags. "From a shop" (*pāpaṇika*) means a rag fallen at the door of a shop.

The meaning is that it is also permissible if one takes [the robe] and gives it for the purpose of the *kathina* ceremony. The remainder should be understood by reversing what has already been stated.

However, regarding this point—the question, "With the spreading of the *kathina*, how many qualities arise," and so forth—as much as has been stated in many commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), all of that is actually included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) of the *Parivāra*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method presented therein.
For by its being spoken here, nothing is lost for one who has performed the *kaṭhina*-spreading (*kaṭhinatthāraka*).
Having thus shown the *kaṭhina*-spreading, he now spoke the passage beginning with "And how, monks, is the *kaṭhina* suspended? in order to show the suspension (*ubbhāra*).
In that context, "matrix" (*mātikā*) means "mothers"; the sense is "progenitors. For the suspension of the *kaṭhina*...

These are the eight origins. In these, the *pakkamana* (departure) occurs within [the robe season]; thus it is called "originating from departure" (*pakkamanantikā*). The remaining [origins] are to be understood in the same way.
311. Discussion on the Group of Seven Regarding Taking Up:
"They will not return" means they will not come back again. However, regarding this *kathina*-suspension originating from departure:

First the impediment of the robe is severed, afterwards the impediment of the residence. For one who departs in this manner, the impediment of the robe is severed right within the boundary, while the impediment of the residence is severed upon crossing the boundary. This has also been stated in the *Parivāra*:
"The suspension of the *kaṭhina* at the time of departure was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun."
"And I shall answer this: first the impediment of robes is severed;
afterwards the impediment of the residence is severed.
"Taking the robe" means taking an unmade robe. "Having gone outside the boundary" means having gone to another neighboring monastery.
"It occurs thus" means that upon seeing the comfort of the lodgings or the excellence of companions in that monastery, it occurs in this way.
However, in this case of the suspension of the kaṭhina at the end of the [rainy] season, the obstacle of the residence is severed first;
for it is severed as soon as the thought "I will not return" arises. And this has been said:
“The completion of the robe-making season is the cause for the suspension of the kaṭhina, as declared by the Kinsman of the Sun.
Regarding this, I shall explain: first, the obstacle of the residence is severed;
when the robe is finished, the obstacle of the robe is severed.”
By this method, the meaning should also be understood for the rest of the analysis of the matrix (mātikā). However, this is the distinction:
"In the case of one who has reached a final decision, even both obstacles—'I shall not have this robe made' and 'they will not return'—are cut off simultaneously as soon as the thought arises.
For this has been said:
“The removal of the kaṭhina by formal resolution was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun;
this I shall explain to you: two impediments are severed simultaneously, neither before nor after.
Thus should the severance of impediments be understood in all cases of the removal of the kaṭhina. Furthermore, because it is by this aforementioned method...
It can be known by the fact that they have arrived with their retinue; therefore, it has not been stated in detail. This, however, is the summary here:

first, the impediment of the dwelling (*āvāsa-palibodha*) is severed when [the robe] is lost near the place of residence; the impediment of the robe (*cīvara-palibodha*) is severed when the robe is lost.
Because the impediment of the robe is severed when the robe is lost, it is called "severed at the point of loss" (*nāsanantika*).

In the case of the "near-hearing" (savanantika) [robe], the impediment of the robe is severed first; therefore, for that person, the impediment of the residence is severed simultaneously with the hearing.
In the case of the "cut-off expectation" (āsāvacchedika), the impediment of the residence is severed first. When the expectation for the robe has been cut off, the impediment of the robe is severed.
However, as for this [other type], because he thinks: "I obtain it without expectation; I do not obtain it through expectation; it occurs to him: 'Right here [I shall keep] this...'"
The teaching on the mixed [cases] along with other exemptions—such as the method beginning with "I shall have a robe made, I will not return"—is of many varieties;
therefore, it has been explained separately in detail later on and is not mentioned here.

However, immediately after the *savanantika* (the end of hearing), the *sīmātikkantika* (crossing the boundary) is mentioned. In that regard, the obstacle of the robe (*cīvara-palibodha*) is severed first.

For him, the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) is severed outside the boundary. When carried out together, two impediments are severed simultaneously, neither before nor after the other.

(316–325) Having thus shown the seven ways of the suspension of the *kaṭhina* in the section on "taking" (*ādāya*), those same [seven] are again shown as applicable, as far as possible, in the section on "undertaking" (*samādāya*) regarding a robe that has been left unfinished, as well as in the sections on both "taking" and "undertaking.
Following that, within the boundary: "I shall return..."

Without touching upon this procedure [of "I shall not return"], those instances that are applicable by touching upon this very [formula] "I shall not return" and by way of the method beginning with "without having determined," have been shown. Thereafter,
having repeatedly demonstrated the "cutting off of hope" (*āsāvacchedika*) by way of mixing it with the others through the method beginning with "he departs in expectation of a robe," again—

The removal of the kaṭhina has been shown as applicable in the cases of "completion" (niṭṭhāna) and "living in comfort" (phāsuvihārika), by way of going to another region and by way of living in comfort respectively.

Having thus shown the removal of the kaṭhina according to its divisions, [the text] now shows their opposites—those obstructions which are said to be severed by each respective removal of the kaṭhina—by stating: "Bhikkhus, these two... [regarding the kaṭhina].

He said, "Obstacles," and so forth. Therein, "by that which has been relinquished" means: that mind by which the residence has been relinquished is called "relinquished"; [the residence is relinquished] by that relinquishment.
The same method applies to "vomited" and "released. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Kathina-kkhandhaka is finished.
8. The Chapter on Robes (Cīvarakkhandhaka):
The Account of Jīvaka’s Story. 326.
In the Chapter on Robes—“Skilled” (*padakkhiṇā*) means clever and proficient. “Arrived” (*abhisaṭā*) means having come. By whom have they arrived?
"By needy people, by needy people": here, having used the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental, it is said "of the needy, of the needy people.
"And he goes for fifty at night" means he goes at night after taking fifty kahāpaṇas.
"Negama" refers to a group of householders.

327. Regarding "he caused the courtesan Salavatī Kumārī to go forth": the citizens gave two hundred thousand [pieces of gold], the king gave one hundred thousand—thus three hundred thousand—and having given other portions such as monasteries, groves, and vehicles, they caused her to go forth;
the meaning is that they established her in the position of a courtesan. "She goes for a hundred pieces a night" means she goes for a hundred pieces during the night. She was ill.
"Paṭivedeyyaṃ" means one should make known one's state of illness. "Kattarasuppe" means on a worn-out bed.
(328) Why did he ask, "Who is my mother, O King, who is my father? It is said that when other royal children were playing and a quarrel arose, they would say, "He is motherless;
he is fatherless. And just as for other children, at festivals and such occasions, there are maternal grandmothers, maternal uncles, and so forth...
When they sent some gift, no one sent anything to him in return.
Thus, having reflected on all this, and in order to know whether he was truly without a mother, he asked, "Your Majesty, who is my mother? Who is my father?
Then he thought, "What if I were to learn a craft? What if I were to learn the craft of medicine? Regarding him—
It occurred to him: "These arts of elephant-riding, horsemanship, and so forth are connected with the harming of others;
the art of medicine, however, is preceded by loving-kindness and is connected with the welfare of beings. Therefore, referring specifically to the art of medicine, he thought:
"What if I were to train in this craft? Furthermore, more than a hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time of Padumuttara...

Seeing the physician who was the Blessed One’s attendant—whose virtues were renowned throughout the four assemblies as "this is the Buddha’s attendant"—he thought, "Oh, may I too attain such a position!
Having given alms for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Blessed One, I too shall be your attendant; [I am] the physician named So-and-so."
He made this aspiration: "May I become like him, an attendant to a future Buddha.
Urged by that previous aspiration, he thought, referring specifically to the craft of medicine: "What if I were to train in this craft? 329.
*Disāpāmokkho* means known, famous, or preeminent in all directions. And at that time—
Merchants from Takkasilā went to see Prince Abhaya. Jīvaka asked them, "Where have you come from?
When they replied, "From Takkasilā," he asked, "Is there a teacher of the medical craft there?
Upon hearing, "Yes, Prince, a world-renowned physician resides in Takkasilā," he said, "In that case, when you go, [inform me...]"
“Inform him,” he said. They did so. Without asking his father’s permission, he went with them to Takṣaśilā.
Therefore it was said: “Without asking Prince Abhaya,” and so forth.
“I wish to learn a craft, teacher,” [he said]. It is said that when the physician saw him approaching, he asked, “Who are you?”
“Who are you, dear? he asked. He replied, “I am the grandson of the great king Bimbisāra and the son of Prince Abhaya. “But why have you come here, dear?
Then he said, “In order to learn a craft from you; O Teacher, I wish to learn a craft. And he learned much, unlike other princes and such.
Having given wealth to the teacher, they learn without performing any work at all; he was not like that.
Rather, without giving any wealth, being a *dhamma-antevāsika* (a student by way of the Dhamma), at one time he performs work for his preceptor, and at another time he learns.
Even so, a clansman endowed with resolute intention, through his own intelligence, [attains] much...
He grasps it, he grasps it quickly, he retains it well, and what has been grasped does not escape his memory.

Regarding the statement, "Even though I have studied for seven years, no end to this craft appears," it is said that here Jīvaka learned everything that the teacher knew— which others take sixteen years to learn.
He mastered it in seven years. Then it occurred to Sakka, the king of the devas:
"This man will become the foremost attendant and most trusted confidant of the Buddhas; come now, I shall instruct him in the preparation of medicines.
Having taken up residence within his teacher’s body, so that he might cure all remaining diseases—save for the result of past karma—with a single medicinal formulation, [Sakka] began his instruction.
He was able [to learn], and so Sakka instructed him in the preparation of medicines. However, Jīvaka thought, "I am learning in the presence of my teacher.
Therefore, as soon as he had been released by Sakka with the words, "Jīvaka is now capable of practicing medicine," he reflected thus and asked his teacher.
But the teacher said, "This was not learned through my power; it was through the power of a deity."
Knowing that he had indeed received it, [the Buddha] said, "In that case, recite it," and so forth.
"Wandering for a league all around" means wandering for four days, having gone out through one gate each day. "He gave me a small amount of provisions" means he gave only a little.
Why? It is said that this thought occurred to him: "This is the son of a great family; as soon as he has departed..."
"He will receive great honor from his father and grandfather; therefore, they will not recognize the excellence of my craft or my own merit.

However, when his provisions are exhausted on the way, he will surely put my craft to use and come to know the excellence of both me and my craft"—thinking thus, she had him give the protective charm (paritta).
The Story of the Wife of the Treasurer, etc.
330. *Pasatena*: with a single handful. *Picunā*: with a layer of cotton-wool. *Yatrahi nāma*: indeed, that which is called.
*Kimpimāyaṃ*: what indeed is this to me? *Upajānāmetassa saṃyamassa*: [I shall reflect] upon this self-restraint and the subsiding of the disease thus produced.
The intention is that he recognizes [the other's] assistance.
331. Regarding the words "May all your ornaments be yours," it is said that the king thought: "If he takes this, I shall place him in a position of appropriate authority;
if he does not take it, I shall make him a trusted inner counselor. Thus he reflected.
He spoke thus. The thought also arose in the mind of Prince Abhaya and the actors, "O, would that he did not take it!
He too, as if knowing their thoughts, said, "This, O King, is the jewelry of my grandmothers;

it is not fitting for me to take it," and spoke the words beginning with, "Enough, O King. [The phrase] "the service done by me" refers to the favor rendered by the King when he said, "May the King remember my service."

"May the Lord remember me"—this is the meaning. The king, being pleased, gave him a house endowed with every excellence, a mango grove and park, a village yielding a hundred thousand [coins] annually, and great honors; then he said, "In that case, speak," and so forth.
This is the story concerning the merchant of Rājagaha.
332. But why did he say, "Can you do it, householder? It is said that by changing one's posture, the brain matter does not settle;

knowing that his brain matter would settle if he remained motionless for seven days, [the Buddha thought: "Perhaps, having promised for seven times seven months, he might even lie down for seven times seven days."
He spoke thus. Therefore it was said later: "But I knew it beforehand.
"Having peeled back the skin of the head" means having removed the scalp. "Having opened the suture" means having spread open the seam.
"I am not able, Teacher," he said, because a great fever had arisen in his body; that is why he spoke thus. "In three weeks" means in three periods of seven days each.
333. "Having cleared away the people" means having had the people led out.
334. Regarding the story of King Pajjota:
"I am disgusted by the snake," it is said, for this king was born from a scorpion; [he spoke thus] for the sake of counteracting the poison of the scorpion.
And because ghee is a medicine that is repulsive to scorpions, he spoke thus. "He will give up a spray" means he will emit a belch.
"It is capable of fifty yojanas" means it is able to go fifty yojanas.
Not only did the king have this female elephant; there was also an elephant named Nāḷāgiri who could travel a hundred yojanas, as well as Celakaṇṇa and Muñcakesa.
Two horses can travel two hundred *yojanas*, while the servant Kāka travels sixty *yojanas*.
It is said that one day, when a certain son of good family was sitting down to eat before a Buddha had appeared in the world, a Paccekabuddha arrived and stood at his door;
a man reported to him, "The Paccekabuddha has come and gone. Upon hearing this, he...
“Go, bring the bowl quickly! he said. Having had it brought, he gave him all his own prepared food and sent him off.
The other, having brought it back and placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, made this aspiration:
“Venerable sir, by virtue of this service I have performed for you, wherever I am reborn, may I be endowed with vehicles.”
He did so. He is now born as this King Pajjota; through that aspiration, he has attained this excellence of vehicles.
"Having made him drink ghee" means having given him ghee to drink; and having explained the rules for the food and conduct of his attendants.
"Having scraped out medicine with his fingernail" means having applied the medicine with his fingernail; the sense is "having put it in. "He expelled" means he purged.
The Discourse on the Pair of Siveyyaka Cloths (335).
What is called *siveyyaka* is a cloth from the Sivathika cemetery in Uttarakuru, which is considered inauspicious.
It is said that there, people wrap the dead in that cloth and set them down; perceiving it as "a piece of meat," the *hatthisoṇḍaka* birds [devour it].
Having lifted it up and placed it on a peak of the Himālayas, they remove the cloth and eat.
Then, forest-dwellers, seeing the cloth, bring it to the king. Thus was this obtained by Pajjota.
In the kingdom of Sivi, skilled women spin thread with three spindles; they say that the cloth woven from that thread is called *enta*.
The Discourse on the Thirty-fold Purgative (Samattiṃsavirecanakathā). 336.

Regarding the phrase "he should administer oleation": why is it said that the Blessed One’s body was not coarse? It is because the deities always add divine nutritive essence (*ojā*) to the Blessed One’s food.
Furthermore, the drinking of oleaginous substances moistens the humors (*doṣa*) everywhere, making the channels supple.

He did so; therefore, he spoke thus. "Three handfuls of lotuses" means: one for the purpose of removing gross faults, one for the purpose of removing medium faults, and one for the purpose of removing subtle faults.
"Before long he became of natural constitution" means that when his body had thus returned to its natural state, the citizens offered alms. Jīvaka came and said this to the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One, the citizens wish to give you alms today; do not enter the village for alms.
The Elder Mahāmoggallāna thought: “From where indeed should the Blessed One receive his first alms today?
Then he thought: “The merchant’s son Soṇa, from the time he began the cultivation of his field, [has performed deeds] not shared by others...”
"He eats the rice of fragrant *gandhasālī* paddy, which has been raised by sprinkling it with milk and water; therefore, I shall bring almsfood for the Blessed One.
Having gone there by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), he showed himself on the terrace of that palace.
Taking the elder’s bowl, he gave him excellent almsfood. And seeing the elder’s intention to depart, [the king said], "Eat, venerable sir."
He said, "Venerable sir, please eat; I shall give something else to the Blessed One.
Having fed the Elder, he wiped the bowl with perfumes, filled it with almsfood, and gave it to him. The Elder brought it and gave it to the Blessed One.
King Bimbisāra, thinking, "What will the Blessed One eat today?", came to the monastery and, as soon as he entered, [saw this].
Having smelled the fragrance of the almsfood, he became desirous of eating it. Devas placed nutritive essence (*ojā*) into two of the Blessed One’s almsbowls:
that which Sujātā had given, and that which Cunda the smith’s son offered at the time of the Parinibbāna.
They placed this essence into every other mouthful as well; therefore, knowing the King’s wish, the Blessed One ate only those portions into which the essence had not been added.
He had a small amount of almsfood given to the king. After the king had consumed it, he asked, "Venerable sir, was this food brought from Uttarakuru?

"No, Great King, it was not from Uttarakuru; rather, it is the food of a householder’s son who lives in your own kingdom," he said, and then he described Soṇa’s prosperity. Upon hearing this, the king desired to see Soṇa.
Having made the offering, he sent for Soṇa along with eighty thousand clansmen according to the method described in the *Cammakkhandhaka*.
Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, they became stream-enterers. But Soṇa, having gone forth, established himself in Arahantship.
It was for this very purpose that the Blessed One had the king provide almsfood.
The Discourse on the Request for the Marriage-Alliance (Varayācanakathā). 337. When the Blessed One had thus finished his meal, Jīvaka Komārabhacca took that pair of Siveyyaka cloths...
[as before] ...and said this: "Regarding the phrase 'the time for the choice has passed,' the detailed explanation here is exactly according to the method stated in the Mahākhandhaka."

It should be understood. "The Blessed One, venerable sir, is a wearer of rag-robes, as is the Saṅgha of bhikkhus"—for from the time the Blessed One attained Buddhahood until this robe was [offered], during these twenty years, no one accepted a robe from a householder;
all were wearers of rag-robes. Therefore he spoke thus. "A robe from a householder" means [robes] from householders.
"A robe that has been given. "With a talk on the Dhamma" means with a talk connected to the benefits of giving cloth.

"Even with this or that" means even with something of little value or great value; the sense is "with whatever [is available]. "A woolen rug" (*pāvāra*) refers to varieties such as cotton-wool and the like, including the hair.
"I allow you, monks, a *kojava*": here, only a natural *kojava* is permitted, not a large back-covering *kojava*.
It is not permitted. *Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojava* refers to a cloak made of wool, similar to a *pāvāra*.
[This concludes] the discourse on the authorization of blankets (kambala), etc., section 338.
"The King of Kāsi" means the king of the Kāsis; he was a half-brother of Pasenadi. Regarding the term *aḍḍhakāsiya*: here—

“Kāsī” refers to a value of one thousand [pieces of gold]; that which is worth this is called a *kāsiya*. However, this [robe] is worth five hundred, and therefore it is called an “*aḍḍhakāsiya*” (half-*kāsiya*).
For this very reason, it says: “suitable for half-*kāsiya* cloth.

“Of various kinds” (*uccāvacāni*) means both beautiful and not beautiful. What is called “mixed” (*bhaṅga*) is made by blending the five types of thread, such as *khoma* and so forth; some also say it is made of flax alone.
340. “Only one robe was permitted by the Blessed One, not two”—thus they thought, and regarding this [rule], they perceived its meaning as being:

“either from a householder or from a rag-heap. “They did not wait until they had returned” means that as long as they had not yet returned from the cemetery, they did not stay; they simply departed. “They did not give a portion unwillingly” means...
It should not be given against their will; however, if they consent, it should be given. "They waited" means they remained in the vicinity.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Monks, I allow you to give a share to those who are waiting, even if they are unwilling.
But if people give [the goods] thinking, "Let those who have already arrived take them," or if they go away after making a sign, thinking, "Let those who arrive take them," [it is permissible].
They reach all those who have arrived. If they have abandoned it and departed, he alone by whom it was taken is the owner.
"They entered the charnel ground together" means they all entered simultaneously; or alternatively, it means they entered in the same direction.
"Having made an agreement" means having made an agreement outside [the monastery], thinking, "We shall divide and take whatever rag-robes we find."
342. "Receiver of robes" (*cīvarapaṭiggāhaka*) refers to one who receives robes being given to the Saṅgha by householders.
Regarding the phrases "one who would not fall into favoritism" (*chandāgati*) and so forth:

among the receivers of robes, it refers to one who, out of a nature prone to greed, either receives first those who arrive later—such as his own relatives—or receives them while showing partiality toward certain individuals.
Or, by diverting it for oneself, one is said to fall into favoritism (*chandāgati*). Or, taking [the gift] later out of anger even though someone else arrived first;
or taking it while showing contempt for those of low birth; or creating an obstacle to the Saṅgha’s gain by saying, "Do you have no place to store it in your house?
Take what belongs to you and go"—in such ways, one creates an impediment to the Saṅgha’s acquisitions.
Or he goes to a wrong course through hatred. But he who is muddled in mindfulness and lacks clear comprehension goes to a wrong course through delusion.

Furthermore, one who accepts [robes] first out of fear of powerful people who arrive later, or who does so out of timidity, thinking, "This position of robe-receiver is a heavy responsibility," goes to a wrong course through fear. "I have accepted this and that..."
One who knows, “This and that have not been accepted,” is said to know what has been accepted and what has not.

Therefore, one who does not proceed by way of favoritism and so forth, but accepts according to the order of arrival without making distinctions among relatives, strangers, the wealthy, or the poor; who is endowed with virtue, conduct, and right practice;
who is mindful, wise, and learned; and who is able [to explain] to donors with clear speech and well-rounded words and phrases—[such a person is a true recipient].
One who expresses approval should be appointed in order to generate confidence;

such a person is to be appointed. And as for the statement, "In this way, monks, he is to be appointed," here it is indeed permissible to appoint him by means of this aforementioned formal act (*kammavācā*), or by means of a motion (*apalokana*), whether within the monastery, in the midst of the entire Saṅgha, or even within a delimited boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
One who has been thus appointed should not reside on the outskirts of the monastery or in the meditation hall.
Rather, he should sit in the main residence where people who come and go can see him easily; having placed his fan at the side, he should remain well-robed and properly covered.
"Having discarded right there" means that, having said, "The burden of receiving is ours," they go away after discarding [the robe] in the very place where it was taken.
"One who lays down the robe" refers to the person who takes possession of the robe.

Regarding the phrases "one who would not fall into partiality" and so forth, the analysis should be understood here and in all subsequent instances according to the method already stated. There is also a formal decision (*sammuti-vinicchaya*).
It should be understood exactly according to what has been stated.
Regarding the discussion on the authorization for a storehouse (bhaṇḍāgārasammuti) and so forth [in section 343]:

in the passage beginning with "or a vihāra," that which is situated in the middle of a monastery (ārāma), not secluded from monastery attendants (ārāmika) or novices (sāmaṇera), and serves as a meeting place for all—this is the meaning.
Whether it be a monastery (*vihāra*) or a large hall (*aḍḍhayoga*), it may be formally designated; however, a bordering lodging (*paccantasenāsana*) must not be so designated.
Furthermore, it is not permissible for this storehouse to be designated by those sitting within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) after having gone to that partial boundary;
it must be designated right in the middle of the monastery itself.
"One should know what is guarded and what is unguarded": herein, that which has no defect whatsoever in its roofing and so forth is "guarded.

However, that for which the roof-tiles or the roof-bricks have fallen off anywhere, whereby it leaks when it rains, or where there is entry for mice and the like, or where there is a hole in the walls and so forth, or where there are termites—[that is "unguarded"].
Whatever [doors] remain open, all that is called "unguarded. Having observed this, one should take remedial measures.
During the cold season, the doors and windows should be well-shut, for garments become stiff with cold.
During the hot season, they should be opened from time to time to allow air to enter. One who acts in this way is said to know what is guarded and what is unguarded.
Furthermore, these three— the receiver of robes and the others— must each know their own duty.
In this regard, first, the receiver of robes should recognize whatever people offer,
whether they call it "timely robe-cloth," "untimely robe-cloth," "urgent robe-cloth," "rainy-season garment," "sitting mat," "bedspread," or "face-towel."

If they give [these items] together, one must not take them all by making them into a single heap and mixing them; rather, having separated them individually and taken them, one should hand them over after explaining them exactly as they are to the robe-storer.
The robe-storer, when giving them to the storekeeper, must also hand them over only after explaining: "This is the timely robe... this is a face-wiping cloth."
The storekeeper, too, should likewise set them aside, making a distinct mark for each one.
Then, when the Saṅgha says, "Bring the timely robe-cloth," only the timely robe-cloth should be given... and so on, up to: when it is said, "Bring the face-towel," that very item should be given.
Thus the Blessed One authorized the receiver of robes, authorized the storer of robes, authorized the storehouse,
and authorized the storekeeper— not out of abundance or lack of contentment, but rather for the sake of supporting the Saṅgha.
For if the monks were to take whatever was brought and distribute it, there would be nothing that had been brought and nothing that had not been brought, and nothing given and nothing not given.
They would not know whether it was obtained or not obtained; they might give whatever was brought, either from the seat of the elders or by cutting it into pieces.
This being the case, there would be improper consumption, and no inclusion of everyone would have been made.
However, when the robes are kept in the storehouse and there is an abundance, [one may give] three robes to each individual monk.

"They will give either two or two, or one robe each; they will know what has been obtained and what has not been obtained, and having learned that some have received nothing, they will think to provide for them.
"Monks, the storekeeper is not to be dismissed"—here, others who are likewise not to be dismissed should also be understood. There are four.
Indeed, these should not be made to leave: one who is senior, the storekeeper, the sick person, and one who has received lodging from the Saṅgha.
In this context, the senior person should not be made to leave by one who is junior because of his own seniority;

the storekeeper, because he has been appointed by the Saṅgha and assigned to the storehouse; the sick person, because of his own sickness; and as for the Saṅgha, [it should not be made to leave] a learned person...

If one provides a comfortable residence for someone who is of great assistance through giving expositions, answering questions, and so forth, and who carries out heavy burdens—making it a place where he need not perform manual labor—then, because of his helpfulness and because he has received [the robe] from the Saṅgha, he should not be made to relinquish it.
"It becomes abundant" means it is heaped up in great quantity; it does not fit within the storehouse. "By one who is present" means within the inner boundary (upacārasīmā).
"By one who stands. "To distribute" means to distribute in order by calling out the names.
"He raised a clamor" means he made a great noise, saying, "Give it to our teacher! Give it to our preceptor!
One who gives a costly robe even when it does not reach monks who are his peers among those assigned to the distribution of robes falls into favoritism.
It is called "going to a state of fault" when, although a costly robe has reached other more senior monks, one gives an inexpensive one instead.
It is called "going to a state of delusion" when, being utterly bewildered and ignorant of the proper procedure for giving robes, one acts out of delusion.
It is called "going to a state of fear" when, out of fear even of talkative novices, one gives a costly robe to someone who has not actually reached it.
He is said to "go. One who does not go in such a manner, but is like a scale for all, being impartial and serving as a standard of measure, is the one who should be appointed.

Regarding "knowing what has been distributed and what has not been distributed": one who knows, "So many items have been distributed, so many have not been distributed," is said to "know what has been distributed and what has not been distributed."

"Having selected" means having sifted through the cloths thus: "This is coarse, this is fine, this is thick, this is thin, this has been used, this has not been used, this is this much in length and this much in width.
"Having weighed" means having determined the value thus: "This is worth this much, this is worth that much. "Praise and blame..."
"Having made [the lots]" means: if each person receives exactly one lot worth ten coins, that is well;
if not, then having tied together a lot worth nine or eight coins along with another worth one coin and another worth two coins, and by this means having established equal shares—this is the meaning.
"Having counted the monks and formed a group" means...

If a single day is not sufficient for giving to each individual, then counting ten monks at a time and binding ten portions of robe-cloth together into a single unit, I authorize that they be set aside as a bundle of robe-portions;

this is the meaning. When the robe-portions have been thus set aside, a *kusa*-grass lot must be cast. Those monks, having again performed the casting of the *kusa*-grass lot, should then divide [the cloth].

"Regarding 'half a share for the novices': here, those novices who are independent and do not perform the duties that must be performed for the Saṅgha of monks, but instead apply themselves to recitation and questioning and perform their duties of service only toward their own teachers and preceptors, and not toward others—to these, half a share should be given.
But as for those [who perform it] both before and after the meal..."
If they perform duties that ought to be performed for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, an equal share must be given to them.

This refers specifically to out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*) that arose during the season for back-robes and were kept in the storehouse; however, in the case of seasonal robes (*kālacīvara*), an equal share must indeed be given.
Regarding the *tatruppāda* (arising there) and *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) requisites, such as brooms and binding materials, these are to be used by performing services for the Saṅgha.
It should be accepted. This is the duty for everyone here.

Regarding the robes in the storehouse, if novice monks come and say, "Venerable sir, we cook rice-gruel, we cook meals, we prepare snacks, we clear away the greenery, we bring tooth-sticks, and having made the dye-skin allowable, we give it;
what is there that we have not done? [the robe should still be taken].

They raise a shout; [in such a case] an equal share should be given. This was said with reference to those who perform [the act] while skipping over [their turn], and those whose status as performers is not recognized.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "If novices request, saying, 'Venerable sir, why do we not perform the Saṅgha-act? We shall perform it,' an equal one-fifth share should be given."
“Desirous of crossing over” means desirous of crossing a river or a wilderness; the meaning is that, having obtained a caravan, he wishes to set out for a certain direction.

“To give his own share” means that when robes have been brought out from the storehouse and piled up, and the bell has been struck so that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has assembled, one who wishes to go with the caravan, thinking “May I not be left behind by the caravan,” [says this].

It was said with reference to this matter. Therefore, it is not permissible to give [the robe] while the robes have not been brought out, or while the bell has not been struck, or while the Saṅgha has not assembled.
However, when the robes have been brought out, the bell has been struck, and the community of monks has assembled, the distributor of robes [should say]:
"This portion for such-and-such monk must be of this much."
Having weighed it by way of the guiding principle, the robe-cloth should be given. For it is not possible to give with absolute mathematical precision, as if measured on a scale;

therefore, whether it be less or more, what is given in this manner according to the guiding principle is well-given. One need not give again what was deficient, nor should one accept what is excessive.
"By way of an excess portion": there are ten monks and ten cloths; among them, one cloth is worth twelve [pieces of money], while the rest are worth ten each.

When the lot has fallen to all of them by way of the ten-piece value, the monk to whom the lot falling to the twelve-piece value has fallen thinks, "With this much my robe will suffice," and he desires to go away with that excess portion.

The monks said, "Friend, this is an extra portion belonging to the Saṅgha. Having heard this, the Blessed One said, "I allow you, monks, when an extra portion has been given," in order to show that there is no such thing as "little" regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha or to a group;
restraint must be exercised in all cases, and one who takes it should feel remorse.
In this context, "extra portion" (anukkhepa) means whatever [is left over].
"Appropriate goods" (kappiyabhaṇḍa) refers to what should not be rejected and should be supplied.
The meaning is: when any kind of appropriate good worth as much as the surplus of his share is given. Regarding "having satisfied the deficiency":
here there are two types of deficiencies—the deficiency of robes and the deficiency of persons. The deficiency of robes...
Indeed, everyone has five robes and five bowls; there are others as well, but each one does not receive them.
They should be cut and given away. And by those who cut them, they should be made into pieces sufficient for half-moons and so forth, or for sandals, bags, and so forth;
at the very least, even a piece four finger-breadths wide [should be given].
It is permissible to cut it into pieces sufficient for a robe and give them; however, one must not render it unusable.

In this way, the insufficiency of the robe constitutes a "deficiency of robes" (*cīvaravikalaka*). Once it has been cut and given, that [person] is satisfied, and then the drawing of lots (*kusapāta*) may be performed.
Even if there are one or two pieces of cloth in the portion of a single bhikkhu...
If they are not sufficient, one should set aside another minor requisite (sāmaṇaka-parikkhāra) there;

having given that portion to whoever is satisfied with it, the drawing of lots (kusapāta) should be performed afterwards. This is also called "deficiency of robes" (cīvaravikalaka), as stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.
"Deficiency of persons" (puggalavikalaka) refers to when those counting ten monks each to form a quorum find that one group is incomplete.
There may be eight or nine [shares]; those eight or nine portions should be given with the instruction: "Take these and divide them separately.
This deficiency in the number of persons is what constitutes a "deficiency of persons" (*puggalavikalaka*). When they are given separately, that [person] is satisfied;
having thus satisfied him, the "falling of the blade of grass" (*kusapāta*) should be performed. Alternatively, "having satisfied the deficient" means:
If the portion of robes is insufficient, it should be made up by equalizing it with other requisites, and then the cutting with the blade should be performed. 344.
Regarding the discussion on dyeing robes:
"With chagaṇa" means with cow dung. "With pale clay" means with reddish-brown clay. Among the root-dyes and so forth, turmeric—
With the exception of all root-dyes, it is permissible. With the exception of mañjiṭṭhika and tuṅgahāra, all stem-dyes are permissible.
Tuṅgahāra is the name of a certain thorny tree; its stem-dye is the color of green palmyra leaves.
With the exception of lodda and kaṇḍula, all bark-dyes are permissible. [Also permissible are] allipatta and nīlipatta.

It is permissible to dye with everything except for *pattarajana* (dye from the *patta* plant). However, it is permissible to dye once with *allipatta* (dye from the *alli* plant) that has been used by a householder.
With regard to floral dyes, it is permissible to use everything except for the *kiṃsuka* flower and the *kusumbha* flower.
Regarding fruit dyes, however, there is nothing that is not permissible.
“Sītudaka” means unboiled dye-water. “Uttarāḷumpa” means a circular support;
the meaning is that I allow [the use of] a support placed in the middle of the dye-pot and the dye to be poured around it.
For when it is done in this way, the dye does not overflow. “In water or on the surface of the nail” means, if it is fully boiled, in a water-basin.
A small amount given does not escape quickly; even when it has not escaped onto the back of the fingernail, it remains there.
*Rajanuḷuṅkaṃ* means a dye-vessel. *Daṇḍakathālakaṃ* refers to that very same [vessel] with its handle.
*Rajanakolambaṃ* means a dye-pot. *Omaddantī* means they rub together. *Na ca acchinne theve pakkamituṃ* means as long as the drop of dye has not fallen away.
As long as it has not been washed, one must not go elsewhere. "Hard" means stiffened because of being over-dyed.
"To throw into water" means to place it after having dropped it into water. When the dye has been removed, that water should be discarded and the robe should be wrung out.
"Ivory-colored robes" refers to those worn after being dyed once or twice until they have become the color of ivory.
The Discourse on the Allowance for Tattered Robes (Chinnakacīvarānujānanakathā): 345.
“Tied with cross-lines” means tied in a four-square checkerboard pattern. “Tied with long lines” means tied with long boundary lines extending both in length and in width.
“Tied with short boundary lines” means tied with short boundary lines interspersed here and there. “Tied in a criss-cross pattern” means—
In the place where it has gone by piercing through the boundary from one boundary to another, it is "joined at the crossroads"; the meaning is that it is shaped like a quadrangle (*catukka*).
"To arrange" (*saṃvidahituṃ*) means to construct. "Are you able, Ānanda? means "Are you capable, Ānanda?
"I am able, Blessed One," he says, showing that he is capable according to the method granted by the Blessed One. "Yatra hi nāma" means "He who indeed. *Kusim*... [text fragment]
Regarding the terms *nāma* and so forth: *kusī* is a designation for long leaves such as those of the *āyāma* and *vitthāra* trees, which grow in the direction of the wind.
*Aḍḍhakusī* is the name for the short leaves interspersed among them. *Maṇḍala* refers to the large circular patch on each section of a five-piece robe (*pañcakhaṇḍika-cīvara*).
*Aḍḍhamaṇḍala* is the small circular patch. *Vivaṭṭa* refers to both the circular and the semi-circular patches.
The middle section is sewn together by joining [the two pieces] on one side.
On both sides of that, there are two sections called *anuvivaṭṭa*. A *gīveyyaka* is another patch sewn with thread, added for the purpose of strengthening at the place where it encircles the neck.
A *jaṅgheyyaka* is likewise [a patch] at the place reaching down to the shanks.
The *saṃsibbita-patta* (sewn-together robe). They say that this is also the name for the sections at the neck-position and the shank-position.
*Bāhantaṃ* refers to one piece on the outside of each of the side-seams (*anuvivaṭṭa*). Thus, it is considered a five-piece robe (*pañcakhaṇḍika-cīvara*).
Alternatively, *anuvivaṭṭa* refers to two [pieces] from one side of the main seam (*vivaṭṭa*), and two from the other side—thus four [pieces] in total.

*Khaṇḍāna* is its name. *Bāhanta*: when one who is putting on a robe of the measure of a *suppa* folds it up and places both ends over the arm, those two ends remain facing outward; this is the name for them. For this very method is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
This concludes the discussion on the permission regarding the three robes (*ticīvara*).
346. *Ubbhaṇḍikā cīvarehi*: having made a bundle (*ubbhaṇḍa*) with the robes; that is, having made them so that they are like a lifted-up bundle;
the meaning is that they have been reduced to the state of a lifted-up bundle. *Cīvarabhisim*:
here, "bundle" (*bhisī*) refers to two or three robes joined together and rolled up into the form of a bundle. Those monks, it is said, [from Dakkhiṇāgiri]...
Thinking, “The Blessed One will return quickly,” they went there, left the robes they had obtained at Jīvakavatthu, and departed.
But now, thinking he would take a long time to return, they took them and set out.
"In the interval between the two months" means during the eight days between the months of Māgha and Phagguṇa. "It did not become cold for the Blessed One" refers to the Blessed One.
It was not cold. [The Buddha] thought: "Even those sons of good family... The Blessed One did not say this because he did not know that they had not sat outside in the open air;
rather, he acted in this way for the purpose of instructing the great multitude. "Cold-naturesd" means those whose nature is cold; those who are naturally distressed by the cold.
"A double-layered outer robe" means an outer robe made of two layers. "A single-layered one" means one made of a single layer.

Thus, in order to eliminate the opportunity for the statement, "The Blessed One maintains himself with four robes, yet he allows us only the triple robe," he allows a double-layered *saṅghāṭī*, while the other two [robes] are single-layered. For in this way, they will have four [robes].
This concludes the discussion on extra robes and so forth.
348. "One should patch it" means one should attach a piece of cloth to the place where there is a hole. "Washed once" means washed a single time.
"Removed from the weather for a long time" refers to worn-out rags; that is, pieces of cloth [removed] after a long period of exposure to the elements—this is what is meant by "rags.
"From the market" refers to rags or robes obtained from a shop. "Effort should be made" means a search [for such materials].
[These things] should be made. However, there is no fixed limit here; even a hundred patches is permissible.
All this is stated with reference to a monk who consents [to such repairs]. "The patch is sewn" (*aggaḷaṃ tunnanti*): here, a piece that is removed and then attached is a "patch" (*aggaḷa*);
what is stitched together with thread is "sewn" (*tunna*). Making it by rolling it up is "rolling" (*ovaṭṭika*). "A *kaṇḍusaka*" is called a button (*muddikā*).
*Daḷhīkamman* means a piece of cloth used for fastening by sewing it to the dwelling without first removing it.
349–351. The story of Visākhā has its meaning explained [in the commentary]. What follows after that has already been determined previously.
*Sovaggika* means having heaven as the cause for attainment; for this reason, he said "sovaggika. *Sokanudaṃ* means that which dispels grief. *Anāmayā* means...
"Healthy ones" means those reborn in heaven. "In the heavenly body" means those who have attained rebirth in heaven.
"Ordinary persons free from passion for sense pleasures" refers to those who have attained meditative absorption (jhāna).
"Seen" means a mere acquaintance. "A friend" means one with whom there is shared enjoyment; a firm friend. "One with whom one has conversed" means...
When told, "Take whatever you wish from what belongs to me," one lives under the name of any one of these three;
having taken [the robe], one is satisfied. Thus, trust established through such taking succeeds.
This concludes the discussion on robes and so forth that fall under the latter alternative.
359. "Made from rags" (*paṃsukūlakata*) means made from discarded rags. "It becomes heavy" means it becomes heavy by the addition of patches in places that are already worn out.
"To make the seam with thread" means to make the patch with thread itself; this is the meaning.
"It becomes skewed" means that when they sew by cutting the thread repeatedly, one corner of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) becomes long. "To remove the skew" means...
"To cut off the long corner" means to cut away the protruding edge. "They drip" means they leak from the cut corner. "They fray along with the wind" means both along the wind and around the border.
"The bowls are ruined" means that the threads placed at the large openings of the bowl-rims come loose, and consequently the bowls are ruined.
"To make an eight-patch design" means to sew the opening of the bowl with a covering of an eight-patch pattern.

360. "To add even more" means to give even an incoming bowl. However, this [additional bowl] should be added only when one's own is insufficient. If it is sufficient, an incoming bowl is not permitted; it must simply be cut down [in size]. 361. "And not, monks, what has been given in faith":
in this regard, if one gives to other relatives, one indeed causes a downfall. But if one's mother and father, being established in royalty, should desire [something], it should be given to them.
362. "The sick" means one who, due to illness, is unable to go having taken [the bowl]. "The rainy-season agreement" refers to the four months of the rainy season.
"Within a month": one must eat a meal on the far bank of a river. Regarding "a monastery protected by a bolt":

in all these cases—namely, during the period of illness, the robe-season (*vassika*), when making an appointment, crossing a river, and when the *kaṭhina* has been suspended—the protection by a bolt alone is the criterion.
For it is permissible to leave these items in a monastery that is protected by a bolt and go outside, but not in one that is unprotected. As for a forest-dweller...
However, if the monastery is not well-guarded, one should place the robe in a basket and, having set it down in a well-concealed place such as a hollow rock or the hollow of a tree, one may depart.
This concludes the discussion on the acquisition of robes belonging to the Sangha.
"363. 'They are yours alone, monk, even those robes taken away after being seized elsewhere' means that they are indeed yours;
no one else has mastery over them. Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with 'But here,' in order to show that in the future they will take them without scruple.
'Those robes belong to him alone until the dismantling of the Kathina'—if [the robe] is for the purpose of completing the quorum..."
If monks receive [robes], the kaṭhina is considered spread for five months; if it is not spread, it is only for one month of robe-giving.

If they give [robes] saying, "We give them to the Saṅgha," or "We give them for the sake of the Saṅgha," or "We give them to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," or "We give them as a rainy-season gift"—even if this includes a deceased monk's robe that has not yet been distributed—

They enter that monastery; all of that belongs to that very bhikkhu. Furthermore, whatever *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe fund) he receives from an investment made for the purpose of the rainy-season residence, or from a deposit set aside, or from the local produce—everything is properly acquired.
This is the characteristic here: any article that has arisen for the Saṅgha in whatever manner [is his].
For one who has performed the *kathina* ceremony, [the robe] reaches [them] within five months; for one who has not performed the *kathina*, it reaches them within one robe-month.

However, that which is given after having been said, "We give this to the Saṅgha who has spent the rains retreat here," or "We give a rains-retreat gift (*vassāvāsika*"), reaches even one who has not performed the *kathina* within five months. But whatever rains-retreat gift arises thereafter—
One must ask: "Is this *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-cloth) for the past year, or for the future year? Why? Because it arose during the period of the dry season (*piṭṭhisamaya*).

"At a time other than the rainy season" means a time other than the rains. Regarding the phrase "taking those robes and going to Sāvatthī," in this context, those robes remain the property of the Saṅgha in every place they have been taken;
the only criterion here is that they were merely seen by the monks.
Therefore, if some people coming from the opposite direction ask, "Where are you going, friend?
and upon hearing that matter, say, "Friend, are we not the Saṅgha? and then divide and take [the requisites] right there, they have taken them correctly.
Even if he, having left the road, goes to some monastery or a rest-house and, while wandering for alms, enters only one house...
Or he enters [the village], and there the monks, seeing him, ask about the matter and take [the requisites] after having shared them;
these are indeed well-grasped. Regarding the phrase "he resolves": here, the one resolving must know the proper procedure (*vatta*).
Therefore, that monk, having struck the bell and announced the time, should wait a short while; if, by the sign of the bell or the sign of the time, the monks [arrive].
If they arrive, [the robes] should be shared with them. If they do not arrive, one should resolve: "These robes fall to my share.
When resolved in this way, all of them belong to that person alone, yet the formal determination (*ṭhitikā*) is not established.
If, having set aside each one, one says: "This first portion falls to me; this second portion... [and so on].
He takes them up, and what has been taken is well taken; the formal resolution (*ṭhitikā*) remains established.
Even for one who takes them after having thus brought about [the conditions], it is indeed a valid determination (*adhiṭṭhita*).

However, if he takes them—whether by striking the gong or not, or whether by making a proclamation or not—thinking, "I alone am here; these robes are mine alone," they are improperly taken (*duggahita*).
Now, if one takes it thinking, "There is no one else here; these [robes] fall to me," they are properly taken.
Regarding "when the *kusas* have been thrown down": as soon as even a single bundle of *kusa* stalks has been thrown down, even if there are a thousand monks, the robe is indeed considered taken.
A portion must not be given against one's will. However, if they wish to give it out of their own inclination, let them give it.
The same method applies to the portion of food as well.
Regarding "with robes": thinking, "We shall give even the timely robe to the Saṅgha from this very source;
if it were prepared separately, it would take too long," they quickly made the meals together with the robes. "Arising upon the arrival of the elders" means they arose quickly through faith in you.
"‘They give robes to the Saṅgha’ means they give them very slowly throughout the entire robe-season.
However, regarding the first two cases, because the giving was interrupted, it is said ‘they gave. ‘A number of elders’ refers to the elders headed by those who are experts in the Vinaya.
This story, together with the previous story of the two brothers, [occurred] after the Parinibbāna."
[The thought] arose regarding the Blessed One, and these elders had previously seen the Tathāgata;
therefore, in the preceding cases, they spoke according to the method established by the Tathāgata himself.
This is the account concerning the case of Upananda the Sakyan.

364. "He went to the village residence" means he went there specifically after observing the time for the distribution of robes, thinking, "Perhaps while they are dividing the robes, they will include me as well. "Will you accept? means "Will you take it?
And here, although no portion falls to him, [they say this] because they think, "This man is a town-dweller and a talkative preacher of the Dhamma."
The monks said, "Will you accept it? "Whoever should accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Now, although this is a light offense, nevertheless, those items that have been taken must be returned to the place where they were taken from. Even if they are lost or worn out, the liability for their value falls upon him alone.
If he is told, "Give [them back]," and he does not give them, then upon his refusal to comply, he is to be made to pay the value of the goods.
"Ekādhippāyaṃ" means one intention; the meaning is: "Give [the probation] to one person only.
Now, in order to show how that should be given, he establishes the formal rule (tan tiṃ) by saying "Idha pana...
and so forth. Therein, if [the monk] stays for half [of the time] in one place and half in another—meaning, if he stays for one day in each, or for seven days in each—in each [place],...
Whatever one person receives in a monastery, half of that and half of that must be given [to the other]. In this way, it is considered "given with a single intention.

Or, regarding the phrase "where there is more": if one staying in one monastery causes dawn to rise during the seventh-day interval in the other, then he is said to dwell "more" in the former; therefore, [the share] from that which is more is [to be given].
A share of the [monastery] residence must be given to him from the dwelling he has occupied. In this way, too, a gift is considered given with a single intention.

This has been explained in the case of different acquisitions, different precincts, and dwellings within a single boundary; however, in the case of dwellings within different boundaries, the formal taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*) ceases.
Therefore, in that case, a share of the robe-cloth does not accrue. But as for the remainder—food, medicine, and so forth—all of these are available everywhere.
It reaches one who has gone inside the boundary. Regarding the Discourse on the Basis of Illness (Gilānavatthu):
"They laid him down upon a couch"—having thus washed him and dressed him in another robe, they laid him down upon a couch.
And having laid him down, the Venerable Ānanda washed the robe that was soiled with urine and excrement and prepared a bed on the ground.
"Monks, whoever would attend upon me, he should attend upon the sick. This means: whoever would attend upon me by carrying out my advice and instructions, he should attend upon the sick;
one who acts according to my advice is the one who should attend to the sick—this is the meaning here.
The meaning is as follows. One should not take the meaning here to be that "attending upon the Blessed One and attending upon one who is ill are exactly the same.

Regarding the phrase "he should be attended upon by the Saṅgha": this refers to a visiting monk who is traveling alone and for whom these [supporters], such as preceptors and others, are not present in that monastery;
he is the responsibility of the Saṅgha, and therefore he must be attended upon by the Saṅgha. If they do not attend upon him, [the responsibility falls] upon the entire...
It is an offense for the Saṅgha. However, among those who take turns guarding, the offense belongs only to the one who does not guard during his own turn.

Even the senior monk of the Saṅgha is not exempt from his turn. If the entire Saṅgha places the burden on one person, or if a single monk endowed with virtue undertakes it, saying, "I myself will guard," then the Saṅgha is released from the offense.
366. In such passages as "approaching one who is approaching," the meaning should be understood as follows:
he does not discern, as it really is, a disease that is increasing, thinking, "This increases for me when I consume this; this diminishes when I consume that; this remains stable when I consume this.
*Nāla* means not suitable, not fit, or not proper to attend upon. *Bhesajjaṃ*.
"Unable to provide" means he is incapable of preparing medicine. "One who has material gain in between" (*āmisan-tara*):

this means that material gain (*āmisa*) is his "in-between" (*antara*). "In-between" (*antara*) refers to a cause; the meaning is that he attends [upon a person] desiring alms-gruel, rice, bowls, and robes for the sake of material gain.
The Discussion on Property Belonging to the Deceased.

367. “Kālaṅkatā” means one who has passed away. Regarding the phrase “to give to those who attended the sick,” here, even if it was given by means of the formal act (kammavācā) mentioned immediately before, or even if it was given after seeking permission (apaloketvā), it is indeed considered given; it is permissible. 369.

Regarding the phrase “whatever there is that is light property” and “whatever there is that is heavy property,” we shall explain the distinction between light and heavy property further on. However, regarding the acquisition [of requisites] for those attending the sick, this is the analysis starting from the beginning:
If he passes away while the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus is attending to him, all are the owners.
Now, if he passes away when some have taken their turn and others have not yet done so, regarding this, some teachers say:
"They should all perform it when their own turn arrives; therefore, all are the owners. Others say: "By those by whom he was attended..."
"Only they receive [the inheritance], others do not. When a novice has passed away, if there is a robe, it should be given to those who attended to him while he was ill.
If there is no robe, whatever else there is should be given. If other requisites exist, a portion for the robe should be set aside and then given.
If both a monk and a novice attended to him equally, an equal share should be given. Now, if it was the novice alone...
If the monk merely makes the arrangements while the novice does the actual serving, the senior portion should be given to the novice.
If the novice merely has the rice gruel cooked with water brought by the monk and performs the act of receiving it,
while the monk serves it, the senior portion should be given to the monk.
Many bhikkhus attend together in harmony; an equal share should be given to all of them.
However, for one who attends with particular distinction, a special portion should be made for him.
Furthermore, whoever—even for a single day—has provided rice gruel or cooked food as an attendant to the sick, or has prepared a bath, he too is indeed an attendant to the sick. Whoever...
If one sends medicines, rice, and so forth without coming near [the patient], this person is not a nurse.
He who comes after having searched for and caused [the items] to be brought is indeed a nurse.
One attends out of a sense of duty; another attends out of expectation. At the time of death, both expect [a reward]; for both of them...

It should be given. If one attendant, having stayed with the patient, goes elsewhere—either on account of the patient's duties or his own duties—with the intention, "I will return and look after him," it should be given to him as well.

If one who has attended for a long time, thinking "I am no longer able to do so now," lays down his burden and departs, even if the patient should pass away on that very day, the portion of the attendant should not be given.
Whether he be a layperson or one who has gone forth—even if it be a woman—all those who attend to the sick receive a share.
If that bhikkhu possesses nothing other than his bowl and robes, all of these must be given to the attendants of the sick.
Even if [the property] is worth a thousand [pieces of gold], they do not receive any other requisites besides that.

It belongs to the Saṅgha alone. If the remaining goods are both numerous and of great value, while the three robes are of little value, then having taken [the robes], the requisites for the three robes should be given.
All of this is obtained from what belongs to the Saṅgha.
However, if he, while still alive, renounced all his own requisites and gave them to someone, then [that person]—
Or if it was taken on trust: whatever was given to whom, and by whom it was received, belongs to that person alone.
By his own consent, the attendants to the sick receive [the items]; without giving them to others, even requisites placed far away belong there to the Saṅgha alone.
It is the property of two persons, undivided; when one has passed away, the other is the owner. Even in the case of many...
The same principle applies to property belonging to one's own [community]. In all such cases, it belongs to the Saṅgha.

Even if they give it to their *saddhivihārika* (resident pupil) and others without first dividing it, it remains as something not properly given. However, if it is given after being divided, then it is a proper gift. In that case, even when those individuals have passed away, it belongs only to the *saddhivihārika* and others, and not to the Saṅgha.
[This concludes] the discussion regarding the prohibition of garments made of *kusacīra* (grass-cloth) and so forth.
371. Regarding *kusacīra* and the others: *akkanāḷa* means made of *akkanāḷa*. *Potthaka* is said to be made of *makaci* (hemp).

The remaining terms have been explained in the commentary on the first *pārājika*. Among these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) only for *potthaka*; for the others, there are offenses of grave wrongdoing (*thullaccaya*).
Furthermore, *akkadussa*, *kadalidussa*, and *erakadussa* belong to the same category as *potthaka*.
372. All robes that are entirely blue and so forth should be washed and then dyed again before being worn.
If they cannot be washed, they should be made into bedspreads or inserted into the middle of a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*).
Their various colors are to be understood in the same manner as described for sandals. Those with uncut fringes or long fringes should be worn after the fringes have been cut off.
Having obtained a *kañcuka* (a coarse woolen cloth), it is permissible to split it, dye it, and use it.
The same rule applies to a *veṭhana* (a turban). However, a *tirīṭaka* is made from tree bark; it is permissible to use that as a foot-wiping cloth.

374. Regarding "to a suitable recipient": if a certain monk takes it thinking, "I shall accept it for him," the meaning is that it should be given. Thus, among these twenty-three types of persons, sixteen do not receive [the robe], while seven do receive it.
376. Discussion on the Occurrence of Robes when the Saṅgha is Divided:
"The Saṅgha is divided" means that, having split, it becomes two factions like the monks of Kosambī.
To one faction—that is, to one group—they give the water of dedication and perfumes and so forth; to the other, they give robes.
"Belonging to the Saṅgha" means this applies to the entire Saṅgha, including both divisions; after striking the gong, it should be distributed together by both factions.

"Belonging to a faction" means that when it is given in this way, whatever portion receives the water belongs to that [faction] alone; whatever receives the robe belongs to that [faction] alone. Where...

However, the water of dedication (*dakkhiṇodaka*) serves as the standard; in that case, since one group has received the water of dedication, they receive the robes, while the other group has received only the robes themselves.
Therefore, both groups, having come together, should divide [the goods] according to seniority.
This, it is said, is the "mark of the foreign ocean," as stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Regarding the phrase "in that very group": here—
But the other side has no power at all. The grounds for sending robes are indeed well-known.
379. Discussion on the Eightfold Matrix of Robes:
Now, in order to show the field for obtaining the robes mentioned from the beginning, [the Blessed One said]: "Monks, there are these eight..."

He spoke the words beginning with “the matrix” (*mātikā*). “He gives within the boundary” (*sīmāya deti*) and so forth are stated by way of the method of reference to individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhānanaya*).
Herein, giving within the boundary is the first matrix; giving by agreement (*katikā*) is the second... [and so on] ...giving to an individual is the eighth.
Therein, when one gives while pointing to the boundary, saying, “I give within the boundary,” it is called “giving within the boundary. This same method applies everywhere.
Regarding the phrase "gives to the *sīmā* (boundary); it should be divided by as many bhikkhus as have entered within the *sīmā*" and so forth in the exposition of the *mātikā*:
first, concerning "gives to the *sīmā*," there are the following types of boundaries:

the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), the common-observance boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*), the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*), the gain boundary (*lābhasīmā*), the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the town boundary (*nigamasīmā*), the city boundary (*nagarasīmā*), the inner boundary (*abbhantarasīmā*), the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), and the country boundary (*janapadasīmā*).
Fifteen kinds of boundaries should be understood: the boundary of a kingdom, the boundary of a realm, the boundary of an island, and the boundary of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

Among these, the "broken boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*) has already been explained in the discussion on boundaries. The "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) is delimited by the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or, in the case of one not enclosed, by the area suitable for an enclosure.
Furthermore, it extends from the place where the monks regularly assemble.

The boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) should be understood as being within two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of two stone-throw) from the edge of a dining hall or from a permanent residence where monks dwell.
Furthermore, it expands when the residences expand and contracts when they contract. However, according to the *Mahāpaccarī*, "it also expands when the number of bhikkhus increases."

Thus it has been said. Therefore, if monks seated together with those assembled in a monastery occupy a space extending even a hundred yojanas as a single continuous unit, that area of a hundred yojanas constitutes a *upacāra-sīmā* (proximity boundary), and the gains accrue to all of them.
Both the *samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā* (boundary of common residence) and the *avippavāsa-sīmā* (boundary of non-separation) have already been explained.
What is called a *lābha-sīmā* (gain boundary) was neither authorized by the Perfectly Enlightened One nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.
Furthermore, kings, royal ministers, or great officials, having caused a monastery to be built, delimit an area of four *gāvutas*,
half a *yojana*, or one *yojana* on all sides; they then plant inscribed pillars declaring,
"This is the boundary for the acquisition of our monastery," and establish the boundary, saying, "Whatever arises within this area, we give it all to our monastery."

They establish [it]; this is called a "boundary for acquisitions" (*lābhasīmā*). The boundaries of villages, market towns, cities, interiors, and water-throwing (*udakukkhepa*) have already been explained.
A "country boundary" (*janapadasīmā*) refers to the fact that within kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala there are many districts; therein, each individual district limit is a country boundary.
A "kingdom boundary" (*raṭṭhasīmā*) refers to the limit of a kingdom such as Kāsi or Kosala. A "royal domain boundary" (*rajjasīmā*)...
The "territorial boundary" (*nāma-sīmā*) refers to the area over which the authority of a single king extends, such as the "Coḷa territory" or the "Kerala territory.

The "island boundary" (*dīpa-sīmā*) refers to great islands and intermediate islands delimited by the edge of the ocean. The "world-system boundary" (*cakkavāḷa-sīmā*) is delimited by the world-system mountain (*cakkavāḷa-pabbata*) itself.
Thus, among these boundaries, when one sees the Saṅgha assembled for some formal act (*kamma*) within a "local boundary" (*khaṇḍa-sīmā*), [one should think]: "Right here..."
When it is said, "I give this to the Saṅgha within the boundary," it must be divided by as many bhikkhus as have entered within that specific section of the boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
For it accrues only to them; it does not accrue to others, even those standing in the intermediate boundary (*sīmantarikā*) or the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
However, for one standing upon a tree or a mountain situated within the section boundary, or for one situated below or in the middle of the earth [within that same boundary], [it does accrue].

It indeed reaches [them]. However, what is given with the words, "I give this to the Saṅgha within this precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā)," reaches even those standing in the intermediate spaces between partial boundaries (khaṇḍa-sīmā).

But what is given with the words, "I give this to the Saṅgha within the common-residence boundary (samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā)," does not reach those standing in the intermediate spaces between partial boundaries.
What is given within the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā) or the robe-keeping boundary (lābha-sīmā) reaches those included within those respective boundaries.
What is given within village boundaries and the like reaches those who are situated even within a boundary that has been formally demarcated inside those [village] boundaries.
What is given within an inner boundary or a water-splash boundary reaches only those included therein.
The same legal decision applies to the boundaries of a district, a kingdom, a realm, an island, and the world-system as it was stated for village boundaries and the like.

If, however, while standing in Jambudīpa, one gives saying, "I give to the Saṅgha in Tambapaṇṇidīpa," then even a single person coming from Tambapaṇṇidīpa is entitled to receive a share for all. Even if a single fellow monk there takes a share for his fellows, he is not to be prevented.
This, first of all, is how the decision regarding the gift of one who gives by specifying a boundary (sīmā) should be understood.

But if one does not know how to specify "in such-and-such a boundary," and knowing only the mere word "boundary," goes to a monastery and says, "I give to the boundary," or "I give to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary," he should be asked:
"There are many kinds of boundaries; which boundary do you have in mind? If he replies, "I [mean] such-and-such a boundary..."
“I do not know; let the Saṅgha residing within the boundary divide and take it. Within which boundary should it be divided? The Elder Mahāsīva said:
“Within the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā). Then they said to him: “The so-called non-separation boundary extends even for three *yojanas*;

if that were the case, those staying at a distance of three *yojanas* would receive the gains, and those staying at a distance of three *yojanas* would perform the duties toward newcomers (*āgantuka-vatta*).”
Having filled [the bowl], he will enter the monastery; being about to depart, he will go three yojanas and then take leave of his lodging;
for one undergoing formal dependence, the dependence shall be suspended upon exceeding three yojanas; a monk on probation must cause the dawn to rise after having traveled three yojanas;
and a nun standing at three yojanas [from her destination] shall enter the monastery.
"Whatever must be requested, all of this is permissible to do by way of delimiting the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) itself.
Therefore, it should be divided within the precinct boundary alone.
Regarding "by agreement" (katikāya): it means by an agreement for equal distribution of gains. For this very reason, he said: "Many monasteries have equal gains."
In this regard, the agreement should be made in this way: when the monks have assembled in one monastery,
those who wish to take charge of another monastery and desire to make its gains equal to their own, should mention the name of that monastery— whether it be because it is ancient,
or because it was inhabited by the Buddha, or because it has few gains— and state whatever reason there may be, such as, "This monastery [shall be joined] with this monastery."
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha to share the gains together"—this should be announced three times.
Up to this point, even one sitting in that monastery is as if sitting here; likewise, in that monastery, the Saṅgha should act in this very same way.
Up to this point, even one sitting here is as if sitting there. When the gains in one place are being distributed, in the other...
