It is permissible to take a share from one who is staying there. In this way, many monasteries may be made to share a single distribution of gains along with a single monastery.
Regarding the phrase "in the designation of alms-food": it refers to the place where one’s own relinquishment is designated. For this very reason it is said:
"where permanent works are being done for the Saṅgha. Its meaning is: in whichever monastery the property of this giver of robes [is used].
The Saṅgha’s turn for cooked food may be current; or there may be a monastery where the monks, taking it upon themselves as their own responsibility, always feed him at home;
or there may be a dwelling built by him, or where meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) and so forth have been regularly assigned;
but in the case of one who has established the entire monastery, there is simply nothing to be said—these are called "permanent benefactors" (*dhuvakāra*).

Therefore, if he says, “I give it where my permanent maintenance is provided,” or “Give it there,” then even if there are permanent maintenances at many places, it is as if it has been given everywhere.
But if there are more monks in one monastery, they should say: “In your permanent maintenance...”
"In one place there are many monks; in another place there are few. If he says, "Take it according to the number of monks," it is permissible to divide and take it accordingly.
In this regard, even small items such as cloth or medicine can be easily divided.
However, if there is only a single bed or a single chair, one must ask for permission; [this applies] whether it belongs to a specific dwelling or even to a single cell within that dwelling.
Or, it should be assigned to whichever dwelling he considers for himself.

If he says, "Let such-and-such a bhikkhu take it," that is permissible. But if, after saying, "Give it to my permanent attendants," he departs without further consideration, it is also permissible for the Saṅgha to assign it.
It should be assigned in this way: "Give it to the place where the senior of the Saṅgha resides."
It should be stated: if his lodging is full, it should be given where there is no space.
If a single bhikkhu says, "In my place of residence, there is no furniture for the use of lodgings," it should be given there.
"He gives to the Saṅgha" means that having entered the monastery, he gives, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha. "To those who are present" means...
The Saṅgha standing within the boundary of the precincts should strike the bell, announce the time, and then distribute [the robes].
Even one who is staying within the boundary but has not arrived should not be prevented from taking his share.

If the monastery is large and robes are being distributed starting from the seat of the Elder (Thera), and the Great Elders, being of a lazy nature, arrive late, [one should say]: "Venerable sirs, for those of twenty years..."
One should not say, "Your turn has passed," but rather, having set aside the turn, one should give to them first and then give according to the turn.
It is said that when they hear that much robe-cloth has arisen in such-and-such a monastery, monks come even from monasteries a league away.
It should be given starting from the place where those who have arrived and those who have not yet arrived are standing.
Even for those who have not yet arrived, if they have entered the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) and their pupils and others are receiving [the offering], it must indeed be given.

If they say, "Give to those standing outside the boundary of the precinct," it should not be given. However, if they have entered the boundary of the precinct and are joined together as one continuous body at the door of their own monastery...
Or if they are within the monastery itself, the boundary is said to be "increased" by way of its pervasion; therefore, it must be given.

Even when it has been given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, it must still be given to those who arrive later. However, if the second portion is given once the seat of the Elder (therāsana) has been ascended, the first portion does not reach those who have arrived;
from the second portion, it should be given according to seniority (*vassaggena*).
In a certain monastery there are ten bhikkhus; they give [robes] saying, "We give these ten robes to the Saṅgha.

They should be divided individually. If they take them all, thinking, "These will come to us," and depart, then because they were improperly offered and improperly received, they remain the property of the Saṅgha wherever they go. However, having set aside one [robe], [they should say]: "This..."
When [the donor] says, "It falls to you," and gives it to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, saying, "The remainder falls to us," it is permissible to take it.
If they bring forth a single robe with the words, "We give this to the Saṅgha," and they take it without dividing it, saying, "It falls to us," it is both improperly offered and improperly received.
However, if one makes a mark with a knife, turmeric, or the like, and [designates] one portion...
Having presented this portion to the senior monk of the Saṅgha with the words, "This place belongs to you," it is permissible to take the remainder with the thought, "The rest belongs to us.
However, it is not permissible to make a demarcation by means of a mere flower or a fold on the cloth itself.
If one were to pull out a single thread and say, "This place belongs to you," [to the senior monk of the Saṅgha...]
If, after it has been given, they take it thinking, "The remainder falls to us," it is permissible. It is likewise permissible if it is divided by cutting it into pieces.

In a monastery with only one bhikkhu, when robes accrue to the Saṅgha, if that bhikkhu takes them all according to the method previously described, thinking, "They all fall to me," they are properly taken;
however, the formal distribution (*ṭhitikā*) does not stand. If...
Having set aside each one individually, he takes it, thinking, "This falls to my share," and thus the distribution remains fixed.
In that regard, if another robe-cloth arises while the distribution has not yet been finalized, and a single monk arrives, it should be divided in the middle and taken by both.
If another robe-cloth arises while the distribution has already been finalized, and a junior monk arrives...
If someone arrives, the standing place descends; if an elder arrives, the standing place ascends.
If there is no one else, it must be taken back by oneself after having reached one's own position.
Or, by touching the Saṅgha in some manner, saying either "We give to the Saṅgha" or "We give to the community of bhikkhus."

However, what is given by the Saṅgha is not permitted for those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlikas*), because it has been stated: "I reject the householder’s robe; I undertake the practice of wearing rag-robes.
This is not, however, because it is unallowable (*akappiya*). Even if it is given after having been formally authorized by the Saṅgha of monks, it should not be accepted.
But that which a monk gives from his own possession is called "given by a monk" (*bhikkhudattiya*) and is permitted.

However, it is not rag-robes (paṃsukūla). Even so, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is not broken. But when it is said, "We give this to the bhikkhus," or "We give this to the elders," it is permissible even for those who wear rag-robes.
It is also permissible if it is given with the instruction: "We give this cloth to the Saṅgha;
let them make sandals, bags for bowls, waist-bands, shoulder-straps, and so forth from it."

If many [pieces of cloth] have been given for the purpose of making sandal-bags and so forth, they are sufficient even for the purpose of robes; therefore, it is permissible to make a robe from them and wear it.

However, if the Saṅgha distributes surplus cloths that have already been apportioned by cutting them up for the purpose of sandals, bags, and the like, then it is not permissible to take them from there.
For only what has been specifically assigned by the owners is permissible, and nothing else.
Even if it is said, “We give this for the sake of Dhammakaraṇa cloths and so forth for the Saṅgha of those who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūlika),” it is permissible to accept it;
for requisites are desired even by those who wear rag-robes. Whatever surplus there is therein may also be applied toward robes.
If they give thread to the Saṅgha, it should be accepted even by those who wear rag-robes. This, first of all, concerns the monastery...
The decision regarding when [the robe] has been given by entering [the monastery] and saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha.
However, if one sees monks traveling on a journey within the boundary of the precincts and announces to either the senior monk of the Saṅgha or the junior monk of the Saṅgha,
"I give them to the Saṅgha," even if the assembly stands filling a distance of a *yojana*.
If it is a single continuous whole, it accrues to all. However, it does not accrue to those who have not reached the assembly within twelve handspans.
Regarding the phrase "gives to both Saṅghas," even when one says, "I give to both Saṅghas," it means: "I give to the Saṅgha in two ways;
I give to the two Saṅghas; I give to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha."
Even when it has been said [in this way], it is indeed given to both Saṅghas. "Half should be given" means that having divided it into two equal parts, one part should be given.

When it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas and to you," if there are ten monks and ten nuns, then having made twenty-one portions, one portion should be given to the individual, and ten to the community of monks.
Whatever has been obtained as an individual gift for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhunīs, that may also be taken by the [individual] Saṅgha itself according to its own *vassa* (rainy-season retreat).
Why? Because it was included under the heading of "for both Saṅghas.

The same principle applies when it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas and to the Cetiya. However, in this case, there is no portion belonging to the Cetiya that reaches the Saṅgha; rather, the portion is exactly like the portion obtained by a single individual.
When it was said, "For both Saṅghas, for you, and for the Cetiya," twenty-two portions were made;
ten were to be given to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, ten to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, one to an individual (puggala), and one to the Cetiya.
In that regard, the individual—even if they belong to the Saṅgha—is permitted to take back [their portion] according to their own seniority, whereas for the Cetiya there is only one [portion].
But when it is said, "I give to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and to the bhikkhunīs," one should not divide it in the middle;

rather, having counted both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, it should be given. However, when it is said, "To the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, to the bhikkhunīs, and to you," the individual does not receive separately;
he receives only one portion from the place where the distribution reaches him. Why? Because by the mention of the "Saṅgha of bhikkhus," [the bhikkhus are already included].

Because it has been taken [as a share]. Even when it is said, "For the Saṅgha of monks, for the nuns, for you, and for the Cetiya," a single individual's share is obtained for the Cetiya, but no separate share is obtained for the individual;
therefore, having given one share to the Cetiya, the remainder should be divided by counting the monks and the nuns.
Even when it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs," it should not be given by dividing it in the middle;

it must be distributed according to the number of individuals. Even when it is said, "To the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, and to you and to the cetiya," the cetiya receives one share per individual, while the individual has no separate share [from that]; [the distribution is] for the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs.

And having counted [the members], it should be divided in that very way. Just as the method was set forth beginning with the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), so too should it be applied beginning with the community of nuns (*bhikkhunisaṅgha*).
When it is said, "For the community of monks and for you," the individual does not receive a separate portion;
it must be taken according to the seniority of the rains-residence (*vassagga*) alone. But when it is said, "For the community of monks and for the shrine (*cetiya*),"...
A separate share for the cetiya is obtained. Even when it is said, "For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for you, and for the cetiya," it is obtained for the cetiya alone, not for the individual.
Even when it is said, "For the bhikkhus and for you," no separate [share] is obtained. When it is said, "For the bhikkhus and for the cetiya..."

But when it is said, "It is obtained for the Cetiya," or even when it is said, "For the monks, for you, and for the Cetiya," it is obtained separately for the Cetiya alone, not for the individual person. The same should be applied starting with the Saṅgha of Bhikkhunīs.
Previously, they gave gifts to both Saṅghas headed by the Buddha; the Blessed One sat in the middle, and to the right...
The monks sat on the left and the nuns sat on the right; the Blessed One was the senior elder of both communities.
At that time, the Blessed One himself enjoyed whatever requisites he received and also caused them to be given to the monks.
But nowadays, wise people, having established an image containing relics or a cetiya, offer alms to the dual community headed by the Buddha.
Regarding teeth: having placed a bowl on a stand before an image or a cetiya and having offered water for the dedication, one says, "I give this to the Buddhas.

Then, when they first offer fresh and cooked food, or bring it to the monastery and say, "We give this to the cetiya," and offer alms-food, garlands, perfumes, and so forth—how should one proceed in such a case?
First, garlands, perfumes, and so forth should be offered at the cetiya; banners should be made with cloth, and lamps with oil.
As for alms-food, honey, molasses, and the like, they should be given only to that person—whether a monastic or a layperson—who is the designated caretaker of the cetiya.
In the absence of a designated caretaker, one may eat the brought food after setting it aside, performing the proper ritual observances.
It is permissible. Even when the time has nearly passed, it is indeed permissible to perform the duties after having eaten.
Regarding garlands, perfumes, and so forth, if someone says, "Take this and make an offering to the Cetiya," one may carry it even a great distance and offer it.
If someone says, "Carry almsfood to the Saṅgha," it may likewise be carried. However, if [someone says], "I..."
If he says, "I am going for alms; there are monks in the assembly hall, they will bring it," and [the donor] replies, "Venerable sir, give it to you alone," it is permissible to eat it.
However, if he is carrying it with the intention, "I shall give it to the Saṅgha of monks," and while on his way the time draws near, it is permissible to take it for oneself and eat it.
"He gives it to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence" means: having entered the monastery, he gives it saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence.
As many bhikkhus as have completed the rains residence in that residence—namely, those who have completed the preceding rains residence without interrupting it—it must be shared among them;
it does not accrue to others. This applies even to one who has gone abroad during the rains.
When there is a recipient, [the robe-material] must be given until the dismantling of the kaṭhina;

however, if it has been given after saying this during the winter while the kaṭhina has not yet been spread, those who know the characteristics say that it reaches even one who has completed the rains-retreat in the following year. This, however, is not discussed in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
If, however, standing outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), he says, "I give [this] to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," it accrues to all who have arrived.

If he says, "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence at such-and-such monastery," it accrues only to those who completed the rains residence there, up until the suspension of the Kathina. If, moreover, starting from the first day of the summer season...
When one speaks [of a gift] there, it reaches all those who are present. Why? Because it arises at the time of the back [of the rains].

If one says, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," only those who have completed the rains receive it; those whose rains-residence was interrupted do not receive it, but only those who have dwelt for the rains.
However, if during the robe-month one says, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," it is only those who have entered the rains-residence during the later period who receive it.
It accrues to those who have entered the rains residence during the first period, but it does not accrue to those whose rains residence has been interrupted.

From the month of the robe-giving season until the final day of winter, if it is said, "We give the *vassāvāsika*," then whether the *kathina* has been spread or not, it accrues only to those who have completed the rains residence of the past year. During the summer...
However, from the first day onwards, the following schedule (mātikā) should be set forth:
"Five months of the past rains-residence have elapsed; four months remain until the end of the future [rains]. To which rains-residence does one give [the robe]?
If he says, "I give it to those who have completed the past rains," it reaches only those who actually completed the rains within that period, even if they have gone away to other regions.
Those who belong to the same community are permitted to take it.
If one says, "I give this for the rains-residence in the future," it should be taken on the day of the entry into the rains-retreat, setting that [future gift] aside.
Then, if [one says], "The monastery is unprotected; there is fear of thieves; it is not possible to set it aside, nor can we carry it about after taking it..."
If, when asked, he says, "I give it to those who have arrived," it should be divided and taken [by the monks].

If he says, "Venerable sirs, I did not give my *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering) for the third year from now; I give that," it accrues to the monks who have resided during that particular rainy season.
If they have departed for various directions and another trustworthy person takes charge of it, it must be given to them. But if only one person remains, [he should take it himself].
The rest have passed away, and everything accrues to one person alone. If not even one remains, it belongs to the Saṅgha, and it should be divided among those who are present.
“He gives by specifying” means he gives after having specified or delimited [the recipient]; in the phrases “with rice-gruel” and so forth, this is the meaning:
he gives by specifying rice-gruel... pe ...or medicine. Herein, the construction is as follows: “to the monks, either for today or for tomorrow, with rice-gruel...”
Having invited them, she gives rice-gruel to those who have entered her house;

having given the gruel, once it has been drunk, she says, "These robes are for those by whom my gruel was drunk," and thus they come to belong to those very people who were invited and drank the gruel.
However, as for those who pass by the door of the house while on their alms-round...
If those who have entered [the village] receive gruel, or if their bowls are brought from the assembly hall and carried away by people, or if they were sent by the elders, it does not reach them.
However, if many others besides the invited monks come and sit filling both the interior and exterior of the house, and the donor says: "The invited..."
Whether they were invited or uninvited, those to whom he gave the rice-gruel all received these robes;
however, those who had received the gruel from the hands of the elders did not receive them.
Then, when he says, "Let it belong to all those by whom my gruel was drunk," it reaches everyone. This same principle applies to the solid food and soft food as well.

"Regarding robes": if someone has previously spent the rains retreat and given robes to the monks, and after feeding those monks he says, "Let this robe, or thread, or ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, belong to those very ones to whom I previously gave robes," then everything accrues to them alone. Regarding lodgings...
When it is said, "Let this belong to whoever dwells in the monastery or the cell built by me," it belongs to that person alone.
Regarding medicine: when it is said, "We give ghee and other medicines to the elders from time to time;
let this belong only to those who have received them," it belongs to those very people.
"He gives to an individual" means he gives either in the person's absence, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so," or in their presence,
placing it at the feet [of the recipient] and saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you. However, if he says,
"I give this to you and to your pupils," it reaches both the elder and his pupils.
There are those who come to receive the recitation and go away having received it; for them also, [the merit] accrues.

When it is said, "I give this to the bhikkhus who travel in regular association with you," it accrues to all those who, having performed the duties toward their private recitation teachers (*uddesantevāsika*), travel about receiving the recitations, the interrogation of the text, and so forth.
This is the analysis regarding the phrase "he gives to a person."
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Cīvarakkhandhaka is finished.
9. The Campeyyakkhandhaka.
The Story of the Bhikkhu of the Kassapa Clan (Kassapagotta) 380.
In the Campeyya Khandhaka—at the edge of the Gaggarā lotus pond, on the bank of the pond constructed by a woman named Gaggarā.
"Bound by the cords" means bound by the cord of duties to be performed in that residence. "He also showed zeal regarding the rice-gruel," and so forth.
When people arrive as guests, it is appropriate to make an effort only at the place where it was said, "You should point them out," and not at any other place.
"Go, monk," the Teacher said because he saw that very lodging was suitable for that monk; therefore he spoke thus.
382. Regarding the phrases "performing a factional act (vaggakamma) contrary to the Dhamma" and so forth, the distinction will be explained later in the text itself.
385. "Performing an act contrary to the Dhamma" means they perform an act that is not in accordance with the Dhamma; or this reading may be "performing an act apart from the Dhamma.
An act performed on the basis of a factual matter is called "performed according to the Dhamma"; the meaning is that they do not act in such a manner.
"An act apart from the Vinaya, an act apart from the Teacher’s instruction"—the same principle applies to these as well.

Here, "Vinaya" means both the formal accusation (*codanā*) and the reminder (*sāraṇā*). "The Teacher’s instruction" means the perfection of the motion (*ñatti-sampadā*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana-sampadā*);
the meaning is that they perform the act without these. "That which is censured and done" (*paṭikuṭṭhakata*) means both censured and performed.
The meaning is that they perform even such a formal act (*kamma*) as is both censured and yet performed when others are protesting against it. 387.
Regarding the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, there are these six kinds of formal acts that are illegal acts" (*adhammakamma*), the word "Dhamma" is a designation for the Canon (*pāḷi*).
Therefore, whatever is not done according to the aforementioned Canon should be understood as an "illegal act. This is the point here.

This is the summary; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the Pāḷi itself, and that is specifically in terms of formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) and a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*).

Since there is no reduction or alteration in a formal act consisting of a mere motion (*ñattikamma*), as there is in the cases of the *ñattidutiya* and *ñatticatuttha*, and since a formal act consisting of a mere notification (*apalokanakamma*) is performed only after having made the announcement, those two types of formal acts are not shown in the Pāḷi.
We shall explain the detailed determination of all these actions further on. 388.
Regarding the discussion on performing [formal acts] by a quorum of four and so forth:
now, as for this sixth type of action known as "a legal act performed by a complete assembly," we shall explain by which Sanghas it should be performed.

To show their classification, it is said: "There are five kinds of Saṅghas," and so forth. "One who has reached the stage of formal acts" (kammappatta) means one who has attained [the status for] a formal act, one who is connected to a formal act, or one who is worthy of a formal act;
the meaning is that he is not unfit to perform any formal act whatsoever.
(389) "If, monks, a formal act is to be performed by a quorum of four, and a nun is the fourth," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of showing the failure of the formal act due to the assembly.
It has been stated. Therein, by the mention of "one who has been suspended" (ukkhitaka), one who is of a different communion through formal act (kamma-nānāsaṃvāsaka) is included;

by the mention of "one of a different communion" (nānāsaṃvāsaka), one who is of a different communion through doctrine (laddhi-nānāsaṃvāsaka) is included. "A quorum of four standing in a different boundary" (nānāsīmāya ṭhitacatuttho) means that it constitutes a quorum of four even together with one standing within arm's reach in either a boundary interval (sīmantarikā) or outside the boundary.

393. The passage beginning with “with one on probation as the fourth” is stated for the purpose of showing the failure of the assembly regarding the formal acts (kamma) such as probation; we shall explain their detailed analysis later.

394. The passage beginning with “For some, monks, a protest within the Saṅgha succeeds” is stated for the purpose of showing whether a formal act performed against one who has protested is valid or invalid.
“Of one who is regular” means of one whose virtue is unimpaired and who has not committed a defeat (pārājika).
"Ānantarikassa" means one sitting immediately next to oneself.

395. The discourse beginning with "There are these two ways of removal, monks," and so forth, is for the purpose of showing the susceptibility or invulnerability of kamma based on its objective basis (*vatthu*).

It has been said. In that context, the statement, "He has not reached the point of being sent away; if the Saṅgha sends him away, he is rightly sent away," refers to the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*).
For it is by means of the act of banishment that they send one away from the monastery; therefore, that is called "sending away" (*nissāraṇā*).
And because this person is not a corrupter of families, he has not reached [the grounds for expulsion] by way of his specific characteristic. Because...
It was said, "If the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of banishment against him"; therefore, he is one who has been properly sent away.
"If the Saṅgha sends him away" means: if the Saṅgha sends him away by means of an act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) and so forth, because in that case [the rule states]:
"Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of censure against three monks... [and so on].
"One is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
one is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and unrestrained;
one dwells in association with householders through improper associations with householders"—thus, expulsion was authorized for each individual factor; therefore, he has been properly expelled.
396. *Osāraṇā* means admission. In this context, "if the Saṅgha admits him" means it admits him by means of the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).

"Admitted" (*osārita*) means one who has been admitted. Even if he has been ordained a thousand times, he remains unordained, and both the preceptor (*ācariya*) and the teacher (*upajjhāya*) are guilty of an offense;
likewise for the rest of the performing Saṅgha—no one is released from their transgression. Thus, these are the eleven persons who are incapable [of being ordained].

They are improperly restored (*dusārita*). However, the thirty-two types of persons such as those whose hands have been cut off, when properly restored (*susārita*), become fully ordained (*upasampanna*) once they have received the ordination;
nothing can be said against them. But the preceptor (*ācariya*), the teacher (*upajjhāya*), and the Sangha that performed the act are guilty of an offense;
no one among them is released from their transgression.

397. Furthermore, monks, the passage beginning with “In this case, there is no offense for a monk to be seen” is stated in order to show that an illegal procedure (*adhamma-kamma*) is based on a non-factual matter, whereas a legal procedure (*dhamma-kamma*) is based on a factual matter. In this context, “should be relinquished” (*paṭinissajjitā*) means “should be relinquished.
[End of] the Discussion on Upāli’s Questions.
In the *Upāli-pañha* as well, legal and illegal procedures (*dhamma-adhamma-kamma*) are analyzed according to their subject matter (*vatthu*). Therein, there are two methods:

that which has a single root and that which has a double root. That with a single root is indeed straightforward. Regarding the double-rooted method, just as a single question is asked concerning the verdict of mindfulness (*sativinaya*) together with the verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*), so too are the verdict of past insanity and the others treated together with the procedure of further penalty (*tassapāpiyyasikā*) and so forth. At the conclusion, however—

"One who is worthy of full ordination, he ordains"—this constitutes a single phrase. Hereafter, for the monks as well, beginning with the verdict of mindfulness (*sativinaya*), the remaining phrases should be combined one by one with each [of these].
The Discussion on the Act of Censure (*tajjanīyakamma*).
407. Furthermore, monks, here a monk who creates strife and so forth—having constructed a wheel by way of these cases:

"an illegitimate act by an incomplete assembly," "an illegitimate act by a complete assembly," "a legitimate act by an incomplete assembly," and "an act resembling the Dhamma by an incomplete assembly" and "an act resembling the Dhamma by a complete assembly"—this is for the purpose of showing failure regarding the seven formal acts, such as the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), and regarding their pacification.
It has been stated. In that context, "without a precedent" (*anapadāna*) means devoid of a precedent. A "precedent" (*apadāna*) is said to be a limit;

thus, the meaning is "devoid of the limits [regarding] offenses. Following that, in order to show the various types of censurable formal acts (*kamma*), that very same canonical text was spoken in conjunction with the phrases beginning with "an act not performed" (*akataṃ kamma*).
In this regard, there is nothing that cannot be understood by following the canonical text; therefore, we have not elaborated upon the commentary.
The commentary on the Campeyya Khandhaka is finished.
10. The Kosambaka Khandhaka:
The Discourse on the Controversy at Kosambī.
451. In the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*: "They suspended that bhikkhu for not seeing an offense. Herein, this is the sequential account:
It is said that two bhikkhus were living together in one residence, a master of the Vinaya and a master of the Suttantas.
One day, when the Suttanta-master bhikkhu had entered the restroom, he went out after leaving the remainder of the water used for rinsing in a vessel.
The Vinaya-holder entered later; seeing that water, he went out and asked the monk, "Friend, was this water set aside by you?
"Yes, friend. "Do you not know that there is an offense here? "Yes, I do not know. "Is there an offense here, friend? "If there is, I shall confess it. "If..."
"But, friend, since this was done by you unintentionally and through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense. Thus, he held the view that there was no offense for that transgression.
The holder of the Vinaya also informed his own dependents, "This master of the Suttas does not even know when he incurs an offense.
When they saw his dependents, [they said], "Your preceptor, even after incurring an offense, [does not recognize] the state of being an offense..."
"He does not know," they said. They went and reported this to their own preceptor.
He said, "This master of the Vinaya previously stated it was 'no offense,' but now he says it is 'an offense. He is a liar.
They went and, saying, "Your preceptor is a liar," thus increased their mutual quarreling. Then the master of the Vinaya [sought] an opportunity...
Having obtained [the confession], they performed an act of suspension against him for his refusal to see an offense. Therefore it is said:
"They suspended that bhikkhu for his refusal to see an offense. 453.
Regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split," it is not yet split; rather, it is as follows:
Just as when it rains, one says, "Now the crop is harvested," even though it will certainly be harvested [only later], so too, for this reason, it will certainly be split in the future;
and that is by way of quarreling, not by way of a formal schism in the Saṅgha.
Therefore, it is said, "it is split. And here, the repetition (āmēḷita) should be understood in the sense of urgency.
454. Having spoken this matter, he rose from his seat and departed. Why did he depart after speaking thus?

For had the Blessed One said to those who had suspended [the monk], "You have suspended that bhikkhu without cause," or to those who followed the suspended one, "You have fallen into an offense," they would have cried out, "The Blessed One is on their side! The Blessed One is on their side!"
Having spoken thus, they might harbor resentment; therefore, having set aside that very thread and spoken this matter, he rose from his seat and departed.

455. Regarding the phrase "by oneself or another": here, one who sits on the side of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma (*adhammavādin*) when they have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and having heard the tenets of both them and the others, thinks, "These are speakers of what is contrary to the Dhamma."
If one generates the thought, "The others are proponents of the Dhamma," while sitting in their midst, one becomes of a different communion from them;

one invalidates the formal act (*kamma*), and because one has not come within arm's reach of the others, one invalidates it for them as well. In this way, one makes oneself of a different communion from oneself.
Regarding the term "of the same communion" (*samānasaṃvāsaka*): here too, it refers to one who sits on the side of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.

“Those here speak contrary to the Dhamma; those others speak in accordance with the Dhamma”—thus he enters into their midst, or else, sitting on this or that side, he takes up the position that “these are the ones who speak in accordance with the Dhamma.
This should be understood as one who makes himself a member of the same community (samānasaṃvāsaka) as himself.
456. Regarding “bodily action” and “verbal action”: here, those who strike with the body exhibit bodily action; [those who speak] harshly... [exhibit verbal action].
It should be understood that they "speak" means they manifest verbal action.

"Grasping each other by the hand" means they grasp one another with their hands out of anger. "While performing unrighteous acts" means while performing deeds contrary to the Dhamma. "While behaving without mutual courtesy" means while behaving without mutual courtesy;
or rather, this is the reading: "while engaged in conversation without mutual courtesy. Regarding "conversation without mutual courtesy":
The meaning is "while [the recitation] is not being chanted. Up to this point, one should sit having formed two rows and leaving a space between them;
however, while the *dhamma* is being recited and the friendly greetings are taking place, one should sit in the interval between the seats, sitting with each seat serving as an interval.

457–458. Regarding the passage beginning with *mā bhaṇḍanaṃ*, one should understand the meaning as follows: by taking the phrase *akattha* as a textual supplement (*pāṭhasesa*), it should be read as *mā bhaṇḍanaṃ akattha* (“do not engage in quarreling”).
The term *adhammavādī* refers to one of those who follow a suspended monk (*ukkhitānuvattaka*).
However, this bhikkhu is a well-wisher of the Blessed One; his intention (*adhippāya*) is as follows: “These bhikkhus are overcome by anger [and thus disregard] the Teacher’s word.”
“They do not accept it; let the Blessed One not weary himself by instructing them”—thus he spoke.
But the Blessed One, out of compassion for them, thinking, “Even later they will receive the perception [of danger] and desist,” brought forward a past incident and spoke.
In that context, *anatthato* means “disadvantage from this”; what is meant is, “This man is a disadvantage to me. Alternatively, *anatthato*...
"Causing harm. The rest is self-evident.
Regarding the verses beginning with "A person of loud voice": one who has a "loud voice" (*puthusadda*) is so called because their voice (*sadda*) is widespread (*puthu*) or great.
"Ordinary people" (*samajana*) refers to common folk (*samāna*), that is, people who are alike; all these people who engage in quarreling are "of loud voice" because they emit sound from all sides.
And it is said that they were alike. "No fool did anyone imagine" means that not even one among them thought, "I am a fool";

rather, all of them considered themselves wise. "They imagined nothing more" means that not even one thought, "I am a fool," nor, while the Saṅgha was splitting, did anyone imagine anything else, such as, "Because of me..."
The meaning is that he did not consider this reason [for thinking], "The Saṅgha is split.

"Parimuṭṭhā" means those whose mindfulness is lost. Regarding "vācāgocarabhāṇino": the long vowel *rā* has been replaced by its short equivalent; they have speech as their range (*vācāgocarā*), not the range of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
And how are they speakers? They speak as much as they desire for the exertion of the mouth, as far as the mouth [reaches].

The meaning is that they wish to stretch [their tongues] out; having stretched them out as far as they can while speaking, not even a single person, out of respect for the Saṅgha, refrains from contracting their mouth.
"By which they were led" means by which quarrel they were led to this state of shamelessness.
"They do not know that" means they do not realize, "This [quarrel] has such a disadvantage."
"And those who harbor resentment toward him" means those who harbor resentment toward such forms as "He reviled me," "He struck me," and so forth. "Sanātana" means ancient.
"Others" refers to those other than the wise—namely, quarrelsome people who are called "others. While they are creating strife here in the midst of the Saṅgha, they think:
"We are restraining ourselves, we are exerting ourselves; we are constantly and continuously going into the presence of Death."
They do not know. And those who understand therein are the wise ones who understand: "We are going into the presence of Death.
Then they settle their strife; for knowing thus, they arouse wise attention and proceed toward the pacification of strife—that is, quarrels.
The verse beginning with "Aṭṭhicchinnā" was spoken with reference to Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu.

Even they had such a meeting; why should it not happen for you, whose parents' bones have not been shattered, whose lives have not been taken, and whose cattle, horses, and wealth have not been seized?
The verse beginning with "If he should find... is spoken for the purpose of illustrating the praise and blame of a wise companion and a foolish companion.
"Having overcome all dangers" means that having overcome both manifest dangers and concealed dangers, one should dwell with him, contented and mindful.

"Like a king his conquered realm": the meaning is that one should live just as the Great King Mahāsudassana and King Arindama lived alone, having abandoned their own conquered realms and the great multitude of people. "Like an elephant in the forest, a Mātaṅga":
*mātaṅga* means an elephant; *nāga* is a designation for something great. For just as one who supports his mother...
"The Mātanga elephant wandered alone in the forest and committed no evil deeds. What is meant is: "Just like the one at Pālileyyaka, one should wander alone and commit no evil deeds.
This is the account of the journey to Pālileyyaka.
467. “He dwells at Pālileyyaka in the protected forest grove” means he dwells in the protected forest grove in dependence on Pālileyyaka.
“An elephant-nāga” means a great elephant. “By elephant-calves” means by young elephants. “By elephant-cubs” means by very young suckling calves.
“With their tips broken off” means that as they go one after another in front, the tips [of the grass] are broken off by them.
He eats grasses that resemble stumps, with only their chewed remains left behind.

"Broken down, broken down" means it has been repeatedly broken off from its high places and felled by that elephant king. "Its branches and twigs" refers to the branches and twigs belonging to this [tree] which they eat.
"Turbid" means the mud and water have been stirred up by them as they descend first to drink.
He drinks. He plunges in while standing at a ford.
"By the elephant, the elephant" means by the elephant-lord, the Buddha-elephant. "Of the one with tusks like chariot-poles" means of him whose tusks resemble the poles of a chariot.
"When he alone delights in the forest": because this elephant-lord, like the Buddha-elephant, delights in the forest, being solitary and secluded.
Therefore, the mind of that Nāga was in harmony with [the Buddha’s] Nāga; the meaning is that it became identical through the delight in oneness (*ekībhāva-rati*).
Regarding the phrase "having dwelt as long as he desired," it should be understood that the Blessed One dwelt there for three months.
Up to this point, the report spread everywhere that the Blessed One, being harassed by the people of Kosambī, had entered the forest and lived there for three months.
Then, indeed, the lay followers of Kosambī—having heard this exchange of conversation—[acted].
468. Regarding the eighteen grounds for schism, beginning with "non-Dhamma as Dhamma," we shall explain them in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
475. "Having reinstated that suspended monk" means: having taken him, gone to the boundary, caused him to confess his offense, and reinstated him by means of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
"The Uposatha is to be performed at that very time" means: on that very day, the Uposatha of concord must be performed according to the method explained in the Uposatha Khandhaka.
"Having gone to the root from what is not the root" means not having gone to the root from the root; the meaning is "without having decided upon that matter.
Upāli, this is called a concord of the Saṅgha that is devoid of meaning but possessed of the literal expression;
it is removed from the sense, yet possesses the mere verbal form "concord of the Saṅgha."
477. "In matters for the Saṅgha" means when duties to be performed by the Saṅgha have arisen. "In consultations" means in consultations regarding the Vinaya.

"When issues have arisen" means when matters concerning the Vinaya have arisen. "In their adjudication" means in the legal decisions on those very same matters. "Of great benefit" means highly helpful.
"One who is to be urged forward" means one who is called upon to exert effort.

"Blameless in virtue by the first" means, for the time being, that one is blameless in terms of virtue (*sīla*) at the very beginning. "One who observes conduct" (*avekkhitācāra*) means one who has observed conduct;
it refers to one whose conduct has been examined according to the method beginning with "acting with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside.
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated as "one whose conduct is unrevealed" (*appaṭicchannācāra*).
"Visayha" means having overcome. "Bhaṇanti anuyyutaṃ" means speaking what is connected, what is permitted, and what is not departed from [the context].
Because he speaks what is connected, and does not speak that which has departed from the reason—either out of envy or by way of going on an improper course—he does not fail in the meaning.
However, one who speaks out of envy or by way of going on an improper course fails in the meaning and the reason.

He does not give [an answer]; therefore, when he has entered the assembly, he both falters and trembles. To show who it is that does not act in such a way, [the text] says: "one who is worthy of being encouraged.
Furthermore, there is the verse beginning with "In the same way, the question," the meaning of which is as follows:
just as one does not fail in the meaning while speaking when questioned, even so, when asked a question in the midst of the assembly, he neither broods nor...
And he becomes dejected. For he who does not understand the meaning broods; he who is unable to speak becomes dejected.
But he who both understands the meaning and is able to speak neither broods nor becomes dejected.
"Arrived at the right time" means arrived at the time appropriate for speaking. "Worthy of an explanation" means because it conforms to the meaning of the question.
"Appropriate to the explanation" means speaking words; the sense is that one utters such speech. "Pleases" means satisfies.
"An assembly of the wise" means a gathering of those possessed of discernment.
"And in his own teacher's doctrine" means in his own master’s teaching. "Sufficient to examine" means to investigate various reasons.
"One capable of weighing with wisdom" means one who is able to evaluate through discernment. "Skilled" (*paguṇa*) means one who has practiced and gained proficiency.
"In what should be spoken" (*kathetave*) means in that which ought to be told.

"Expert in the points of failure" (*viraddhikovida*) means skilled in the circumstances where a failure occurs. This verse was spoken to demonstrate the kind of person who is proficient in what should be spoken when adversaries approach.
This is the meaning here: by such speech as is spoken, adversaries undergo defeat and the great multitude undergo persuasion;
"persuasion" means bringing about understanding. And while speaking, one does not abandon one's own position or one's own teacher’s doctrine;
rather, in accordance with the matter upon which the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) has arisen—
"Being skilled in speaking when answering a question that should be answered in such a way as not to cause harm.
Regarding "capable in the work of a messenger": because he is endowed with the eight qualities of a messenger, he is competent in the Sangha’s duties as a messenger.
"He grasps thoroughly" means *samuggaha*. This is what is meant: just as they grasp an offering (*āhuna*), that is, a mass of offerings (*āhutipiṇḍa*).
Thus, with a mind born of joy and gladness, he is one who takes up the duties of the Saṅgha;
the meaning is that he is the receiver of each respective duty among the duties of the Saṅgha. "Acting according to his word" means acting upon what has been said.

"He does not conceive on account of that" means that because of that performance of the word, he does not give rise to conceit or overweening pride, thinking, "I am doing it; I am fulfilling the burden of the Saṅgha."
"In as many bases as one falls into an offense" means: in whatever number of bases one falls into an offense, one falls into it.

"And how the emergence occurs" means: how the emergence from that offense occurs. "These are the Vibhaṅgas" means: these Vibhaṅgas are the elucidators of these two points—namely, in which bases one falls into an offense and how the emergence occurs. "Of both" means: [of the offense and its emergence].
"Both [should be] his. "Welcome" means "well-come. "Skilled in the basis for emerging from an offense" means proficient in the causes for emerging from an offense.
"And those things which they practice"—referring to quarreling and so forth, by practicing which one undergoes banishment through such measures as a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of condemnation).
"The reinstatement of that person who has completed that [period]" refers to the reinstatement of the individual who has lived out that period of conduct (*vatta*).
It should be done; he knows this as well. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Kosambakakkhandhaka is finished.
[End of] the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
The *Aṭṭhakathā* on the Mahāvagga is completed.
